speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I had to revise my speech several times.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I realised through the revisions, they have helped me better understand what is at stake in this year’s Budget.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, it is not all that bad being the second last speaker.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I cannot speak for Mr Saktiandi Supaat though.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This House has heard impassioned pleas from hon Members on the focus areas for this year’s Budget.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For instance, there have been clarion calls to further increase social spending to take care of less fortunate people and improve their social mobility, address more issues associated with the ageing population, and providing better opportunities for all, young and old.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: At the same time, all hon Members have agreed that we need to ensure that the Budget is financially prudent.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There are divergent views on how this can be achieved.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is important that we in this House try our best to build a consensus on at least the broad areas of strategy that this Budget represents.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Everyone must agree that we should not dissent for the sake of dissent.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, what should be the framework for us Members to build this consensus?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But before that, I want to, first, deal with a point made by hon Member Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin in her speech yesterday.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: She further cites a report in support of the view that the Government is excessively prudent with its large Reserves.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: She then asked how much is then enough for us.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: She also said "every tilt towards the side of pragmatism is simultaneously a tilt away from the side of our ideals".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With respect, I do not see pragmatism on one hand and being true to our ideals on the other as binary choices giving rise to a zero-sum game.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This kind of approach would give rise to polarising views which would make it harder for us to reach a consensus on what is the right approach to be taken in our Budget.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Ms Kuik asked how much is enough for us.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In a financial crisis, the value of assets, especially those marked to market will shrink.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We saw that in the Global Financial Crisis when the international bank shares dropped.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We cannot predict with any certainty how much we need to overcome the next big crisis that will hit us.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As an analogy, think of the Indian Ocean tsunami.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Using the pragmatism/idealism dichotomy that she raised, what should the Government then do?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Should it be idealistic, assume that the world is kind and, if Singapore, a small country with no natural resources, needs help to prop up its finances, it will get help, and it will be treated fairly, equally and equitably?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With due respect, is this a realistic assumption?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Or should it be pragmatic, because it is a steward of 3.6 million Singaporean lives and that of their progeny, and ensure that the Reserves can be tapped to save us from the next crises whenever it may happen?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As a father who has a stake in the future of his children, I am clear in my mind what the Government should do.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What is more important, I would respectfully suggest, is to appreciate whether the approach taken in this Budget is in keeping with our values.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is how I suggest we can forge a consensus as Members on the Budget.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Members of this House would recall the debate on the Government White Paper on Shared Values in 1991 in this House during the tenure of the second-generation leaders led by Emeritus Senior Minister Goh as Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The first three shared values are: (a) nation before community and society above self; (b) family as the basic unit of society; and (c) community support and respect for the individual.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Investment in economy and infrastructure is needed to secure the future of Singapore as a nation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is not growth for growth’s sake, as emphasised by Minister Heng.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is about making sure that our families remain intact and we and our family members enjoy a good standard of living.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is also a healthy dose of idealism in this Budget.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Just look at the plans that the Minister has suggested to take advantage of the opportunities within Asia and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: At same time, the funding of the investments is done in a prudent way, which is also in keeping with our values in putting our nation first.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Member for Aljunied, Mr Low Thia Khiang, said reference to this is a distraction and unnecessary.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With respect, I fail to see how this can be so.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We have already been committing to expenditure well into the 2030 and beyond.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Surely, a responsible Government should also signal how it plans to raise the revenue for the same period.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Reserves are not being used to fund expenses.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I endorse this forceful point that was made by hon Member Mr Christopher de Souza yesterday on the danger of using proceeds from land sales, which make up our Reserves, to fund expenditure.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: That is not to say Reserves cannot be used.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The way the Budget is pitched, it represents a fair usage of Reserves and allocation of responsibilities between the present and future generations.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Payment obligations on the loans would also fall on the future generations.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The 50% NIRC rate, in my view, represents a fair balance between ensuring a bright future as a nation and the present funding needs of the community.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is no loading in favour of one or another.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Once we change this, it will be a slippery slope and there will be a tendency to adjust a higher percentage to accommodate for higher expenditure.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is my answer to the hon Member Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan who suggested in his speech yesterday that the Government listen to views expressed by some Singaporeans that the NIRC rate should be increased.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: (In Tamil):   Yesterday, Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan spoke about the Government listening to the people's concern on raising revenue.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As such, the Government should consider and decide which approach will be suitable for the people, and then the Government should explain its decision clearly to the people.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: (In English): Next, the concrete steps in providing greater support for families recognise the primacy of the family as the basic unit of society and the important role it plays in nation-building.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For these reasons, I support the Budget because it accords with our shared values.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Before I leave this point, I would like to return to an aspect of the speech Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin made in reference to JC and polytechnic students she spoke to, constantly using the word "uncertain" when asked to describe their future.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If I were there at the discussion, I would acknowledge that, indeed, our future as a nation and as individuals has and will always be uncertain.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We survived because we remained together, worked hard putting the nation before community and community before self.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would point out that we are in a better situation than before because of a prudent and forward-thinking Government.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would highlight the importance of being resilient and the need for the students to be the best they can be for themselves, their families and our country.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If our youths can accept this, we can be sure that we will have a strong future.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Having said that, I have three observations to make on the Budget.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Minister Heng decided to extend WCS to overcome near-term challenges because, in his words, "Some firms remain concerned about business costs" even though our economy has picked up.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We, therefore, will see a second extension of WCS which has been running since 2013.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In 2015, when the Government first proposed the extension of WCS in Parliament, concerns were raised in this House.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Member Assoc Prof Randolph Tan warned that WCS may land up in delaying the adjustments that businesses should make in order to complete restructuring.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In other words, WCS should not unwittingly become a wage subsidy crutch.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Deputy Prime Minister Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam explained then that there is a need to adopt a phased approach whilst the foreign manpower policy is tightened and the labour market becomes tighter.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Otherwise, there would be an impact on weaker businesses, especially startups.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is also a need to support those who are rejoining the economy and may need time to enhance their skills and increase their productivity.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I support this approach but, given that this is the second time an extension is being sought, I am of the view that the WCS criteria should be sharpened so that we focus on the firms which are concerned about business costs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I do not see why a muscular company, say, a Government-linked company or a listed company, can benefit from WCS in the same way as a small enterprise.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Also, the drivers for WCS, when implemented in 2013, were the need to improve productivity and the tight labour market.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In light of the improved situation, why does the Government see a need to further extend WCS by another three years, which is a year longer than the first extension, which was for two years?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Minister Heng Swee Keat identified the forging of strong partnerships as a third key enabler to capture future opportunities, especially in Asia and ASEAN in particular.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He pointed out: "Competition is not the only driving force in our economy.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Cooperation is also key." He went on to identify platforms for partnership, such as Partnerships for Capability Transformation (PACT), Global Innovation Alliance, ASEAN Innovation Network, and announced the setting up of the Infrastructure Office.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I support the focus on capturing future opportunities in Asia and ASEAN to grow the Singapore economy.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is, however, a need to overcome the default mindset of companies which are used to competing with one another.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Also, PACT contemplates large organisations to partner small companies.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Recognising this, in a Business Times article published on 8 November 2016, Mr Lim Hwee Seng and Ms Bernadine Huang of PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC), stated as follows: "This scheme remains out of the reach of the smaller-scale small and medium enterprises (SMEs).

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: More often than not, large organisations will choose to work with the bigger SMEs, and not the smaller ones.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We suggest for PACT to be extended to allow bigger-scale SMEs to work together with smaller-scale SMEs and not just large organisations vis-a-vis SMEs." How would the Government promote the forging of strong partnerships in these circumstances?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In particular, how would it ensure that the smaller SMEs would benefit from PACT?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is especially important in the technology space where there are a good number of startups and small companies which could potentially benefit from venturing overseas in partnership with large organisations.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I note that the 2001 Economic Review Committee, in its report which was issued in 2003, a similar call was made.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It promoted a cluster approach amongst companies venturing overseas, where larger companies lead a cluster of enterprises, including SMEs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What lessons can we draw from the past?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Final point ‒ strengthening social safety nets for those in need.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am very heartened to note the concrete plans for Budget 2018 to build on the SG Cares movement.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: One big contributor is Tote Board, through its grant-making activities across sectors, such as Arts, Community Development, Education, Health, Social Service and Sports.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This amounts to about 17% of the donations.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Casino entry levies have not changed since 2010, not even adjusted for inflation over the past eight years.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But I think Mr Murali has done great justice in terms of trying to wrap up some of the points made by other Members.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am not sure whether I should try and keep it brief or try to be on point.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: But I find that the Budget takes a very detailed approach to the challenges that Singapore will face in the next five years and the Minister for Finance has scrutinised the various revenue platforms and carefully considered how best we should manage this against our expenditure, especially on building the infrastructure necessary for the future and the rising expenditure on healthcare and security.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The hallmark of this Government has always been to plan ahead, including this time round, providing forward guidance on its fiscal plans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Based on the past two days' debate, I think it has also led to a healthy discussion on our fiscal sustainability and reserve adequacy as well.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: This is an important issue to lay bare, in particular, for a small and open economy such as Singapore, as huge amounts of money move in and out of Singapore all the time.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: This is of benefit to us, especially as a financial centre, but it can bring with it risks that we need to buffer against, so as not to take risk leading to major job losses.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: And I think that is the penultimate key issue ‒ the job losses that might arise from this.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: After yesterday's debate, I was looking at statistics overnight.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: This S$400 billion is what actually leaves Singapore's shores, and we will need money to rebuild for jobs if this goes out.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: And I remind Members again that this is only 30% of the FDI amount.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: So, we are fortunate to have a good team handling our Reserves.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: They have been able to secure good returns from year to year to supplement our Reserves.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I must, at this point, congratulate them and the Ministry of Finance (MOF) for an excellent job.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The point made by Ms Kuik Shiao Yin in her speech yesterday about being pragmatic and shifting from pragmatism and moving away from idealism, I think is the point that I shared just now in terms of statistics.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: So, being pragmatic today is actually quite important so that tomorrow's kids can have a space to realise their dreams and ideals.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: At this juncture, Mr Speaker, please bear with me.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I am trying to share a bit in terms of using a localised version of the island parable sketched by the late American economist Paul Samuelson of Massachusetts Institute of Technology to set the context about the overlapping generational issues that we face before my comments and questions later on.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Let us assume we have this island which is home to unusually tall rambutan trees ‒ Samuelson uses cocoa trees and I am using rambutan trees here to give a localised version ‒ and also hungry people ‒ one young and one old generation ‒ and little else.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The rambutan trees are our surpluses and reserves, and the fruits are our returns from our reserves.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: So, the young among the people would climb the trees and pick the fruits.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Take note that the fruit must be eaten quickly before it is spoilt by the hot weather.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The older people are physically incapable to climb and pick the fruit.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Neither could they buy fruit from the young, as they have nothing to offer in exchange.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: So, if the elders had saved the fruit from their youth, it would not work.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The stockpile would have rotted with the passage of time.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: So, the solution: the young gives to the old the fruit they pick and, in return, the next generation will do the same for them when they, too, grow old.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Thus, the young sort of pays it forward.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: This also serves as a link between two generations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The scheme works, Samuelson pointed out, only because “new generations are always coming along”.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I will pause at this moment and say this may be an oversimplified world I am painting, but the same core values and principles have been applied in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: So, past and current generations always looking forward and thinking about the future and caring for the less fortunate.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: In Singapore’s context, things have evolved with practical policies introduced in the past 50 years.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Our young can acquire a durable asset, say, a Housing and Development Board (HDB) flat, and our Government buys reserve assets and can replant half the rambutan fruits or seeds to grow more rambutan trees.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: At a future date, they sell these to cash out and take care of themselves.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Thus, when the young get older, they can rent or sell the HDB flat to the next generation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: In most cases, this kind of saving and investing does far better to serve the people.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Capital accumulation enlarges the economy’s productive capacity, thereby creating wealth.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Saving and investing both store value and add to it, turning one rambutan fruit into a whole tree.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Retirees can, therefore, expect to get more out of their investment than they put in, not to mention other long-term initiatives that we have already built up over the years, such as Central Provident Fund (CPF) and ElderShield, for future retirement and healthcare needs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: So, Mr Speaker, my first question is related to the fruits from the replanting of the rambutan trees.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: We should make sure we continue to plant more rambutan trees and not go down the path of eating too much rambutans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: In fact, we should have a balanced diet ‒ our NIRC (or rambutans) ‒ when we can find other sources of food or tax revenue.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: After all, too much rambutans may not be good for us.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Besides, even when we take other sources of food from other plantations or trees, we have consistently taken care of those plantations with fertilisers and tender loving care by offsets and other measures to ensure all is well and more fruits can be produced in the future.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: So, back to my first question to the Minster, will the trees continue to bear fruits at a rate we need?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Can we and future generations continue to plant trees, even as some of the older trees wither and die?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: It would be good, too, if the Minister could say whether or not we can continue to expect such returns from the Government Investment Corporation (GIC), MAS and Temasek in the next few years or decades.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I wholeheartedly agree that it is important to save for rainy days and keep a substantial Reserve.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I am glad that the Government is looking at ways to address the overlapping generation usage of our future infrastructure, especially in the next economic phase of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: In particular, the issue is about optimal financing and that the user pays.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Rather than just building up funds now for future infrastructure projects, I am glad that the Budget highlighted efforts to fund infrastructure projects by a debt structure to finance the construction of infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: In principle, under such a debt structure, the cost of funding the infrastructure project should be amortised over time, so that each generation pays for the benefits they get from using the infrastructure project.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: In our case, it may be useful to earmark a certain amount of Reserves or NIRC to use to “guarantee” the bonds or borrowings for an infrastructure project.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: To segment spending for infrastructure projects and other expenditures in our Budget explicitly would give taxpayers a better picture of where their money is going to, and how they will benefit from it.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: In fact, this is a feedback from one of my residents ‒ trying to give a better picture of where the money is spent and how you benefit and the usage of Reserves as well.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: So, the key word here is “earmark” for the guarantee to lower the financing costs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: But the returns from the infrastructure project must make sense.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: If future users cannot afford to pay, lenders can tap on that collateral and assume ownership of it.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: For example, in the context of the rambutan story, build a fence around one rambutan tree and use that as collateral to borrow money to construct the bridge to the next island, so that we can build more rambutan trees there, and not sell the rambutan tree.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: We can use the toll for the bridge to next island to eventually pay for the bridge.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Most importantly, the future users of that bridge will pay for the bridge.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: No need to chop down the rambutan tree.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: So, it is an issue and concern I have.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Contingency liabilities could build up for future generations, affecting the ability to obtain funds in future.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Does the Ministry see an issue in the build-up of contingent liabilities for future generations?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Moving ahead, we will also have to evaluate how a GST increase in the near future would impact on the lower-income and middle-income groups.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: If GST is to be increased, how much of it is expected to be ploughed back to reach those in need?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Will more resources be pumped into existing assistance schemes to mitigate the impact of rising living costs?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: It would be prudent to explore means to collect the revenue efficiently, and quickly and fairly allocate it to reduce further inequalities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Furthermore, as the Government moderates the pace of various Ministries' budget growth and looks out for ways to be more efficient and effective, there will be decision inflexion points with tradeoffs at the margins.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I have visited and met students and staff of ITE as part of the Council for the Development of the Singapore Malay/Muslim Community's (Yayasan MENDAKI’s) Future Ready Unit's efforts to enhance the awareness of the younger generation about being future-ready and to instill the importance of SkillsFuture and lifelong learning.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Without a doubt, the Government has provided excellent support and resources to ITE.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: In the last 25 years, ITE has made tremendous progress to provide skills training for full-time students and Continuing Education and Training (CET) skills upgrade for in-service workers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Another ITE programme, which in my view is excellent, is the Global Education Programme (GEP).

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: This programme provides ITE students with a holistic education by exposing them to new skills, global mindsets and perspectives, and a better understanding of the culture and lifestyle in other countries.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: This is even more important in Singapore’s next phase of development where skills meritocracy is essential.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Another resource that I hope will not be affected are the financial assistance support for ITE students.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The application and checks because of means testing can be very onerous for these families.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The Government is clearly seeking solutions to do so without putting too much burden on the current generation and these efforts should be lauded.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I hope there will be no more rambutan trees being cut.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: After 54 speakers and a short detour on how speakers are rostered, Minister for Finance.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I am glad that the Budget has sparked many thoughtful conversations among citizens and fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Many Singaporeans have shared their perspectives with me in the course of various consultations and engagements, as well as with the other Ministers.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I am grateful for the feedback that has helped us to refine our thinking and ideas along the way.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is important because the Budget is not an accounting exercise.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is a strategic and integrated plan for the future, about how all of us can come together to achieve our shared aspirations.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As we learned in Our Singapore Conversation, many aspire for a home where we can make a good living and fulfil our potential, regardless of where we start in life; where we can live purposeful lives, and enjoy our silver years surrounded by the care of family and community; and where we feel assured that our aspirations and needs can be met.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This Budget is about how we allocate resources to achieve these aspirations, through: (a) a vibrant and innovative economy, with diverse opportunities for all; (b) a smart, green and liveable city that we can be proud to live in; (c) a caring and cohesive society where people look after one another, especially the disadvantaged and the vulnerable; and (d) a sound fiscal system that provides for Singapore’s needs in a fair and sustainable way.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our Budget theme is "Together, a Better Future".

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I am glad that many Members agree that we can achieve a better future if we work together.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: My Ministerial colleagues will talk about the respective issues under their purviews at the Committee of Supply (COS).

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: First, I will explain our approach to revenues and taxes, and why this is the sustainable, responsible and fair way to meet our future needs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Second, I will talk about the urgency of transforming our economy.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Third, I will speak about how we can, together, build a more caring and cohesive society.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In this debate, two main questions have been raised: why do we need to spend more?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: What are the roles of taxes, Reserves and borrowing in meeting our revenue needs?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: First, let me explain why we need to spend more.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I explained in the Budget Statement that we face structural and sustained increases in expenditure in a number of areas – healthcare, security and other social spending.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: First, we will spend more due to an ageing population.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Already, Government subsidies for seniors' healthcare needs are more than six times that of a young person.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Second, the number of citizens who have chronic conditions is rising.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Without taking action on diabetes, the number of diabetic patients aged 18 and above could rise from 450,000 in 2015 to 670,000 in 2030.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We are working hard to arrest these trends.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Third, new medical technologies, new treatments, procedures, diagnostic tools and drugs can lead to a higher quality of life, but they could also cost more.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Next, annual security spending is also expected to rise by about 0.2 percentage points of GDP as we invest more to counter rising threats.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The scale and magnitude of terror attacks around the world in recent years are signs that the terrorism threat has heightened.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This threat has come closer to our shores, given the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria's (ISIS’) ambition to establish a caliphate in the region encompassing Singapore.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As ISIS loses ground in Syria and Iraq, ISIS fighters’ return to Southeast Asia presents a serious threat to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The recent Marawi crisis in southern Philippines is a sign that extremist terrorism is now endemic in the region and may take many years before the security problem is rooted out.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Around the region and at home, we have also seen more cases of self-radicalisation.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In addition, the range of threats has widened.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In recent years, we have seen an increasing number of high-profile and damaging cyberattacks around the world, like the WannaCry ransomware incident, which affected computer systems around the world.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: With rising security threats and a wider range of threats, we will need to continue to invest in security to keep Singapore safe.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is a vital investment in our future generations, ensuring that they have a good start in life.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Two in three preschoolers will have a place in a Government or Government-supported quality preschool, up from one in two today.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Apart from these recurrent expenditures, we are investing in key infrastructure to build a better home and ensure we remain one of the world’s leading global cities.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And we have to be prepared that expenditures could rise further than what we project now.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Healthcare spending, even in countries that are prudent like Japan and Germany, is around 10%-12% of GDP.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: A sudden escalation in terrorist threats or geopolitical tensions could significantly increase the security spending required.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: A decade ago, we could not have predicted the rise of ISIS and the speed with which terrorism has spread and evolved around the world.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our responsibility is to ensure that we make timely decisions and have enough revenues to meet our future expenditure needs readily, amid an uncertain future.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In making the additional investment, we are doing so on a strong foundation.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Government spending to date has achieved good outcomes.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is less than half of what the OECD countries typically spend.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We think carefully about how to design and organise our underlying delivery and funding systems and consider the roles of all stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is a chart showing how 15-year-olds from different countries do on the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) test for science, compared with how much the government spends on education.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: One group is the Nordic countries, which typically spend about 7% to 8% of GDP.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Various OECD countries form a second group, around the OECD average.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: They typically spend about 4% to 6% of GDP.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: A third group comprises East Asian societies – Japan, Hong Kong, South Korea.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: They tend to spend less, with PISA scores on the higher end.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We spend about 3% of GDP and do well compared to other countries.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The conclusion is the same even after we consider private expenditure on education, such as enrichment classes.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is not just in taking tests that our students do well, but other skills like collaborative problem-solving.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And this does not capture the immeasurable character-building work that our schools do in cultivating traits in our students, such as perseverance, responsibility and valuing hard work.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The next chart shows healthy life expectancy against government and statutory healthcare spending.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Countries to the right of the chart spend more of their GDP on healthcare, while those to the left spend less.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The higher up a country is on the chart, the longer its residents live in good health.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Green points represent the younger societies, while red points are the more aged ones, and amber ones are somewhere in between.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Many governments spend around 6% to 10% of their GDP on healthcare.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As Members can see from the charts – 6% to 10%.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Even with population ageing, we expect to spend less than other countries with similarly aged populations.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is despite our spending being at the lower end when compared to various jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: That said, Singapore must stay vigilant as a society and as a country.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: How have we been able to achieve this so far?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In education, we achieve good outcomes because we have invested in our schools and a dedicated corps of educators who believe in developing every child to their fullest potential.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We have engaged parents who do their best for their children’s education.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We have community groups, charitable foundations and individual donors who support students and families in need.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In healthcare, we are able to lead long and healthy lives because we have a well-designed healthcare system and dedicated healthcare professionals, with a system of incentives aimed at delivering value, rather than volume of treatments.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We have citizens who take responsibility for their own health and strong families who look after their aged parents.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And we have caring and dedicated voluntary welfare organisations (VWOs) that run many services in the community.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In security, we enjoy safety today, not only because we have built up robust and sophisticated systems and a strong corps of Home Team officers.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is also because we have National Servicemen and volunteers who serve with pride, and a united, law-abiding and vigilant community that stands against crime.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is the power of partnership, and of a whole system that encourages everyone to take responsibility.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It explains how a tiny country like Singapore with no natural resources can have world-leading outcomes with moderate levels of taxation and spending.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is the Singapore way and we must continue to build on this ethos.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In particular, managing the cost of healthcare must be a whole-of-nation effort.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We all need to do our part to keep healthcare cost growth sustainable.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In this respect, I appreciate the useful suggestions by Ms Sun Xueling on how we can be more efficient, effective and smart in spending.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The Ministry of Finance (MOF) will elaborate more on how we are doing so at the Committee of Supply.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: While we must instill prudence as a value in managing our resources, we must also appreciate that the major structural expenditure drivers that I have spoken of will entail billions of dollars of additional spending a year.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The needs they address cannot be met by just squeezing more out of every dollar.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Having explained why we need to spend more, let me now talk about how we plan to finance this in a fair and sustainable manner.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling and other commentators have asked if we could fund the increased spending for the future with a windfall surplus like the one we had in FY2017.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The main increase came from an exceptional Statutory Board Contribution from MAS due to unexpected currency translation gains and investment gains from a global rally in equity and bond markets.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The increase in Stamp Duty collections was generated by the recent property market pick-up.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We cannot fund our plans to secure Singapore’s future on the basis of episodic windfalls.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If we are fortunate to have these occasional windfalls, we should do the responsible thing and save most of it for our future needs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The Government is also sharing some of the surpluses through the SG Bonus.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: There are essentially three ways of doing so: raise taxes; borrow; or draw on our Reserves.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Each of these ways serves a purpose; each involves risks and tradeoffs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We have decided on our approach only after deep and serious study – first, of our spending needs, followed by the options available to fund them.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Louis Ng can be assured that in the process, many public officers from MOF, MOF agencies like the Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority (ACRA), Customs and the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore, and other agencies spanning different policy and operational areas, debated the ideas rigorously with me and their own bosses.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In the process, they pushed back on many ideas but also gave me fresh perspectives and feedback.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: They were certainly not afraid of speaking up or disagreeing with me or with the other Ministers for that matter.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, let me now turn to the roles of each of these methods – taxes, borrowing and Reserves.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is not an option that we have taken lightly.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Not just because raising taxes is unpopular, but because the Government should, as far as possible, avoid taking people’s hard-earned money and deciding on their behalf how the money should be spent, unless it has to do so for critical social, economic or national needs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Certainly, we should not shy away from addressing the need for taxes, where we see areas of collective need that can be better met by Government provision.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: These include areas like healthcare, supporting the elderly and retirees, investing in our people through preschools and SkillsFuture, and strengthening our security.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As Mr Liang Eng Hwa reminded us, many Members in this House have fought for the Government to do more in these areas.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But we should also consider the costs and how to fund them.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Looking ahead, we have needs that occur year after year.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The responsible way for us to fund such spending is to raise taxes.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As Er Dr Lee Bee Wah pithily reminded us, you do not fund recurrent spending needs by hoping to strike 4D.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Each generation should strive to pay for its own spending through sustainable means, instead of drawing down more than is prudent from the Reserves or by borrowing and passing on the cost of current spending to future generations.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In particular, for the broad-based needs that I have mentioned, a broad-based tax like the GST is appropriate.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As then-Minister for Trade and Industry, Mr S Dhanabalan, said at the Debate on the GST Bill in 1993, it is critical to have a “tax system that will make an immediate and direct connection between demands for public service and the private purse”.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is important so that we understand that whenever we increase demands for public services, we should also pay more.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan gave us all a timely reminder that when the Government pays, it is the taxpayers who pay.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: First, there have been questions on the timing of the GST increase that I have announced.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In planning our finances, we take the long view.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We seek to understand major trends holistically and how they may affect Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: By announcing the GST increase early, we are being honest and upfront about our national needs and setting out what needs to be done.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We are giving ample notice to citizens and businesses that we will need to raise GST.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Members of Parliament (MPs), such as Mr Lim Biow Chuan and Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan, have spoken about why we need to do this, to set out a clear direction for the future.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I hope that it helps everyone to understand our shared challenges in the coming years.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Indeed, we must have such important discussions about our future, well in advance.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is important because it is not just Government finances that will be impacted by trends like ageing, but individual citizens and their families.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We must all prepare for what is to come.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This will also help us to better determine an appropriate offset package that can help with the adjustment.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But we know that there are always uncertainties.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: That is why we have given a timeframe of 2021 to 2025 as to when this increase would need to take place.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Before we move to raise GST, we will carefully assess the prevailing economic conditions as well as our needs at that point.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Second, let me address questions over how the GST increase is sized relative to our needs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This estimated amount is before we account for the amount needed to fund the enhanced GST Voucher (GSTV).

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is thus the prudent and responsible approach to raise GST in good time, instead of hoping for expenditure to fall.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Third, let me address concerns over the fairness and progressivity of an increase in GST.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I understand that some are worried about the impact of a GST increase on the cost of living, not just among the lower-income, but also among many middle-income households.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As I have mentioned in my Budget Statement, GST should be seen together with the rest of our taxes and transfers system, including the GST Voucher scheme.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The Government provides structural GST offsets through the GST Voucher.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is a permanent scheme, an integral complement to GST.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is a targeted way of making the GST package a progressive one.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: For retiree households, they also get significant GST offsets.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In addition, we have schemes and programmes to support the less well-off.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This includes the Workfare Income Supplement and Silver Support.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: From education to healthcare and housing, our social programmes provide higher levels of support for the lower- and middle-income households than they do for the well-off, with lower-income households benefiting the most.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: First and foremost, our approach to supporting the middle-income is to create good economic growth, as the best form of social security is a good job.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Second, we keep the tax burden low, so that Singaporeans get to keep as much as possible of what they earn.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, when you look at the overall balance of taxes and transfers, lower- and middle-income households receive significantly more benefits from transfers than what they pay in taxes.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As I have mentioned in the Budget Statement, we will continue to absorb GST on publicly subsidised education and healthcare.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: When we eventually raise the GST, we will enhance the permanent GST Voucher scheme to provide more help to lower-income households and seniors.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We will also implement a transitional offset package, with lower- and middle-income households receiving more support, to help them adjust.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan and Er Dr Lee Bee Wah also asked if we intend to set up a Committee Against Profiteering (CAP) to combat any illegal profiteering due to GST hikes.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: When we last raised the GST in July 2007, most businesses did not use GST as an excuse to raise prices beyond the GST increase.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The then-CAP looked into the complaints to manage profiteering.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Similarly, when we raise the GST to 9%, we expect businesses not to exploit the situation and use the GST as a cover to raise prices.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If necessary, the Government is prepared to convene a similar CAP.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: There have also been concerns that consumers may choose to shop abroad for daily products and there will be more attempts to evade GST.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Today, we limit the value of goods that can be brought into Singapore for their personal use without GST.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Customs and Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA) officers enforce this, and we will continue to have an appropriate level of enforcement when the GST is raised.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: While we have announced the GST increase this time, we continually consider all other taxes and sources of revenues to meet our expenditure needs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Some Members have asked if we are doing enough to tax wealth, and if those with higher income are contributing a fair share.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Dr Intan Mokhtar has suggested raising personal income taxes (PIT).

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We also introduced a cap of $80,000 on PIT reliefs, taking effect from YA2018.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Under the present PIT structure, about half of our workers do not pay personal income tax.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Among those who do, the top 10% pay about 80% of our PIT revenue.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Any review of PIT rates must ensure that Singapore remains attractive.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Just yesterday, Hong Kong has announced a reduction in PIT in their Budget.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We will be moving in the opposite direction if we are to raise PIT when all jurisdictions are competing for talent, including our Singaporean talent.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We will continue to monitor and review our rates but, for now, our view is that PIT rates are reasonable for us to remain attractive, given the intense global competition for talent.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Ong Teng Koon and Mr Yee Chia Hsing suggested that we look closely at wealth taxes.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Aside from taxing income, our current approach to taxing wealth is mainly through taxes on assets that cannot be tax-planned away easily, unlike other methods like estate duties.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: That is why we have enhanced our property tax regime in the last decade to make it more progressive, and to meet our spending needs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: For residential properties, 86% of property tax collected comes from non-owner-occupied residential properties, and owner-occupied residential properties with an annual value of $30,000 and above.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In this Budget, we have made moves to improve the progressivity of our stamp duty regime, so that those who can afford a higher-value residential property pay more taxes on their purchase.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is a significant proportion of our revenues.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We will continue to review this area closely.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Yee Chia Hsing and Ms Foo Mee Har suggested reviewing taxes on alcohol and gambling.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We regularly review such duties and we will take these suggestions into consideration.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: On the introduction of GST on imported services, Mr Thomas Chua mentioned the $225 billion worth of imported services reported by the Department of Statistics.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I wish to clarify that this includes all business-to-business (B2B) services, and vastly overstates the imported services which we will introduce GST on.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our move to levy GST on imported services will not affect most businesses.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is because most businesses can claim full refund of the GST they incur on inputs that they procure for their businesses, including imported services.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Thus, businesses affected by the GST on imported B2B services are primarily financial institutions and residential property developers which do not get such full refunds.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But let us be clear that this is a move to defend our current revenue base from being eroded as more transactions move online.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Dr Intan Mokhtar has made suggestions to raise corporate income tax rates, particularly for MNCs and large firms.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Around the world, there are significant changes and uncertainties in the global tax environment.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: There is ongoing discussion worldwide on international tax rules for combating tax avoidance under the Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) project.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In 2018, the US reduced its headline corporate income tax rate from 35% to 21%.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It also made other changes to make it more attractive for US companies to invest at home.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This may spur cuts in corporate income tax rates around the world.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Singapore must remain sensitive to these global trends that impact us.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We are a small and open economy, subject to the full forces of competition in a globalised economy.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is important for us to remain a competitive and business-friendly location.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The increase in GST is not expected to impact our competitiveness significantly, which is a concern raised by Dr Lim Wee Kiak.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The future GST rate of 9% is not high by international standards as this chart shows.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, our new rate is less than half of that.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Among countries in the region, many others have GST standard rates that exceed 9%.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Japan, for example, plans to raise its consumption tax rate from 8% to 10% in October 2019.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In summary, we have taken a principled approach to meet the general population's future needs through a broad-based GST increase, while ensuring that our overall system of taxes and transfers remains fair and progressive and is supportive of growth.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I have spoken at length on the first way of financing our needs through taxes for recurrent needs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Borrowing is a reasonable option for major long-lived capital investments with high capital expenses, because the benefits of these assets are enjoyed mainly by future generations, in fact, many years down the road.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is an option that we are pursuing for major long-term projects like Changi Terminal 5.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling and Mr Saktiandi Supaat raised concerns on whether borrowing will result in unsustainable debt and interest payments and they have raised an important point.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Indeed, we aim to live within our means.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We should not over-borrow and burden future generations with unsustainable debt, as we have seen in other countries.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The stark difference is that unlike some other countries, we borrow not to spend on recurrent needs like healthcare, education and security, but to invest in long-term infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Such long-term investments will continue to yield economic benefits and position Singapore well for the future.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We are strategically leveraging the strength of our financial position to optimise our borrowing.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: To reduce financing costs, the Government is considering the provision of guarantees to back borrowings by our Statutory Boards and Government-owned companies.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The Government is consulting the President's Office and the Council of Presidential Advisors (CPA) on this proposal, including the details of how it will be structured.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, many of the points that Mr Saktiandi mentioned earlier on will be discussed in great detail.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This way, we can tap on the Government's triple-A credit rating and the strength of our Reserves without directly using it.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is how we are helping the current and future generations.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We are able to do so only because we have planned our finances soundly and accumulated strong Reserves.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We are one of only 11 countries in the world, and the only Asian country, which has a triple-A credit rating, which represents the solid foundation and safety net that our forefathers left for us.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We do not and cannot take our credit rating for granted.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I am glad that Members, like Mr Sitoh Yih Pin, Mr Liang Eng Hwa and Mr Ong Teng Koon, think that this is a sensible approach and recognise the value in this.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Now, I will talk about the third way we have been financing our needs, which is our Reserves.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our Reserves have been painstakingly built up over half a century by our Pioneers and previous generations.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We have inherited this nest egg and must act as responsible stewards.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: That is why, over the years, we have carefully deliberated and developed a comprehensive set of rules to safeguard and manage the use of our Reserves.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our Constitutional rules protect our financial assets and land as past Reserves.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As land sales convert physical assets into financial assets, the proceeds from land sales are rightly fully protected as past Reserves as well.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is irresponsible to mislead people that the principle suddenly does not apply when we use just, say, 20% instead of 100% of land sales proceeds.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Pritam Singh made such a suggestion and if I may use an analogy: suppose our forefathers left us with five plots of land and, each year, we sell one plot, 20% and use that money.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In five years, there will be no land left.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, that is the fallacy of using 20%.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Now, instead of using the proceeds of land sales, or any part of it, for spending, the proceeds of land sales are added to our Reserves, which are invested in a globally diversified portfolio.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This achieves a balance between supporting the needs of the current and future generations.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Today, contributions from Reserves are already the largest contributor to our revenues.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It seems relatively painless to do so compared to raising taxes.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And you may be wondering why do I not take a painless way?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But is it the right thing to do?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: To amend the rules as a first resort is ill-disciplined and unwise.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This would defeat the purpose of enshrining the 50% cap in our Constitution.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Moreover, if as soon as we need more money, the first thing we do is relax the rules, that is the surest way to change Singapore's basic orientation, from saving and building for the future, to living for today and letting tomorrow look after itself.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We must not give in to the temptation to chip away at our strategic national asset.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Indeed, as many Members agreed, we should not over-rely on NIRC, which is already the largest source of our revenues.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: An over-reliance will hurt our ability to respond to changing circumstances in the future.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We are stewards of the Reserves for our future generations, as what our forefathers had been for us.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It was thanks to the astute Dr Goh Keng Swee and other forefathers, who had the foresight of investing our Reserves in a long-term and diversified portfolio early, that Singapore has built up a nest egg.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Since then, each generation of Singaporean leaders has upheld that discipline of running balanced budgets, setting aside surpluses, having professional managers manage our Reserves for long-term gain.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our founding generations resisted the temptation to spend more from our Reserves.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: What if Dr Goh and our other forefathers had said, "We are saving too much of our surpluses", "we should spend more on ourselves and leave less for our children and grandchildren"?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Would we have this inheritance from which we are now benefiting so handsomely and debating how to use more of it?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Today, the constitutional arrangements for the use of Reserves represent this discipline we have set for ourselves.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As the Prime Minister said in 2008, it is about "our commitment to continue growing our Reserves, while allowing the Government to tap on part of the investment income for current spending".

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Deviating from these rules in a sustained way will put this critical balance at risk and may compromise the long-term health of our Reserves and the country.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Be it NIRC or land sales proceeds, we must uphold the discipline in tapping on our Reserves in a sustainable way.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And to be clear, we prepare for the future not only within our own lifetime, but our children's and children's children.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The average life expectancy of a Singaporean child born today is over 80 years.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: A lot can happen in such a lifetime.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Just think about what the world has gone through in the last century.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In the first 50 years of the 20th century, a person would have lived through two world wars and the Great Depression, the advent of nuclear weapons and the establishment of the Bretton Woods system that governs the international financial order today, including the setting up of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In the next 50 years of the 20th century, a person would have lived through the Vietnam War, the formation of ASEAN, major advances in technology, such as the space race and the Internet, the rise and fall of communism and the Asian Financial Crisis.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As we now come into the 21st century, we are moving from a unipolar world to a multipolar one, with growing tensions between major countries and concerns about global and regional stability.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If anything, developments that we are witnessing today remind us that the future is ever-changing and uncertain, as recognised by Mr Liang Eng Hwa and Mr Henry Kwek.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: What is clear is that in the aftermath of a crisis, be it financial or geopolitical, there are usually many years of subsequent weak economic performance.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Employment and economic output tend to fall for a sustained period.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In turn, with crises like these, Government revenues are likely to decrease, at the very moment when we need resources to support our people and economy, a view shared by Assoc Prof Randolph Tan.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: That is why our Reserves are critical to help us overcome such challenges, especially since we have no natural resources.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin raised the IMF's general guidance on reserves adequacy.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: IMF's guidance is meant to specifically address capital flight risk, which is the risk that the Singapore dollar deposit holders will switch out to foreign currency because there is a loss of confidence in our currency.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: That is but one of many scenarios which our Reserves have to deal with.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, the examples I gave of the last century, and all the major events and the potential impact, should serve as a very important reminder about the role of our Reserves.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Also, even major countries, very well-developed countries, whether it is the US or the EU, are not immune from financial or economic crises.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In fact, ironically, the last global financial crisis originated in the most developed parts of the world.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But its impact was felt all around the world.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, however much that Singapore develops, however much the world develops, we must be cognisant and we must be prepared to deal with unforeseen events, to deal with crises which can have a very significant impact on Singapore and around the world.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We need to be prepared for crises that go beyond just a currency crisis.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: More importantly, we must have the humility to recognise that we can never predict what will happen in our lifetime, much less our children's lifetime, or their children's lifetime.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, what we must do is to give them the best chance of a better life, whichever way the winds of change may blow.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: What we have inherited from the past, we also owe to the future.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Members of the House, what I have elaborated on is on the overall approach that we are taking to fund our growing needs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I have listened carefully to the speeches of Members of the Workers' Party to see if they could offer an alternative approach.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But as far as I can tell, the Workers' Party supports the thrusts that I spoke of.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In fact, no one has asked the Government to cut back on any specific item.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: On the contrary, they have asked the Government to do even more.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh asked the Government to do more in many areas, like giving Silver Support to those living in large flats.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Dennis Tan asked the Government to enhance elderly care support.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Ms Sylvia Lim spoke about inequality and what we must do.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Not a single one of the MPs, except Mr Pritam Singh, even mentioned what it would cost, nor how to fund it.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In fact, not a single one mentioned about how much it would cost for each of the ideas that you articulated.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Only Mr Pritam Singh spoke about other ways of funding it.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: He suggested using revenues from land sales and increasing the NIRC cap.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I have explained earlier, clearly, why we cannot, and should not, use this.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: He even suggested that through our Smart Nation efforts, we can increase tax collection from self-employed hawkers and taxi-drivers!

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: These are distractions, and Mr Low Thia Khiang asked us not to be distracted, so I hope that you could have a discussion with Mr Low Thia Khiang.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Instead of taking a principled stance, Mr Pritam Singh would rather withhold his support for the GST increase by adopting a "wait-and-see" posture.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is easy to fall back on politically expedient options and pretend that they will solve our long-term challenges.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But this is a dishonest and irresponsible approach.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If we were to do this, future generations of Singaporeans could easily end up in serious deficit.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Then, we will be having a very different conversation about our future.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I think the Workers' Party should come clean to the people.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Do they want the Government to increase healthcare or social spending?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Does the Workers' Party want the Government to increase healthcare or social spending, as all its various MPs have spoken, item by item?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If yes, how does the Workers' Party propose to pay for the increase?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, I am glad that Mr Low Thia Khiang, who is not here today, appreciates our longer-term challenges and the significance in positioning Singapore as a Global-Asia node.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But I was puzzled that he characterised the GST debate as a distraction, and that he would rather debate this at election rallies.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The Workers' Party MPs have been elected into Parliament!

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Parliament is exactly the place to debate serious issues affecting our nation's future.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I have set out, as clearly as possible, why our spending needs will rise and the options for meeting these needs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: All your MPs have spoken and said let us do even more.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I have also given very clear notice, way in advance, of the need to raise GST.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And I am prepared to answer your queries.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, I really hope that the Workers' Party MPs, having run on a slogan of a First-World Parliament, is not just using attractive election slogans, with no real intent to take your Parliamentary responsibilities seriously.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I hope that when the elections come around, the Workers' Party will not turn around and use the GST to distract people from the longer-term issues that we face.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: These are serious long-term challenges that we should do our best to address and not take this as electioneering or as political play.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We owe it to Singaporeans to do the right thing.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Ultimately, as many MPs and Nominated MPs have pointed out, our fiscal approach is about giving expression to our shared values.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Embracing the virtue of work and responsibility, where each generation works, earns and contributes its share.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And being good stewards of what we have been given today and doing our part to leave behind something better for our children and grandchildren.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This approach reflects who we are as a society, not one based on narrow notions of individualism, where each generation lives for itself and demands a chunk of the pie, but one based on notions of family and mutual support, where all generations take care of one another, and come together to build a better, stronger nation.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As the Malay saying goes: "Serumpun bak serai, sesusun bak sirih" − we are not only stronger when we come together as one, we look good, too.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Another way in which we safeguard our future is to ensure that future generations of Singaporeans inherit a green and liveable city.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This will help businesses lower their energy costs and potentially more than offset the impact of the tax.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: By taking early action, companies that improve energy efficiency and reduce emissions can become more competitive internationally.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: There are many exciting opportunities in the cleantech sector.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: When Deputy Prime Minister Teo and I visited the Energy Research Institute @ NTU (ERI@N) last year, we were very encouraged to see that our support for research and development (R&D) was enabling our researchers to do good work, like on perovskite cells, which Mr Leon Perera mentioned.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: These cells have the potential to be cost-effective in generating solar energy.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: These efforts will allow us to compete and collaborate with companies around the world that are making a big push on the green economy.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Households can also do their part to reduce energy consumption.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I hope that these moves will foster a change in mindset and our energy consumption habits and evolve into a wider green movement that will make Singapore a cleaner, greener and even more liveable city, as Dr Teo Ho Pin mentioned.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources will share more on our efforts on environmental sustainability and the Year of Climate Action at COS.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: While the announced increase in GST rate has received the most attention, let me remind everyone that the most critical challenge that we are facing is in transforming our economy.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Growing our economy is not only the best way of ensuring strong and sustainable revenues, it is also the most important way for our people to realise their aspirations.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This task is growing more urgent by the day, as structural changes in the global economy and technological advances disrupt the status quo, as pointed out by Mr Ang Wei Neng.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our strategy is to position Singapore as a Global-Asia node of technology, innovation and enterprise, which Mr Lee Yi Shyan spoke about and supported.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This means fostering pervasive innovation throughout our economy.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It means building deeper capabilities in our firms and our people; and it means forging stronger partnerships at home and abroad, to build scale and ride on the region’s growth together.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I am glad that many Members, including Mr Sitoh Yih Pin and Assoc Prof Randolph Tan, agree with our strategies to position Singapore for the new global economy.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Members have raised thoughtful questions on the progress of our economic transformation and preparing our workers for the jobs of tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: More than eight in 10 said that they had expanded their operations overseas, up from under six in 10 in 2016.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As Ms Foo Mee Har highlighted, we need to urgently press on with the implementation of our Industry Transformation Maps (ITMs) to achieve economic transformation.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I urge all stakeholders – businesses, trade associations and chambers, the Labour Movement and Government agencies – to double down on transformation efforts and to communicate the importance and urgency of transformation to their members.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Some of our companies are developing know-how to move into higher value markets.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: From a clean room supplier for MNCs in 1978, it has reinvented itself as a developer of innovative medical devices, such as the Miri Time Lapse System, which is used to improve the success rate of in-vitro fertilisation (IVF) procedures.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We have seen how companies in traditional industries are transforming their businesses through innovation.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: One example is LHT Holdings, which started off as a saw miller in 1977.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
