text: With support from the Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR), it became the first company in Singapore to commercialise radio frequency identification (RFID)-tagged wooden pallets in local and overseas markets.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This means more resources for our startups to scale.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: One success story is PatSnap, which has developed innovation intelligence software that uses deep learning artificial intelligence (AI) to decipher global trends in innovation.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: PatSnap’s founder, Jeffrey Tiong, interned in the US as part of the National University of Singapore (NUS) Overseas College Programme.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: There, he found intellectual property (IP) due diligence extremely cumbersome.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In 2007, Jeffrey set out to develop a platform that would make IP due diligence cheaper and simpler, with support from NUS Enterprise and some initial grant support from the Government.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: PatSnap now has over 4,000 clients in over 40 countries, tapping on engineering talent from all across the globe.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Another example is Multi-Currency Exchange and Data Acquisition (M-DAQ), a home-grown financial technology (fintech) firm headquartered in Singapore, which has developed cutting-edge foreign exchange solutions to process local currency transactions for some of the largest global e-commerce platforms.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The company processes more than $3 billion worth of transactions per year from this line of business alone.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Behind these successes lie the spirit of innovation that Mr Azmoon Ahmad and Ms Chia Yong Yong spoke about.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We must press on with our efforts to support a culture of innovation, as Ms Denise Phua reminded us of.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Google has substantial operations in Singapore, with more than 1,000 staff in functions, such as engineering and R&D.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Just yesterday, in collaboration with the Nanyang Technological University (NTU), Alibaba opened in Singapore its first joint research institute outside China, to undertake research on AI.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: These are encouraging signs of progress and we must build on this momentum.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Over the years, our broad-based schemes have built awareness about productivity and innovation.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In 2016, about 85% of small SMEs in the Singapore Chinese Chamber of Commerce and Industry’s (SCCCI's) Annual Business Survey reported that they adopted productivity measures, such as automation, digitalisation and upgrading worker skills.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We are making a push for firms to deepen their capabilities at every stage of growth through a comprehensive range of targeted support.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Even so, we must always bear in mind that Government grants are meant to catalyse companies’ transformation and should not become permanent support.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Murali Pillai and Dr Lim Wee Kiak asked about WCS.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is a transition scheme that we extended but will taper down.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It provides temporary support for businesses that raise wages for Singaporean workers while they press on with efforts to transform and become more productive, as Mr Chong Kee Hiong mentioned.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We must continue to invest in our people to ensure that they are equipped with relevant skills to take advantage of new opportunities, as Ms Sun Xueling and Miss Cheryl Chan observed.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Arif Rahman has made good use of such programmes.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: After his GCE "O" levels, Arif took various odd jobs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Last year, he underwent a Tech Skills Accelerator Web Development Immersive boot camp.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Today, he is a full-time front-end web developer at Indorse, a social network for professionals to showcase their skills.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The effort to upskill and reskill our workers requires close partnership among employers, the Labour Movement and the Government, as Mr Heng Chee How and Mr Patrick Tay highlighted.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This tripartite approach is a key strength of our system.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Even as we support Singaporeans in the pursuit of opportunities, we need to ensure that Singaporean workers remain sufficiently protected, as Mr Ang Hin Kee and Mr Ong Teng Koon spoke about.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: For those who are self-employed by choice, we aim to better address their concerns and challenges, for instance, in legal protection, social security and skills development.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: For those who would prefer regular employment, we are keen to help them do so.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The tripartite workgroup we formed last year has identified several key common challenges that self-employed persons faced.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Zainal Sapari and Dr Intan Mokhtar have brought up the situation of low-wage workers and suggested reviewing employer CPF contribution rates for older workers.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We support low-wage workers by encouraging sustainable wage increases underpinned by regular work and productivity growth.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We provide additional support for low-wage workers through Workfare and assistance for healthcare, housing and their children’s education.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: However, in mandating higher CPF contributions for older workers and better benefits for low-wage workers, we must be mindful not to impose too many barriers to their employment.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Ms K Thanaletchimi and Assoc Prof Daniel Goh have brought up the concerns of women at work, and Ms K Thanaletchimi also spoke on flexi-work arrangements.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The Minister for Manpower will share more about the various schemes to help our workers at COS.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Businesses have asked about the role of foreign manpower in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As Mr Melvin Yong and Mr Heng Chee How highlighted, our ageing population and shrinking resident workforce are major challenges.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Economic growth will slow, unless our businesses make full use of this narrow window, before our workforce shrinks further, to redouble their efforts to raise productivity.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: China, the world’s most populous country, launched its "Thousand Talents Plan" or "千 人 计 划" in 2008, to draw in the best talent from around world for strategic projects.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Today, China has far surpassed its initial targets.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: For us to thrive, we must be equally strategic to develop our Singaporean talent and to draw in the right complement of international talent.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As Ms Foo Mee Har observed, in this way, we can draw in the skills mix to support new industries that create better jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is not the first time that we are making a major push to transform and upgrade our economy.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: All of us have a part to play: Singaporean workers, to continually upgrade their skillsets to be ready for the future; Businesses, to press on to innovate and build deep capabilities and partnerships; trade associations and chambers (TACs), to step up to encourage firms to do more, and do better together.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As Dr Tan Wu Meng put it, we must move ahead boldly to safeguard our continued survival and prosperity.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Let us have confidence, keep our eyes on the horizon, and move forward together.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: All our efforts to steward our resources and grow our economy are ultimately about forging the kind of society we want.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: First, we need to stay cohesive and united as a society, with opportunities for all; second, we need to build a caring society, with people who are passionate about contributing to the common good.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Ms Chia Yong Yong put it well when she said that Singaporeans should have "minds unafraid to dream", surrounded by a community with hearts big enough to accept failure.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Ms Jessica Tan, Mr Ganesh Rajaram, Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin and Mr Kok Heng Leun have talked about the importance of addressing inequality, fostering opportunity and enhancing social integration.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I agree with them that we cannot allow social stratification and inequality of opportunity to erode our precious social harmony.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Singapore must continue to be a society where everyone, regardless of background, has the opportunity to do well based on personal efforts and talent.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: How we achieve this is inextricably linked to our economic strategy.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As Ms Jessica Tan and Dr Tan Wu Meng have pointed out, diversified and broad-based growth creates opportunities for Singaporeans to pursue their aspirations, and this is the best way to help all Singaporeans progress in life.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Rather than focus on how the pie is divided, we should grow the pie so that we can all enjoy a larger slice.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Ganesh Rajaram shared a powerful story of how he was able to move up in life.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Indeed, many in my generation were fortunate to benefit from our system of education and meritocracy.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As our economy grew, and our society becomes more settled, the rate of mobility slows too, and we must redouble our efforts.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our approach is to give Singaporeans a good chance of realising their potential at various stages in life.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We are investing significantly in the early childhood sector to provide our children with more accessible, affordable and quality preschool.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We started the KidSTART pilot in 2016 to provide children from low-income families with early access to health, learning and development support.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We ensure that all our students, whatever their family background and circumstances, have access to a quality education.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And that is the extent to which our education system and our parents' efforts have been able to uplift.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, in other words, our system and our collective effort have enabled them to surpass their international peers in a similar socioeconomic position in their own societies.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Some have academic interests, some have more specific skills-based interests, others want to be entrepreneurs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We have been systematically moving beyond fixed streams and excessive focus on examinations, towards enhancing the education system to nurture all talents and skills and the holistic development of every student.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This has been the Ministry of Education's (MOE's) approach for many years.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Budding entrepreneurs have programmes to support their interest, including the NUS Overseas College that Mr Jeffrey Tiong of PatSnap embarked on.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We prepare our students to participate in the global economy through initiatives, such as ITE GEP.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat can rest assured that we will continue to invest in ITE and offer financial support to students in need.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And beyond the schooling years, we are investing strongly in SkillsFuture.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It gives everyone the opportunity to move into new areas of the economy in line with their aptitude and interests.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked about longitudinal studies on social mobility.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: There is also an ongoing longitudinal study on child cohorts being conducted by NUS.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But bridging the social divides is not just a matter of fostering opportunities and closing the income gap.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As a society, we must be mindful not to allow invisible, intangible divides to fester.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I agree with Mr Ganesh Rajaram that divides can only be bridged if Singaporeans work together to ensure that every child is equipped with perseverance, confidence and resilience to succeed.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As the Government, we also invest heavily in our common spaces.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The hawker centres which are an integral part of our daily lives and our cultural heritage; the parks which bring us together in appreciation of our City in a Garden; and the HDB neighbourhoods which eight in 10 of our resident households call their home.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Apart from creating common spaces, perhaps the best way to bridge social divides is to nurture our common values, by building a caring society.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: A good society is not just one where each of us is able to do well for ourselves.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It should be one where we all feel a sense of responsibility towards one another, a spirit of caring.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Just as we have achieved good outcomes in healthcare, education and security by working together, all of us play a part in building such a society.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh and Mr Darryl David spoke about the importance of mutual care and support within the family.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Indeed, most of our seniors are able to count on their family for support.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And we must strive to keep families strong.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The enhancements to the Proximity Housing Grant will help to do so.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Desmond Choo and Ms K Thanaletchimi spoke about the stress that caregivers face.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Caregivers play a vital role in our society and deserve great respect for the support they give their families.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Besides the financial schemes that defray the costs of caregiving, we also offer tangible support to caregivers through respite services in some of our senior care centres and nursing homes, so that caregivers can rest and recharge.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We are also expanding the Community Networks for Seniors (CNS), which will better link up different stakeholders with needs in the community.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The Prime Minister's Office (PMO), MOH and the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) will say more about Government support for caregivers at the COS.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As Ms Joan Pereira, Ms Tin Pei Ling and Miss Cheng Li Hui have suggested, we will continue to review our policies to enable our seniors to contribute meaningfully, stay active and independent, and age with confidence.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But no single stakeholder has the resources to meet the community's needs alone, to address the structural shift in our demographics, or to foster opportunities for all.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As Ms Rahayu Mahzam said, the community's involvement in initiatives, like the Silver Generation Ambassadors programme and CNS, is necessary to strengthen our social support networks and last-mile delivery.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: That is why this Budget seeks to strengthen partnerships between the Government and the community, and to encourage a spirit of giving in every Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We want to foster a caring society through the SG Cares movement, bringing together individuals, informal groups, community organisations and corporates to partner one another, and better reach out to those in need.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Ms Denise Phua asked if we can encourage people to donate their SG Bonus.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We are studying how to facilitate this and will provide more details later in the year.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Everyone can be part of this ecosystem of giving, regardless of age or background.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I met Asyraf at an ITE graduation ceremony.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Asyraf dropped out of school at Primary 4 as his mother was unwell and did not even sit for his Primary School Leaving Examination (PSLE).

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: NorthLight School gave him a second chance, which he was determined to seize.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: He did well enough to move on to ITE, continued to excel, received a scholarship in 2014 from the Building and Construction Authority (BCA) and, in 2017, graduated from Singapore Polytechnic.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Before National Service (NS), Asyraf went back to NorthLight School and volunteered his time by supporting the teachers in teaching Facility Technology, and by sharing his experience with his juniors.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: He is now on the NorthLight School Alumni Council, even while he serves NS.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Asyraf shows us that anyone can give back.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And as Ms Denise Phua and Mr Vikram Nair have reminded us, for those who have done well, it is even more important to think about how you can give of yourself to help others.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This partnership and spirit of working together is not just a good to have.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is the best way forward, towards a nation which shares a set of common values, and a better home for all of us.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As I said from the start, this Budget is about our future.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Over the past two days and earlier this morning, this House has reaffirmed our vision for the kind of future we want.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Such a future will not be ours unless we do the hard work for it and make preparations.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As Mr Christopher de Souza put it, it starts with being rigorous and working on options that matter rather than being ideological.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Ultimately, the test of what we do is whether it works.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our success will depend on our unity of purpose and our collective spirit of enterprise and caring.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is by working together, and pooling our resources, that we have built up a strong fiscal foundation and the Reserves to protect and provide for us through the ages.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is by working together and deepening partnership that we can build scale, create value and ride the growth of the region together.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And it is by working together, and partnering one another as a community, that we can best reach out to and care for our fellow citizens in need.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Together, we have built, and are continuing to build, a nation that we can be proud of.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Together, let us make a renewed commitment to pass on a better country for our children and grandchildren – a country where a child is given the best start in life, no matter her parents’ background; where she can grow up in a green, safe and globally-connected city; where she can apply her talents in an economy full of exciting, fulfilling jobs; where she can live a long, healthy and meaningful life with many opportunities to give back to the rest of her community; and where she can have some assurance and protection from the vagaries of the world over the course of her life, through the financial provisions that we have made.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is the kind of commitment that those before us made, so that we have a better life today and a strong foundation on which we can build our dreams.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is the kind of commitment that I hope all of us, not just in the Government, not just in this House, but Singaporeans everywhere, will come together to make in this Budget to build a better future for all of us, and give our children the best chance of a better life.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is how, together, we can ensure that Singapore will continue to thrive and prosper, generation after generation.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Question is, "That Parliament approves the financial policy of the Government for the financial year 1 April 2018—".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Yes, Sir, I have clarifications for the Finance Minister.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have four clarifications for the Finance Minister.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But before that, I would like to thank him for touching briefly on longitudinal studies.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I will be taking this matter up further with MOE at the COS.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On the first clarification, the Finance Minister referred to Mr Low Thia Khiang's speech yesterday.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I am sorry Mr Low is rushing to Parliament right now after attending to some family matters.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And he mentioned that somehow, the Workers' Party was not being upfront because we did not want the Government to distract this debate by announcing the GST.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Now, if I heard him correctly, actually, his speech was focused on supporting the Government's accurate identification of the challenges going forward with becoming a Global-Asia node and so on.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He did actually specifically say that it is fine for the Government to announce the GST hike, or intended hike, in advance of time and we can actually have a separate debate about it.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: His main point was that by doing it in this Budget, it distracts the debate from the other things that are being done in the Budget because everybody is focusing on this thing which is not even a Budget measure.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And of course, there was a bit of a cut and thrust about whether we should debate it at the election rally and we do welcome the early announcement because we think the voters should also make a decision on this.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Now, the Government itself is not definitive about when this is going to happen.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And, of course, we do note that in the run-up to the Budget discussion, there were some test balloons being floated up about the fact that the Government needs to raise revenue.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And immediately the public seized on the fact that Deputy Prime Minister Tharman and perhaps other leaders had earlier said that the Government has enough money for the decade.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, the public pointed out, "Hey, you know, is this a contradiction?" And I rather suspect, myself, that the Government is stuck with that announcement.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Otherwise, if the announcement had not been made, perhaps we would be debating a GST hike today.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Earlier on, Minister Heng also said that the Government has not made a decision on when, because it has itself to look at prevailing conditions, economic conditions and also our needs at that time.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Similarly, I do not think we will be in a position to take a stand on that until the information is available at the relevant point in time.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, I think it is ridiculous for the Government to expect us, as a responsible Party, to support something when all the information is still not available and we do not have a crystal ball.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The third clarification, I think the Minister touched on why it is not prudent to use land sales as part of Government revenue.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is an issue that we have debated before.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But the analogy he gave was, we have five parcels of land and if every few years, we sell one parcel, there will be none left.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But I think the Minister can clarify that it is not quite like that.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is not a case of it being gone forever.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Or even 10 years for the commercial leases.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, is it not really comforting for our poorer students to tell them that they are doing better than their poorer counterparts in other countries when really, in their class, they are actually further behind them, on the average?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: First, on the first point about my reference to Mr Low Thia Khiang's point.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Actually, when I was listening to him yesterday, I thought, I was very happy that he supported the point that I made, about making Singapore a Global-Asia node of technology, innovation and enterprise.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: He went on to talk about the various moves that the Government made over the years to look ahead and position Singapore to be able to meet new challenges and secure new opportunities because the world is changing very quickly.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, he made a very good speech on our engagement, particularly with China.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I was very surprised that towards the end of that very good speech, he then got distracted by this statement.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: He said: "Sir, the unfortunate thing about this Budget is that it is looking forward too hastily for future revenue streams by prematurely announcing the GST hike.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This has become an unnecessary distraction from the vision articulated in this Budget, and is a real distraction causing the Government to lose its focus in getting buy-in for the vision".

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is, in fact, a real distraction because, in fact, if the Workers' Party truly believes that all the things you and your Members have advocated − spend more on this, spend more on this group, spend more on these others − and that you agree that all these will require new revenue measures, then why do you not just say that "Yes, we are very happy to support this so let's now talk about how we are going to position Singapore for the future." I will be very happy to discuss this with the Member, who can file a Motion, a separate Motion, to discuss that.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But bear in mind that this is a Budget Debate and if we do not talk about a tax increase, we do not debate the tax increase in this very forum, in this very session for the Budget Debate, then where else are you going to do it?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And to suggest that you do it at the election rally is just a complete distraction.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Does the Member want to be constructive and say that in any election we talk about serious things, about how we are going to position Singapore for the future, how we are going to create a better life for all Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Rather than to seize on issues that will make people unhappy and say, "Oh dear, you know, the Government is going to tax you and all that and, therefore, you know, this is a bad move." You must square your position.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Is it not right for us to say that we know that there is one item that is definitely going up and we will not even have enough to manage that one item?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If you know, as an individual, that you do not have enough money to even pay for your basic meals, should you not provide for some of that?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Never mind that I do not know what other things we have to spend on.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, I am very grateful that previous Finance Ministers, Governments and Prime Ministers, have been extremely prudent in making sure that when we know something is coming, do not avoid it, do not pretend that it is not coming and then mislead our people and say that "Therefore, without knowing, I cannot support".

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The question for me is very simple, "Do you support all those increased spending?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Or are you contradicting all your MPs' positions yesterday where everyone spoke about doing more?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Do you disagree with the fact that our healthcare expenditure will go up and, if you do not disagree, then the question is how do we find the revenue sources to meet that?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, that is the answer to your first question, and also your second question about why your Party's position, about why you cannot support at this point.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, now that I know that it is your Party's position, I am even more puzzled because I wonder why all your MPs, every single one of them, spoke about "let's do more".

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In fact, none of them had suggested that "No, no, no, you should cut back on this item or that item.” In fact, “Very good, whatever you do, double up, do more." So, the question is, if I accept all your proposals, I have to redo the expenditure sums again and look at what else we need to do.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, I think that is quite a distraction.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I hope Mr Low was not distracted somewhere.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Now, as to your point about the land sales, and why my five land parcel analogy is not a correct one.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If you sell that land for 99 years, you are not going to get back that land until 100 years later.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Several MPs had spoken yesterday that even for building infrastructure, we should be considering lifecycle costs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, I think we better do our financing properly.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Then, on the Member's point about the PISA score and the students, we are not saying that we have a perfect education system.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In fact, there are many things which I am very happy that Minister Ng Chee Meng and Minister Ong Ye Kung are continuing to do, building on the works of previous Finance Ministers, to continue to raise —

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Well, they continue to build on this good work.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: That all these changes have taken place for many, many years and the fact that our students are doing so well, it is really a tribute to our educators, our parents, to the many self-help groups.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The numbers which I have shown are done by the OECD study, not just of PISA but, in fact, of various areas in which they are looking at our kids, including in areas like collaborative problem-solving.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our kids are ranked best in the world in this.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As a former Education Minister, I can tell you that the reason why collectively we are ranked so high, the very important reason is this: in every country, you can find one good school, one of the best schools which the elites would go to.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In Singapore, if you look at the performance of students across our schools, you can see what a high average it is.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, when I say "Every school, a good school", it is not just a feel-good thing.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Because I really think that we must give credit to all our educators, to all our principals, to all our parents for the hard work that they put in so that, regardless of which school you go to, the child has the best chance of success.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Beyond the basic foundation as they move into post-secondary education, that we have many more pathways for them to excel.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is right and proper that we look at what have been achieved, rather than look at what has not been achieved and, therefore, pick on that one narrow area and discredit the work that has been going on by so many good people.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One of the hardest things I had to do with this Budget actually was to try and assess how a GST hike can be staved off, given the Government's Budget.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, when the Minister says that the Workers' Party is irresponsible and dishonest, I respectfully have to disagree with him on that account.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With that as a preamble, I have five questions for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Does this tentatively suggest that the Government actually has more income from NIRC than it originally planned to have, with more likely to be realised in the future, in view of the fact that the NIR formula tends to smoothen out investment cycles?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The second question has to do with the point I raised in my Budget speech, which is whether there is any scope for raising NIRC from 60% to 70% for a short period of time to oversee large infrastructure spending, with the view to return this back to 50% on the condition that the revenues from such infrastructure must be returned to the past Reserves.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This would free up more of the Government's Budget in the respective financial years for recurrent spending and this was one suggestion I put forward to stave off the GST hike, and I am not sure whether the Minister replied to that.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Fourthly, how does the Government determine which investment entity – MAS, Temasek or GIC – gets a larger component of land sales revenue for investment, in view of the different risk thresholds that each entity assumes?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, in that regard, that is why I said, it is now the single largest source and, therefore, we should be careful in having a more diversified source of revenue.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The Member asked about whether the fact that the overall NIRC contribution is 3.4%, when the Deputy Prime Minister Tharman Shanmugaratnam has said that it is between 2% and 3% over the five-year period.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But bear in mind one thing, the NIRC is about long-term investment.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And, therefore, we cannot work based on short-term fluctuations and decide that well, henceforth, in the future, we would have this 3%, 4%, 5% that we can rely on.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I was at the MAS when the Global Financial Crisis happened.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I can tell you that I spent many days and nights and weekends looking at the market and how it was going to affect us.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I attended so many meetings among global central bankers, Chief Executive Officers (CEOs) of companies, of financial institutions, with finance ministers in the developed world and with major central banks.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: There were warnings about some of these by some analysts, but none foresaw the problem, and the impact was huge.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We must accept that there will be market volatility which you cannot predict.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: You do not want to have a situation where financial markets are doing very well, that the Government spends a lot more, and then when the markets go down, which is probably when we need the resources most, that you have very little to meet those needs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Let us be very careful about over-interpreting the number.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The Member's other comment about raising the NIRC contribution to 60%-70% for a short period for infrastructure, is this not another way of touching your Reserves, changing the formula, to use it and say, at some point, I would put it back?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I do not see the logic of that argument.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In fact, what we are doing, or what we are hoping to do, is that we want to have proper discipline and scrutiny of borrowing for infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: That is why we are going to discuss with the President and CPA.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We think that a proper way of doing this is to issue bonds in the market so that investors can scrutinise those numbers and see that these are viable projects.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Then, seeking the approval of the President and CPA to provide a guarantee.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, again, there is another layer of check but, at the same time, that layer of guarantee allows us to access funding at probably a better rate.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, we are using the strengths of the Reserves strategically but without touching the Reserves so that the Reserves can continue to be invested for long-term gains.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: That is the approach and, therefore, whether you are taking 50%, 55%, 60% or 70% for a short period of time, it sounds like it is a costless option.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The way that we are proposing is conceptually sound and financially sound.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The Member's last question about the basis of the Reserves for the strength of the Singapore dollar, let me clarify.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: There has been a lot of misunderstanding on this point.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Certainly, strong Reserves help us to anchor confidence.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But MAS' needs in terms of what it does as a central bank is very different from almost all central banks in the world.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: All central banks in the world adopt an interest rate policy.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Whether it is the US Federal Reserve (Fed), the European Central Bank (ECB) or the Bank of Japan (BOJ), the central bank announces certain policy rates and then they undertake certain operations to get to that rate if they need to, but the announcement itself and the anticipation of the announcement have very major impact on the economy.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In our case, our monetary policy is centred on the exchange rate.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Again, I must give great credit to Dr Goh Keng Swee and his team very early on, for deciding on this most unusual way of dealing with our monetary policy.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The reason is this: the exchange rate has a far bigger impact on the state of the economy than interest rates.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We are a very open economy and, therefore, the exchange rate affects economic activity in a far more significant way.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The MAS regularly updates our trade numbers and updates our economic model to see if that remains valid.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: From looking at the studies that they have done, I am convinced that it remains the right policy: to have an exchange rate-centred policy to be able to manage the economy.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The MAS manages our official foreign reserves and it undertakes operations in the market in order to get to the desired band.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It also makes policy announcements regularly so that the market is clear about the official assessment of the economy.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The market may or may not agree and, in which case, you will see currency movements.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But I must say that MAS has done a very good job over the years and so the market generally accepts MAS' policy announcements.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: When speculators were speculating on the positions of other currencies, they did not touch very much the Singapore dollar because they know of two very fundamental reasons.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: All these firms who are doing credit ratings look at the numbers very carefully before they give us a triple-A rating.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, those are the very important defences that we have for the Singapore dollar, and the very fact that the Singapore dollar has risen is not just because of our monetary policy.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The fundamental reason is that our economy has been doing better, that the real economy has got its position correct, that we have been upgrading and revamping the economy over the years and, therefore, the currency moves up, in order to play the equilibrating role.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Can I seek a clarification from Ms Sylvia Lim who said that there was a trial balloon when the Prime Minister spoke last year, and because of the public reaction, the Government backed down but was stuck with this announcement and, therefore, this announcement has been made of a future GST increase.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Can I invite her to agree that that is a thoroughly hypocritical and dishonest statement, and typical of the statements she makes in this House?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Would Ms Sylvia Lim agree that the Prime Minister first talked about a tax increase during the National Day Rally – I think it was in 2013?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And that the Finance Minister talked about the tax increase in the Budget last year, a year ago?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Prime Minister, when he spoke about the likelihood of a tax increase late last year, referenced to the Finance Minister's statement earlier in the year.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Given that the positions have been consistent and Ms Sylvia Lim will also know that, for example, that when we first talked about GST, it was mentioned in 1986, but it came into force much later, in 1994.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, given those sets of facts, would Ms Lim be prepared to withdraw the very serious allegations she makes, that this Government announces something late last year, trial balloon, public reacts, we quickly backed down, but we are stuck; basically, making an accusation that the Government is behaving willy nilly, dishonestly.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And if she will not withdraw those baseless suggestions, will she set out what the facts are for making the suggestion, whether she still stands by the suggestion, and repeats it?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I can understand why he wants to accuse me of various things, because he probably was not happy about past debates where I had disagreed with some of his legislative changes, and in typical fashion, he always accuses me of dishonesty, when, as far as I am concerned, I acted honestly.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: As to the chronology of events that the Minister recited, I do not have them on hand, I have to go back and check – to be fair to him – but this is my honest belief.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The implication, based on what you have said, is that a trial balloon was floated with the obvious intention that a tax increase was going to be announced now, but because of the public reaction being so severe, the Government has backtracked and has changed its mind, and has announced it as a future tax increase.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if that is not what you are saying, please say so clearly.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: If Members can wait until I call them.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, am I not entitled to have a view?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We now have confirmation that there was a suspicion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Does Ms Lim agree that it does not accord with the standards of a First World parliament and honest debate, for someone to come here and start talking about, "This is my suspicion", "I cannot back it up", "It is contrary to all the facts", "In fact, I have not checked the facts; now that you have recounted the facts, I'll go back and check.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I have my suspicions." Would she agree that that is contrary to the standards of a First-World parliament?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think a phrase, a Latin phrase will be ringing in her mind: "suppressio veri, suggestio falsi	".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Somebody very eminent, a High Court Judge, said that about Ms Lim.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I do not agree with the Minister that I am somehow not up to standards.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: This is what we as Members of Parliament have to do to get better clarity on matters of public interest.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Of course, the Government can rebut our speeches robustly – that is fine.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: But I do not think I am disentitled to come to Parliament to advance honestly-held beliefs or suspicions.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I want to thank my colleague, Minister Shanmugam, for reminding me that I have not answered this part of Ms Lim's question.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Ms Lim says that she is saying this on suspicion.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I believe Ms Lim is a lawyer and also a Police Officer before.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I, too, have been a Police Officer before.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, we both know that the first thing when we have a suspicion, is to go out and interview witnesses as part of our investigations.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If you were to look at circumstantial evidence, why did I not set a timeline for that?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I said that it depends on the prevailing economic conditions, it depends on a number of factors which I will continue to carefully monitor.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And that we must not get distracted with one-off events, one-off surpluses.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I made that very clear in my Statement.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Having told Ms Lim that I have been working on this ever since I became Finance Minister to look at all our revenue projections and expenditure projections again and discussed with the Prime Minister and Deputy Prime Ministers – that the statement is correct.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It was not a case of floating any trial balloon.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If you remember, I said it at the last Budget that we have to look for revenue measures.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I said it again at a constituency visit at Cairnhill-Moulmein a few months after that.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Then the Prime Minister said it in November last year.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, on the basis of all the evidence that I am offering, will Ms Lim withdraw her comments?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I still feel that there is nothing wrong with what I have said.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I have a request and a clarifying question.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The request is: can I request that slides be made available to the public and that MOF engage with youth educators, specifically for GP, Social Studies and Economics, to help them facilitate a deeper conversation with young people about this?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Because I think it is a conversation that is going to come up again and again.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Many teachers actually feel very inadequate at explaining this and may give a wrong understanding.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: For the clarifying question, I understand that the full size of the Reserves can never be revealed for strategic reasons, but the absence of public information about the size of Reserves and the rate of return makes it quite hard for the average lay person, especially the educators, to have a meaningful conversation about it.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The problem with the vacuum of information is alternative narratives are filling the gap – some are obvious, deliberate misinformation and some are just different from the Government's story.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I read an Overseas-Chinese Banking Corporation (OCBC) Economist's suggestion that we could split the Reserves into two parts: one as a base for generating the NIRC that can be publicly disclosed; and the other that is used to deter currency speculations can be kept secret.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I was wondering if the Finance Minister could give his take on this suggestion.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: On the first request: can we make the slides and the information available to our people and our educators?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And if there are particular information or analyses that she thinks are useful, I would be happy to get my colleagues to work on that, because I think an informed discussion is important.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I hope she appreciates that, in a world of major currency transactions every day, even the size of our Reserves is tiny by international standards.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is tiny by the amount of transactions that are going on around the world every day.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, the answer to the suggestion on whether we can split it into two parts: I have actually considered that, but I do not think it is sound because there will still be speculation as to how big that part is.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is publicly available as to how big the MAS' official foreign reserves are.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: A way of thinking about it is that that forms one part of it, but, as for the rest, should we look at it more?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Having gone through the Asian Financial Crisis – I was serving as Principal Private Secretary to Minister Mentor then – and I was looking at how various countries were managing their reserves and managing the currency speculators, it was the most important lesson for me as a young officer then.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Never underestimate how the profit motive can destroy countries.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It happened very, very swiftly and I have to say that, rather unfortunately, many of the countries that were very deeply affected, adopted policies that looked very good at that point in time.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It seemed like they were doing the right thing, but the reserves were gone very, very quickly, and it took them years and years to rebuild them.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Having gone through the Global Financial Crisis when I was running MAS, I was even more concerned.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We all thought that maybe only developing countries are vulnerable to financial crises.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But when this crisis happened, it originated from the most developed economies in the world, amongst the most sophisticated financial centres, in the US, in Europe, and then it spread to all the rest of us.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We, in Asia, were lucky that all those new products and new innovations had not had such a strong foothold yet, although they were coming.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Let us be very careful about dealing with finances, dealing with our Reserves, dealing with our global financial market.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is easy to suggest, "Let's do this, and that".

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But we really have to think through the implications very, very carefully, and we must continue to monitor how global financial markets are developing.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Even as I speak, new rules are being made; not only about global finances but about global taxation.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In my Budget speech, I spoke about how the centre of economic activity is moving towards Asia.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I also added a line that the global order will change.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I think Mr Low Thia Khiang hoisted that point.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Therefore, let us think very hard about all the things that we need to do and make sure that we provide sufficient buffer.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And on that the note, the Question is, "That Parliament approves the financial policy of the Government for the financial year —"

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Question is, "That Parliament approves the financial policy of the Government for the financial year 1 April 2018 to 31 March 2019." As many as are of the opinion say "Aye".

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And after the debate that we have in Parliament, the Workers' Party has not made clear its stance on the Government's financial policy.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, I either have a clarification from Ms Sylvia Lim now that she supports the financial policy of the Government, or I would ask for a Division, Sir.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Ms Sylvia Lim, would you like to respond?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: But the GST announcement was an announcement which is not being implemented in this Budget.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, in accordance with the usual procedure, I do not think we are voting on the announcement; we are voting on the measures.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Minister for Finance, would you like to proceed with a Division?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Therefore, the financial policy includes the policy to raise GST in the coming years, between 2021 and 2025.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, I think I will ask for a Division, Sir.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: As many as are of that opinion say "Aye".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Speaker, to make clear, we are unable to support the announcement on the GST hike.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: For this particular Motion, we are voting on the Budget Statement.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Will hon Members who support the Division, please rise in their places?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Minister for Finance, you have called for a Division, would you like to proceed with a Division?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: You should only start to vote when the voting buttons on your armrests start to blink.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Members are advised to check that their names are registered according to their vote indication when the voting results are shown on the display screen.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Deepening economic transformations continue to be the focus, with various schemes streamlined and better integrated, such as the Productivity Solutions Grant (PSG) and the Enterprise Development Grant (EDG), the piloting of the Open Innovation Platform to spur partnerships and the enhancements of various tax incentives, such as IP licensing, amongst others.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I will speak on the economic measures during the MTI Committee of Supply (COS) debate.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am glad that the introduction of the carbon tax would be phased in gradually to monitor the impact and applaud the Government’s commitment that the projected $1 billion revenue collected over the first five years will be used to support projects that will achieve greater emission reductions.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I also welcome the measures to further improve social mobility, such as increasing the annual Edusave contributions, updating the income eligibility for the Edusave Merit Bursary and enhancing the MOE Financial Assistance Scheme, among others.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I appreciate the Government sharing this way ahead of time so that Singaporeans and businesses can better prepare for the increase.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It will also give the Government time to work on offset schemes to further enhance the progressivity of our GST system, something quite unique to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We know the reason why we need more revenues.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our expenditures have been rising rapidly, with healthcare and infrastructure spending among the main drivers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the next decade, this trajectory is likely to continue with even higher healthcare and other recurring expenditures.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In some ways, as Members of Parliament, we have a part to play in these rising expenditures.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To progress as a society and to improve the well-being of Singaporeans, we are relentless in pushing for more spending in many areas, such as education, housing, healthcare, transport and others.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We asked for more subsidies to help low- and middle-income families; we ask for more facilities in the constituencies we represent.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, I must admit I am one of those.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, I requested the Minister for Health for a polyclinic in my constituency three years ago.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am glad that construction will start this year.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But I know that it would cost the Government tens of millions of dollars to build a polyclinic and, when completed, it will incur recurring operating and maintenance expenses in perpetuity.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I have made another request to the Minister for Health for a Senior Care Centre, which I understand will cost about $1 million to build and, of course, will come with its operating costs thereafter.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But such facilities and the various expenditures are necessary to improve lives.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Between not spending on these items or cutting spending, I would rather the Government spend prudently but look for more revenue sources so that we can continue to provide more to improve the quality of life for our people.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I believe most Singaporeans can understand why the expenditures are rising.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The question is how do we find more revenue to pay for these rising expenditures.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Some had suggested why not increase the share of Net Investment Returns Contribution (NIRC) beyond 50% and asked if the Government is too prudent or conservative in managing the finances.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, let me offer my thoughts on this.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: When I studied Civil Engineering at the Singapore Polytechnic, one of the structural engineering concepts that I learned was this term known as the "Factor of Safety".

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Essentially, what it meant is that whether it is a building or a structure like a bridge or a tower, engineers will design and build structures with a load carrying capacity way beyond the expected or intended loads ‒ often between two and three times.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is to reduce the probability of the structure collapsing due to unforeseen factors to a negligible level as you can never be 100% sure that the inputs that you use will be accurately captured in the calculations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There could be unexpected extreme wind loads or seismic movements due to major earthquakes nearby, for example, or other possibilities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, buildings and structures are purposely built much stronger than needed for normal usage, with a "factor of safety” added to, hopefully, cater for the extreme unexpected emergency situations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Similarly, when we look at the long-term finances of a country, should we not also load a “factor of safety” so that, as a country, we will never be caught in a position where we are unable to decisively respond to an unexpected crisis or disaster?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Should we not want to ensure that we have the ability to fight back and recover from an extreme risk event?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And these risk events could be known unknowns to us or total unknown-unknowns to us.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It could be weather calamities, severe global or regional economic crises or even geopolitical crises in the region.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Last year, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, UAE and Egypt cut diplomatic relations with Qatar and imposed an air, sea and land blockade, with the aim to isolate Qatar’s economy.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Qatar’s huge reserves have certainly come into play in how they cope with the crisis.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We are smaller than Qatar in size, with no oil or gas underneath us.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our economy heavily depended on external trade and investments to sustain our economic livelihood.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Any changes to the global economic and trade order can have severe direct impact on our economy, more than any other countries in the world, due to our openness as an economy.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And given our inherent circumstances with almost no domestic hinterland, we will always have to be an open economy to seek opportunities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our domestic consumption can never sustain growth in our economy and will certainly not earn us the foreign currency needed to pay for the imports that we need and want.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As we transform into a more innovative, entrepreneurial and internationalised economy, our risk exposures to the volatility of the world market will increase, not decrease.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The other reality of a small economy is that we will always be a price taker in the fiercely competitive world out there.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Today, we have a vibrant and viable economy.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We have strong export capabilities and we continue to be able to attract good investments into Singapore.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But one day, if this global economic order changes and turns against us or countries decide to impose unfair trade barriers on us, we may really need to count on our reserves to help us buy time to turn	things around.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, I asked myself – what can go wrong for a country like Singapore to be more conservative in managing our finances?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What are the downsides for doing that and what are the upsides?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our solid financial position helps us to maintain our position as one the few countries in the world with a triple "A" credit rating – very few left in the world.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It helps us to keep our Singapore dollar strong ‒ an important counter-inflation tool.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It strengthens our position as an international financial centre, ensuring our connectivity and relevance to the world and, of course, creating very good jobs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Imagine us not having NIRCs or much lesser NIRC, our spending and subsidies of programmes would have been much lower and/or we may have to raise even higher taxes.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Parliament had debated the NIR framework in the past and had agreed on a 50-50 split between spending now and saving for the future.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is a fair balance between the current and future generations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I voted in support of the framework then and my position remains firmly unchanged.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is always tempting to go for short-term painless solutions.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our forefathers were resolute in not taking that easy path and so should we.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Rather than use more of the returns for current spending, we should let the power of compounding returns do the work by re-investing the other 50% so as to grow the principal amount of the reserves and contribute to bigger value of the NIRC in the future.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Going forward, we actually need a bigger NIRC to keep our tax system competitive and, importantly, progressive as well.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, what are the downsides of being more prudent or conservative?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Well, there may, indeed, be some years where we do collect more taxes than needed, such as in FY2017.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are many factors that can result in higher than forecasted surpluses ‒ better-than-expected economic performances, actual expenditure and revenue deviating from the forecast, better investment returns, among others.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As the Government ‒ like most other governments in the world ‒ adopts a cash accounting approach, as opposed to accrual accounting like companies, the annual Budget position can be significantly affected when there are changes to payment timings for big ticket items.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Whenever there is a Budget surplus situation, the Government does have the practice of redistributing the surpluses, whether it is from the current Budget or past surpluses from the current term of Government, to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The payment of special GST Vouchers and the one-off SG Bonus are good examples where payouts are tilted in favour of the low and middle-income.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Here, I hope the Minister for Finance can affirm this surplus redistribution arrangement as part of our social compact.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Besides helping to mitigate the impact of GST and rising costs, it can also help manage the income disparity that we see widening in our society.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Of course, in the years ahead, we can never be sure of any surpluses or the extent at which our social expenditures rise and where the additional tax revenues are meant to be used for.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, in years where the country has done well, we should be targeted in distributing the surpluses to the low to middle-income.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This approach would also instil spending discipline as any further rise in recurring expenditures would have to be funded through more taxes.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This in-built discipline will help to keep our operating budget sustainable and fairer as well.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This pre-funding approach demonstrates commitment and ensures that there is sufficient funding for projects with very high capital expenditures, such as the Cross Island MRT Line.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I also welcome the new financing approach for projects that generate future economic returns to be undertaken by Statutory Boards or Government-owned companies where they can look to borrow to finance the projects and could potentially draw on the Government guarantee to lower the financing costs of these long-term borrowings.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Government is a net creditor and does not need to borrow, other than the issuance of Singapore Government securities which are to help create a risk-free bond market yield curve.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, for the entity that builds the Government-invested infrastructure, borrowing at the project level does require higher financing costs because of the risks associated, such as construction risk.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This could result in a negative situation from the Government's standpoint where borrowing rates may be higher than the returns derived from investing the reserves.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, it makes smart sense to tap on the Government guarantees to reduce the borrowing costs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to talk more on this issue and seek buy-in from Singaporeans on the approach that the Government is taking.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Importantly, to expound on our value system about each generation – past, present and future – doing our part to shoulder the funding of a socially cohesive and economically vibrant future Singapore.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To a certain extent, this Budget has brought to attention this issue and offers some clarity on how we intend to achieve this inter-generation equity.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And beyond just about living within our means, Budget 2018 acts to grow the means for better living in the future.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, the most balanced way to look at this year's Budget is not just seeing it from today’s standpoint but imagining that we are in 2030 and looking back at the measures that we have put in place today.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With that, Mr Speaker, I support the Budget.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is prudent yet aspirational, as it plots a path to a visionary and sustainable future for our country.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Singapore’s economy grew at a faster than expected pace, with encouraging growth in productivity, real wages and output.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This is to cater for expected expenditures in the next decade for infrastructure developments and an ageing population.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Even though it would have been more convenient to do otherwise, I appreciate the Minister's courage to be upfront and begin the uncomfortable conversation of "money not enough" now, in order to give Singaporeans plenty of time to prepare.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is understandable that no one likes a GST hike.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We can take comfort that this increase is not immediate with the exact timing of between 2021 and 2025, depending on the state of the Singapore economy, how much expenditures grow and how buoyant existing taxes will be.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: As a principle, I urge the Minister to try and delay the need to raise the GST rate.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: First, with the recovering Singapore and world economies and the shift in global economic weight towards Asia, these shifts represent significant opportunities for our firms and people.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: One optimistic scenario sees Singapore’s economy continuing to outperform our forecasts over the next few years, with recurring Budget surpluses.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Under these happy circumstances, we should review the need for a GST rate hike.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Second, I would like to call on the Government to continue studying all other possible streams of revenue.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: For example, expanding the scope of GST to cover the rapidly growing e-commerce market will plug tax leakage to online sales and level the playing field for offline companies that have struggled to compete.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Indeed, with cross-border transactions expected to account for more than half of online sales, the plan to levy GST on all imported digital services by 2020 represents a significant step in broadening the Government’s tax revenue streams.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I hope that the tax on imported digital services will pave the way for a broader e- commerce tax on goods and services when complexities of an effective tax collection mechanism for low-value imported goods can be resolved.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Given the projected exponential growth of e-commerce, its potential for GST contribution must be worth the effort to get it right.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The Government should also consider introducing sugar tax in the light of growing concerns over diabetes.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Other tax avenues could include introduction of a capital gains tax or increase in property tax for non-resident property owners, as imposed by countries, such as the UK, Australia and New Zealand.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: When GST hike becomes inevitable, I call on the Government to offer more in the Offset Package, to help lower- and middle-income households and seniors cope with increases in the cost of living.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The new package should help people understand how support provided actually "offsets" taxes they pay on their expenses.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The Government must do a better job to assure Singaporeans that a GST increase will be implemented in a progressive manner and that the authorities will moderate the impact of this increase on those who struggle to make ends meet.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Under the existing NIRC framework, 50% of expected net investment returns is already contributing the single largest source of funds for Government expenditure.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Its contribution has risen steadily over the years, such that $1 in $5 of Government spending now comes from NIRC.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This high dependency on NIRC, I think, represents a significant vulnerability for Singapore, given the volatility that comes naturally with any investment portfolio.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Even the best investment managers will admit that they can only manage risks, not returns.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: To ensure a sustainable fiscal position, there may be a need, some time in the future, to consider a limit upon which Government spending can tap NIRC to avoid over dependency, over and above the current NIRC framework.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The latest being the Government's consideration of using reserves to provide guarantees against long-term borrowings to build critical national infrastructure at lower financing costs.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This is a much better way to tap on the strength of our reserves without having to draw directly on them.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: While I support this approach, I would like to ask the Minister how these borrowings against reserves can be structured and operationalised.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: What is the expected difference in borrowing costs versus investment returns from the reserves?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I am pleased to see broad-based schemes such as the Productivity and Innovation (PIC) Scheme, replaced by targeted measures to foster innovation and R&D, go international, build capabilities and forge partnerships.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: There are, however, three critical areas we need to address.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: First, companies are still very concerned that Government regulations have not kept up with the times.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I spoke in the last Budget about the need for the Government to create enabling environments, within which companies can become nimbler and more innovative, in order to cope with the rapid pace of innovation and increasing competition, even from within the ASEAN region.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Companies do recognise that selected agencies have tried to do things differently, but they often voice their frustration of being tripped up by "last-mile" regulations.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: A whole-of-Government approach is needed to create a dynamic ecosystem, with coordinated efforts across agencies to update related rules and regulations.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The Industry Transformation Maps (ITMs) are still a work-in-progress.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This effort will need to speed up, their implementation is urgent.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: ITMs were supposed to be a joint effort between industry partners, trade associations and public agencies, all coming together to support the sector’s transformation.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The Government’s role was to bring industry stakeholders together to catalyse action, yet industry players feel that the private sector has not been adequately involved in the process.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
