text: Given the pivotal role ITMs are meant to play in the future economy, all stakeholders, including the companies themselves, must start pulling its own weight for this important venture to succeed.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Many firms complain that they are not able to embrace the push for companies to go digital and adopt new technologies, amidst a severe tech talent crunch.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Shortage of skilled talent will constrain our efforts to transform our economy, with the problem becoming more acute as economic growth gains pace.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It lays out a roadmap for a fiscally sustainable and secure future for Singapore in the face of considerable challenges, including an ageing population and infrastructure.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It calls on us to face down these challenges today, so that when we deal with them, we do so from a position of strength.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: As the old Chinese proverb goes, "The best time to plant a tree was 20 years ago.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The second best time is now." Mr Speaker, I support the Budget. 12.00 pm

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: During the Budget debate last year, I mentioned that there is room to make our tax system more progressive and that those who can afford must contribute more.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am glad that this has been introduced this year, although I must say that the Finance Minister is very kind to increase the marginal rate from 3% to 4%, as I had earlier suggested a much higher marginal rate of 10%.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Another progressive measure which I noticed is that the levy for foreign domestic workers (FDWs) has increased.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: During the Second Reading of the Stamp Duties Bill last year, I suggested setting up a special department to look at creative ways to raise more revenues and also look out for existing tax loopholes which should be closed.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope the Ministry is looking at this proposal.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: First, I would like to repeat my suggestion last year to introduce the tender of SG-series registration number plates for cars.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I noted that the front page of the Straits Times Budget Special covering the Budget Speech by the Finance Minister also featured a white car with a SG2018 number plate!

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am convinced that the tender of SG series registration car number plates would raise good revenues which will help boost our Government coffers.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Second, I would like to suggest altering the duties payable for dutiable luxury goods, such as cigars and high-end wines and alcohol.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: According to the Singapore Customs website, for most wines, there is no customs duty payable and the excise duty is $88 per litre of alcohol.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Tobacco products are charged by weight and its excise duty rate.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Similarly, a top-end Cuban cigar is taxed at a rate of $427 per kilogramme, which is a similar rate to normal cigarettes, even though it may cost many times more.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Understandably, this may incur more work for the customs office.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, I am hopeful the Ministry can look into my proposal.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Raising more revenues from luxury items, such as special car registration numbers, high-end wines and cigars, is not only progressive but also discretionary in nature as there is consumer choice.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Once again, I would like to thank the Finance Minister and his team at MOF for presenting a well-balanced and forward-looking Budget which prepares Singapore for the years ahead.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In his Budget speech, the Finance Minister spoke of three major shifts in the coming decade.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The rise of Asia was observed some years ago but the colossal scale of the change only became apparent to many with the conception of China's global One Belt One Road (OBOR) initiative.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Technological disruption is mind-blowing, if not downright terrifying for some.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The sight of agile robots from Boston Dynamics on our Facebook feeds, driverless vehicles and news of medical initiatives in cloning herald a world that was considered to be fictional only one generation ago.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The prospect of an ageing society, however, was not sudden.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Successive Governments have identified it, with the second generation PAP leadership establishing the Inter-Ministerial Committee on Ageing which published its report in 1999 and with at least four other high-level committees on ageing since 1982, putting the issue squarely in the public imagination.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Economic growth is at the centre of our existence and an economy that exhibits a certain verve and vitality is critical to the well-being of our people.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While the Government has got the headline issues right, as it had with identifying ageing almost 20 years ago, what will matter most is how its vision of looking after Singapore and Singaporeans is translated operationally and executed on the ground.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My speech will cover education, fiscal sustainability and taxes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In his Budget speech, the Finance Minister spoke of Industry 4.0, a reference to the technological shift from computer systems to integrated cyber, physical, biological and intelligent systems.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: They are our younger Singaporeans – many of whom are still in school today.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On 19 February 2018, The Straits Times carried a fictional article that sought to imagine what Singapore would look like in 2030 for one young Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It spoke of the story of Alex, whose life was transformed by the Committee of the Future Economy (CFE) report of 2017.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Alex interpreted the report to mean that entrepreneurship was the way of the future.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: By 2023, his fictitious company was awarded a contract to supply MOH with mechanical parts for robot-assisted surgery.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With a local foothold, he expanded his business into Southeast Asia.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Alex’s story was fascinating to me particularly when I contrasted it against the speech of the former Head of Civil Service, Mr Lim Siong Guan, who gave a series of lectures as part of the IPS-SR Nathan Lecture Series on Singapore late last year.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Most striking was Mr Lim’s observation of how we in Singapore pile accolades on those who reach the pinnacle of success, with others often remaining unnoticed and unmentioned.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The call for innovation, a central pillar in this year’s Budget, requires – in Mr Lim's view – for our people to try more and fail; and to be recognised not only for their success but their effort, and to be proud of trying their best in exercising their talents and abilities.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In a second equally compelling and parallel anecdote, Mr Lim spoke about how Israeli mothers in the past wished their children to be doctors and lawyers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Fast forward 20 years and this scenario has apparently changed completely, with Israeli mothers wishing their children to be CEOs of start-ups.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The situation is similar in Estonia and Finland.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In Mr Lim's words, "Singapore has to get there and be exceptional in our own way".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I have my doubts about whether Alex’s parents are ready for him to forget how they changed addresses to get him enrolled into a better school before he entered Primary 1 and how they spent thousands of dollars in tuition fees so that he would be streamed for the best outcomes to secure a stable and lucrative career.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: More pointedly, unless Alex comes from a rich family, I am not sure he would be in a position to give up an education in accountancy in favour of entrepreneurship, given our cultural biases to what qualifies as a good job, school, university or career.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Without a doubt, the education system has progressively evolved for the better, but do we have the luxury of time to undertake its transformation for the new economy, a transformation that is arguably as urgent as the economic transformation we desire?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With our people as the only natural resource, we must begin from the starting point that each and every one of our students, each and every one of them, regardless of race, language or religion, can not just succeed, but excel in the economy of tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The focus cannot be on acing examinations alone as a means of securing a child's future, as is overwhelmingly the case today.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even as our education system has correctly made adjustments to allow for a minority of students to benefit from aptitude-based entry points across the education system, this may not be enough.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There are no evident signs of this tuition culture abating.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even PAP Members have raised questions in this House about stress and anxiety levels in our students.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Parents naturally equate poor PSLE results with relatively poorer opportunities and outcomes for their children in Secondary school.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: They fear that poor PSLE results will evince a bleak future, with their children condemned to schools dominated by problematic students who, in their estimation, do not like to study or cannot communicate well, hence, setting their own children up for mediocrity.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Such fears, amongst others, correct or not, drive the tuition industry and the stress both in parents and, by extension, in students.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But there is another downside – and a very important one – that requires us to hasten educational transformation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is particularly since our educational culture is weighted in favour of parents with means, and naturally so, and those who can pile on enrichment classes and tuition, and even consider paying educational professionals to work out long-term strategies to game Direct School Admission exercises.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government has previously looked at broad-based schemes like the Productivity and Innovation Credit (PIC) to drive productivity, only to shift now to more targeted measures for specific industries through the ITMs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In similar vein, the Government should start identifying the specific policy changes needed to alter behaviour and drive cultural change in favour of learning.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The time has come to squarely look at our tuition culture and, ironically, how it may actually be holding us back rather than spurring and motivating our students in a healthy manner.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The tuition industry is an important stakeholder in this undertaking.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Rather than spend time and money on tuition, would our students not be better served by an education in various regional languages, more debates, better communication skills, financial literacy, problem-solving and negotiation, and on field trips rather than cramming model answers and methodologies for exam-based outcomes only for them to be forgotten very quickly thereafter?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How critical is streaming and even the PSLE examinations for success in life in the future economy?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If it is not critical, are there persuasive arguments that remain for their continued existence?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The need of the hour today is different from that of the past.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A radical shift in direction needs to take place to set up our future generations of workers and employees for the future economy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Alex’s plans to become a successful entrepreneur with an appetite for risk – and for his story and Singapore’s economic future not to be a fictional one – depend on it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How much of it do we need to protect the Singapore dollar from currency speculators is a valid question, given that yearly revenue from land sales alone ensures that our reserves continue to grow in size.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Similarly, there have been calls to consider only a temporary increase in NIRC to fund non-recurrent, lumpy infrastructure investments, such as the high-speed rail, new MRT lines and Changi T5 terminal.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In his Budget speech, the Finance Minister made a fundamental distinction to set out the Government's thinking on recurrent spending which directly benefits current generations and that the responsible way to pay for such expenditure is through taxation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, it is no secret that Singapore's approach to budgeting is highly conservative, with land sales excluded from the Government's income, even as more resources are required to take care of our elderly population through to 2030 and beyond.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Reasonable Singaporeans take the view that there is scope to consider how elderly Singaporeans can be better protected in their twilight years, with the burden of additional taxes like the GST held off for as long as possible.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One novel, if not relatively radical approach in view of the current orthodoxy, is to reconsider the role land sales can play in recurrent spending.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government is, by far and away, the largest landowner in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The majority of all land here comprises 99-year or less than 99-year leasehold properties.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Seen in this light, should not the current generations be allowed to benefit from some percentage of today's land sales with the knowledge that such land regenerates itself in value for future generations, providing successive Governments with the recurring source of income?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Should Singaporeans, who are now expected to live well into their 80s, reap more benefit from land sales so as to justify better social protection for them?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even as land is scarce in Singapore, it is also highly valued, with land sales likely to be very healthy in the decades to come right until our HDB flats run down their leases and well into the second half of the century.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As much as the development of the port in Tuas will cost money, the move of port facilities from Tanjong Pagar will free up prime and valuable waterfront land adjacent to Shenton Way.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: After 2035, a massive tract of land where the current Paya Lebar airport sits, massive by Singapore's standards at least, will be available for sale to the Government of the day.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In between, the Government, as the largest landowner, has many sites open for development that will ensure steady growth of the reserves for the foreseeable future.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On the Government's "Factually" website, the argument against including land sales for budgetary spending is two-pronged, apart from constitutional restrictions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, this argument can potentially be addressed with a cap on spending revenue from land sales, for example, not more than 20% of the value of average land sales over 20 years, or 20% of land sales for that year, whichever is lower.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This would give no good reason for an ill-advised government to ramp up land sales when in government to increase its own income.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The second argument on the "Factually" website posits that income from land sales is invested and is already available to the Government for spending through the NIRC framework.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While this is a stronger argument and certainly true, not co-mingling the income from land sales with other reserves for investment also brings with it the prospect of greater transparency to the public and of mitigating the consequences of poor investment decisions most dramatically highlighted by GIC's partial divestment of its stake in UBS and losing billions in the process, as reported last year.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This also promotes a healthier discussion of fiscal issues amongst our population.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Of course, the money has to come from somewhere.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But there are two ways of framing this conversation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One, is to say that proposals that seek to improve and suggest better social protection for Singaporeans are tantamount to raiding the reserves.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The other is to take a strategic perspective of our reserves position – something only the Government can holistically do in view of the significant information asymmetries – look at how quickly the world is changing and always assess how Singaporeans can be better protected ahead of time.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To reiterate, allowing a portion of the revenue for land sales will also not stop the reserves from growing.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: They will continue to grow and disproportionately benefit future generations.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But looking at using land sales also gives the Government of the day more flexibility to ensure that current generations of elderly Singaporeans' healthcare needs, for example, are adequately budgeted for, leaving more scope for the Government to strengthen social protection for the current generation of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Inter-generational equity is a subject that deserves greater discussion.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The importance and willingness to prepare for the future cannot be underestimated, especially since the very technological disruption the Finance Minister spoke of will, like globalisation in the past, have its discontents – those who cannot be readily retrained to assume higher-value jobs, those who may not be able to build new capabilities, those who, for example, cannot stand for too long and for whom job redesign is only a catchphrase, and those who may not be able to adapt to what they fear is a brave new world.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: GST may not have to rise but Singaporeans could be more likely to accept it if the Government considers the pros and cons of moving from the established orthodoxy and considers new approaches that improve social protection thresholds for all, and elderly Singaporeans in particular.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As expected, the Budget drew much attention on the Government's plan to raise GST from 7% to 9% sometime in the future.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, there was inconsistency in the treatment of some additional taxes that will no doubt add to the Government's coffers before that.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, no estimates were provided on the likely additional revenue that would be added to the Government's income with the inclusion of the GST on imported services.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In addition, the journey to become a Smart Nation – another plank of this year's Budget – is likely to make Singapore more efficient in tax collection.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There is also the question on the move to become a cashless society and the impact this will have on sectors which have traditionally been thought to under-declare their income, such as self-employed hawkers and taxi drivers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This prospect will become less probable with the advent of more electronic transactions and, in turn, is likely to have a positive effect on tax revenues.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Furthermore, with borrowing backed by Government guarantees proposed for large infrastructure projects, more spending for such projects can potentially be allocated elsewhere for recurrent spending.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These are necessary investments to keep the Singapore economy humming along.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, the people who keep it humming must be equipped to succeed in tomorrow's economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This Budget is of tremendous importance because it adds further strength and connectivity to the efforts that had already begun in previous Budgets to pave the way for Singapore to embark upon the future economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In that sense, Budget 2018 cannot be looked at in isolation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: It is clear to anyone who has followed the sustained efforts of the last few Budgets that the determinants of where to apply the limited resources in order to maximise the benefits of the fiscal impulse are long-run social and economic objectives rather than short-term relief.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The economy’s transformation is based on ensuring greater efficiency in the use of resources, and a crude fiscal push with only short-term gains should be avoided.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: At best, such a move could crowd out the private sector in the competition for resources already in short supply, especially manpower.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: At worst, it could detract from the careful efforts already under way in each of the industry transformation maps and accompanying skills frameworks to deepen the push for future readiness.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: These include evidence of fortified strength in the labour market situation, the continuing improvement in competitiveness in external-oriented sectors and the revival in productivity performance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In the labour market for instance, redundancies have stabilised, unemployment continues to be low and re-employment is encouraging.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In industry competition, what we find is that businesses are beginning to rationalise their dependence on foreign manpower.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In productivity performance, the situation is certainly something we have to continue to watch out for, but the recent uptick in productivity performance is something that we should be able to link to the efforts over the last few Budgets to improve the productivity situation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The main question is: what have we to continue to do in order to sustain these gains?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, against these positive signs, there are accelerating effects of long-term challenges, especially demographic shifts and national security, which are continuing reminders of our vulnerabilities as a small, open economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In this Budget, the programmes that are already well-funded continue to be so, with increases in social spending and infrastructure expected to continue in the years to come.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: But in the longer term, as spending needs grow, we will have to decide how to meet those needs in a responsible manner.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Depending on potentially volatile and unanticipated increases in Budget surpluses is not ideal.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The unusual Budget surplus that we saw in last year's Budget is a welcome surprise in this case because of currency movements that had gone unexpectedly in MAS’ favour.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: But market movements which present large upside surprises in one year could also contain the potential to do the opposite.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: With sufficient diversification and vigilance, the chances of a downside surprise can be minimised but not eliminated.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This is not a reliable recipe for funding long-term national commitments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Despite criticisms about the extent of social spending, the incontrovertible fact remains that Social Development expenditures in Singapore account for the largest share of the Budget and has done so with rare exception in recent years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: I pointed out before that we should not ignore the fact that the pace of increase in social spending must be managed in order to ensure the competition with other areas of spending does not drive up costs of limited resources.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This is a rate of growth that will double spending every seven years or so and this is way in excess of the rates of growth that we see in economies, like Sweden, which have taken a long time to reach the point that they are at, at this point in time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Such spending increases are an improvement that have been made possible by Singapore's continuing economic progress.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: There are many areas of Social Development, no doubt, that require urgent attention.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: New areas of needs arise as society develops and the economy matures.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Sustainable solutions to such challenges require a focused and targeted approach.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Even advanced economies, Sir, have to continue to defend their vulnerabilities against unforeseen national security threats as well as sudden external economic upheavals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The competition to prioritise certain areas of spending should not lead to a softening of emphasis on areas of basic necessity, such as defence spending and the shoring up of our economic defences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: At any point in time, there are security threats in various parts of the world which may have an impact on shipping lanes and flight routes vital to our trade linkages.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: As a sovereign developed nation, it is our responsibility to be prepared to bear the burden of maintaining these vital connections.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The building of national defence capabilities is a fundamental priority that cannot be ignored.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The experiences of other advanced economies show that the failure to maintain up-to-date defence capabilities could lead to a diminished capacity to play a full role in defence partnerships.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Just as with our national infrastructure, ensuring that our defence capabilities are continually upgraded to meet future needs is critical.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In recent years, there has been growing criticism from a vocal minority about the growth in Singapore’s reserves and what the reserves are needed for.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: As demonstrated by the last crisis, however, developed economies could actually be more exposed to certain types of crises than less developed ones.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The cost of confronting that crisis, Sir, was a costly affair for many governments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: But as the experiences of several countries have shown, a strong response with a decisive and sufficiently large package of measures meant that the cost of the responses could usually be recovered if the intervention successfully revived asset valuations that had been downgraded by the crisis.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In order for this to occur, the resources needed to mount the rescue packages had to be available in the first place.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Our role in financial markets is not small and these examples are not irrelevant.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Our own experience during that crisis was no less informative.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: If those reserves had not been readily available, the consequences would have been unimaginable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This is why there is a need to protect and grow the reserves through a disciplined fiscal approach that includes responsible taxation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This Budget is a cogent demonstration of these principles of forward thinking and responsible planning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: It recognises, for example, that taxing undesirable behaviour is necessary, but not a constructive approach to funding long-term needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: A secure economy will provide the foundation for strengthening social programmes, supporting the needy and expanding opportunities for future generations.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Residents ask for financial help, they want lower transport fares, they appeal for more bus services to bring them to their specific destination; they ask for low-cost rental flats, they ask for blue CHAS cards, for higher healthcare subsidies and they ask for less expensive medical treatment at clinics and hospitals and the list goes on.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For many of these requests, I am sympathetic as these residents are usually low-income.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Any reduction of costs or living expenses would be greatly welcomed by them.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: However, what some people do not remember is that it is not the Government who just pays for the subsidies.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The financial burden would be borne by other taxpayers.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Not all residents understand that the Government is a trustee of sort to manage the taxes paid by Singaporeans and Singapore companies.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In doing so, the Government has to be prudent in its spending and judiciously decide how to allocate scarce resources.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Many of us have unlimited wants but there is only so much resource available for distribution.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: We do not have oil reserves, no timber forest or coal or natural minerals at our disposal.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But despite the lack of natural resources, Singapore has remained successful with good economic growth and has accumulated respectable financial reserves.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I attribute this to good government as well as a hardworking and intelligent citizenship who have helped built Singapore to what it is today.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Our Budget theme for this year is "Together – A Better Future".

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In the Budget Statement, the Finance Minister explained that the Budget is a strategic and integrated plan.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: More will also be spent on education and security.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: These priorities of the Government resonate with me.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Indeed, healthcare is always a concern for many Singaporeans as there will be more and more seniors as we live longer.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Many elderly citizens whom I speak to worry about high healthcare costs, especially those who suffer from chronic diseases or had suffered stroke or require long-term medication for cancer.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In my constituency walkabouts, I see more and more residents on wheelchair or needing help with their mobility.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: More spending on healthcare will make it affordable for those who need help in their retirement years.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Having improved infrastructure will also allow better accessibility and convenience for many people and create a better environment for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Lower transport fare is welcomed because public transport is a necessity and public transport should be kept affordable.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: An increase in education spending is also welcomed as it will prepare our children for the future challenges in the world.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Increasing the financial support for students from lower-income families will mitigate the gap between the well-off students and lower-income families.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: With increased terrorist activities, security should also be an area of priority and, indeed, we should ensure that whatever we have today should be protected from those who wish Singapore to fail.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: However, the devil is always in the details.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In allocating more resources to these areas of priorities, I urge the Government to consider and to ensure that the lives of all Singaporeans would improve.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I understand the need to take better care of the poor and needy and those with low-income.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But I urge the Government not to forget the struggles and difficulties of the rising number of middle-class citizens who may feel sandwiched by Government policies.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They perceive some of the policies as not helping them.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Hence, I urge the Government to implement policies which would help those in need and, at the same time, be fair to citizens who have contributed to build Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Thus, for incentives like S&CC rebates or GST vouchers, please consider helping those who live in bigger flats but with lower-income.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Please do not just assess based on house type.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Review the income ceiling for those who apply for CHAS card or those who should receive Silver Support.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Keep an eye on the retirees and the middle-income Singaporeans so that they, too, can share or enjoy the growth of the country.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Schemes like the Housing Grant and Proximity Housing Grant are good schemes that help the middle-income own HDB flats with large subsidies from the Government.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The increase in GST was voted in November last year.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: When the idea was floated, I said that there is always a political cost if you cannot persuade the ground that a hike in taxes is necessary.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Nobody likes a tax increase as it takes away disposable income from the citizen and transfers it to the Government to manage.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The Prime Minister had previously said that in this current term of Government, which ends in 2021, it has enough revenue.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Thus, I am glad that the GST increase is not taking effect next year or the year after.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In my view, it is fair and prudent to take a longer term view of the needs of the country.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It is not always possible to expect the Government to keep increasing the spending on healthcare, security and other social spending without thinking of how to fund such spending.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In particular, if the increase in GST would help reduce the healthcare burden on all citizens, if it helps subsidise transport costs, if it provides more care for the lower-income, it should be something that we should all support as we are helping the majority of Singaporeans, for the lower-income, middle-income and seniors.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: When the GST increase is implemented, there will also be an offset package later.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, with respect to Mr Pritam Singh, I would not agree that GST in the Singapore context is regressive.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In fact, I am surprised at the Workers' Party's reservations on GST increase.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Because if the Workers' Party agrees to increase social spending for healthcare, education and security, where can the funds come from to pay for these recurrent expenditures?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Minister Heng had said, "In the next decade, between 2021 and 2030, if we do not take measures early, we will not have enough revenues to meet our growing needs." Thus, to me, it is clear that the Government is planning not just for a few years later but for the next decade!

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For those who say that we should use the Budget surplus last year to fund the increase in expenditure, I respectfully disagree because it is fiscally unsustainable to rely on a surplus which is not a constant or a guaranteed source of revenue.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Last year’s surplus was an extraordinary gain and Minister Heng had explained how the surplus came about.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Details of the surplus were also published in the media yesterday.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Surely, we cannot expect currency translation effects or increases in stamp duty to be always available in future Budgets.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For those who advocate that we use more than 50% of the expected NIR and keep less in the reserves, I would urge the Government to be cautious.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It is always easy to say spend more today and save less for the future.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: What should be the right balance is a question that everyone has an opinion about.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: To me, we should exercise prudence and try to spend within our means, especially if our expenses are on recurrent spending on healthcare, security and other social spending.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: We have been fortunate that our NIR has been increasing year after year.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: What if the NIR falls in the future years?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Would we then say take more from the NIR again?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: As for using proceeds from land sales, as suggested by Mr Pritam Singh, I want to sound a word of caution: once land is sold, the asset is gone.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If we to use any part of the sales proceeds to fund recurrent expenses, does that mean that we are taking the monies away from the reserves?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, I humbly submit that we should allow our reserves to grow in tandem with the economy.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Before I conclude, allow me to seek a few clarifications from the Minister.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Can we not rely on our other resources or borrow from our reserves and pay interest on those loans?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: With that, Mr Speaker, Sir, I support the Budget.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: He made a statement to say that once the land is sold by the Government, it is gone.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: But does he not agree that actually the Government's definition of land sales includes leases.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, it is not quite accurate to say that once the land is sold, it is gone.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: The funds, once they go back into the reserves, would be gone for that period.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: For you to get back the land, you have to wait 99 years for it to come back.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, again, I would like the Member to confirm that it is not accurate for him to say that once the land is sold, it is gone.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: I am afraid I cannot understand what Ms Sylvia Lim is asking.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: You are going to wait 99 years for the monies to come back before it goes back into reserves.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Then, you are spending funds that would be gone for 99 years.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, Members of Parliament, good afternoon!

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Today, my topic is: a strategic and long-term Budget which helps businesses grow sustainably.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: A key highlight of this year’s Budget is that it materialises the framework promulgated by the Committee on the Future Economy through the introduction of a series of targeted measures to assist businesses.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Before announcing this year’s Budget, the Government had widely sought views and feedback from trade associations and chambers.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The various measures now introduced by the Budget have matched the expectations of the business community.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: This year’s Budget is very far-sighted, as it is making preparations for a better future.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Going forward, Singapore will increase public expenditure in healthcare, security, long-term infrastructure and education.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: We believe our people and businesses will benefit from public spending in these areas.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: When I listened to the Minister for Finance as he delivered the Budget Statement, what I thought about the most was the question of how we can increase our revenue sources while curbing our expenditure, 开源节流 in Chinese.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: I am glad that the Government will, hence, observe the principle of 开源节流 when constructing large-scale infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Because such investments are huge, the Government is looking at allowing Statutory Boards and GLCs, like LTA, to fund them by borrowing or issuance of bonds, in order to avoid tapping into the national reserves.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The Government is also considering providing guarantees for long-term borrowings for such infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: As a country with no natural resources, our reserves are like a financial linchpin that provides the country stability and should not be tapped into so easily.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, mobilising resources from the society to continuously obtain funds to finance such construction is a wise decision.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The other manifestation is to moderate the pace of Ministries’ budget growth.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: As Singapore is already an ageing society, there will be more and more areas that will require spending in the future.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: We need to stringently control Ministry spending, monitor closely the policy implementation processes, plug loopholes in the abuse of Government resources, raise the quality of public projects and avoid the vicious cycle of problems arising from Government spending and then having to spend more money to resolve problems – this is truly how 开源节流 could be meaningfully carried out.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: They are worried that following the GST increase, many consumers will swarm into Malaysia, particularly Johor Baru, to shop for daily products.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: These retailers believe that this is very likely to happen because the Singapore-Johor Rapid Transit System Link will start operating in 2024.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: With the ease of travelling, more convenient customs clearance, easier conveyance of goods and the strength of the Singapore dollar vis-à-vis the Malaysian ringgit, the lure across the Causeway would only grow greater.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Come 2026, the surge in north-bound traffic could be even higher, as the Singapore-Kuala Lumpur High Speed Rail is projected to be operational by then and there will be many convenient places to shop along the route.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: To local businesses that provide similar services, this is a long-awaited equitable measure.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Such purchases include software applications and a variety of Business-to-Business (B2B) services, including accounting and IT.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: On the other hand, once this GST is levied, many purchasers, especially SMEs, will face pressure arising from an increase in their operating cost.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: However, on-line transaction of services is a complex matter.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Whether it is the provision of services through the B2B or B2C model, there is a likelihood that charges from both ends may exploit technical or policy loopholes to gain an advantage in areas, such as during the transaction, the computation of tax assessment and tax rebate.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: There is a need to strengthen supervision in theses aspects.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Only when our companies thrive and develop, they could then contribute more to Government revenue.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The Government has continuously been helping our companies to transform and upgrade.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Next, companies themselves have to be more proactive to push the pace of transformation and innovation.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Workers need to learn new knowledge, new skills, while bosses must use a new mindset to develop new markets.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Transformation is like stretching the body, where periodic pains are unavoidable.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: There is no guarantee that transformation will definitely succeed, but not transforming means certainty of elimination.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: There is another Budget measure that is welcomed by businesses.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses passionate about charity have always enjoyed support through Government policies.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In the last two years, donations to Institutions of Public Character (IPCs) are entitled to enjoy 250% of tax deduction.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: At the start of a new year, the Government has introduced a Budget that is strategic and with a long-term vision.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Following this, it will require all the stakeholders in the society to proactively take action to execute all the measures that have been introduced.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I highlight that ageing is not uniformly experienced, and that men and women experience ageing and are affected by ageing very differently.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are, therefore, gender inequalities we need to tackle if we are to meet the challenges and opportunities of ageing successfully.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our policies targeted at ageing must factor in the gender differences for them to be effective.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I focus on three sets of issues, namely, issues related to the gender income gap, issues with supporting caregivers and the economic and health security of seniors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A study using data from MOM last year showed that the gender pay gap has not improved in the decade from 2006 to 2016.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is unacceptable that we have not made any progress in closing the gender pay gap in 10 years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need to tackle the gender pay gap because it will affect our future senior women and their retirement security.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Already, women are living longer than men and CPF LIFE is structured in such a way that discriminates between gender, with women paying a higher premium and getting less payouts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The gender pay gap has, therefore, a compounding effect on the retirement security of women.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There has been some attention on the gender pay gap in the finance sector and in senior management, but I think we should actually pay more attention to the majority of our women workers who are labouring in other sectors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The health and social service sector impacts ageing and our seniors the most.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is also a sector that is, arguably, the most susceptible to what Minister Ong Ye Kung has noted as a key factor underpinning the gender pay gap, that is, the social norms and expectations placed on women.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Nursing makes up the bulk of the health and social service sector and most nurses are women.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Nursing is also in high demand because of ageing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A strong professional body of local nurses is essential for us to successfully meet the challenges of ageing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For many decades, there has been an erosion of status and value attributed to nursing, which culminated in the 2013 Population White Paper footnote mistake in classifying nursing as a low-skilled job that is difficult to offshore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The apology and correction from Deputy Prime Minister Teo Chee Hean then was swift and right, and I believe there has been a narrowing of the prestige gap between nursing and other professions since 2013.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But there are still two other associated issues.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, while wages for nurses have been improving, there is still a lag.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is not too different from similar ratios for OECD countries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, when compared to small countries with a similar demand profile for nurses, we are behind.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, the ratio in Israel is 1.4.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In Australia, where ageing is also a major challenge for society, the ratio is 1.2.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Given the high demand for nursing because of our ageing society, there is scope to further increase the wages of nurses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Second, it has been a longstanding fact that most nurses are women, which has entrenched the perception that nursing is a female occupation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This gendered composition and perception of nursing will continue to exacerbate the supply shortage of trained nurses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Increasing the wages of nurses will kill several birds with one stone.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As most nurses are currently women, increasing the wages of nurses will help close the gender pay gap.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It will also signal the increased social value and respect that is attached to nursing; that nursing is far from being a low-skilled job; that, on the contrary, nursing is an especially precious skillset for the ageing society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We all know that nursing is a very demanding job.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is emotionally straining, time consuming, especially with the shift work and overtime, and is also physically draining.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Increasing the wages of nurses will make the remuneration more commensurate with the passion that is demanded of nurses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Increasing the wages of nurses will also help to shift the mindset over time, so that more men would take up the calling and not be put off by the opportunity cost of higher pay for men in other professions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Another issue related to the gender pay gap is the income security and prospects of women who have become mothers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Part of the reason for the gender pay gap is linked to women returning to the workforce after taking a prolonged break due to pregnancies or childcare responsibilities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Little recognition is given by employers and the Government to the years women spent in service to the family and to the nation to bear and raise children, unlike men who are often given a salary premium for the two years spent in National Service.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The current emphasis on lifelong learning and continuous retraining exacerbates the issue.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: By the time women try to return to the workforce, they face the triple challenges of making sure their skills stay relevant, discrimination against older workers and wage stagnation compared to their male peers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Last year, during COS 2017, I proposed the SkillsFuture Mommy Awards to make re-entry into the workforce for mothers less challenging.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have the social and policy infrastructure to resolve this issue.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is an area that SkillsFuture Singapore and Workforce Singapore should look into.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, again, we see gender closely connected to ageing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As with nurses, getting our policy right in supporting caregivers is essential for us to successfully meet the challenges of ageing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we can resolve these two issues, we will be able to support a strong body of caregivers who would form the bedrock of our silver care system, close the loop between healthcare and community care, and allow our seniors to successfully and actively age in place.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The numbers should have gone up by now.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is not a small number, as it represents around 10% of our resident workforce.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is despite the fact that 49% of caregivers in this survey had the support of foreign domestic workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The same survey shows that caregivers living in private property and, therefore, assumed to have better means, experienced lower stress, while caregivers who were working and who were facing more financial problems due to caregiving experienced higher stress.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is only one of the many surveys and studies that have shown consistent results.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I think it is time we recognise that caregiving is full-time work, which prevents caregivers from realising their employment potential and affecting their financial security.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How can we better support caregivers in this respect?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Two years ago, during COS 2016, I asked the Government to consider giving means-tested refundable tax credits to caregivers, so that caregivers who do not work or work part-time would get some cash refund.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This would lessen their financial burden and improve their retirement adequacy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Senior Minister of State Sim Ann then replied that the Government’s approach focused on direct subsidies of services to lessen the costs borne by caregivers, rather than providing cash allowances to people looking after family members.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am of the view that the two do not have to be mutually exclusive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Cash allowances to caregivers suffering from extreme negative financial impact would allow them to access the subsidised services.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we recognise full-time caregiving of seniors as unpaid work, then it is not far-fetched to consider them as low-wage employees who need income supplement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should rethink the orthodoxy and provide income support to caregivers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is already one scheme that is suited for this purpose – the Workfare Income Supplement (WIS) Scheme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: WIS is means-tested and, with older workers receiving higher payments, it will ensure the benefit will go to needy caregivers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Also, since 40% of the payment is given out in cash and 60% in CPF contributions, this will help take care of the immediate financial needs and enhance the retirement needs of the eligible caregivers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second issue is the stress faced by caregivers of seniors, which, in the worst case, can lead to depression and anxiety.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Studies of caregivers in Singapore have consistently shown high stress levels among caregivers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Caregivers of seniors with dementia experience higher stress.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Female caregivers of seniors, namely wives and daughters, tend to experience a lot more stress than male caregivers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These female caregivers reported feeling rundown and exhausted and experienced restless sleepless nights.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many of them reported the desire to be involved in culturally relevant recreational activities, such as a game of mahjong, but they lack the social networks to get involved.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our caregivers are a heroic bunch with strong Asian family values.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Another study has shown that caregivers often report concerns about the caregiving and much less about the effect of caregiving on their own physical and mental well-being.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What this means is that while they know and are driven to care for their loved ones, the caregivers do not know how to care for themselves and tended to neglect their own well-being.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I think these are great initiatives, but we are starting from a very low baseline of no support for caregivers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is a lot more we can do, especially given the general reticence of caregivers to seek help for themselves.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I suspect the caregivers are not too forthcoming in seeking caregiver support services at the SCCs and AICareLinks centres.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It may well be that we would need to use the Social Service Offices (SSOs) and Family Service Centres (FSCs) infrastructure to bring the support to the caregivers to enhance their well-being.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I understand the logic to integrate health and social support for seniors under MOH and empowering AIC to be the central implementing agency to coordinate the services announced in the Budget Statement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But I hope this integration will not come at a cost to the cross-functional integration between MOH and MSF, and between AIC and the SSOs when it comes to needy seniors and vulnerable caregivers of seniors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In fact, with seniors ageing in place and in their communities, the delivery of services is most effectively achieved by leveraging the community networks of the SSOs and FSCs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I turn now to the third and last set of issues, which are directly related to the retirement security of senior women.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are two issues here I would like to highlight: economic security and health security.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, existing cohorts of elderly women and soon-to-be senior women cohorts are experiencing economic vulnerabilities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This gap is narrowing for younger cohorts as gender equality improves with better educational attainment by women in recent decades.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, this problem will remain with us for at least another 20 years, as the gender CPF gap is similar for those aged 45 years and above.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Back in 2008, HDB found that just over half of elderly residents living in HDB flats planned financially for retirement, with women much less likely to do so.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many elderly women, much more so than elderly men, are dependent on their spouses and children for financial support and many continued to work in low-paid jobs to supplement their meagre income.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One study in 2011 showed that 26% of those aged 55 years and above reported they perceived occasional or regular financial inadequacy, with more women reporting this than men.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This means that among the working elderly, 41% had income from work, family members and state assistance amounting to less than 40% of the median income in the workforce.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This suggests that many seniors are working past retirement age not just because they want to, but because they had to, and many in this category are women.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It does not look like this issue is going to abate in the next decade.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Instead, the scale of the economic insecurity problem will increase due to the doubling of the number of seniors to 2030.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One possible line of attack would be to look at how social service and community development agencies helping to place the elderly in jobs could also help the elderly draw up favourable contracts for service and provide advice and retraining opportunities to improve their income prospects.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the meantime, the Silver Support Scheme could be enhanced to mitigate the problems faced by the elderly working poor.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As many of the seniors are dependent on their spouse and children for their housing needs, we should make sure this housing dependence does not erode the efficacy of state assistance to support the needy seniors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Silver Support Scheme payouts to needy seniors are currently tiered according to the HDB housing types they are living in.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is unnecessary as the beneficiaries of the scheme are already means-tested.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A needy senior living in a 5-room flat receiving $300 a quarter and a needy senior living in a 2-room flat receiving $750 a quarter are already means-tested to be facing low household support, with a monthly income per person in the household of not more than $1,100.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One may be living in a bigger flat, but they are facing the same financial difficulties of meeting their everyday needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The 5-room flat is a long-term asset and cannot be simply unlocked to support their everyday needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How is the size of the HDB flat related to the provision of household support to the elderly poor?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our seniors are now living longer, fruitful lives and receiving better healthcare.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While women are living longer than men, women are also facing more downsides in health security than men.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Senior women spend more years in disability than men, and women are two-and-a-half times more likely than men to report difficulties in carrying out typical activities of daily living.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Senior women are also more prone to suffering from dementia and higher rates of depression, which are more home-bound diseases that compound the caregiving burdens faced by female family members.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The concern is that women are caught up in an inter-generational vicious circle of caregiving and deterioration of mental well-being.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need a more targeted approach to tackle dementia and mental well-being among seniors and the general population at the national level.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Gender budgeting involves analysing the Government’s annual Budget and programmes for their different impact on men and women, and then adjusting allocations and programme details to promote gender equality.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I especially like the part on targeting benefits at those in need.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To promote gender equality is thus to be strategic and integrated, as this Budget seeks to be.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I wish to state right here that I fully support this year's Budget.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Fifty-three years on, our challenges are now different.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Our education system prepares students for PMET jobs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The rising impact of disruption caused by changing business models, technology and global competition has significantly increased our risk of job obsolescence or, as some people call it ,"jobsolescence", as well as job loss.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: General wage levels have risen but there is a need to continue efforts to transform low-wage industries for better earnings and prospects.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: For Singapore as a whole and for the Labour Movement, these changes and realities will dictate our priorities as we continue to pursue our mission to care for our population and to care and value all working persons.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: For the Labour Movement, we continue to want to work closely with the Government and employers to develop that better future for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: To that point, there are three key priority areas where the Labour Movement could help Singapore and Singaporeans do better.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: First, in the area of "High Age", and this is shorthand for the unavoidable ageing of our local workforce and its implications.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Over the past several years, dedicated efforts by the Tripartite Partners have brought about hard-earned tangible improvement in the terms of work for lower wage workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The road ahead remains long and arduous, as structural improvements require sustained transformation of mindsets, skills, technology and procurement practices on the part of employers, service buyers, workers and regulators.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Just because a growing proportion of the workforce comprises PMET jobs does not mean that every PMET employee is secure in his job.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: With changing technology alone, for example, artificial intelligence (AI), Internet of Things (IoT), Manufacturing 4.0, Robotics and others, many longstanding routine PMET jobs will be redesigned or may be rendered redundant and be replaced by new roles and requirements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Add to that the continuing pressure to de-layer and flatten organisations and to outsource jobs and functions to more cost-competitive countries, we can see the need to help not only today's unemployed find jobs, but also to help those who may be more at risk of becoming "tomorrow's unemployed" manage their risks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This will entail proactive Tripartite partnerships to spur transformation at the industry, company and job levels and to improve the conditions for prompt and seamless skills upgrading and conversion to take advantage of new income opportunities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: It would also include enhancements to job-matching and job-switching machinery for both traditional and emerging ways to earn a living, as well as the corresponding safety nets to help the displaced find their feet again quickly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Labour Member of Parliament, Mr Desmond Choo, will speak of the value that youth will bring to our nation and share how the NTUC is reaching out to them even before they join the workforce.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Touching on the issue concerning the "Double Middle" group, that is, middle-income and middle-age, and wherein there is a growing number of PMETs, my fellow Member of Parliament, Mr Patrick Tay, will share how we must value every such worker and how to keep them relevant.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Labour Nominated Member of Parliament, Ms Thanaletchimi, will call on all to value the family behind every worker, particularly for women, who often have to juggle between work and family commitments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: With the rise of the gig economy, Labour Member of Parliament, Mr Ang Hin Kee, will remind us not to underestimate the value that freelancers and the self-employed bring to our economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: While fellow Labour Members of Parliament have touched on various worker groups, my Labour Member of Parliament colleague, Mr Zainal Sapari, will put the emphasis on the low-wage workers, whose contributions we must continue to value.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: As we all spend our time at the workplace, Labour Member of Parliament, Mr Melvin Yong, will speak on the value of the life of every worker and how we can render every workplace safer and healthier.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: In years to come, there will be more citizens above 65 than there are those below 15.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Well, that means that Singapore may be headed for a triple whammy, if we are not careful.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: First, there will be the peaking of the citizen workforce around 2020 and thereafter plateau and then decline.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
