text: Second, the shrinking citizen workforce and loss of relevant experience through retirement of older workers will impact the ability of companies to operate optimally, unless, of course, they are able to raise productivity or, perhaps, if they could increase the proportion of foreign manpower in their workforce, or profitably and sustainably retain the services of mature workers longer.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The constraint on company growth will, in turn, lead to lower-than-potential corporate tax contributions to Government revenues.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The third one, the growing senior segment of the population, will lead to more social spending and support in healthcare and welfare, especially if structural unemployment or downward pressure on the income among seniors increases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The combination of these three factors will mean that the shrinking working population and companies will shoulder an increasingly heavier tax burden to support the reducing tax contribution from the senior population as they leave employment and as they incur higher living expenses linked to ageing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: In short, the earlier the older segment of our population ceases to be able to contribute economically, the earlier and more painful we can expect the tax increases that the working population and companies would have to bear in support.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The raising of re-employment age to 67 actually was contained in the recommendations of the Tripartite Committee on the Extension of the Retirement Age back in July 1997.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: It is very important but not something easy to do and it took us 20 years to move to 67.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Going forward, the question is what do we do and whether this broad tactic of prolonging employment across the board by law is going to be as doable as in the past 20 years or would it face additional challenges.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: That said, investments in the use of assistive technology and age-universal process and job design and redesign must continue relentlessly, so that we are able to compensate for the physical declines of the workforce to the greatest extent possible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And in this, schemes like WorkPro should continue and be refined to produce more substantive and pervasive outcomes wherever such opportunities exist so that we maximise this benefit.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Hitherto, technology was used mainly to improve efficiency of work processes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Today, technology goes beyond that to drive Business Model revamps.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: What this means is that a person’s job may change or disappear much faster than before, not only because his company is not doing well, but because entire occupations, organisational layers and how value is created, delivered and captured in an industry may fundamentally change.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: A person displaced for this reason will have a hard time finding a similar job because the job category itself may be fading.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: While this scenario may confront a worker of any age, the average older working person may face more and higher hurdles in the adaptation and switching process, on top of ageist attitudes among some employers, and may be displaced out of the workforce long before reaching the re-employment age.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: With such pervasive technology, rapid digitalisation and changing business models, how can companies stay competitive while tapping on mature workers who bring value, insights and experience to the table?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Could we try harder in making the workplace more conducive for mature workers to contribute?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: How about training them to be more digitally aware and technologically competent, placing them in growth sectors?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: When we travel to another country with a different plug and socket design for their appliances, we all know that it would be very troublesome if our appliance does not have the right plug design.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Even if the appliance itself is functioning well, you cannot use it because you cannot connect to the power source.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: That is why we find the multi-adaptor plug so useful on trips.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We also know that if we go to a country whose language we do not know, we will encounter many difficulties even to get very basic things done or to have ourselves understood.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Conversely, if we understand and speak the language, we will be as a duck takes to water.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I say this as an analogy for the employment and employability of working people of all ages because, increasingly, it will be like becoming a multi-adaptor plug and being able to understand and use the language of a place.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Workers who can learn and adapt repeatedly in their working lifespans will last longer and earn better, whilst those who cannot or will not do so will face increasing difficulties in employment and re-employment, regardless of whatever law you pass or wage subsidies that the Government may put in.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: In this rapidly changing world of work, skills requirements change quickly with the flux of competitive business models, technology and innovation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Old areas of the economy fade away even as new opportunities emerge.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Some growing job areas would be brought about by this very ageing of the population, such as in personal support services, healthcare and eldercare.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: That is why working persons must keep up with the changing requirements or else find themselves of the "wrong plug design" and become powerless.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Businesses and Industry Associations must take the lead, with the support of the Government and the Labour Movement, and to do this without delay.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Here, I want to remind everyone not to unconsciously fall into the mind trap of thinking that industry transformation involves only the younger working population or only the local population.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: A chain is only as strong as its weakest link.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: A company’s workforce is typically both young and mature, both local and foreign.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: If a company or industry focuses transformation only on one part of its workforce and neglects or dismisses the other parts, it is, actually, short-changing itself.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: If Singapore, therefore, neglects the segment of its workforce that is growing the fastest – and here, for the local workforce, that is the mature segment – then it is downright counter-productive for these reasons that I have discussed earlier.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: From the perspective of the company, it would be both sacrificing its own potential capability as well as practically inviting higher corporate tax burdens on itself sooner.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This includes how the implementation of the Industry Transformation Maps must include the upgrading of mature workers and the speeding up of progress toward more age-universal workplaces.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I further call for a special focus on confidence building for mature workers in digital awareness and competencies in working with robotics and in using data smartly to finesse the supply of and demand for goods and services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This is the new language in the world of work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We should proactively and aggressively promote their learning and use, just as we had in promoting basic literacy and numeracy through BEST and WISE courses, and IT confidence through the National IT Literacy Programme (NITLP) in years past.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Facility and adeptness are not innate attributes or in-born.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: These are growing areas of job opportunities and they also allow our mature workers actually to play to their strengths.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The NTUC and Labour Movement stand ready to actively partner and support the Government and the business community in all these areas to build this critical dynamic employability in our older working persons.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And we will do that with our network of unions, social enterprises and U-Associate partners.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The better we are at pursuing these objectives, the more we will avert that triple-whammy I described and, in fact, turn adversity into advantage and a concern into strength.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: A better future is possible, but it never comes from just hoping for the best.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: That future must be invested in, slogged for and cherished together.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Time is ticking away and the consequences of our actions or lack of actions will become clearer by the day and month.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We must succeed so that our mature workers and citizens' future in Singapore will remain one of hope and promise.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Critical to this transformation are the social and career foundations that we are putting in place for the workforce.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I will touch on how we can strengthen our social and career foundations further to help Singaporeans, especially younger Singaporean workers and families, to prepare for the changes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Ever more rapid technological disruptions will continue to fundamentally change how work is done.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Singapore's limited resources meant that we have ever narrower margins of error to prepare ourselves for the new economy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our workforce, especially the workers of the future, must be able to take on future challenges quickly and adroitly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Ideally, employers and employees are aligned in the ITMs and work towards redesigning jobs for the future, promote innovation and seek and seize opportunities to go international, where possible.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Because this transformation requires fundamental structural changes, ITMs will, understandably, take time to be pervasive.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Two recent surveys done, one on businesses and another on students at the Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) hinted that we need to intensify our transformation efforts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, many training programmes require time away from work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But in a tight labour market, workers are prioritised for operational purposes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The schemes announced in the Budget, such as Productivity Solutions Grant, will go in some way to aid companies to innovate and build deeper capabilities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, there is still a missing link of a last mile connection of turning transformation plans into transformative actions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our future workers might also need to be primed for the transformation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our younger Singaporeans are the future of Singapore’s workforce.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They need to be part of this transformation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Out of the 17% who said they have heard about ITMs, the level of understanding about them was only 6.5, out of a scale of one to 10, whereby 10 denotes that they fully understand the information.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It meant that, for most students, the industry that they are studying hard for would have changed in no small measure by the time they graduated.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But they would not know this until they have entered the workforce.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Students in the IHLs who are poised to enter various industries need to understand these plans so that they can gear up for the changes in the sectors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While the roll-out of ITMs is not yet complete, the communication of the ITMs need to be stepped up so that businesses, workers and students are plugged into the plans and development within their sectors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In both cases – for businesses and students – there is a "last mile gap" in connecting available schemes with the target groups and stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I would suggest that the Labour Movement could play a bigger role in bridging the gap for both businesses and students.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Recently, I visited the workers from the SATS Workers' Union (SATSWU) at their workplaces at the airport.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They proudly showed me the new technologies, such as automated check-in and bag-drop.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They could now attend to more passengers and guide them – adding value where they previously could not.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There were important developments that would improve workers’ productivity and allow workers to work for longer in better jobs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: So, I asked, "How is this possible?" They shared that because the industry changes were shared in advance, gaps were identified early and their skillsets were identified in advance.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: SATSWU also worked with the company to train its workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, it was also noted that the operations also depended in part on sub-contractors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The passenger experience was dependent on the capabilities of these smaller companies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These smaller companies might lack the resources to train their workers and undertake productivity initiatives.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Labour Movement can coordinate with these companies and their bigger unionised counterparts on training needs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Then, the training modules can be placed on board NTUC’s ULEAP bite-sized training platforms, so that workers can be trained without significant downtime.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Before I left the airport, I asked the workers, "Can we continue to do better?" They shared with me and said, "Of course, we can.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Transformation is not new to us, changes at the airport are constant.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As long as workers are involved early, productivity gains are shared, workers' value are unleashed to take advantage of transformation and workers' energies and ideas to make airport processes better".

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For students, ITMs must be made accessible to them so that students can understand the key thrusts of our economic transformation for their desired industry or profession.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: NTUC, through its youth wing, can help the students navigate the ITMs through industry tie-ups and youth career networks.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The latter peer-to-peer systems are more accessible and less top-down.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is shared from an industry peer to another student.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Information is personalised, curated and more readily accepted by our millennials and younger generation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This would then give SMEs greater access to young talent.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The changes brought about by our economic transformation will require workers to be nimble and ready to take on new challenges.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Thus, our social system must also be enhanced.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: More social support should be given to our workers to balance their work and home responsibilities better.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Young parents, for example, would require more support in the new economy as they can be considered as "double sandwiched" – middle-income and also having to take care of young children and older parents.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As Singaporeans are marrying later, families are getting smaller and people have longer life expectancy, the responsibility of taking care of both young and older parents can converge at such a point in a young couple's life and for a prolonged period.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I am confident that as long as the Tripartite Partners work together, we can tackle the challenges and successfully transform our economy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We plug the gaps, we gear up our workers and students for these challenges and we provide greater support for them and their families.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Together, we can create a better future for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: If you ask me how I would describe this year's Budget, I would say it is a Budget with its "Feet on the ground, hand on the heart and eyes to the future”. "Feet on the ground" because we ground ourselves on solid footing and fundamentals.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We ensure our businesses and enterprises do well, so that our workers benefit through better jobs and pay, and stay employed and employable. "Hand on the heart" because of it having the courage to confront the difficult fiscal challenges, share the fruits and to ensure no one is left behind. "Eyes to the future" because of the clarity of focus to build our country, the curiosity to test new ideas and innovations and the conviction to stay the course and prepare for the future.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I am worried for a group of workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: My fellow Labour Member of Parliament, Senior Minister of State Heng Chee How mentioned it earlier – it is the double-middle group.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: They are our Professionals, Managers and Executives (PMEs) or what we often call the "sandwiched class".

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The latest labour market report, as well as the labour market trends, do not auger well for them.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Structural unemployment, under-employment and unemployment are three challenges which confront our workers in Singapore, especially PMEs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The three "Ds" – Digitalisation, Disruption and Demographics will transform or make redundant traditional jobs, while creating new specialised jobs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In the new normal, skills acquisition will have to increase in frequency, while working people will progressively experience more transitions in their employment life-cycles.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: A working person may be in a multi-national corporation today, a small and medium enterprise tomorrow, and possibly opt to freelance in the near future.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The future of work, workers and workplaces will transform.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In the Labour Movement, we value every worker and we are, therefore, concerned about employment and employability of all, especially the PMEs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: There was no longer a need for bank tellers, greeters, cash officers and service bankers in the branches.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In their place were 130 multi-skilled, universal service bankers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Job roles requiring a single skill were eliminated.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The new job role consolidated adjacent skills and role requirements into one role.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In two years' time, the Universal Service Bankers' role will also evolve and may also not exist as more digitisation and digitalisation are adopted.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Sales jobs have also been impacted as people prefer to procure services via the Internet or through mobile apps.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: For example, chatbots are likely to eliminate telephone marketing and support jobs as people prefer not to wait to talk to a person when they have a query; they want to have their query keyed in online and receive an immediate response in their digital environment of choice, for example, in Facebook.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In the accountancy sector, the traditional maker and checker roles to assess compliance in assurance, audit and tax will be transformed.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: With adoption of technology, the process of consolidating and making sense of information will be made easier.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Employees will need to possess broader skills in areas of understanding technology.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: An example is a Tax Technologist who must also understand fraud detection systems.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The audit role has to shift to one which helps the client to manage the risk and compliance issues of the business.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: If it is of any relief, many jobs will continue to require uniquely human skills that artificial intelligence and machines cannot replicate, such as creativity, collaboration, abstract and systems thinking, complex communication and the ability to work in diverse environments.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The companies that fare best in this new disruptive era will be those that embrace these changes rapidly and effectively.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Put simply, new jobs and economic growth will accrue to those who embrace technology, not those who resist it.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: At risk of not becoming acquired fast enough?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We need to not just skill our workers to be great at their jobs today but also skilled so as to be prepared for the jobs of tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Our working people typically take about 15 years to prepare themselves for their first job with the expectation to progress to more challenging and better paying jobs thereafter.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Paradoxically, people generally spend less time and effort to prepare and upskill themselves for their next job.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Given the time pressures, financial and family commitments, it would not be practical to set aside another 15 years to upskill working people for their next job.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The adult learning model thus has to be reworked to enable working people to upskill and remain marketable and relevant and enhance their opportunities for career progression.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We need to re-tool at a faster rate.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: That is why, in NTUC, we are reworking the entire adult learning model.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We want to develop modules which are bite-sized and just-in-time for continuous learning.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The speed of demand for new skills is faster than the speed of supply of new skills.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: For every company which has lost out in the digital race, such as Kodak and Borders, there are new companies which are flourishing, such as Carousell and Airbnb.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: There is a need to make available bite-sized and just-in-time training so that our working people can keep abreast of the latest developments in their work domains.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: For example, a cybersecurity practitioner needs to keep up with the latest cybersecurity threats and such training should be delivered within 24 hours through bite-sized two-to three-minute updates on-the-go.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In the same manner, a safety professional in the construction industry would need to keep abreast of industrial accidents so that they can learn quickly from them and apply the learning at their workplaces.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This is a challenge that the world is facing and if Singapore gets this right, our workers can be one step ahead.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The traditional mode of curriculum development in Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) is a long one.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: IHLs have to take time to figure out the market demand, design the curriculum and mobilise workers to be trained.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: To shorten the development phase, the way forward is to work with companies to design bespoke training to be conducted in-company to upskill their workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This can shorten the development phase of training substantially as the company knows what skills it wants its workers to be trained in and can mobilise the workers to take up the training.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The need to continually upskill applies to both employees and freelancers – all working people should take personal responsibility to prepare and upskill in relevant areas for future jobs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It is imperative that freelancers take on the responsibility to keep their skillsets relevant, too.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Increasingly, it is not just a question of encouraging people to learn new skills, but of finding new ways to help them acquire the skills they will need.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In this respect, I have three suggestions on what employers and employees need to do.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I call it the three Cs ─ Change Mindsets, Communicate and Collaborate.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Employers tend to fear that the benefits of investing in training are lost when employees leave.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Instead of viewing training as a short-term cost, employee development should be regarded as a long-term investment that allows staff to add value to their roles and take up expanded job scopes.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The better employees become at their jobs, the easier it is for organisations to attain the level of productivity projected.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Employers, when hiring, need to do skills-based interviews to assess skills, experiences and fit with organisation's culture and values and not just look at paper qualifications and age.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Be open to hiring mature and older workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Our Labour Movement's recent research reveal that employers prefer to hire skilled, trained and experienced staff instead of training their existing staff for these new jobs or hiring someone untrained and train him up.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In short, they want "plug and play" employees.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We have a tight labour market and an ageing workforce.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Employers will find it tough to find the perfect match.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I, therefore, urge employers to change their mindsets on "plug and play" and adopt a "hire then train" approach.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Lastly, the responsibility for skills development and acquisition does not reside solely with the employer nor the Government.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Individuals must have a learning mindset in the course of their careers so as to remain able, agile and adaptable.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We need to bring people together sector by sector to collaborate, transform our companies and then take proactive and concrete steps to train, re-skill and up-skill employees to match the in-demand skills and competencies.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Besides our Tripartite Partners, the Labour Movement has started working with industry partners, training providers and IHL, for example, the Labour Movement’s Multi-Union, Multi-U Associate alliance to uplift standards and improve the employability of workers in the OPEC industries by uplifting standards of process technicians and engineers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: By doing so, this will create accreditation of the process technicians' trade and raise the standards whilst boosting transferability of their skillsets.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The Labour Movement is also partnering the Institute of Engineers, Singapore, to raise engineering and technical competencies in the profession.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: More importantly, the Industry Transformation Maps must be operationalised to benefit the workers on the ground, and stakeholders must join hands to make this happen.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In this rapidly changing landscape, transformation is critical and requires strong partnerships between unions, our working people, enterprises, education and training providers, professional guilds and the Government to enable meaningful and mutually-reinforcing transformation for the benefit of all stakeholders and our economy.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It is important to align all stakeholders and identify what the future jobs and skills are and communicate effectively to all.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Besides just looking at job losses and gains, concerted action needs to be taken to identify jobs at-risk of displacement.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This is what I urge every sector and every company to do.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: To proactively and pre-emptively identify the jobs at risk in their organisations and help their employees, our working people, to stay Ready, Relevant and Resilient – Ready with the new skills, Relevant for the new jobs and also Resilient to the new changes.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Our workforce has to be Able and equipped with the skills to take on these new jobs, Agile to move across sectors and Adaptable to change.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This reminds me of the Wallet Ninja, I have it here.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It is a multi-purpose pocket multi-tool, it reminds me of the importance of multi-skilling and making our skills work for us in a variety of scenarios and conditions as and when the situation and need arises.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It is also made of four times' treated steel, to remind us to steel ourselves for changes ahead.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Putting our hand on heart and communicating the jobs and skills at risk.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Focusing our eyes on the future by helping the unemployed land into future jobs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We can never change the direction of the wind but we can adjust our sails to always reach the destination.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Before I end my speech, I wanted to respond to what hon Member Assoc Prof Daniel Goh spoke on earlier.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: He spoke about the future of women, plight of nurses, caregivers and seniors.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: He suggested we spend more and more to help them.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I was Executive Secretary and Advisor of the Healthcare Service Union since 2006, more than a decade ago.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In fact, we have set up a Tripartite Committee and they have been looking at this issue for the past decade, working very closely with the major employers, including MOH, in particular, looking at how we can upskill and raise the career prospects to attract more into this sector where we are in need of workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: So, it is not right to say that their futures and their careers have not been looked after, or neglected.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Since a decade ago, from job redesign, then to a one-race to the top, and then now to the Industry Transformation Maps, we have been working very closely with Tripartite Partners, we have made significant headway.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: If you speak to any healthcare worker in the public healthcare institutions, they can share with you some of the initiatives and programmes that they have done and embarked very tenaciously on.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In Singapore, more than two decades ago, we have adopted, at a Tripartite level, a very flexible wage system and a competency-based hiring and progression structure and framework.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Therefore, I am surprised to hear that, with these structures and systems in place, some people are short-changed.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Yes, maybe perhaps there may be some form of discrimination here and there in small pockets.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: He has made many suggestions on increasing our country's spending but did not really talk about where the money should come from and whether it will be sustainable.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I think that is something very important ‒ it must be sustainable.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It is this very reason that we want to ensure our healthcare workers are looked after and our healthcare costs are managed that we have this year's Budget.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We are concerned and we do not want anyone ‒ whether young or old, male or female ‒ to be left behind.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This Budget 2018 is very imperative and its focus is to help each and every one of our Singaporeans navigate a path and be future-ready, and to build up our resources and stay focused.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I am heartened that the Budget is all-inclusive and it embraces both the short-term and long-term needs of Singapore.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: On operationalising Industry Transformation Maps in our journey of economic transformation, I agree that the approach of Industry Transformation Maps (ITMs) for the 23 industries was a good start.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: We need to work on the strategies to operationalise them.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The ITMs were a product of Tripartite efforts and should be treated beyond a paper exercise.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: All relevant stakeholders should continue to come together and implement the ideas on the ITMs.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The Singapore healthcare system is confronted with an ageing population with increasing chronic conditions, coupled with a slower workforce growth and rising healthcare costs.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Minister Gan presented three "beyonds", that is, beyond healthcare to health, beyond hospital to community and beyond quality to value to ensure our healthcare system meets the three core objectives of accessibility, quality and affordability.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The future directions for the healthcare industry have been put forward clearly in the ITM.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, it is important to operationalise the ideas effectively.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I shall now speak on national skills framework.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: First and foremost, there is a need to develop a national skills framework for current skills in demand and future skills.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: We should continue to look at other healthcare professions, such as Therapy Assistant and Community Nurse, in view of the shift towards community care.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: We should also consider other job positions in the administrative job group to ensure that the relevant skills and training are mapped out for their career progression.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: There is fear amongst administrative and ancillary staff group, like the health attendants, that, with automation and robotics, will their job be redundant.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: PWM will help to increase wages of healthcare employees through skills upgrading and productivity improvement.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Another way would be to gradually move away from only recognising academic qualification to purely skill-based remuneration to break the glass ceiling.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, the shift towards modularised training is highly recommended.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The Institutes of Higher Learning (IHL) should develop such modules to deepen the skills of healthcare employees.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In return, the healthcare institutions, both public and private, should embrace and recognise these skills attained by the employees and remunerate them accordingly.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: These are the secretaries for the clinical department in the hospitals.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: They have no room for growth or career advancement unless they obtain higher academic qualifications, that is, diploma or degree.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This should not be the case if we truly embark on skills-based PWM and elimination of the glass ceiling.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Next, it is also crucial to identify jobs at risk and work out feasible plans for affected employees to ensure smooth transition of employees from existing jobs to new jobs by engaging MOH, public healthcare clusters and various healthcare institutions.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: For example, the jobs in medical records departments in various healthcare institutions would be replaced by National Electronic Health Record (NEHR).

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Essentially, we need to engage the relevant stakeholders early to minimise disruption to employees’ livelihood.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: While we look at existing jobs at risk, it is equally important to identify future jobs to work out the skills and training required.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, other support schemes, such as the Professional Conversion Programmes (PCPs), Career Support Programme and Work or Career Trial, would supplement the existing efforts in attracting local talents into the growing manpower demand in the healthcare industry.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: We need to find ways to shorten the PCP programmes and improve the quality and standards of healthcare professionals, especially for career switchers.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In this aspect, we need to draw in the expertise and wisdom of the professional licensing body.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: With the shift to community nursing and the focus on the Intermediate and Long-Term Care (ILTC) sector, we will need more nurses with the relevant skillsets and attributes.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: First, provide opportunity for workers in other industries who are potentially in danger of retrenchment or whose industries are in the sunset industry.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Work with the relevant stakeholders, licensing body, IHL and professional group to review the current training programme and provide them with bite-sized curriculum.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Two, invite non-practising nurses to return to nursing, especially in community nursing and the ILTC sector.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Provide them with the specific skillsets required for community nursing and allow flexible work arrangements.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Though the return-to-work programme has been fairly successful in healthcare, we can tweak it to make it more attractive for such groups of non-practising nurses who are mainly housewives.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Third, tap the mature workforce to create supporting roles, such as healthcare assistants or healthcare attendants.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Provide training for them so they have the relevant skills.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: These are decent jobs that will allow our mature workers to join the healthcare sector.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Last but not least, I would like to put forward the idea of setting up a Healthcare Academy at the Tripartite level with the participation of relevant stakeholders.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I mooted this suggestion at the last Budget debate.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The verticals of the skillset training must be seen in parallel with the horizontals of the soft skillset.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This is all the more important as we are seeing an increasing number of healthcare professionals bringing healthcare services to patients at home.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: As the home setting is an uncontrolled environment compared to a controlled hospital setting, we need to equip our healthcare professionals with the relevant skills to deal with unforeseen situations and in managing their emotional and mental well-being.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: As a society, we embrace inclusivity and, as corporations, we should embrace corporate social responsibility where human capital, regardless of gender, has to be nurtured and retained.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I concur with Labour Member Desmond Choo that more can be done to help our young parents thrive in the new economy.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It is particularly challenging for women who often have to juggle work and family commitments.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I will be speaking mainly on family-friendly workplaces and the employment and employability of women.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The topic on family-friendly workplace has been a discussion point without much yield.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The slow adoption of the Tripartite Standards on Flexi-work Arrangement is rather concerning.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore remains a rather conservative country when it comes to caring for and valuing the family that is behind every worker.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The burden of caring for the young and elderly often fall on the shoulders of women.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Companies in various sectors can do more to help female workers.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The relationship with her Reporting Officer (RO) became strained after her RO refused to grant her flexible work arrangement as she could not find any person to take up parts of her duties.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: She related her experience to the union but decided not to take it up with the human resource department as she did not want to cause any trouble.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: (In Tamil):   At this juncture, I would like to share a case of a nurse whom I know working in a healthcare setting who had to give up her job because she was not granted flexible work arrangements as she had to look after her children.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The relationship with her employer became bitter after her reporting officer refused to grant her flexible work arrangements as she could not find any other nurse to take up part of her duties.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: She related her experience to the union but decided not to take it up with the higher-ups as she did not want to cause any trouble.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: (In English): Similarly, another female staff, who devoted most of her working life to one employer had requested for flexible work arrangements as she has to look after her school-going children and ailing mother-in-law.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: She, too, had had her request turned down.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: While the top management of most companies are supportive of flexible work arrangements in principle, however, it does not seem that such support trickles down to every level within the organisation.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Departments and supervisors do not know exactly how to implement flexible work arrangements successfully.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: They have KPIs to meet and, therefore, tend to take a hard stand with such requests.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In both cases, they typically involve women who are burdened and who are financially strapped.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: These women will need support throughout their lifetime if they are not working or fall out of employment for such reasons.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I agree there must be progressive efforts made to create awareness.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: There is also a pressing need for sharing best practices in a more pervasive manner.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, we must change before more women at child-bearing age fall out of employment.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This will surely pose social problems as our population ages.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: A young mother, whose child was admitted to hospital due to several bouts of epileptic attacks, had to take leave to care for her child.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Her supervisor was unhappy that she took too many days of leave to care for her sick child.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The young mother needed her job so that she could continue to support her family and her child’s medical expenses.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: She approached the union for help and managed to settle the issue amicably with the union’s intervention.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This brings me to my point about Government mandating caregiving leave.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Not many employers are adopting such good practices where staff feel cared for and, in return, employers will get 100% loyalty and support from the staff when the company needs them during dire situations without counting hours worked.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Generally, the behaviour of many staff will fall into the category of “good deeds beget good deeds”.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: As a developed country, while we are concerned about economic growth, it should not be at the expense of social needs.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: About 50% of our population are women and, increasingly, men, too, are embracing caregiving roles.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It is, hence, essential for the Government to look at this from a broader viewpoint.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The third issue which I would like to raise specifically for women is to mandate the allocation of lactation room in all new commercial buildings as well as industrial workplaces where offices are located.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Government consider calling on owners of the buildings to set aside a certain percentage of the gross floor area for lactation rooms, with some incentives given?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: For existing buildings, we should evaluate the possibility of creating space for this purpose.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: With lactation rooms, we are promoting breastfeeding and, inadvertently, branding the workplace as a baby-friendly workplace.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: We need the Government’s support in this area.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: (In Malay):   The third issue which I would like to raise specifically for women is to mandate the allocation of lactation rooms in all new commercial buildings, as well as industrial workplaces where offices are located.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Government consider calling on owners of the buildings to set aside a certain percentage of the gross floor area for a lactation room, as well as offering some incentives to building owners?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: For existing buildings, we should evaluate and identify the possibility of creating a space for this purpose.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: By having lactation rooms, we are promoting the benefits of breastfeeding and, at the same time, branding such workplaces as workplaces that are conducive for female workers who are mothers with babies or infants.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: We need the Government’s support on this issue.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The rate of gestational diabetes mellitus in Singapore is among the highest in the world.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Mothers with this condition are also seven times more likely to develop Type-2 diabetes.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: However, a longer period of breastfeeding showed a correlation with a reduction in the risk of women developing Type-2 diabetes.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: (In English): We need companies to understand this.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Studies have shown that a mother should breast feed her infant for the first six months and up to two years of the child's life for the benefit of the child and mother.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: With four months of maternity leave, mothers tend to give up breastfeeding and switch to baby formula because of the lack of lactation rooms at the workplace.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Office building owners, which have not used up the permissible gross floor area will be able to tap on the funding to put in place the facilities.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Can we do more to increase the take-up rate?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Let us make Singapore a socially responsible society at all levels.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: On women in the STEM or Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics industry.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, the employment and employability of women, especially in the STEM industry is a major concern.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: With a shrinking workforce, the reliance on women to set foot in all industries becomes dire.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I certainly would like to believe that there is no gender-specific or gender-biased industry at present in Singapore but more so the preference of women to be working in certain specific sectors.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I urge the Government to do more to nurture the next generation of female students to be well-geared in STEM subjects and, at a later age, join the STEM industry.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: We must do all we can to change the mindset of parents, employers and workers.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: There is a growing need to grow the workforce in the STEM sector as future jobs are more likely to be generated in this sector.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: While we embark on the Return-to-Work (RTW) Programme, especially for mature women, we need to be more targeted.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Mentors are of great help in those identified professions as they can handhold the individual, providing them with confidence and assurance.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: There should be a longer work trial period for complex jobs.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I hope the Government can do more for the Return-to-Work Programme so that it can be more pervasive.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Let us embrace and employ "different strokes for different folks".

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Indeed, among the 200,000 self-employed persons or freelancers, many operate by using new technologies that either disrupted traditional businesses or created new markets.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this last category, the workers may be deployed as freelancers at the workplace and not counted as the company's headcount.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, they report for work and comply with the company's guidelines which are no different from salaried employees.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These companies may have infringed the Employment Act and should be flagged out to MOM for investigations.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In fact, all allegations, including possible tax evasions by freelancers who under-declare income, should be made to the relevant authorities.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is the only responsible way of ensuring that the issues are properly dealt with.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should do all we can not to wedge a divide as to which self-employed file tax properly and who under-declare their income.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For hardworking cabbies, I hope we do not undermine their integrity by making unfounded, sweeping statements that they under-declare income or may have under-declared their income.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On the contrary, Mr Speaker, Sir, we have been working with IRAS very closely to ensure that volunteer groups come into the taxi community to explain to the drivers how to file income tax returns and to do them properly.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Fortunately, the majority of our self-employed persons ensure that they do the responsible thing and, in fact, we are glad that the majority of self-employed persons are in their preferred occupation.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Day to day, they face new platform intermediaries, such as Grab, IO Talents, Caregivers Asia, that are transforming the way businesses are run, making matching of services hassle-free.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: More consumers and self-employed persons now go to a common platform to find each other.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, whether you need a cleaning service, photography service or chauffeured ride service.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Consumers now have easier access and more choices when it comes to selecting services.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some, however, do so voluntarily, contributing to the self-employed persons’ MediSave account or even providing insurance cover.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Instead, they can easily remove freelancers from their platforms, have huge control over payment and work arrangements, and freely set their own commission rates.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Their impact will be more significant, now that the number of gig workers using such platforms may be increasing.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, before penalising or removing self-employed workers due to the fact that they receive poor service ratings from their customers, has there been enough thorough checks done to ensure that those allegations are properly investigated?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some freelancers shared with me that they are affected by delayed payment, unexpected cuts to the fees or the rates and changes in incentive payment at the last minute, without giving them due recognition and information ahead of time.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: New technologies do bring dynamism to our economy.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But with only vague and non-transparent guidelines, freelancers using such platforms are potentially at risk.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As these intermediaries gain bigger market share, they also grow in power and, if left unchecked, they can dictate tougher terms over the self-employed persons and even consumers who use their platforms.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope to see more being done to support our self-employed persons.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A case in point is the Tripartite Standard on the procurement of services from media freelancers that was launched in November last year.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This was jointly developed by Info-communications Media Development Authority with NTUC and stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is an industry-specific Tripartite Standard that addresses the concerns of media freelancers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Back in 2014, LTA, together with the National Taxi Association and taxi operators, also set up a mediation system to allow taxi drivers to resolve payment disputes with their taxi operators.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: MOM also commissioned a survey on self-employed persons in 2016 to gather more information and understand their concerns.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have recently submitted our recommendations to the Minister and we look forward to more specific support and targeted assistance for self-employed persons.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I will share more during the Committee of Supply when we debate on the MOM budget.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Budget 2018 is a Budget that prepares us for the future.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should not underestimate the value that self-employed persons bring to the economy.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope the support for self-employed persons can be widely adopted to help them sustain their career choice and thrive in this new economy.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With that, Mr Speaker, I support the Budget.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: My fellow Labour Members of Parliament have touched on various worker groups but we must not forget our more vulnerable low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One of the core missions of every labour movement anywhere in the world is to look after its workers, particularly the more vulnerable workers in its midst.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is also a responsibility that our Government shoulders and commits to this mission in order to improve the livelihood of our people.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Low-wage workers will always be part of our labour landscape.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Not by design but because there will always be those who form the lower tier in the income hierarchy.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: More importantly, the work they do forms an important part of our social fabric and contributes to our economy.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Their struggles, hopes and aspirations give us reason to be their voice to pave a better future for them.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, for our Labour Movement, the Budget presents an opportunity for us to do good, do more and do right by them.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Indeed, I believe that with everyone's help – Government, union and employers – low-wage workers can have a sense of hope that their lives will be better year after year and, more importantly, that the future for their families and themselves are that much brighter.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To date, the efforts of the Labour Movement to help low-wage workers have paid off with the strong support provided by the Government and our Tripartite Partners.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The long hours put in by policymakers, unions, companies and every one of us sitting here today have resulted in the implementation of many policies to better support and protect these workers’ wages and their employment rights.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We believe that PWM has also caused a ripple effect that has led to the increase in wages of low-wage workers in other sectors as well.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In fact, from 2012 to 2017, the wages of those in the 20th percentile have shown the largest increase.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This has, hopefully, eased the ever-increasing cost of living for these workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Other schemes implemented over the years, such as Workfare Income Supplement (WIS), have also gone a fairly long way in making life easier for these low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They have a better chance of bringing home higher salaries.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Under the Workfare Training Support Scheme, they also have better opportunities for upgrading their skills through available training programmes at heavily subsidised rates, giving them some confidence to be relevant to the workforce today.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Amendments to the Employment Act, such as requiring employers to issue pay slips and employment contracts, will go a long way to offer better protection to our vulnerable low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The road to improving the lives of low-wage workers cannot just end here.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The sad reality is that many of the current lowest paying jobs in our country are held by elderly workers with little education and limited skills.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: During our engagement with our union leaders to arrow in on the plight of low-wage workers, the issue of ensuring workers' retirement adequacy, especially for low-wage workers, stood out prominently.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Of all the suggestions given on retirement adequacy for low-wage workers, there were some prominent ones that I would like to put up for the Government's consideration.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Currently, the employer's CPF contribution rate decreases progressively after the worker reaches 55 years of age.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The different CPF contribution rates tagged to different age bands were introduced in 1988 with good intentions to ensure our companies could remain competitive.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, the assumption to rationalise why older workers should have reduced employer's CPF contribution rates may no longer be valid today.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many workers, regardless of their age, are already being paid based on the job value as we have moved away from a seniority-based wage structure.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Moreover, given longer life expectancy, workers need to build on their retirement savings.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This would help workers build their retirement savings and would be especially beneficial for elderly low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is also in our best interest to ensure that workers can meet their retirement sum as it would reduce the burden on social services in later years which would have to be shouldered by the current working population.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Such a review would no doubt add cost for the companies, but I believe that we need to move away from the 1988 policy which has indirectly created a class of "cheaper, older" labour.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Employers must value our mature workers as an important resource who can still contribute to their businesses, especially in this tight labour market.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many of us assume that all workers get the 13th-month bonus (AWS) at the end of the year.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But the sad reality is that the very group that needs it the most is not receiving it.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I believe this 8.3% increase in salary will bring back much more than its worth in monetary value when it comes to making our vulnerable low-wage workers feel a sense of fairness, recognition and appreciation for the work they do.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: After all, this nation was also built on the backs of these toiling workers who had also played their part to pave the way for a better future ‒ a future that we, today, enjoy.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Third, the union leaders felt that more can be done to help low-wage workers cope with medical cost.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While a clear majority or 86% of employers do offer outpatient benefits beyond the required statutory requirements on a voluntary basis, it is the low-wage workers who are being hurt the most by the limited coverage under the Employment Act.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Perhaps, the various Ministries may want to consider this as a leverage to incentivise companies to care more for their workers, particularly the low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am aware that the suggestions I am making may cause some pain not only to employers but also to us as final consumers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But, again, if there is no pain, there is no progress.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):   The rapidly changing current economic landscape and job situation can affect many workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am very concerned about the fate of low-wage workers who are mostly older and do not possess higher qualifications.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Although many training opportunities have been made available to help them upgrade their skills, it is essential that the training is suitable to their age group and learning capabilities.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Helping low-wage workers, by having employers pay for the costs of their outpatient treatment at polyclinics, can also relieve their burden.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): In conclusion, in the past and also very recently, I have written several blogs to highlight the bread-and-butter issues of low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I know that some of my entries might have caused some discomfort to some readers, particularly my most recent post entitled "Slavery of the poor".

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But there is nothing I would change about the message I intended to convey.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It was not a blog post I wanted people to scroll past, nor was it a post to exaggerate the struggles faced by these workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It was a post that echoes the sentiments of our low-wage and elderly outsourced workers who exist in our society.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must not fool ourselves to think that, as a society, we are doing enough in being fair to all our workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While there are policies in place today to help our low-wage workers, many of them are still being taken advantage of.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They struggle to make ends meet, let alone save for retirement, no matter how hard they work.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The stark realities faced by vulnerable workers do not have to persist year after year.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must have a bigger heart and mind to ease their livelihood.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must value their contributions and think more about them and less about us.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But while we continue in our quest to peer into the crystal ball and try to divine the future, we must not forget that the bedrock of our industries, present and future, are our workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: My fellow Labour Members of Parliament have, in turn, argued for the various initiatives that the Government should embark on to enable workers to take on the jobs of the future – low-wage workers, high-age workers, middle-income, middle-aged workers, PMEs, including freelancers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They have also highlighted the value that each of our workers brings to the table.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, we will need a fit and healthy workforce in order to be able to take on these jobs in the first place.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Singapore is suffering from two worrying trends that will continue to have a profound impact on our labour force.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A Business Times news report published late last year forecasted that 2018, this year, will see, for the first time in our history, the same percentage of those aged 65 years and above matching those younger than 15 years old.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Every worker is, therefore, a precious resource and we must value the life of each and every worker.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As many of us spend most of our waking hours at the workplace, we need to do more in terms of workplace safety and health to keep our precious resource safe and healthy.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is certainly encouraging to see that the sustained collective efforts by our Tripartite Partners to tackle workplace fatalities have borne some fruit.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, every death is a tragedy and every accident is preventable.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We must, and we should, do more to ensure that our workplaces are safer.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: One area that we can do better moving forward is to encourage better near-miss reporting, so that we can reduce the occurrence of accidents.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Does it mean that the dip in fatal accidents was simply down to luck?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A structured and well-participated near-miss reporting regime would help to better identify dangerous work conditions, and early interventions can help bring down the accident rate.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To make the next quantum leap in reducing workplace fatalities in the next decade, we will need bolder strategies to make Workplace Safety and Health (WSH) more pervasive in every workplace.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: During a recent Tripartite study visit to Finland, we learnt that Finland mandates that there must be one elected Occupational Safety and Health representative in workplaces where there are at least 10 employees working regularly.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This has helped Finland achieve a workplace fatality rate of below 1.0 per 100,000 workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Should Singapore, too, have a mandatory WSH officer in every company?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For a start, perhaps a more practical approach would be to make it compulsory for companies to appoint a WSH representative as part of the certification for BizSAFE Level 3.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There is, currently, no such provision for companies applying for BizSAFE Level 3.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For now, companies must appoint a Risk Management Champion (RMC) for BizSAFE Level 2.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With proper training, the role of these RMCs can be expanded to serve as WSH representatives.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While it is important to have preventive measures to mitigate workplace injuries, it is also equally important to help workers return to work in the unfortunate event of an accident at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is where we can do more to improve the Return-To-Work (RTW) Programme, which was recently started in November 2017.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The RTW grant is currently restricted to Small and Medium Enterprises.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To promote and deepen the RTW culture, the Government should consider extending the grant to large corporations, too.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In the event an injured worker requires a change of employer and work scope due to a workplace accident, the current RTW grant does not cover vocational rehabilitation.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
