text: The RTW grant should be extended to cover such cases.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And "Health", as the final letter in "WSH", often gets neglected.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Talks of occupational health issues, such as physical health and mental well-being, are often missing in our WSH conversations.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But as our workforce ages faster than before, we will most certainly see more workplace health issues in the next decade.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With many workers today doing desk-bound jobs and leading a sedentary lifestyle, it is important that we encourage regular exercise to prevent health problems, such as high cholesterol and high blood pressure, as we age.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Health Promotion Board (HPB) has a Healthy Workplace Ecosystem programme to encourage busy office workers to take part in physical activities and eat healthier options.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To date, there are 30 participating Healthy Workplace Ecosystems.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But more needs to be done to get more companies and employers on board to bring healthy lifestyle programmes to our workplaces.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It was announced recently that Singapore is one of the founding cities of the Active Citizens Worldwide project, which seeks to get people in cities to be more active.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is a good step forward and I encourage Sport Singapore to partner HPB to create more workplace healthy lifestyle programmes for our workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Of course, a big part of being healthy means eating healthy.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As we continue in our war against diabetes, we must do more to help shape the eating habits of Singaporeans and lower the barriers to healthy eating.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In many of my union visits, I have seen many staff canteens at the workplaces.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A good place to start would be to encourage these staff canteens to sell healthier food.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We check on what food and drinks are sold in school canteens to ensure that our children eat well in school.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Perhaps it is time that we start a Healthy Canteen programme at our workplaces to ensure that there are healthier food options at our staff canteens.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: One common complaint is that healthy food is often more expensive.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If you eat at our NTWU canteens, it is cheaper to buy brown rice than white rice.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We also encourage our canteen operators to serve coffee and tea without sugar as the base drink.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But if you want to add sugar, there is a sugar counter at the side.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But of course, we also put up posters at the sugar counter to remind you of diabetes.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, please do not add too much sugar when you go to the sugar counter.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For individuals, one of the biggest push factors for them to embark on a healthy lifestyle comes from knowing their own health status.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And surprisingly, 80% of these bus captains who had issues with their health, were doing a health screening for their first time.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This shows the importance of early detection and early intervention.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I, therefore, urge all employers to make free annual health screening a norm in their staff welfare benefits.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The final big pillar of occupational health that is rarely broached in most of our WSH conversations is the issue of mental health.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The stressors of everyday life can take a toll on even the most strong-willed individuals.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Like physical health, we must focus our attention on the early detection and prevention of mental health issues.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A study was recently launched by the Institute of Mental Health and the NUS School of Public Health to examine the association between physical health and mental health, with the results expected to be released in 2021.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As we work on the major physical health pillars under the umbrella of occupational health, the benefits to mental health should also be examined in the coming years, as our workforce faces increasing stress, having to adapt constantly to the rapidly changing economy.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Every worker is precious and more can be done to value the life of each and every worker.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As we work on upskilling our workers and transitioning to the new economy, we must also not forget to ensure that we have safe workplaces and healthy workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We should and must do more to provide safer workplaces and build an ecosystem for all our workers to stay healthy.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With that, Mr Speaker, I support the Budget.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: With the recent spike in en bloc activity and the general meteoric rise in asking prices of properties, what is the simplest way to make sure that such gains go towards the majority of Singaporeans, rather than the rich who buy and sell property?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: How do we ensure that we are able to stretch the value of every Budget dollar, every tax dollar, for all Singaporeans to lead better lives?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is the sort of simple socialism which has informed Singapore policymaking since our Independence and still does much of the heavy lifting in the redistribution of wealth today.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Our socialism is captured by one simple phrase ─ that all of us work together for the well-being of that individual Singaporean who needs help.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: There are two elements which I would like to speak on today that relates to this year’s Budget ─ the use of NIRC and the need for greater equality in Singapore today.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The heavy redistribution that our socialism demands takes place today, in the main, within one generation, that is, the rich of today are taxed to help the poor of today.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: There is also a sense in which the rich of today are taxed to help the poor of yesterday, that is, those a generation or two earlier than them.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But by and large, our socialism does not leap over time.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We make each generation pay its own way, as far as possible.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is the first characteristic of Singapore's socialism and that is why we resist the populist call to spend more of our NIRC.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Since 2008, we have seen an increasing reliance on the NIRC.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is, as we all now know, our number one source and contributor to our revenue base.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: My views and questions to our Finance Minister are as follows.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: What if the investment climate takes a turn for the worse?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Would we be able to continue to finance or do we need to draw down on some of our welfare programmes?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And is it fair to deprive future generations of the wealth that they would have enjoyed had we allowed the interest to compound?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Since the 2008 amendment to our Constitution, we have taken a less conservative approach to the use of the income from our reserves.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We have, since then, seen about 11 instances where the percentage of NIRC to be used has come up in Parliamentary debates.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Members of Parliament from either side of the House have called for this percentage to be increased.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Such an argument is, in a way, understandable because it is an easy and popular course of action.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I think our socialism commits us to raising the percentage at some point but we do not know when or by how much.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: That is to say, it does not commit us to holding steadfast to a certain percentage, only to a certain way of spending.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Which brings me to the second characteristic of our simple socialism – the striving towards a more equal society.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I have spoken before about how complete equality is an impossibility because human beings are not widgets and we are irreducible into one another.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: What we can do, however, is to strive towards equality in basic human experiences – a safe home, a good and meaningful job, a chance for our children to prosper and find their purpose in life; to value each and every one of our Singaporeans and ensure that, for generations to come, they are able to build better lives in this garden city we call home.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And this means that we need to put flesh on what it means to have a collective destiny.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This means we need to address the challenges of poverty, the lack of opportunity; we need to compensate for the poor luck that fate might have dealt on any Singaporean – whether an illness or an abusive spouse, or even with an addiction to gambling.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: As a society, we help those who are most vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It may be true that Singapore as a whole is so affluent that a family with a five-figure income may still feel deprived and feel entitled to even more subsidies.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: He has two boys: one in Primary school and the other a teenage – in Secondary school.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: He has an HDB flat, just $60,000 shy of full payment.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But he has to pay the financial institution 4% in finance costs for his loan.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Peter had originally taken this private loan over an HDB loan because, at that point in time, the starting interest rate offered by the financial institution was 1.17% and the housing agent then had told him that it was a better deal.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Of course, over time, the interest rate went up.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Incidentally, I should add here that although I would consider Peter a savvy man about finance, it is well-known that the cognitive tax on the lower-income is higher.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: When Peter tried to refinance with HDB, unfortunately it was not approved.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: While I understand the need for some of our policies to follow the principles of efficiency of the market, our commitment to equality demands that we change this rule to bring about greater equality.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The financial institution is a commercial profit-making entity, but I think HDB can perhaps take a different goal as its guiding objective.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I also understand that one cannot pick and choose; that if you enjoy low interest when the market is flushed with capital, you cannot decline when the rate is hiked.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The choice is between stability and perhaps a slightly higher rate with HDB and the ups and downs of the private market.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: To do so does not require us to incur more expenditure ─ it merely shifts the interest profits from the bank and puts half of this in Peter’s pocket and, the other half, in a sense, in the Government.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This, of course, may over simplify the process, and I do oversimplify the process.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Of course, this shifting of loans will mean messier policy implementation.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I merely sound this out as a possibility for the Ministers here to consider.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It is something that will be of great help to some lower-income families, like Peter, struggling to pay the monthly loans they had taken with commercial financial institutions.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Second, Peter usually pays $40 a month for his boy's school bus.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: He also enjoys a few other benefits under the MOE financial assistance scheme ─ free text books, a waiver for fees and 50% subsidies for buses.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Because he earned $75 dollars a month too much last year due to overtime pay.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is a man who has bought health insurance for both his wife and his sons.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In fact, he has planned carefully so that when he is 65, he can count on an endowment policy maturing.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Peter ha,s in a way, planned, has prospered slowly and carefully.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But he has also laboured under some rules that weigh a bit more heavily on him.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This requires a new way, possibly a whole-of-Government approach to dealing with such specific instances.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: There is much that remains to be done in Singapore to make our society more equal.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Our simple socialism demands that we make difficult choices.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We must recognise that even relatively well-off people can have a legitimate experience of relative deprivation, when compared to the very wealthy.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: At the same time, we must see the need to allocate resources more urgently to men like Peter.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It is only when we do not have enough to cater to men like Peter that I feel we should consider raising the percentage – not as a means of populist hot air balloon for everyone who demands a specious equality with their neighbour.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Herman Daly wrote that there should be a moral limit to growth.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So too, should there be a moral limit to the consumptive nature of man.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In the 52 years since the founding of Singapore, our socialism has evolved, with our welfare net cast a lot wider and deeper than before.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is as it should be, as our resources and wealth have grown over time.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: At the same time, we must recognise that the NIRC is already called into service to a very large extent.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In this, we ought to be more generous to men like Peter and find ever more ways in the name of equality and justice to bring him and his family along with us and ensure his two boys fight for a land they believe in.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: If we do, indeed, collectively care for his family, all for one, and value the contributions that they have contributed to this country; then, in return, they will feel that they are Singaporean and work for our collective future.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Of course, human beings in every era view their era as a time of modernity and change.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But the era we are living through is seeing many fundamental economic and geopolitical changes to the post-World War II status quo, changes that are making the past a less and less reliable guide to the future, changes that underline ever more strongly that the strategies that brought us here today will not be the same ones that enable us to navigate successfully tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Geopolitical and economic weight is shifting towards Asia, particularly China, and to a lesser extent, India; while Japan and Korea remain major economies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Regional powers, including ASEAN, have the potential to carry much more weight.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Meanwhile, inequality, both within and between countries, is adding to the unpredictability, triggering political shifts like what happened in the US with the election of President Trump and, in the UK, with Brexit.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And climate change marches on, even as the world struggles to cope, using the Paris accords that the US abandoned.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The first broad point I would like to make in my speech is, while we pay special attention to Asia – and I agree that we should do this – as our home region and the world's fastest growing major economic region, let us not write off the West.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In spite of the structural issues faced by some western countries – which range from fiscal deficits and state debt to low productivity growth to inequality-fuelled populism and chronic crime in some cities – western countries still have unmatched soft power.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In fields, such as R&D, entertainment, academia and information and communications technology (ICT), not to mention military technology and diplomatic clout, the West still leads the world, even if the size of that lead is diminishing.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should ensure that our efforts to engage North America and Europe are well-maintained, so as to draw learnings and forge partnerships, whether in the public or private sector realms.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should not assume that Asia will continue to outgrow the West in a linear fashion.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some western countries have shown a tremendous resilience, an ability to rebound from setbacks.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The recent victory of President Macron in France underlines that ability to self-correct and renew.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, Mr Speaker, Sir, I would like to talk about industry disruption but, specifically, in the context of Asia and, in particular, ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The world economy is teeming with disruption, which both destroys and creates anew.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many of these are coming together in interesting ways.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, iOT could generate vast quantities of data for AI to work on so as to improve processes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And this is not even mentioning sharing economy industries like private car-hire, whose disruptive effect is already quite mature in some cities.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As these technologies become increasingly mainstream, they will transform the economies of Asia.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Indeed, that is already happening, in both mature and emerging Asian economies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How can Singapore be relevant to this process of the unfolding of disruption in Asia?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our economic agencies have, for a long time, conceived and implemented initiatives to help Singapore develop a role vis-à-vis the Asian region in these respects.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These initiatives have helped to create and sustain many good-quality jobs and high value-added economic activities.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How could Singapore position itself to play such roles vis-à-vis the unfolding of disruptive industries in Asia?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For a start – and this is the second broad point in my speech – we could focus on ASEAN above all.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I was glad to note some ASEAN-related initiatives in the Budget speech.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is our region and our destiny is inextricably linked to its.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is also the region where our efforts to make Singapore’s economy relevant are pushing on an open door, given the vast size, presence of strong domestic industry players and market barriers that exist in other regions of Asia, such as China, India, Japan and Korea.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A Singapore that is deeply engaged and co-prospering with ASEAN will help ensure that ASEAN will be a fruitful intersection point between the great powers of China, India and Japan, rather than becoming in the future their battleground at some point in the decades to come.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How can Singapore be relevant to the rise of disruptive industries in ASEAN?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The example of Grab may hold a lesson.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Grab is a Singapore-based firm, with Singapore being its largest R&D centre.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Grab has embarked on growth initiatives in the region.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Along the way, it launched a new business model in Indonesia which is uniquely suited to that vast market – motorcycle-hire, which competes with local firm GO-JEK and others.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It also acquired Indonesian shopping app firm Kudo.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As such, Singapore could host data centres, management teams, R&D labs, financing hubs and so on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singapore, with its multi-ethnic make-up, could also be a test-bed to trial products.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For a start – and this brings me to my third broad point – Singapore could galvanise our base of Autonomous Universities, think-tanks, private consultancies, research agencies and so on, to focus on mapping out the paths which disruption could take in ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At this point, I declare that I am the CEO of a research and consulting firm which operates in the Asia Pacific region and global emerging markets.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We could cultivate the soft power of working in a multi-disciplinary fashion to collect and analyse all relevant data on how disruptive industries could rise in ASEAN countries.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: ASEAN has 10 states of which only two have more than 15% of the total population, meaning it is a rather fragmented region, population-wise.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Each ASEAN state has a different economic, business, financial, technology, governmental and cultural landscape.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such studies could indicate the alternative pathways down which disruptive industries could evolve in ASEAN countries – leading to outcomes like Grab and GO-JEK’s motorcycle private-hire in Indonesia.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The thing about big projects is that they can serve to galvanise a people and boost the economy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: President Kennedy’s goal of sending a man to the moon helped galvanise a massive scientific and organisational effort in the US.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While the goal, by itself, served a symbolic, nationalistic purpose, along the way, it helped seed an aerospace industry in the US that has, over the decades, yielded many new technologies that US industry has made use of, like the business of launching commercial satellites today and the current US private sector space industry.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In Europe, 22 member countries have come together to create the European Space Agency (ESA) for researching and exploring space, which has registered 82 successful commercial satellite launches till 2018.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Europeans also established the world’s largest particle accelerator in 2008, the 27-km long Large Hadron Collider, as well as other particle accelerators in a complex known as CERN.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: More recently, CERN has become a pioneer in grid computing or distributed computing.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But the examples of NASA, ESA and CERN show us what ingredients can go into a bold project that has broad economic spin-off benefits.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We could propose a project that would enable Singapore to serve as a test-bed and hub as the project is rolled out across ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I know that it is never easy or fast to get things off the ground in ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But such a proposal could build on the precedents that have been set and the learning curve that has been gained from pioneering the ASEAN Innovation Network, the ASEAN Financial Information Network and the ASEAN Agreement on E-commerce.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some ideas for such an ASEAN-wide initiative that Singapore could champion are as follows.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The financing for such an ASEAN-wide project could be raised in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The know-how and supply of parts and services for refuelling or, perhaps, I should say, recharging stations as well as manufacture of critical components for the vehicles could be undertaken in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One of Singapore’s core competencies seems to be design, project management and servicing of urban infrastructure, a point I have alluded to in earlier speeches in this House.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We could pioneer new technologies and processes in manufacturing, deployment and maintenance of solar panels.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, though it need not take this particular form, such an initiative could use perovskite technology, which some scientists believe has major advantages over traditional silicon-based solar cells.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some scientists hold that perovskite cells can generate more energy from sunlight on low-light days, which may be helpful, given Southeast Asia's weather patterns.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Though there are also disadvantages of perovskite, like a greater susceptibility to temperature- and humidity-induced instability, which scientists are in the process of overcoming.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The point is Singapore could pioneer best practices in the manufacture, deployment and maintenance of solar panels in dense, urban environments in ASEAN's largely tropical weather conditions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These could be used as a model for deployment in major cities across ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I offer these suggestions in the spirit of demonstrating the contours that a major ASEAN-wide initiative could take, without asserting that these are necessarily the only or best candidates for such an initiative.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Lastly, and in conclusion ‒ in moving away from the main theme of my speech, Sir ‒ I would like to pose two questions for the Minister for Finance.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is there evidence that we have passed a certain threshold in terms of our effort to cultivate a vibrant start-up landscape?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It would be helpful to understand the background to this change, coming at this time.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: It went on to say: "The world's most populous country has become the biggest source of visitors to Singapore for the very first time, while its tourists remain the biggest spenders here".

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: With the rising affluence of its middle-class, Chinese outbound tourism is rising rapidly.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: In this Chinese New year alone, an estimated 6.5 million will leave China.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: This number will rise for a long time, given that only 5% of the Chinese population currently holds international passports, compared to 40% in the US.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: In the broader context, China’s economic heft has been felt around the world.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: For instance, it became the largest trading partner to 120 countries in 2014.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: In 2015, it exported more capital than it received.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: We are entering a new era of global economy, anchored by two juggernauts across the Pacific – China and the US ‒ which will be of the same size in economic terms by 2030.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: For Singapore, we will have to make adjustments swiftly and decisively to leverage China’s rise.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: For a long period after WWII, the US, Western Europe and Japan were the main sources of capital and know-how.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: A good command of English connected us to the advanced economies.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: As a result, we industrialised and developed our workforce skills in a relatively short time.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Unlike the West, which is at least 12 hours' flight time away, the Chinese economy is merely 3.5 hours away.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Such proximity gives us immediate access to the market.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: As China exports its capital to the region, Singapore will also benefit.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Of course, this presumes we know how to add value in this two-way process.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: While this percentage remained stable over the years, many observed that our standard of Applied Chinese had declined sharply.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: The same observation was also made of the usage of Malay at home.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Perhaps, we could consider the comments from the Low brothers.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: (In Mandarin):   Lianhe Zaobao published an interview on 23 February titled "Worries for Singaporeans: the Loss of Hunger".

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: The Low brothers were lucky enough to be able to board this gigantic ship sailing into the world.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: While working in China, they were amazed to see how fast China had progressed over the years.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: At the same time, they were worried for Singaporeans." Low Er Wei said, "In the old days, when we went to China, we felt superior because we felt we were better educated, could speak English and lived in a good environment.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: China is overtaking us in every aspect of life.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: There are many people who can speak English better than we can, not to mention Mandarin.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: We have lost the advantage we once possessed." Low Mi Lun said frankly that when they first set up the company in China, they only wanted to employ Singaporeans because they felt the cost of communication would be low.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: However, in the past seven or eight years, the learning capability of the Chinese people has made a great leap.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Compelled by tough competition, the Chinese people have demonstrated stunning learning abilities and surpassed Singaporeans very quickly.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Low Er Wei said: "Singaporeans find it increasingly difficult to adapt to local conditions.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: They are complacent and have become a stumbling block for progress.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Furthermore, Singaporeans have been comfortable for too long and lost the sense of hunger.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: This is our biggest worry." Low Mi Lun also lamented that, currently, there are still many Singaporeans who believed that they were great and even take pride in not being able to speak Chinese.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: He said, when you compare China with Singapore, you will see how differently people see and do things, showing up Singapore's weaknesses.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: (In English): I do not know the two brothers.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: I thought they perhaps could have established a stronger link with Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: However, the Lows' rather forthright and uncomplimentary comments were rather similar to some of the feedback I received from Singaporean businessmen doing business in China.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Their messages to me are: "China is developing faster than we care to know"; "Singapore faces very keen competition"; "Complacency will set us back"; and "We do not know what we do not know".

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: These blind spots, perceived or real, have serious implications for us in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: It affects our ability to engage effectively with a fast-rising economy.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Our ability to value-add as a knowledge-, investment- and trade-hub to the rising trade and investment flows in the region is not a given, and can be challenged or replaced.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Knowing the language is insufficient; it is equally important to know how the other side thinks and negotiates.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: The Suzhou Industrial Park project taught us this".

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: To shore up our shortcomings, I propose that the Government consider three broad measures.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: One, to support the use of mother tongues outside classrooms and in the larger society.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: In Chinese, I will call it "活学活用, 学以致用".

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: We have succeeded in adopting English as the lingua franca among all races.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Obviously, mastering Chinese will help us connect to its 1.3 billion population.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Mastering Malay will help connect us with 300 million population in Southeast Asia.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: At the strategic level, it is enhancing our ability to connect with the steadily growing markets of Asia.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Many successful small nations speak multiple languages and thrive.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Some examples are Luxembourg, Switzerland and the Netherlands.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: For a start, we should promote the use of mother tongues at Government service counters and public places.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: With programmable signboards, we can easily require multiple language displays without space constraints.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Frequent practice in translation from English to our three other official languages, or even selected international languages at some places, will also help people broaden their mindset and promote inter-racial harmony.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Our public sector will also make less, at times, embarrassing translation errors with constant practice.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: In the public broadcast and media space, we should also encourage the correct use of mother tongues.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Funding of Public Service Broadcast (PBS) should not be based on viewership alone.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: On the contrary, investing in good programming to promote correct language usage will multiply the effectiveness of our bilingual programmes in schools.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Two, encourage learning by immersion and internship (鼓励浸濡, 就地实习).

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: For decades, we have sent our best and brightest students to the top universities in the west.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: This has helped us build up a pool of talents familiar with the West which is synonymous with entrepreneurial capital, advanced technology and know-how.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: All multinationals I know make it a requirement for their top talents to have overseas tours of duty.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: There is no reason why we cannot know Shenzhen as well as we know the Bay Area, and Beijing as well as we know Boston.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Three, invest in infrastructure to access world news, business information and global affairs, especially business news from the region and China, 掌握资讯 帷幄千里.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: While it is true that news consumption is mostly local, Singaporeans, as a people, must not suffer from a myopic view of the world.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: The more we know about the vastness of the world, the larger our ambition.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: The more we know about competition, the faster we run and make changes.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: As a trading hub for centuries, Singapore thrives on making continual adjustments to external market signal stimuli.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Staying open and connected to the world has become our lifeline.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: As soon as we turn inward and insular, we will stagnate and decline.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: The question is: how can we read the world as it is, without subconscious "filtering" or "selective reading"?

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Could we create a media environment where our population watches the news, documentaries and business analyses as if we were part of some larger markets?

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Besides Channel NewsAsia, could we access Caixin Global, 财新传媒, Bloomberg or CNBC for free and on a daily basis?

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Our news source shapes our worldview and our biases.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Could we invest more in our local media for analytical programming of China and the regional businesses to promote widespread learning?

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: But, in reality, they are, in essence, extensions of our bilingual policy beyond the classrooms into society.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Constructing a multilingual environment can only be an advantage for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: After 50 years of bilingual education, I think we are ready to introduce the next phase of language application.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Singapore will soon celebrate its 200 years of founding.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: In the past two centuries, Singapore raced ahead of the region to be an oasis of investments and trade.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Now that the region has caught up, China has risen, we need to make continual and further adjustments to our strategy to sharpen our competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.50 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 3.30 pm until 3.50 pm.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Usually, the emphasis on "economy" and "economics" is so overwhelming.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We hear it on the news, we talk about it with our colleagues, and even the Government tends to use economic benchmarks as a marker for Singapore's success.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But if "a strong economy is not an end in itself", then what is the end?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Why work so hard to attain a strong, robust economy?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In this social contract, when the economy is strong, the fruits of our labour must be shared with everyone, so that we can all achieve a better quality of life.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: As a nation, we progress with everyone hand in hand.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We each have a role to play in society, in building our economy.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Some provide capital, some contribute labour, some succeed and some fail.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But, as we move ahead, no one should be left behind.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: When we benefit from this system, we should give back to the society, to give a leg up to those who are less privileged.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Our social contract recognises that we are all part of a larger whole.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: As such, we need to take care of those who fall between the cracks.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Only then can we say, true to our pledge, that there is justice and equality.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, the fact is, we are some ways away from achieving this ideal.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We pride ourselves for building a "compassionate meritocracy", one which is kinder, more inclusive and more redistributive.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Yes, we hold meritocracy as an important tenet of the society.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But our meritocracy rewards only those who have made achievements – those who have done well in school, those who have succeeded in their jobs.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: What about those who continue to fail in school?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: What about those who work two jobs and still cannot earn enough to feed their family?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: There is no guarantee of equal opportunity when there is no guarantee of an equal starting point.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Those who are better off can and will use their privilege to go to better schools, live in better neighbourhoods, get better internships and job opportunities.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Where does that leave those who begin their journeys on more rocky ground?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Those who cannot rise above their circumstances despite their hard work?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Those who never achieve because the odds are perpetually stacked against them?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Let us not forget that privilege comes in myriad forms — socioeconomic status, family history, gender, race, class, sexual orientation, political affiliation and so on.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: How do we honour our social compact where meritocracy fails?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Now is the time to examine our social compact, to see how meritocracy benefits or fails it.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: What is the quality of life lower-income families have at the moment?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The children are deprived of privacy and a conducive environment to study.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Some do not even have a meal to come home to after school.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: How do you tell these children that meritocracy will help them succeed?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: There are various Government schemes which low-income families can qualify for based on their income level.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: They worry that despite their hard work, their incomes do not match the increasing costs of living.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: How do we tell them that our meritocratic system benefits them, when it does nothing to improve their current living conditions and, ironically, adds to their insecurity?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: With our greying population, we also encounter more elderly people, particularly seniors who are alone and living in poverty.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Some of them share a home with another elderly person because they cannot afford to buy their own property.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Others may realise that escalating healthcare costs have to be financed by the sale of their greatest assets – their homes.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The sense of displacement that these seniors face can be extremely detrimental to their mental health.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In some cases, they take on manual low-paying labour to make a living.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: How do we explain to these senior citizens that despite all their years of work, they are now left on the margins, because they are simply not as productive or competitive as others?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Have our social support structures been developed to cater for these seniors?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Or do our meritocratic convictions in self-reliance and responsibility mean that they should find solutions to their own problems?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: That is to say, funding and activation of manpower are provided for self-help community groups to address these areas.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But we need to provide care and support in a sustained and meaningful way.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: More importantly, how can we provide assistance without making those who need help feel that they have to prove that “they have worked hard but not achieved enough and hence, is worthy of support?” We have been inculcated with the values of meritocracy: hard work will be rewarded, self-reliance and personal achievement are key to our success.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Have we also then made those who have failed to achieve believe in the narrative that it was because of personal failing that one cannot do better and accept this narrative that it is not a dignified existence?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: How then do we tell those who do not succeed by society’s standards that they have not failed?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: How do we tell them there should be no shame in seeking help?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Or do we look at them, and say, "You are not working hard enough, so you do not deserve support"?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: My point is that there are people in our midst who do not succeed despite their best efforts.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Maybe they grew up in a poor household, unable to afford books, educational toys and enrichment classes.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Maybe they grew up in a broken home, with little parental supervision, so they spend their days and nights at the playground.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: By the time these people go to school, by the time they leave school, by the time they enter the workforce, I do not have to say it.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: For every one person who says, "I came from a poor upbringing but now I am a success", there are many others who did not succeed.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: To use an analogy, we are, each of us, individual parts of a machine that has been working well in the course of our history.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Each of us has a different function and capability.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: If this machine is successful, it is because of all the parts, not just the shiny parts, not just the big parts, not just the loud parts.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Every single person plays a role in making an economy successful – from the CEOs to the coffeeshop cleaners, from the highly salaried to the hourly-paid labourers.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Let us not sweeten meritocracy by adding a descriptive word like "compassionate".

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: How do we then achieve a better quality of life for all whilst we grapple with growing inequality?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Is universal coverage of essential services to certain groups the answer to these problems?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I believe it should be one amongst other options that Singaporeans should start considering and we should be having conversations on these, deeply.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We should not just ask what we want for ourselves.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I hope this conversation will start with us looking around us.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Looking at what, besides ourselves, is needed to bring a better quality of life, to all people.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We work hard now, hoping to save for the future.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The Government has said that there will be more expenditure and even have plans for 100 years ahead.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Where is the assurance that the hard work of Singaporeans will contribute to their well-being in the future?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: This larger conversation must be one that involves all Singaporeans across all demographics of society.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It should also be one that is open to difference.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The different ethnic groups, the different religions and beliefs, the different genders, the different sexual orientations and the different political ideology.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: No one should feel or be made to feel left out.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The construction workers who build our homes and roads, the domestic workers who tend to our children and seniors.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It is this diversity that enriches our humanity.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It is this diversity that powers our innovation.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: When we support one another regardless of our differences, we all benefit by becoming collectively stronger.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: This diversity is what will make or break Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We are a land-scarce nation, with no natural resources.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But what we do have is our people.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We need to create a conducive space for them to be creative and innovative, for people to take risks and be applauded for failures as much as successes.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Innovation should not just happen in the workforce in the economy.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We need to be innovative in life, in the social sector and in dealing with our social and political problems.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: To think critically, to ask the right questions, to break rules and challenge the status quo, if necessary.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Are we able to ask the hard questions?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: An innovative culture is one that does not shy away from asking difficult questions.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Innovators often demonstrate different points of views from the conventional or the establishment.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Here, I would like to highlight the work of an important group of people, the NGOs and the activists on the ground.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: They have worked incredibly hard against all odds, over many years, to find means of addressing the plights of the less privileged or accepted groups of people amongst us – the poor, disabled, LGBT people, foreign workers, inmates facing the death penalty and so on.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Some of them have been working at this for more than 30, 40 or 50 years.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Sometimes, their work, while not in opposition to the Government, can confront the Government's position.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Are they agitators who are just concerned about themselves?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: They do this because they have the same vision that Minister Heng had mentioned: to "build a better home and provide for a better quality of life for our people".

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: They raise issues to highlight hidden problems, make the invisible visible.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: They are concerned about solving problems and eradicating prejudice and injustice.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Activists by and large do not want to incite trouble.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: They do not want to be at loggerheads with the state.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, they want to get the state on their side, so that policies can be changed.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: At the core of their activism lies the deep belief in achieving happiness, prosperity and progress for our nation, through a system that is just and equal to all.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Sometimes, when activists feel that they are not heard, they appeal for support from the public, hoping that the public will hear them out.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: This is what a functioning democracy is all about.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Patriotism can sometimes come in the form of thorns in our sides.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But patriotism comes from a good place and demands that we all do better – not only for ourselves, but for our fellowmen and, most importantly, for our country.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: So, what then is the role of the Government in this?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: This is where my experience as an artist comes in useful.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Then, together, we wade through the messiness, sort things out and listen to different views.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Soon, we will find and agree on one brilliant idea.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But we need more than just one brilliant idea.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We need many ideas, working together, serving as many people as possible.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: There are many patriotic people like that in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But this country also needs patriotic people of a different kind.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Those who try to grapple with the increasing inequalities in our midst, those who are compassionate, innovative, fearless in their questioning.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Those who want to improve our system for one and all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: And, lastly, I would like to appeal to this Government to participate in this dialogue; let yourself be a vulnerable observer, a vulnerable listener.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Listen to the voices, to the stories and narratives by first acknowledging your vulnerability as a human being.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: As I shared two years ago in the Budget debate, "When a society is low on opportunity, it is the rent-seekers and owners of old capital who extract profits." But how we grow also shapes how equal a society we become.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: For example, economist César Hidalgo at MIT has found that countries with higher economic complexity tend to have lower inequality.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some of this is because complex industries need skilled workers and supporting enterprises – which means the workers and SMEs have more stake in a more equitable economic structure.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This also contrasts with less complex economies, simpler economies where the income distribution may follow the controlling interests of resource ownership – who owns an oil well, who owns farmland, who owns production facilities.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Another finding from Hidalgo's team is that when you study economic structure, you can see how the pattern of exports evolves over time – usually along what they call adjacencies, which means it diversifies towards products which are similar to the existing exports.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: When you have a diverse economy, more paths for people to rise, more paths for workers and students to do well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Everyone building deep skills, everyone having a stake in the workplace, in industry and in the economy.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And Mr Speaker, we do need to transform.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because, today, all around, there is disruption and also opportunity.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, how do we get ready for the next 50 years?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Looking back, for two centuries, Singapore benefited from geography.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Bespoke and distributed manufacturing 3-D printing where you can build parts next to where they are going to be assembled.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In many Western countries, the mood is not so good about trade.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And technology continues to disrupt jobs every day.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Furthermore, the very idea of economic geography is also being disrupted.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Digital data flow is going to create a parallel world economic order, a world economic order that is digital in parallel to existing geography – whether it is collaboration, competition or opportunity.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Not just digitising today's businesses, but creating new business models.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: For example, if you look at life sciences: data science is what turned DNA sequencing into genomics and is what drives personalised medicine, helping patients around the world.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: E-commerce and retail are more than just going cashless.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is about knowing your customers even better than they know themselves.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Artificial intelligence and the Internet of Things will change factories – assembly lines that adapt, maintenance that predicts what parts are going to fail and better quality control.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, Mr Speaker, how do we ride the wave?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We must ensure that Singapore has a strong position in this new digital economic world order.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This means good external connectivity, good pipelines for data.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: That means when we spend on digital infrastructure, we must see it as an investment and not consumption – the same way we invest in the Tuas Port and growing Changi Airport.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Obvious next steps for a data hub include machine learning and artificial intelligence (AI).

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In 2015, the New York Times reported the US Federal Government spent US$1 billion on AI research.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, we must maintain our reputation as a trusted jurisdiction for intellectual property and data protection.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because in the future, when someone sequences all three billion base pairs of his personal genome, who will they trust, where will they trust that data with?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This means legislation that is up to date or even one step ahead.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It also means investing in better communication security because communication is being disrupted, too.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Traditional public key encryption which your "https" and other forms of online secured socket layers depend on – all that presumes that factorising large numbers into individual prime numbers takes a long time, even with a fast computer.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But quantum computing is promising to disrupt this, by doing that factorising faster than was thought possible.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This may seem like "blue skies research", but I see some of this as what I call "blue ocean research" – practical applications and a big harvest for those who can catch the dividends early enough.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Our fiscal position is better than many other developed economies.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, the next step is to invest and converge investments, technology, talent, infrastructure, to create that critical mass of opportunities for Singaporeans and for Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We may be a little red dot, but we can help build an ecosystem of inter-operable systems to benefit all stakeholders in the region.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: You might even call it: "One dot, one web: One shining little red dot, one web of partnerships and networks".

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, Sir, today, the digital economy is developing rapidly.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: With this, Singapore can continuously increase its prestige and influence.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: At the same time, Singapore should also take advantage of being a first mover and work with neighbouring countries to establish common standards in ASEAN and to establish an ecosystem of inter-operable systems.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: You can call it One Dot, One Web: "One shining little red dot, One Web of partnerships and networks".

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: (In English): The Government has a dual role: minimise risk, maximise opportunity.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: When we minimise risk, we prevent a race to the bottom.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But, if there is too much bureaucracy, too many administrative barriers, it gets in the way of people and businesses racing to the top.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, today, more than ever, the Government can and must be an enabler of opportunity, innovation and growth.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We need to be fast and we need to be able to act fast, especially when speed matters because, in the private sector, in Industry 4.0, a "slow decision" is often the same as "no decision".

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And if there is "no decision", after a while, it becomes a "no" decision when people take their business and opportunities elsewhere.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, we must keep on finding ways to empower that Team Singapore to do even better.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Can we be better at nurturing and promoting our own unicorns – start-ups that are valued at $1 billion or more?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: How can we be more competitive on this?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: How easy is it for SMEs and start-ups to access credit and funding, especially during the early years of the so-called "valley of death", when many enterprises do not quite make it before taking flight?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Can we reduce land cost and rental overheads for businesses?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We can have a market for different kinds of leasing models.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There is traditional upfront capital expenditure, but there can also be models with discounted upfront costs in return for profit sharing, or even some extent of equity ownership, and that equity could even be conventional or preferred stock.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We can have a market of different models to see what works.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We must be a home – a home where the brightest talent of tomorrow will want to settle down and raise children in, while creating jobs, wealth and opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because when a bright young spark grows up in Singapore, there is that emotional attachment to the little red dot.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Sometimes, it is home ‒ home ties ‒ more than any financial incentive that decides whether a company founder keeps that Singapore footprint, even after the start-up goes regional or global.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: As disclosure, I should mention that I do use a Razer mouse.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Razer, a world-class gaming hardware company bought THX, the audio company founded by George Lucas.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Razer's founder, Tan Min-Liang, grew up in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: If he had grown up elsewhere, we would have one fewer star in our constellation of entrepreneurs.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The World Management Survey by John Van Reenen at the London School of Economics studied 12,000 organisations, 34 countries.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: They found that basic management skills account for large differences in productivity and output per worker.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But we also know that children from less well-off families do not get the same access to parental support, to parental experience of having run a business, to other forms of social capital.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Fewer chances to learn how to run a business or get an apprenticeship at an SME through networks.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This is another way we can reduce inequality, grow entrepreneurship, help young Singaporeans to rise up and do well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Today, the economy is being transformed, many policies, many transformations.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But beyond this Budget, we all must have the audacity to dream big.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: To dream big and boldly go where we can position ourselves to ride new trends and new journeys over the next 50 years.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And so, I stand in support of this Budget.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With these challenges in mind, the Budget has laid out specific initiatives targeted at ensuring that Singapore will continue to have a robust and vibrant economy, as well as a healthy stream of tax revenue that we could tap on to support our long-term social objectives.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this regard, this year's Budget is fiscally prudent, measured and well-balanced, with emphasis given to address both immediate concerns and long-term needs.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Two initiatives, in particular, have created much talk on the ground ─ the SG Bonus and the impending rise in GST.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some chatter has likened these two initiatives to the well-worn analogy of giving a chicken wing and taking back a chicken.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While this analogy may draw a few chuckles, I think that it is a somewhat facile one.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Singapore Government has always been committed to sharing the fruits of the country’s development with Singaporeans and the SG Bonus is yet another instance of this commitment.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Linking the SG Bonus with the proposed rise in GST, however, gives an inaccurate perception of a relationship between the two issues.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As this proposed increase will not take place for a few years, I would like to now shift my focus to the present and to look at three specific aspects of the Budget in my speech.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First of all, a vibrant and innovative economy.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Digital technologies have disrupted traditional business models, changed the ways business decisions are made and have transformed how goods and services are delivered and consumed.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many businesses are struggling to keep up with these transformative changes and it is crucial that our firms, especially our SMEs, develop digital capabilities and competencies to compete in this digital era.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The SMEs Go Digital programme has been a timely shot-in-the-arm to help our businesses ramp up their digital capabilities.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While we help businesses transform, we also need to ensure that we have the talent base with the right skills to support that transformation.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe that we need to focus on two areas: to up-skill and re-skill our workforce.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These employees need to be up-skilled and re-skilled to take on technologically-enhanced roles so that they can continue to add value to their employers.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We also need to help employees who are displaced by technological changes and innovations to learn new skills.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Industry Transformation Maps (ITMs) have been developed to help 23 industries reinvent themselves.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As Singapore moves into its next phase of growth, we must ensure that we have the right mix of human capital to support that growth.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The development of human capital is imperative and should also be done in tandem with the development of digital skills.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The second area is to focus on the benefits for families in the area of education.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As an educator, I strongly believe that education is an important leveller that enables social mobility.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While the increase in Edusave contributions will benefit all students, it would also be ideal if we could provide targeted help in larger quantums to those in our community who need an additional leg-up.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, can we consider an enhanced financial assistance scheme where there are different tiers of Edusave grants and top-ups, depending on family income?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Other initiatives that we could consider would include making student care more accessible and affordable by giving higher levels of subsidies to lower-income families and prioritising student care services for children of single working-parents because these families typically do not have the same level of social support that dual-parent families have.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The final area I would like to focus on is that of the enhanced Proximity Housing Grant (PHG) designed to benefit families.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I welcome the different enhancements that the Budget has made to the PHG.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe that these enhancements will, in the long run, promote family ties and encourage family members to live near one another.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Having an extended family living close to one another will provide a much-needed social support network.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is especially important in Singapore’s ageing society where dual-income families are norms rather than exceptions.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As such, grandparents are great sources of support for grandchildren when parents are out at work and the daily interaction between grandchildren and grandparents are wonderful ways to keep the elderly mentally and physically active and engaged.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singles, too, can also play their part in an extended family network.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The difference could be in the tens of thousands, which is quite substantial for a single individual.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Ideally, this principle can eventually be applied to other proximity-based housing grants as well in the future.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Indeed, the next decade will see Singapore undertake several major projects to upgrade our healthcare systems, transportation network, infrastructure and to beef up various aspects of our security.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I understand that the only way for us to ensure that we do not overly burden our future generation is to ensure that we have a fiscally sustainable and prudent Budget now.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Having said that, it is important that the Government also remembers to temper any future tax increases with the appropriate measures and schemes to help those who need assistance and help when that day comes.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With that, Mr Deputy Speaker, I conclude my speech in support of the Budget.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But before that, I would like to make three brief points about the Budget.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We can argue about the precise percentage of NIRC to use, but the important thing is we must continue to grow our reserves.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: If our reserves do not grow, it may not continue to anchor the stability of our growing economy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: As a small city-state, Singapore has been described as a small boat in a large ocean.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: During the last big storm, the 2008 Global Financial Crisis, our reserves served as an anchor, thereby providing us with much-needed stability.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Recently, some have commented that our reserves have already gotten too much and we can afford to spend a little bit more of our reserve income.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: However, I feel that many commentators did not talk about the fact that Singapore's economy is still growing and we are actually a small ship that is continuing to grow in size.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: With geographical uncertainty and the rolling back of financial regulations in US, the only certainty is that bigger and larger financial storms will eventually come to our shores.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: So, if our reserves fail to keep up with our growing economy, maybe not at the next crisis, but a few crises down the road, our reserves may not be of a sufficient size to anchor the bigger Singapore economy then.
