speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And if Singapore flounders, who will save us?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) or World Bank?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Even if they do, at what cost, especially for the average Singaporean?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, we must be wary of the serious implications of not growing our reserves.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Because retirees have no income, they are more impacted by the GST, compared to other Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Some retirees, even those living in private estates, are asset-rich and cash-poor.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: To help them manage the cost of living, I hope our Government can help put some urgency in helping them monetise their assets.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I have spoken about this issue in depth during the recent February Parliamentary Motion on "Support for Senior Citizens".

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, I hope the Government can continue to actively ensure that such options exist in Singapore, either through reverse mortgage of larger flats in private estates, or through specialised reverse mortgage funds like those done in France.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Recently, some commentators have spoken about the effectiveness of the ITMs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For example, the Government can launch a new programme to encourage businesses to use Artificial Intelligence in, let us say, year one.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Major businesses, with their budgetary process, will need up to a year to make major shifts to take advantage of that programme.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The efforts of the business will also take time to impact the bottom line.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: After the bottom line is made, it would still take many more months, even one to two years, before the improvements are reflected in any company’s audited accounts.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And then, more time is needed before the numbers are finally submitted to ACRA and to our Department of Statistics.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: That is why we need three to five years before we can fully comment on the effectiveness of programmes, in terms of economic output numbers – whether it is GDP, Value Added per worker or productivity numbers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In the meantime, I feel that our debate should focus on input indicators of economic transformation, by which I mean the quality and the accessibility of transformation programmes for our businesses and workers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And let us not get fixed on immediate economic output numbers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I agree with Minister Heng that Singapore should be a Global-Asia Node of technology, innovation and enterprise.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: By and large, I think we are making good progress.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: However, I think we can do more to tap a rising ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I am glad that our economic policies are keeping up with a rising ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Beyond the ASEAN Economic Community (AEC), we are also setting up the Infrastructure Office, which is contributing to more infrastructure development within ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We are expanding our Global Innovative Alliance into ASEAN's Innovation Network and we are pushing for the creation of an ASEAN e-Commerce platform.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: A stronger secretariat will improve ASEAN's ability to track and execute various commitments, so as to unlock the full potential of agreed measures.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For example, a stronger secretariat will be able to help us better coordinate action in response to non-tariff protectionist measures within the AEC.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I am also heartened to see the strengthening of talent development programmes.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This includes Professional Conversion Programme (PCP) for Southeast Asian Ready Talent, SkillsFuture ASEAN Leadership Programme, GOASEAN Award, Young Talent Programme, and Infrastructure Development Internship.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that should these programmes prove successful, the Government can quickly scale them up.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The creation of Enterprise Singapore, as well as the rollout of more programmes to support companies to internationalise, will strengthen our efforts.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: However, I feel that much more work is needed for Singaporeans to "Think ASEAN".

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Today, there is a dichotomy between the tremendous opportunities offered by ASEAN and the perception of ASEAN by everyday Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Many Singaporeans I speak to, associate our neighbouring countries with affordable holiday destinations or places where we go abroad to do community service.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, many Singaporeans assume that many parts of ASEAN are backward regions and will stay so for a long time.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But many parts of ASEAN are growing quickly, and these assumptions are no longer true.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: As such, it is very important for us to change the mindset, especially among our youths.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: After all, while our Government and our companies are more involved in ASEAN, the full benefits can truly be realised if our Singaporeans are personally involved in the opportunities.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: So, I would like to propose five ways we can encourage our people, especially our youths and PMETS, to see the possibilities in ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And when they go abroad, we should ensure that our youths see the bright spots and centre of innovations within ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Two, we can promote exchanges between student leaders.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: As a young Singaporean studying in the US many years ago, I was deeply involved in the largest student leader exchange between the US and China.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: That allowed me to understand that lifelong friendships can be forged over time, if the programme is executed well.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: There is scope to do such a programme, linking the future leaders of Singapore with those of our neighbouring ASEAN countries.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Today, many ASEAN officials spend short training stints in Singapore and they are here because they are slated for greater things back in their home country.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, there is scope for us to network our students with them, so that we can benefit from their in-depth insights that are not frequently covered publicly.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: By that, I mean getting our tertiary institutions to teach ASEAN languages, business cultures and political culture through both formal courses and guest speaker series.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Singapore has deep expertise in the region through many excellent institutions, such as the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy, Rajaratnam School of International Studies (RSIS), Asia Competitiveness Institute (ACI) and Institute of Southeast Asian Studies (ISEAS).

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We also have multilateral institutes, such as World Bank, which has a deep presence in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Our leading bankers, lawyers and management consultants have tremendous experience working in ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, we can tap on these institutions and our experts to open up courses and talks to our students and young entrepreneurs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The goal of all of these is to get our people to "Think ASEAN".

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: If we can use our year as ASEAN Chair to start this mindset shift, the opportunities for Singapore and Singaporeans will naturally follow.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: With that, Mr Deputy Speaker, I support the Budget.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am in agreement with the Budget, which has been carefully calibrated and aligned with our key goals.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While we enable innovation and support our enterprises to seize future opportunities, we are also preparing to deal with increasing expenditures in healthcare, national security and infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Indeed, as the Minister had emphasised, we are at a transition point which will present unprecedented opportunities and challenges.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some hard choices, such as raising the GST, will have to be made to ensure that we stay in the black and continue to build up our fiscal fitness.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: GST is one of our key sources of revenue.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This advance notice will help investors, businesses and residents to plan expected expenditures.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Minister has mentioned that the exact timing of the increase has not been confirmed and will depend on the state of our economy, our future expenditures and the revenue from existing taxes.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The GST was introduced in 1994 at the rate of 3%.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It was increased nine years later in 2003 to 4% and, subsequently, in quick succession, to 5% the next year in 2004 and 7% another three years later in 2007.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It will be over 10 years by the time it will be raised again.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Under what circumstances can the Government use other combinations of income instruments to replace the tax contribution from the GST increase?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Also, what is the expected GDP contribution arising from the large-scale infrastructure projects, such as Changi Airport Terminal 5, Tuas mega port and the Kuala Lumpur-Singapore High Speed Rail (HSR)?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How would these go to reduce our reliance on future GST increases?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In addition, will the Government consider a cap on the proportion of GST contribution to total revenue, since there will be future returns on investments made with our current reserves and the infrastructure investments we are embarking on?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We also have to consider if we should set a ceiling on our GST rate in the future.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For now, even after increasing it to 9%, our GST is at the low end of the spectrum, compared to many other developed countries.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: European countries’ GST or Value-Added Tax (VAT) is between 10% and 20%.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The standard rates in Denmark and Sweden are 25%.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While Denmark's VAT is set at one rate, other countries, such as Sweden, Germany and France, have reduced rates applied to essential goods, such as food.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I agree with our Government’s decision to keep our GST at one flat rate to minimise administrative and compliance costs.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, going forward, should our GST continue to increase, we should review and examine other GST models with lower rates on essential goods and services to reduce the burden on the lower-income groups.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In planning for GST increases, we have to take into account both the pace of wage increases that can be attained and the projected inflation rate, so as to reduce the impact of the increase in the cost of living on our citizens.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must continue our investments in innovation and our efforts in structural reforms to boost productivity growth for the long term.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Wage increases and productivity gains must grow in tandem.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The scheme aims to encourage employers to share productivity gains with staff.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The gradual reduction in co-funding by the Government, from 20% this year to 10% in 2020, will ease cost pressures on companies while they undergo transformation to raise productivity.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Another important scheme is the Progressive Wage Model (PWM).

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope the Government will consider expanding this productivity-based wage progression pathway to sectors beyond cleaning, security and landscape sectors.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Doing so will help the low-wage workers in other sectors who are vulnerable and not equipped to negotiate for training, upgrading, better or more productive work designs.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Next, the plan to both save and borrow for future infrastructural projects is a sound one.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I agree that the plan to borrow by our Statutory Boards and Government-owned companies involved in infrastructure will achieve twin benefits.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Providing Government guarantees backed by our reserves would certainly kill two birds with one stone – providing assurance to investors while preserving our reserves to generate future returns.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How will the Government decide which entities and projects will receive these guarantees, the amounts and the timeframes for repayments?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In addition, will there be a cap on the total amount of guarantees to be provided?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As infrastructure projects are supposed to be utilised well into the future, it is important to also apply our vision of building a Smart, Green and Liveable City on such projects as they will certainly impact how we live, work and play.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This would help develop a green bond market of a significant size and add to the vibrancy of the bond market with greater variety of products attracting different investors.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Is it necessary to expand Budgets every year, as long as they are pegged to inflation rates?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Young Singaporeans, in particular, will be excited about building their careers, businesses, fulfilling their dreams in the innovative and vibrant economy which the Minister is planning for.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: A greener and cleaner living environment will certainly be a significant boost to our living standards.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In the face of increasing costs of living and a challenging economy, I am heartened that the Government plans to set aside more resources for those in need.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This is a Budget that is forward-looking and filled with optimism.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I share the Minister's opinion that regional and international partnerships will certainly help to open doors to new opportunities.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I am pleased to see that he is implementing some schemes to achieve this.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Next, even before the Budget, the Government has shared plans to transform industries through the development of Industry Transformation Maps (ITMs).

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: These are aimed at addressing issues within each industry and fostering deeper partnerships between the Government, firms, industries, trade associations and chambers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This is good in principle, but implementation would not be so straightforward, given that every industry, every business, every individual has different levels of expectations and commitment.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Communication and engagement between the different bodies will always pose challenges.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: SkillsFuture will remain a crucial component to help Singaporeans adjust and adapt to the Future Economy.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Thus far, those who have utilised their SkillsFuture credits have found the scheme to be encouraging and, more importantly, they have gained useful skills that will help them in their careers, or even just to enrich their lives and learn something new.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope the Government will consider investing more resources in SkillsFuture, such as giving more credits to those who have already used theirs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I would now like to move on to social issues.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Some of these flats are now at least 30 years old and prone to defects and safety issues.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share future plans for HIP for ageing flats?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Nee Soon South is in a very unique situation.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Half of my flats are built in 1986 and the other half in 1987.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, half are enjoying the HIP while the other half are still waiting, 还痴痴地在等.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I am also concerned about those who have a house but are cash-tight and have little options to right size.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This is becoming increasingly common in the older private estates, where the land lease is expiring and it is difficult to sell their house.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There are also people who live in older HDB flats with a lease of less than 60 years and they find it very challenging to sell their flats.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This is not about monetising the house but getting some money from the sales to cover the cost for the next house.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: As more housing estates start to age, this problem will become more rampant.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: While there is Silver Housing Scheme (SHS) for residents who are 55 years old and above, this scheme requires most of the proceeds to be topped up into the CPF and may not meet the needs of all elderly.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How does the Government intend to address these issues?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What were the factors that were taken into consideration?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The perception from the public is that this is just an exercise to take a cut from all the en bloc homeowners.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is likely that these en bloc owners have to buy another apartment to move to and they will end up being penalised if they buy above $1 million.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Rising living costs and inflation are persistent concerns for every country.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: During my interaction with residents, by and large, residents understand the need for the Government to raise the GST.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, they worry about businesses profiteering by raising prices excessively and, in some cases, in advance.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Back when it was announced that prices of water would be increased, residents said some businesses took the opportunity to raise prices even before the increase kicked in.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope the Government can look into a taskforce to ensure commercial entities do not use the GST increase as an excuse to exploit consumers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The Government is enhancing various financial support and grants which would help mitigate the GST increase in some ways.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: An applicant may have obtained a new job or wage increase which results in disqualification from a scheme, but he or she may have only obtained that income increase recently and still has many outstanding bills to pay off.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I think we should also look at other criteria, such as minimum working period.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Ultimately, we do not want to end up penalising people for getting a job or a better paying one.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Our end-goal is to ensure that children in these low-income families have a conducive environment where they can focus on their studies and self-development without being affected by their parents’ worries.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Beneficiaries should thus be encouraged to find better means to support their family and not feel worried that they will be cut off from much-needed financial support once they do so.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This happened last year when the water price increases were announced.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that the Government can monitor this situation to ensure that commercial entities do not use the GST increases as an excuse to exploit consumers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The Government will also increase various financial support and assistance, which can help mitigate the impact of the GST increase.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: For example, a person who may have just obtained a new job or wage increase could become ineligible.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But we should look deeper whether the person has to settle any outstanding bills that came about when the person was retrenched.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I propose that, apart from the household income, we should look at the person’s period of employment.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Ultimately, we do not wish to penalise someone who manages to secure a better job.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   This Budget pays attention to the ageing issue.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Hence, I would like to raise a few related points.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Old houses tend to have shorter leases and are difficult to fetch a good price, no matter whether it is a private property or an HDB flat.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Hence, it is a challenge for their owners to downsize to a smaller unit and get additional cash.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Old HDB units built between 1987 and 1990 face a special problem.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This has affected the quality of life and safety of the owners and that is why I said that old flats face a special problem.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But the flats are located in Nee Soon South, half built in 1986 and half in 1987.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: One-half is qualified for HIP but the other half will not qualify.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In addition, some illnesses troubling the seniors are not covered by the Government's medical subsidies.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: For example, many seniors suffer incontinence and need long-term treatment.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope the Government can pay attention to this and provide some subsidies.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: After the Government announced the plan to raise GST, some unscrupulous businesses may increase their prices even before the actual GST hike.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This happened when the water prices increased last year.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Government consider establishing a task force to study this problem?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This is a conversation between a husband and a housewife.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The wife said to the husband, "Dear, dear my mother is ageing and my mother has to visit doctors very frequently.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Our children are growing up in their developing age.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I need to buy more fish and meat for their development.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I need to have more money from you." Husband looked at the wife with a smile and he said, "No problem.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I have a piece of good news to share with you.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Last Saturday, early in the morning, as I was at the Community Club, I met our Member of Parliament.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Our Member of Parliament came to visit us before 8 o'clock.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I went to buy the 4D and the number came out as 8481.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I felt that I had hit the jackpot." The wife looked at the husband and she said, "Dear, what I want is the current expenses, I am not talking about one-off type of expenses.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, are you telling me that if you do not win the lottery, my mother does not need to see the doctor?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Are you telling me that if you do not hit the jackpot, my children do not need to eat extra protein?" And the husband said, "That is not a problem.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We still have a house, an asset we can sell." I think this is the problem that one of our Members has described that is worrying.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The understanding is: not a problem; if we do need to finance expenses, we can just utilise the proceeds from the land sale.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The population's age and Government costs are always rising, but no problem!

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The Government can solve them by just selling land.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: One of my residents seems to have seen this coming.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Last Saturday, when I was visiting the coffeeshop, he told me, "Sister Wah, you must remember, even a mountain of gold can be depleted.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: People shouldn't keep thinking about using the savings our grandfather left us.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Don't let us become the unfilial sons who squander the family wealth!"

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is vital that we are discussing this Budget from a position of strength, with a large surplus.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Prudent policies have enabled us to continue to accrue surpluses even as the economy and population mature.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This gives us vital breathing room to manoeuvre as future challenges loom.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is especially critical as one mega-trend is likely to fundamentally change our world.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In the words of Mr Masayoshi Son of Softbank: AI is coming, and it is coming Big Time!

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And it will combine with robotics and automation to change how we work.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While technology is always creating new jobs and destroying old ones, there is reason to believe that the current phase of development is different.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: With machine learning, computers can teach themselves faster than humans can teach them.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: DeepBlue, which beat the chess grandmaster Garry Kasparov in 1996, was rule-based and human programmers taught it how to win at chess.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In contrast, AlphaGo beat the world champion at Go after teaching itself the game.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: AlphaGo Zero taught itself how to beat AlphaGo in 40 days without using a single data from a single human game.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is clear that the impact of technology on the economy and the labour market will be broader, deeper and more rapid than previous technological advances.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Broad – because it will affect many sectors simultaneously.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Deep – because it will affect many different job functions within each industry.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And Rapid – because the rate of adoption of software or cloud solutions is not hindered by the need for physical rollout.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What will result is not just traditional structural or cyclical unemployment.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We will experience a permanent secular shift in the economy, which will change what jobs are available and what skills are in demand.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: History has shown that technological progress has always led to new jobs and an overall improvement in our lives in the long run.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But all of us are going to be there in the long run.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And in the meantime, the transitional pain is going to be very, very real.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: According to research by The Boston Consulting Group, jobs will be lost in roles such as machine operator, production planner, while new roles will be created, such as data scientist and robot coordinator.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many of those displaced will struggle to take on the new emerging roles.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The recently-emerged private hire car industry has served as a refuge for those who have been displaced from other lines of work.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This has allowed them to continue to earn an income.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This has helped mitigate the pressure of job losses from sectors that have been struggling, such as marine and offshore.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, we are not far from the day when all cars will be able to drive themselves.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The move towards Autonomous Vehicles (AV) will have a profound impact on the labour force it will displace.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Is there another industry that can absorb so many jobseekers who may not have any specific marketable skills?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The gig economy – freelance or part-time work – can help cushion the impact, but it is not a long-term solution for many.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They are individuals who are trapped in an endless hamster wheel with no hope of advancement.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This then becomes very fertile ground for radicalisation.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We can, therefore, expect to see a displaced underclass who will struggle to make ends meet.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This Government has had the foresight to put in place SkillsFuture and emphasise training and reskilling.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We are leading the world in this area.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But we need to recognise that a large segment of the population will struggle to learn and apply these new skills.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And when you factor in their families and dependants, the number of people affected gets really, really big.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This raises vital questions around the whole approach to social spending.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Short-term cushioning may not be enough, since we cannot trampoline them back into economic health.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Any support would need to be sustained as well.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Current trend is towards a broad spread of small subsidies.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Is this still the right prioritisation going forward?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As technology advances, wages will likely fall as a share of GDP.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Then, it becomes only right that the owners of land and capital pay a greater share of the burden.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What steps are we taking to prepare for this, in terms of fiscal policy and of preparing the ground and the rhetoric for this possibility?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And what are we doing to prepare the next generation for this new reality?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Our education system has served us well, but can it equip the young for the new challenges?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If you believe that things are changing more quickly, then what is needed is not specific knowledge, but imagination and the ability to learn.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How do we inculcate the values needed for the future, such as curiosity, imagination, critical thinking and persistence?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But the advent of AI is inevitable and there will be consequences.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We cannot be complacent and assume that new jobs will automatically be created.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In many cases, AI will supplement and augment our capabilities.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, now is the time to talk about AI.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This Budget is unique in a few respects.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And not only that, but which is quite upfront about some of the bad news for the next 10 years.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, it is a very straightforward Budget but the most important part of it is the message.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The message is one of optimism, that Singapore is ready for the decade ahead, notwithstanding the challenges we face.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I also think there is a risk that in this Budget, people may take, sometimes, perhaps, too much comfort.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is also important for people to realise what some of the important changes mean and what impact these will have on them.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: First of all, of course, if this vision succeeds, we will have a vibrant innovative economy and a smart, green and liveable city, which sounds very nice.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If we fail, of course, the consequences could be dire.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The opportunities could move to other parts of Asia.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In fact, what you see in places like the European Union, for example, is that opportunities move to the developing parts of that Union.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, there is a chance that even though there is a move towards Asia, we may lose those opportunities because we are less competitive than other parts of Asia.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We may lose opportunities to countries that are cheaper but which can still produce better value than us.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We have to find the way to succeed.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But even if we succeed, the path will not always be smooth-sailing and I think it is important for individuals and companies to recognise that they have an important part themselves in this process.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Government can lay the foundation, it can create opportunities for workers to improve their skills.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It can also create opportunities for businesses to improve and digitise.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But, ultimately, the people who will benefit from doing so are the workers and the businesses themselves.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Even if a business succeeds in digitising and a worker succeeds in picking up skills, it is important for both businesses and workers to realise that this success is not permanent, nor is it guaranteed to last.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, the business that may be successful today may not be successful in a few years' time.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Even if we look at just the last 15 years.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Fifteen years ago, at the turn of this new millennium, some of the more successful companies were, indeed, tech sector, and everyone thought back then in 1999 and 2000 that tech was the way to go.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Nasdaq valuations of many companies exceeded even the mainboard-listed New York Stock Exchange companies.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But that was a very short cycle at that time.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It lasted maybe two or three years before the dot-com bubble burst and many people who had invested in picking up the skills to succeed in that environment were, all of a sudden, jobless.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is the reality of the new market and this cycle has repeated itself many times over, even in the last 10 years.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Shortly after that, from 2004 onwards, a commodity megacycle started, and suddenly, oil and commodity prices started rising and everyone thought that commodity, oil and gas were the way to go.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But in the last three or four years, this sector has had a big pullback as well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: A lot of the investments in that sector will be wasted.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There will be distressed assets going out and this is the reality of the future economy.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Even if workers pick up the skills, even if businesses adapt, they must understand that success is not permanent.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: What works this year may not even work in the next year.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Therefore, it is very important to be nimble.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The fact that you have picked up a skill and that skill has paid off for a few years is a good thing.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The fact that it does not pay off for a lifetime is to be expected.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is the reality of the future that we are going to live with.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is what will happen even if we succeed in having a vibrant and innovative economy.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The nuts and bolts of being vibrant and innovative are the reality that you or your business could become irrelevant very soon because someone else has come up with an innovation that makes you irrelevant.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For countries and big economies that have invested heavily in one area, one sector, for example, the Scandinavian countries back in the days of Nokia and Ericsson, they have also paid a heavy price when those sectors subsequently pulled back when the iPhone, for example, came and took the mobile phone market away.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, even if we succeed, it is important for individuals and businesses to know that things may happen beyond your control that will change the playing field dynamically.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While the Government can enable you to pick up new skills even in that situation, it is normal for this to happen and you have to be able to adapt to that.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Related to this is the second important thing that I think Government can do, and this is part of the Budget – Being a Caring and Cohesive Society.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: On the one hand, of course, the Government is saying that we will try and be there as a safety net.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For those who have low-income, there will be social transfers to help.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Education is now being provided at an even earlier stage, even extending to the preschool sector.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If we start enabling education at an earlier age, that will, hopefully, reduce the risk of inequalities, even at the time people enter Primary 1.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If one studied the Greek wisdom, Plato's Republic is said to be the ideal republic, all children will be taken away from their parents and put into institutions, so that everyone has an equal footing.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Of course, that is theoretical; it is unlikely to happen in practice.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I do not think any parent would want their children taken away.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But the reality is the more you equalise the education playing field, the better you are to have at least equality at the starting point.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This Budget is making important steps in that respect.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Accessible Primary 1 education was the best way to do it 30, 40 years ago.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: More than that, the second part that is important is also the sense of social responsibility.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There are gentle nudges in this respect in terms of encouraging charitable and community work and participation.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is important for people who succeed to also realise that their success is not just because of their own efforts or abilities, but also because of the environment they lived in and also because of luck.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The dynamism in the modern economy, the line between success and failure is sometimes not easy to identify.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Good people may fail, notwithstanding the best of efforts.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: People may succeed one year and fail the next.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is important for people to realise when they succeed that that is a time to be generous and to give back.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This sense of responsibility is something the successful have to understand and accept.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: That is probably going to be the key to being a truly caring society.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: When you succeed, you must understand that it was not you alone and "It is time for me to give back".

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And when that success disappears, maybe someone else will be kind to you at a time when you need it.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is the core of a caring and cohesive society.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But we must realise that our success is not our own and our misery is not always someone else's fault.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, we must take responsibility for our success while, at the same time, be gracious when we succeed.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: With the ageing population, with a shrinking workforce, how were we going to actually fund the increasing social spending needs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We have been blessed to have had a very generous amount in reserves and we have been able to use a fair bit of this through the Net Investment Returns Framework.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The big question is: will this be sustainable and, if so, for how long?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I am grateful the Finance Minister has put forward a plan – to me a fairly reasonable plan – to explain how this can be made sustainable.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These things are dynamic but it is good to know that this is what we have to prepare for.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is never an easy thing to do.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Of course, it is natural for there to be some push-back, for people to say, "Why do we not look at some alternatives?" The Workers' Party has suggested using land sale revenues upfront.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think my colleague Lim Biow Chuan has addressed this.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Some other countries do it but I do not think that is a reason for us to follow suit.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is more responsible for us to put the revenue from land sales or anything we get into the reserves and use any income we have from that.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Because, ultimately, land is an asset, and, I think as some speakers have said, it is our most finite asset.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The best we can do is treat that as an asset even after it is sold, and if there is income, then we can use that as part of the NIR Framework.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, in that sense, all this goes towards making sure that we have a financially sustainable Budget.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If there are investments in long-term infrastructure, then, of course, for this, we can use hybrid models, including, perhaps, borrowing to be paid for with future income from that investment.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: All these are financially sustainable ways and that is probably what the next generation will be most comforted by, that we will do our best to improve Singapore, to create opportunities in Singapore, to make it a place where they and their children will have opportunities.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Even if we succeed, there will be people who will have difficulties and it is important for us to be generous in that respect, with both ourselves as well as the Government, and to make sure that these people have a chance to get back up again.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We have had many analogies from different people on pushing the car, so that it runs on its own as well as a trampoline.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But I think these are all important analogies to let our people know what the real message is, that, ultimately, it is for you to be self-sufficient and to sustain yourself, but there are people there to give you a hand when you are down.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: (In Tamil):   This is an important Budget because it plans not only for the next year, but for beyond the next decade.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The world is changing rapidly and Singapore is changing, too.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The rise of automation is going to change the nature of work and, if our businesses and workers do not adapt, the jobs and opportunities will go elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is, therefore, important for both our businesses and workers to take advantage of the opportunities available to keep up and keep ahead of the times.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore, too, is changing, the biggest being the demographic change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These recommendations, however, are not mine but those of members of the public and civil society organisations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Together, we have brainstormed, edited and edited and edited and crystalised them into these 18 recommendations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My heartfelt thanks to members of the public and groups, such as Architects of Life, Autoimmune Illness Support Group Singapore, Singapore Youth for Climate Action, AWARE and TWC2.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Public Service is the heart of our entire system; they play a crucial role.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The success of this Budget and Singapore relies heavily on them and, this year, I will again focus my speech on how we can strengthen our Public Service.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the past year, I have reached out to public servants through closed door dialogue sessions to better understand their concerns, the difficulties they face and their aspirations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am grateful that they have shared their views with me very honestly and candidly.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They fear that they will be labelled as troublemakers, that their bosses will get angry; they fear that it will affect their appraisal and their promotion.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, Sir, after I delivered my Budget speech about the Public Service last year, there were Facebook comments and I received messages telling me to be careful, I will get into trouble for speaking up too much.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My sister was also passing me messages from her friends, telling me to be careful.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I made it a point to publicly say that I did not get into trouble for speaking up, that this fear is mythical.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Having said that, this fear of speaking up, whether we want to acknowledge it or accept it, is very real.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A panel of academics and former senior civil servants echoed the same sentiments at a forum last year, "that Singapore needs more people to speak up and challenge authority.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They lamented the reluctance of civil servants to pose contrarian views when facing political office holders".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But Prime Minister's wish for Singapore is that we "be blessed with a 'divine discontent' ─ always not quite satisfied with what we have, always driven to do better".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We do have this "divine discontent" but what we need to work on is ensuring we are able to hear it and that people are not afraid to speak up, that they do not accept the status quo and that they will fight for changes that will lead to an even better Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This fear of showing this "divine discontent" was also present in my meetings with the public servants.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I remember one sharing his views during the meeting, which was contrary to mine and halfway through he stopped and said, "Actually, I’m feeling quite afraid of opposing your views, as you are a Member of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And I realise that, subconsciously, I started my sentence by saying 'With all due respect, Sir', in the hope that you will be less offended with what I was about to say".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This culture of being afraid, of keeping quiet, of not rocking the boat, is detrimental to the Public Service, to any organisation and, most of all, detrimental to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This culture results in the loss of good ideas, of better ways of doing things and the loss of good public servants.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As the Prime Minister has so rightly said, "I try not to surround myself with 'yes, Sir' men.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That is important because if all you have are people who say, 'three bags full, Sir', then, soon, you start to believe them and that is disastrous.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: You need people who have their own views, whose views you respect, whom you can have a productive disagreement with and work on ideas which you might not have come up with, or who improve on ideas you had".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to make sure we do not have a Public Service filled with "yes, Sir" men and women.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To demolish this culture, we need to break our entrenched processes and bureaucracy – the same entrenched processes and bureaucracy Minister Ong Ye Kung spoke about at the Public Service Conference in 2017.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We urgently need to cut the extremely long red tape that may be frustrating not just for members of the public but also our public servants.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This will allow employees to review and grade their direct managers, resulting in a holistic 360-degree review, instead of just a one-way top-down appraisal system.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We do have some 360-degree appraisals currently but I understand that this is not regular and does not seem to include all public servants.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Teo had said that "leaders receive 360-degree feedback on their leadership qualities when they attend milestone leadership development programmes".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Again, many public servants I have spoken to fear a bad appraisal if they speak up, oppose their bosses' views and challenge the status quo.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: So, that is first question I am asked, "Will I get into trouble if I speak up and share my thoughts with you".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The second question is, "Even if I meet you and share my thoughts, nothing will change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: So, what’s the point?" The second question to be honest is much more troubling than the first.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It shows that these public servants have given up.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Why try, then get frustrated and then get upset for nothing?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We are in danger of becoming what Calvin, in the comic book Calvin and Hobbes, said, "If you care, you just get disappointed all the time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Some public servants I met also told me directly that it is almost impossible to feel motivated to do more because mediocrity is rewarded.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They want to make a difference, which is why they joined the Public Service, but they do not feel empowered to do so.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Through these meetings, I also learnt that each Ministry or Statutory Board functions differently.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Some public servants shared that they have regular dialogues with their CEO and Permanent Secretaries.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They have pigeonhole sessions where they can share their views openly.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Moving forward, we should continue this open and transparent practice of having all-hands staff meetings frequently, where all levels of public servants have direct communication channels with senior management.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We are all aware of the existing roles QSMs play.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These sentiments are already in the public domain and let me share parts of what Joanne Poh wrote a few weeks ago, in a post entitled "Civil Service: The Ins and Outs of the Iron Rice Bowl", where she provided advice on whether a career in the civil service is for you.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She said: "While there are many perks of working in the civil service, be prepared to work in an environment that some find stifling.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There tends to be a very strict top-down hierarchy where things are done 100% by-the-book.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: So, if you’re a young upstart who is dreaming of doing great things, be prepared to know your place, shut up and just do what your bosses tell you to." "Some people are happy just to be quiet and do as they’re told in exchange for a stable job with good pay and perks.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But if you’re the type who wants to be a superhero and change the world, you won’t find the outlet you seek in the service.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It’s ironic that MPs are calling for civil servants to be 'less rigid' and to 'think outside the box'.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Recently, MP Er Dr Lee Bee Wah, in an interview, even suggested that civil servants give 'cut and paste' answers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Ask any young civil servant and they’ll tell you that their superiors frown upon those who speak up or try to introduce fresh ideas." Sir, we urgently need to change this perception, change this system, recognise that we need to empower our public servants and ensure that the Public Service attracts superheroes and people who want to change the world.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have called for the Public Service to innovate.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And Minister Ong Ye Kung told public servants that, "The main obstacle is ourselves".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We, and by "we", I mean us in this House and the senior management in the Public Service – need to make sure that our public servants work in a system where everyone can speak up and where everyone can be heard.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the words of Napoleon, "The world suffers a lot, not because of the violence of bad people, but because of the silence of good people".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As I had shared in my Budget speech last year, "These are a rare breed who devote their lives towards serving Singapore".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But we now need to make sure that they do not work in a system where they feel they need to be silent, where they feel they need to be "Yes, Sir" men or women and where they feel that nothing will change even if they speak up.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Today, I would like to speak on the Finance Minister’s announcements on the overall national effort to better support our ageing population.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I agree with this new approach, provided the agendas and the targeted outcomes are spelt out clearly from the beginning and the execution details are adhered to in order to achieve the desired aim.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Lives where seniors, with increasing years, can still enjoy active, healthy and fulfilling days, live in their own homes and environment within the community and have little or no dependence on institutional care.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Many seniors prefer such independent living with their loved ones and friends in the community.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The ideal outcome will be a happy populace living well and gracefully.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I want to share my observations and experience in such care.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: In Kreta Ayer-Kim Seng (KAKS) constituency my grassroots leaders and I started Senior Activity Centres with the concept of promoting physical, mental and social well-being of our residents.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The first one was started 20 years ago with the help of Thye Hua Kwan Moral Care.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Three more SACs, run by grassroots leaders using the same concept, were added over the years at different precincts of our constituency.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I have always been an advocate of preventive healthcare because I am a medical doctor.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Hence, we have applied this concept at our SACs from the very beginning and have practised it till today.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The concept of physical, mental and social well-being is to facilitate our seniors to stay healthy through having daily balanced nutrition, getting physical activity and receiving cognitive stimulation.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: So, daily meals and programmes are provided with this aim in mind.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Physical exercise keeps the bones and muscles strong to minimise falls and fractures and to facilitate good mobility and independence.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Social and mental well-being prevents isolation and depression.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Together, all these will enable mobile seniors to be active, healthy and happy and to remain in the community by warding off frailty and dependency.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Frailty is a geriatric syndrome where organ function drops below a healthy level.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: When key organs, such as the heart, kidneys, lungs, muscles and brains, start to function below optimal levels, there will be reduced resistance to diseases, with increased incidence of incapacity and dependency.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Those who adopted a regimen of good nutrition, physical activity and cognitive stimulation were less frail than those who did not.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: In mild cases, their frailty could even be reversed.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Those who fulfilled only one factor, such as eating well but not exercising regularly, did not fare as well as those who managed all three.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Assoc Prof Ng Tze Pin, who led the studies, said, "Frailty is not an inevitable part of ageing and, with the right intervention, we can reduce the number of elderly who need to seek treatment for this syndrome".

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The SLAS, which was conducted from 2010 to 2013 and was first published in 2015 in the American Journal of Medicine, determined that a healthy diet for seniors is one that has sufficient calories and protein.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Assoc Prof Ng Tze Pin explained that, with old age, the body becomes less effective in converting amino acids into muscle, causing the seniors to be more susceptible to muscle degeneration.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: One way to slow down this degeneration would be to consume enough protein.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Through my observations over the years, I noted many of our seniors do not consume enough protein.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: One of the reasons is that protein is more costly.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This nutritional deficit is even more pronounced with those seniors living in 1- or 2-room rental flats.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: In contrast, 16.7% of the robust ones were living in other housing types.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Since Kreta Ayer-Kim Seng SACs have been catering to seniors living alone in the 1- or 2-room rental flats all these years, it will be interesting to find out the incidence of frailty for the seniors living at Indus, Chin Swee and Kreta Ayer precincts.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Perhaps, Prof Ng can be persuaded to send his team there for a comparison study.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Now that MOH will be taking ownership of the Senior Cluster Network (SCN), I hope MOH will promote this concept of promoting physical, mental and social well-being of our seniors and keeping them healthy, active and happy.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This will need the concerted efforts of SCN staff and stakeholders coming on board with a shared mission.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Execution of the programmes daily can run into many challenges as seniors may have their own preferences.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: For instance, one of our difficulties in our SACs is to get our seniors to do more exercises daily.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Some just want to only pick and choose the subsidised daily meals and outings, but are reluctant to participate in daily exercises.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Hence, SAC staff must adhere to the concept of physical, mental and social well-being through coupling the exercise programmes with meals, outings and fun activities to achieve this mission.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Incentives had to be introduced over the years to cajole more to take part in the daily exercises.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Activity, especially in exercise, is much reduced after retirement for many seniors to the detriment of their well-being.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Getting the involvement of grassroots, VWOs, volunteers and befrienders will add value to the SCNs.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Community involvement, especially grassroots assistance, will add a human touch and care to the seniors, especially those in need.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Taking them to festive activities organised by grassroots organisations can bring cheer to many, especially those living alone.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Visiting them, especially by familiar grassroots leaders or befrienders, at their homes when they fail to show up at the centres and giving them medical or social assistance quickly if they are ill are very useful.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: SACs are the choice centres for coordinating befrienders with the seniors and will be a one-stop centre for a targeted approach, preventing duplication for the best outcome.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I hope to see MOH expanding preventive healthcare and community care by setting up more SACs islandwide, especially at 1- or 2-room housing precincts.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Aged-care providers can now work with AIC as the single agency on the delivery of holistic aged-care services to seniors across both the health and social domains.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Preventive healthcare means to prevent getting diseases or disability.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Preventive healthcare also means a better chance of partial or even full recovery if treatment is provided quickly should one get sick.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Mr Tan, not his real name, is aged 88 and a member of Chin Swee SAC.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: He suddenly stopped turning up and was missed at the centre some 10 years ago.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: On visiting him, he was found to have suffered a stroke.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: He was in bed and could not walk.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Social help was arranged for his daily living and food was sent to him daily.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Within six months, from being immobile, he could slowly walk again.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Today, 10 years later, after his stroke, he is attending his SAC and other events organised by the Kreta Ayer-Kim Seng grassroots.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: My appreciation to all my Kreta Ayer-Kim Seng grassroots volunteers here.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Best of all, Mr Tan could continue to live independently by himself, albeit walking with a limp from the stroke episode.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I attribute his achieving partial recovery and independence to the appropriate assistance and support given to him at the very early stage of his illness.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I have other stories similar to Mr Tan’s but, due to time constraint, I can only mention just this one.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: With AIC under MOH being the agency in charge of SACs, seniors like Mr Tan can be referred quickly from the SACs for the assistance required to achieve better outcomes.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This is vital to prevent irreversible conditions resulting in permanent immobility.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Our ageing demographic profile will increase the number of seniors who require assistance in their own homes.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This is inevitable, especially in precincts with many seniors, such as Chin Swee precinct.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Over the years, many more residents have become “housebound” due to medical conditions and chronic diseases like diabetes and hypertension.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Thus, the need for homecare that enables these seniors to remain in their homes.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I want to register my thanks to both Temasek Care and AIC here.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Ageing Gracefully@Home (AGH) is a grassroots initiative of Kreta Ayer-Kim Seng Constituency that is intended to benefit weak seniors living alone in HDB rental flats in Chin Swee, Kreta Ayer and Jalan Kukoh precincts.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: It is a holistic care programme for seniors who are staying alone and are unable to take care of themselves.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: AGH provides, where required, one or more of the following services: daily meals, daily supervision, including daily home visits, befriender services, blood pressure checks, medicine intake checks, home counselling, nursing and homecare, transportation to and from hospital and physical improvements in the home.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: We paired an active elderly, or AGH Befriender, with a frail or immobile one, or AGH Beneficiary, so that the Befriender will visit and socialise with his or her Beneficiary each day.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: We also have a team of full-time healthcare aides and nurses to look after these residents.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This programme enables seniors, who would otherwise be hospitalised or be given some institutional care, to remain in their own homes.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This programme makes seniors happy with graceful ageing in place.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I hope AIC will be duplicating this at other precincts, especially those with 1- or 2-room flats.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: First and foremost, my appreciation to Finance Minister Heng Swee Keat for the delivery of Budget 2018.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, I would say it is a very clever Budget, especially on the fundamental change in the way major projects are to be financed in the future.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: It is a Budget that I consider as inclusive and progressive.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: It is heartening to see a well-balanced palette of offers and initiatives being laid down for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Primarily, this Budget prepares us into the future, both in capacity and economics, based on the three major shifts in the coming decade and yet mindful of the well-being of fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Though I mentioned I am positively impressed with the Budget, I am of the opinion that it is not a perfect one.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I shall not and will avoid being too picky.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Rather, I shall mention those which I believe warrant attention and I hope Minister Heng can reconsider them.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I feel this is missing and I believe this would make a big difference if the Budget could take this as one of the many initiatives to help businesses in the near term.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I would even go one step further – it would be great if we can find a structural solution to this.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Hopefully, we can hear good news in the next Budget year.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Next, I would like to touch on fostering pervasive innovation.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I was glad and delighted when I learned that innovation is mooted as one of the suggested initiatives in pushing forward towards a vibrant and innovative economy.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Upon scrutinising the numerous offerings, while I am appreciative and glad to see good ones on the table, I still felt incomplete.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: From financial tax deduction to the promotion of National Robotics Programme, I thought these are initiatives that touch on the surface.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: At most, it will only give a scratch.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: What I thought was missing is the soul of innovation.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Like I said, the numerous initiatives being suggested are all good.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Being a person myself who has been involved in technology and innovation for more than 30 years, I am very passionate about innovation.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: What I thought worth mentioning is the creation of the innovation spirit.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Unfortunately, I am unable to relate nor equate any initiative which supports the creation and building of the innovation spirit.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I had expected more to be done in our education system and curriculum that foster the spirit of innovation.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I was looking forward to a more fundamental shift which is so pervasive that it will become a basis in reshaping our innovation landscape.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: In Budget 2016, when I was a rookie Parliamentarian then, I did bring up the same topic on innovation and the culture of inquisitiveness.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I mentioned that innovation is an intangible capability and competence which needed to be nurtured with time.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: And it is important that this starts at a very young age and in schools.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I hope the suggested actions can be taken up for further discussion and reconsideration.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: While I am not rejecting nor dismissing any of the suggested initiatives, I thought the fundamental approach to fostering pervasive innovation is still missing.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Thus, Mr Speaker, I would like to suggest that a more fundamental approach towards fostering pervasive innovation to be reconsidered.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: With what is suggested today, I am not confident we will have a sustainable pervasive innovation landscape.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Let us do the right thing and do it right together.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: It is so heart-warming to see current running and new programmes and initiatives being rolled out concertedly, either enhanced or finetuned.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The SG Cares initiative has proven to be alive and serves as a national platform towards the spirit of a caring and giving nation.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Be it for individuals and families or senior citizens, there is always something for everyone.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: While it may not be complete, I believe the carpet has been rolled out and we just have to improve it year on year.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Our success as a nation should not only be measured by economic indicators alone.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: We must instil the sense of civic duty and ensure that everyone is not left behind.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Be it young or senior, able or disabled, capable or not, everyone must and should be taken care of.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: And we have SG Cares as a platform to help us formulate and sustain our system of caring.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The feedback from my interaction with various and numerous community leaders on this matter has been very positive and encouraging.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The continuation of support programmes is highly appreciated.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
