text: It is also worth mentioning that the effort of integration of healthcare and social support for seniors has been very much welcomed.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: This is expected to improve efficiency and efficacy when dealing with intertwined eldercare programmes, which have proven to be needed in our ageing society.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: While we move up the ladder to becoming a gracious and caring society, we should not and must not be over dependent on the Government to fork out grants and subsidies.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Instead, I believe we need to build an ecosystem in which a substantial part of giving is to be generated from the society itself.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: We need to find a way and establish a system which is sustainable, where giving is becoming a pleasure, and giving is highly motivated.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: A system of recognition and reward should be explored in trying to encourage giving.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps a progressive tax system for donors may be worth studying.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I shall be elaborating on this in more detail during the Committee of Supply (COS) Sitting.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: While this is good news, I believe it is not a guaranteed recurring item.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: From my experience in business, it is quite normal for a business organisation to share between 15% and 20% of its net income profit to its shareholders as dividend.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Likewise, the same rule can be applied here, with the remaining to be retained as savings for use in financing near-term programmes.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I thought this is a clever way of managing our finances.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: However, this can only be true if our Reserves yield a return which is higher than the cost of borrowing by the various Ministries when undertaking the major and infrastructural projects.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Based on past data on return on investment on the Reserves, I am confident that this is the case.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: What I would like to point out is that there will be costs incurred for any borrowing.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: There is no such thing as a free lunch.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: As major and infrastructural projects will have to be financed through borrowing, thus, the overall cost of these projects will be inflated by an additional amount equivalent to the cost of borrowing.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: As we all know, at the end of the day, whatever cost incurred will have to be borne by the customer or consumer.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Be it the new high-speed rail project or Changi Terminal 5, it will be no surprise that this additional cost will be at the consumer’s cost.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: In this case, the consumer will not be burdened by the additional cost of borrowing, which is the result of a new financial framework on expenditure of major infrastructural projects.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: (In Malay):   First and foremost, I would like to express my appreciation to Finance Minister Heng Swee Keat for the delivery of Budget 2018.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: It is, by and large, a very interesting one.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: In my view, Budget 2018 is an inclusive and progressive Budget.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: What is even more interesting is the new approach towards financing major and infrastructural projects in the future.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The current SG Care programme is also being finetuned and enhanced.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: New offerings are introduced to further complement self-help efforts by the people, with the aim of making it comprehensive.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Primarily, this Budget aims to prepare Singaporeans into the future, in terms of an advanced and progressive economy, as well as in terms of capabilities.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: It is based on the three major shifts in the coming decade, which are: a global economy that appears to be tilting towards Asia; the emergence of new technologies that are expected to change how we live, as well as the way we work and play; and ageing.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: As a corporate executive who has been involved in the engineering field for a long time, as well as in the largest Asian market, China, I would like to share my experiences.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: My disadvantage at the present moment is that I am unable to communicate fluently in Mandarin.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I am quite weak in the Chinese language and I know only a little bit.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Even so, I was determined and explored the China market.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I feel that mastery of the Chinese language can act as a catalyst if one wishes to explore the China market, which is and will continue to grow rapidly.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The China market and its state economy have been developing rapidly over the past 20 years.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: At the moment, this largest global economic nation in Asia, will continue to expand on the basis of its own economic policies.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Its policies are rather different compared to capitalist economic policies practised in the West.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Its economic policies with a communist character will continue to be implemented so that China can develop into the largest global economy and overtake the United States (US) economy.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: In my view, this appears to be its long-term objective.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: If this occurs, we will have no choice but to face this outcome and deal with it.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: During an economic forum organised by the New York Economic Society in 2015, the Chairman of Alibaba – which is one of the largest firms in the world – Mr Jack Ma said that his country is making preparations so that China will not only remain as a manufacturing and exporting country, but it will also continue to rise and it dreams of being a country that can import and consume.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: When this happens, China’s purchasing power will become a very huge attraction.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: It will also become the centre of the global market which will change the way we do business in the future.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: This is a development that we cannot ignore.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: This can increase the possibility that, in the future, our children can compete more confidently.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I am sure that if our children can at least converse in Mandarin, they will become more confident and have more opportunities in the future.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, the Singapore spirit is prevalent in Budget 2018, as highlighted by Minister Heng.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: In wanting to move forward and progress into the future with certainty, clear themes and strategic initiatives have been outlined and, at the same time, not forgetting to be rooted and stay humane as a caring society.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There is much in Budget 2018 covering key priorities which Minister Heng Swee Keat has outlined in his Budget Statement.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In my speech today, I would like to focus my discussion on social mobility and opportunity.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There is growing concern that the divide across Singapore society driven by inequality of opportunity is leading to social stratification by class.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The very fabric of Singapore and the Singapore Story is based on our people and how they have worked hard to build Singapore and a better life for themselves and their families.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Hence, it is important that our systems and structures must continue to ensure access to opportunity for all Singaporeans to do better and move up in society based on ability and hard work.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: When we talk about social mobility, we can give our attention to growth and how we make the pie bigger for everyone.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I do, however, hesitate to say that the rising tide will lift all boats as we have seen examples in many countries, including Singapore, where this has not always been the case.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While growth is important, if we are to be able to address the widening inequality, growth has to be coupled with access to and, more importantly, the ability of all Singaporeans to take advantage of the opportunities, if social mobility is to be achieved.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Budget Statement each year outlines the Government’s revenue and expenditure for the upcoming financial year and the Budget measures.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Each year, when I listen to the Budget, I pay a lot of attention to the measures because the measures outlined the aspirations of what the Budget sets out to achieve for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: These will provide opportunities and challenges for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: These shifts could improve social mobility or cause an even greater socioeconomic divide.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This will focus our efforts as a country to capture the opportunities presented by the shifts and capture them not just in Singapore but beyond.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It will also create opportunities by developing and attracting growth to Singapore and transform our businesses to be manpower-lean, to enable older workers to continue to contribute.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While this strategy cannot guarantee success, these policies seek to provide appropriate support and equalise access to opportunity.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The measures outline the Government’s intent to enable businesses and individuals to transform, build capabilities and tap on partnerships both locally and abroad to be able to engage and capture new opportunities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: These measures, as the hon Member Mr Azmoon had mentioned, are not exhaustive but they do set out the foundation and direction.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: They will need to be refined and to evolve, given the pace and scale of the shifts that confront us.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But if they are implemented effectively, they will enable companies and individuals to take advantage of these opportunities and have a very good chance at success.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Minister Heng outlined several measures to foster pervasive innovation to support businesses to innovate across the entire value chain.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Minister Heng did indicate in his Budget Statement that this cap is to ensure that smaller businesses will benefit more from this measure.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The feedback from SMEs on this measure as well as the increase of tax deduction for IP registration fees and for qualifying expenses on research and development (R&D) done in Singapore, is that for many of the SMEs that are developing in this space, many have little or no profits.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Hence, they would not be able to benefit from these tax deductions.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: More targeted grants oriented for IP and R&D-related cost would better benefit these smaller companies.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The new opportunities that are presenting themselves would also require new skills, know-how and relationships.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Building deep capability both for our businesses and workers is necessary to enable them to compete on value and skills and not cost.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The various measures announced focus on capability development in internationalisation, digitalisation and productivity improvement.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: These skills are needed to equip Singaporeans and our businesses to be able to have the know-how and skills to take advantage of these new opportunities in Singapore, regionally and globally, and to create value to differentiate and compete.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Another important factor that Minister Heng touched on as well was partnerships, both locally and abroad, to allow our companies to harness one another’s capability.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Because what is important is not just know-how but, to operate regionally, we will also need to build networks and plans that will allow these expansions.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I would now like to touch on the topic of our seniors.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There has been much discussion in the Budget Debate over the last two days on our ageing population and the need to strengthen the support for our seniors.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While I agree that this is important, I do want to talk about how companies can benefit from the mature workers in their workforce.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I have spoken about the movie "The Intern" in this Chamber before and I would like to use the example again.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: First of all, because I do not watch that many movies, so I do not have that many movies to give examples on but, actually, I thought it would help illustrate the point on the value of a diverse intergenerational workforce.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I believe this is an area that we have not tapped.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In the movie, Robert De Niro played a retiree who applies for a position in a "Senior Intern Programme" at an e-commerce company.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: He reports to the young successful founder of the company.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Although he is not familiar with the digital world, he makes the effort to learn and adapts well to the work and his colleagues.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In the movie while he is adapting to the digital world, what he has done is he has applied his experience, his experience as a businessman, his sharing of knowledge and, most importantly, his coaching to help the young founder get through difficult times in her business.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If tapped well, this intergenerational diverse workforce can make a lot of difference.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: All these measures, I was really quite excited about.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: You may ask, "Why is she linking social mobility to all these things about innovation?" It is because, ultimately, if we provide the platform, we enable with skills and we allow that collaboration to happen, then, ultimately, that spirit of innovation will depend on businesses and Singaporeans to do our part, to put in the effort to make the best of these opportunities, and then do better for both the country and for ourselves.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If done well, I believe that this is social mobility in action.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In this new world, with the shifts we are facing, what we are seeing is that when you do not have legacy, you can move a lot faster.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Therefore, it will allow that disruption to allow people to actually do better.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The opportunity to do better can be there.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But creating the environment to do it is what Budget 2018 is laying the foundation for.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I was very pleasantly surprised when the Minister shared the emphasis on the need to build capability and skills in the area of preparing our people to prepare for their financial needs at key stages in their lives.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Financial planning and making informed financial decisions are core skills and have profound impact on the lives of individuals and their families.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This is not a matter of whether you are rich or poor.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In many of the Meet-the-People Sessions (MPS) cases that I have seen over the years as a Member of Parliament (MP), much of the hardship and challenges faced by our residents and their families are usually a matter of lack of financial planning.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: When situations like sudden illnesses, loss of job or unfortunate circumstances occur, individuals or their families have problems coping if they had not done financial planning.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This impacts the person and the entire family in managing their day-to-day expenses, as well as longer-term commitments like housing and medical needs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, it is good that financial education curriculum will start with our youths, as financial planning must start early.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What are the enhancements to existing services at Housing and Development Board (HDB) and Central Provident Fund (CPF) Board to enable Singaporeans to also make better informed decisions in the purchase of their flats and retirement respectively that were mentioned in the Budget?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, Mr Speaker, Budget 2018 sets out to build the foundation and position Singapore for the future and for growth.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: By providing an environment to support access to opportunities and the ability to seize these opportunities will provide Singaporeans with hope and I hope also the aspiration to do better for themselves and their families.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: It clearly takes into account the need to keep up with rapid changes.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: From digitalisation to upskilling, to adoption of smart technologies.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The pressure to make major changes within a short period of time is daunting.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: On top of that, talks of increased spending in various crucial areas like healthcare, enhanced social safety nets and massive infrastructural developments, as well as the possible Goods and Services (GST) hike, have got Singaporeans waiting for this year’s Budget with apprehension.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Amidst a climate of uncertainty, the Minister for Finance has crafted a practical Budget that addresses all these challenges.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: He has outlined ways in which we can keep our economy innovative and vibrant, which means more opportunities for businesses and, in turn, a better future for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Businesses will certainly appreciate the strong focus on the available support for pursuing innovation and increased digital capabilities.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We will be making bigger steps towards our vision of a Smart City that is also green and liveable.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: A few days ago, Hong Kong announced their financial position as well.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In fact, one of the key focuses when I read up on it was how do they continue to invest in innovation?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: At a dialogue session with my residents in Sembawang after the Budget Statement was released, one concern among the residents was naturally on the proposed future GST hike.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The residents were asking whether this was going to make Singapore an even more expensive place for businesses and for us to stay and for tourism as well.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The appeal from the residents was to delay the GST increase as far as possible.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: If it is not 2021, is it possible to push it to 2025?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Better still, have plans to grow the economy, grow the income of Singaporeans, grow the revenues and incomes of all businesses and also let the revenues of the country grow concurrently.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: So, if we can, we can deter the GST increase indefinitely.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I support the Government's ambitious plan to develop a number of mega infrastructure projects and I support the financing framework proposed.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: But the more we build, the more we need to maintain.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Did the Government take into account the maintenance cost after the construction?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: And I am a little bit concerned whether our construction sector and manpower can handle so many infrastructure projects at the same time.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We are worried about whether we have the resources to do so, not just about finance, but also the space and the manpower.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Can we space all these developments a bit further apart?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Next, I would like to move on to our environment, a topic that I have been following closely with every Budget for the last 12 years.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Environmental issues are closely related to our sustainability and living standards.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Hence, it is important for us to continue to review and improve policies regarding this aspect.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The carbon tax, scheduled for 2019, was announced last year, and this year's Budget revealed further details on it.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The carbon tax will no doubt serve as a deterrent for big emitters of greenhouse gases.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: But we need to do more to push for more measures to help companies and households to reduce their energy usage and use renewable energy.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Will the Government introduce incentive measures like grants for projects to help households as well as businesses to achieve lower carbon emissions?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: At last year’s Budget, I spoke about exploring the use of solar energy, and I am glad tangible progress has been made.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: It is heartening news that the private sector, Town Councils and various Government agencies have been major contributors to expand solar capacity in Singapore in recent years.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The private sector accounts for 45.9% of total installed capacity, while Town Councils and Government agencies like HDB account for 44.7%.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The residential sector, comprised primarily of private homes, accounts for 589 installations, but that is less than 5% of total installed capacity.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The way forward is to keep the momentum and increase take-up rates.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: While smaller rooftop systems are less economical than larger ones, making them seem to be poor investments in the short term, increasing awareness on cost-saving abilities and installation procedures can help to generate more interest among private home owners.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In the United Kingdom (UK), the National Network for Low-Carbon Open Homes, an initiative by the Centre for Sustainable Energy, provides a platform for people with energy-homes to share about the technology they use, their experiences and to answer questions.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: For Singaporeans, the use of renewable energy is still in its infancy stage.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: So, perhaps a similar platform could help to generate awareness and interest.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I hope the Government can consider subsidised or free energy consultation to encourage more buy-in from the public.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The Government should also work closely with private developers and residents to facilitate convenient and affordable installation of solar panels for condominiums and other private residential apartments and commercial buildings.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: They can tap on the e-commerce platform for electricity to pick their provider.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: So, now would be an appropriate time to step up on public education and encourage households to make more eco-friendly decisions.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I note that many such clean energy projects are still in the testbed or pilot stage, and awareness and presence are lacking.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Not many residents are aware that their homes are being powered by or will eventually be powered by solar panels on roof tops.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: How many are aware that they will soon have a choice to use renewable energy in their homes and plan to make the switch?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: More importantly, how many Singaporeans see this as a good thing?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: It is important to get Singaporeans excited about renewable energy, and this can only be achieved through greater transparency and public education, even for early-stage projects.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: My next topic is on encouraging acts of charity in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I know the schools have encouraged students to donate an ang pow during the Chinese New Year period to the welfare fund so that needy students can benefit from the fund.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In the same spirit of caring and giving, I would like to propose that the Government facilitate giving by providing an easy option for Singaporeans who are keen to donate their SG bonus ang pow to local charities like the Community Chest or even the President’s Challenge 2018.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Maybe the Government can provide dollar-for-dollar matching to encourage the public to donate.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The goal of the scheme is to encourage employers to give wage increases to their employees.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: However, I would like to know if any study has been done on the effectiveness of the scheme.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: How many employers are doling out salary increases because of the scheme?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: On the flip side, many employers are also concerned with raising salaries as this will permanently increase their manpower cost, whereas WCS is a temporary one.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Most employers would prefer to share the company’s profits with the staff by special bonuses which are one-off and will not permanently increase their manpower cost.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: There are Singaporeans who have utilised all their credits, and there are some, on the other hand, who are waiting for a perfect course to come by.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: They are afraid to waste their current credit on a course that may not benefit them.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Why not top up their SkillsFuture credits since there is a Budget surplus?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: It also promises to shape a nation that is more compassionate and empathetic towards the less fortunate, with the Government taking the lead.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Whether we are considering the impending increase of the GST or the methods to finance future infrastructure projects, the issue of our rapidly ageing population informs every decision we make.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   On the new Budget announced by the Minister for Finance, from the impending increase of the GST, to how to finance future infrastructure projects, the consideration behind these issues is for our rapidly-ageing population.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: An ageing population and a shrinking labour market will bring about social impact and increase the burden on the next generation.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are many Government policies aimed at improving productivity, encouraging the adoption of technology and lifelong learning to maintain sustainable economic growth.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As the saying goes, "It takes 10 years to grow a tree and 100 years to educate a person".

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: After 2030, will this ratio still be a good one to allow Singapore to continue to be a liveable and prosperous nation?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will Singaporeans still enjoy a good quality of life without burdening the next generation?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): We have to address the problem of our ageing population through a combination of raising the fertility rate and controlled regulated measures in selective immigration policies.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Accept those who are self-reliant financially, can contribute good tax revenue for Singapore or who could create quality jobs for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Measures, such as ensuring more healthy golden years for seniors by upgrading their skills, boosting productivity and utilising technology, are all very well and good.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, there is no replacing having more babies, youths and an active workforce in our population.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Minister elaborate on what other options have been considered, resulting in GST being the preferred choice?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What is the average charity donation to IPCs made by Singaporeans per year for the past 10 years and whether it is stable or rising?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will the Government set up another charity fund to support ageing Singaporeans with public donations so that it may help mitigate the need of a GST increase?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These survey results lead us to ponder whether the many good traditions left by our forefathers will be affected by the changes in society.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These good traditions have laid a solid foundation for us.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): An article that I read in The Straits Times written by a very young writer by the name of Ng Chia Wee, I quote, "The family is an economically important societal entity.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Strong families are the bedrock of national fiscal sustainability.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If the family abandons its responsibility to care for its aged members, the Government will have no choice but to step in, leading to greater spending and thus revenue-raising… rising Government involvement in healthcare does not mean falling family involvement.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As Minister Heng remarked, rising amounts of healthcare and social expenditure will place greater demands on families and the Government." Sir, let me go back to speaking in Mandarin again.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin): The important value of filial piety is still very strong in our community and is deep-rooted.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Repaying our parents is universal, regardless of ethnic and religious backgrounds.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Except for a small number, Singaporeans shoulder the primary responsibility of caring for elderly parents.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With small families of only one or two children and increasing life expectancy for our aged, the road ahead will be filled with challenges.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On the other hand, parents love their children and will normally not want to become a burden to them.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many senior citizens I have met told me that they do not want to cause any inconvenience or trouble for their children, and they also want to leave something for their children and grandchildren.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is the case even for those whose children are doing well financially.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In fact, there is a very meaningful tradition in our Chinese community.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe most Members would have heard of it – the last batch of things or money left behind by the deceased – the shouweiqian (手尾钱).

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is the money or things placed in the hands of the deceased before nailing the coffin; the coins are called 手尾钱.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This money will be distributed to the children and grandchildren.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And the ritual is called fen shouwei (分手尾).

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The tradition believes that things left behind by the deceased will bring good luck for the family.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It symbolises the love from the older generation to the next generations, and also the responsibility on the part of the children to carry on the traditions.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To be able to bring luck and fortune to the next generations is considered a virtue according to traditional values which should be passed from generation to generation.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): The same article in The Straits Times that I read, and I quote: "those who do not desire to support the older generation (must) consider that they themselves have, in fact, been supported by this very generation many times over.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would young people have been able to enjoy the quality education, the vibrant economy, the high-paying jobs Singapore has to offer if not for the values and revenue generated by the work put in by those who came before them?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Paying more to support the elderly is merely a form of giving back… paying more now would mean paying less in future because it prevents additional problems arising in future which would require even more revenue-raising... policies to improve the healthcare infrastructure and social safety net will not just ensure better care for today's elderly but also ensure there are proper systems put in place to meet the needs of tomorrow's elderly.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although more top-ups would be needed to maintain these systems, the fact that these systems would already be in place will make things a lot easier for the elderly of tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Young people are, in fact, indirectly contributing to their own future care." Next, I would like to voice my support for the plan to borrow for new infrastructure projects.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Currently, some Statutory Boards are already borrowing, but doing so on a bigger scale is certainly the way forward.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As the Minister had pointed out, this would help to preserve our Reserves while spreading the costs over many years.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With Singapore’s triple-A credit rating, we will be able to attract strong interest and promote our local bond market.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If so, we have to be selective about which projects to be made accessible to the man-in-the-street.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Not all projects will be suitable for individual investors.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For projects involving participation across borders, such as Changi Airport Terminal 5, the Kuala Lumpur (KL)-Singapore High Speed Rail, the Johor Bahru (JB)-Singapore Rapid Transit System Link, foreign entities and investors should certainly be allowed to participate and subscribe.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, for bonds to finance projects like local transportation, we have to be careful that we are not too commercialised in our offerings.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I agree that it is important to keep half of our earnings from our Reserves.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must be mindful to grow it not only for ourselves but also for our future generations, as we earn the substantial interest income in perpetuity.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Having a large, ever-expanding pile of Reserves is our best guarantee against an uncertain future.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is the mountain backing up our Singapore dollar, ensuring its stability and strength.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When foreigners know that we have a good fiscal system, a prudent and responsible Government, they will not speculate against our currency.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our reputation has meant the Singapore passport has been rated the most powerful in the world.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have to continue our public education effort to teach Singaporeans the value of preserving and growing our national piggy bank – our Reserves.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Yesterday, our hon Members have suggested that we use part of the land sale to finance recurrent expenditures.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It may be good to know the pros and cons of the proposal.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: From the prudent and disciplined financial planning angle, the proposal sounds similar to the concept of reducing mortgage policy, enabling long-term asset to meet the recurrent expenditure for retirement needs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, one must know, and I do not think Singapore is going into retirement.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, one may ask whether it is the best policy as we need to work together to bring many more good years together to our children, to our next generation and to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the finance industry, even if you ask for a short-term loan using a long-term asset, a bank or lender would ask for a repayment plan for this short-term loan.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And this is also one of their prime conditions for granting approval.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For retirees, there are also many options, such as the Lease Buyback Scheme, to support their retirement.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I know Member Lee Yi Shyan encouraged us to use more Mandarin, but I am not sure whether toggling back and forth is what he meant.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But thank you to Mr Gan for keeping our interpreters on the ball.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Minister Heng Swee Keat referred to the 2018 Budget as a strategic and integrated financial plan for the long term.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Singapore has long prided itself for planning with a long horizon and being prudent with our fiscal spending, to the extent that some sceptics may say we are very conservative.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In the 2018 Budget, the statistics provided and plans announced are all focused to meet the projected needs in 2030.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: We know there are technological shifts that will impact our economy, an ageing population looms and we need to foster a caring society to strengthen the social aspects supplementing the Government’s efforts.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But beyond awareness of trends, surely, we must do something about it.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: When I first began working, I used to ask myself what is Singapore's Budget about and how does it impact me?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: What is this annual ritual that gets people talking and fussing around the same time of the year?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Like others, short-term handouts and schemes that directly impact us are what we are looking out for.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Longer-term plans that are announced usually do not retain in our thoughts for very long.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: After all, the Finance Minister announces many initiatives or schemes in each annual Budget.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: To many, the crux of the Budget is how much will I receive and how much will the Government take in return?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: To many, they view our Budget on a transactional basis rather than one that is about participative nation-building.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Recently, I had a dialogue with a group of 30 youths and young working adults.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: At the dialogue, we did an instant poll to understand what concerns them most about their future and Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Upon further discussion, I understood where their concerns arise from.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It is heartening to know that some of our younger generation do look forward to understanding what Singapore’s future is and think about how their future fits in the big picture.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Given that Singapore is a mature economy and the nature of jobs are rapidly changing, many are worried whether the economy can sustain at healthy rates and jobs remain available over time.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Unless we maintain a high employment rate and have reasonable income growing in line with inflation, it will be difficult for the working class to manage their living costs, contribute for future needs and save adequately for retirement.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: For a developed economy to maintain a sustainable growth rate of 1% to 3% is not an easy feat.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The real competition is dynamic and beyond our shores.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Regional, global markets with substantive scale and an active hunt for talents are what constitute our competition.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As workers, we cannot rest on our laurels and expect jobs to remain status quo or to remain readily available for us.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Instead, creating opportunities, being innovative and staying relevant are the new normal that we must learn to adapt to.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: We must possess the passion and drive to hunt for the next new and big thing.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Thus, the need for constant upgrading of job skills, value adding in our work scope have readily become a requirement on our part to keep abreast with time.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Many of you know that traditional engineering jobs involve extensive work with long hours.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: When I started out as a fresh engineer, there were many situations that I encountered which are not taught in books.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It seemed there were always new applications to learn, new situations to grapple with that required me to think on my own feet.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I recalled one incident where I was struggling and about to give up.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This was what my then line manager told me: "Do not shy away from the issues.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Always think and go beyond your assigned tasks, continue to evolve, build your skills frequently as the company or even the global market changes.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Someday, you will realise that you are the ultimate beneficiary of all the knowledge and skills that you have acquired in the process." I am glad to have heeded his advice as it has been one of the most practical and useful advice and has since been my mantra for skills upgrade and constant learning even before SkillsFuture emerged.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It has been one and a half years since the economic restructuring efforts began.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: To have a future-ready economy, we need more than just future-ready workers.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The companies also need to be forward-looking and continue in job creation.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In this Budget, much has been spoken about seniors aged 65 and above.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Earlier this month, a Motion about strengthening support for seniors was raised in this House.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In the Motion, we said that we should treasure and value our seniors, leverage and build upon the knowledge that they possess.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But where senior workers are concerned, I do not think the society has fully embraced this.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It is true that skills gaps do exist in the marketplace today.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But when the workers are equipped with new skills, will the industry hire those without prior direct experience or in the same field?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I feel that the largest gap in the restructuring efforts lies with the current hiring process.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Today, hiring managers are very focused on past relevant experience and not the potential or the value-add that each individual candidate can bring to the job.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This will limit how we can leverage the skills of individuals in adapting to uncertainty at the workplace.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I believe this is also one of the factors that stereotype and keep many in the mindset assuming older workers are a burden, whether in terms of health, efficiency or knowledge.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Way back in 1998, Amazon Chief Executive Officer (CEO) Jeff Bezos hired people with a different perspective.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Before he says yes to a new hire, there are three typical questions that he would ask: one, will you admire this person?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Two, will this person raise the average level of effectiveness of the group they are entering?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Three, along what dimension might this person be a superstar?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: He focuses on the value the individual can bring to the team, rather than what they have done in the past.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: With a limited and ageing workforce, I urge all hiring managers across the industries to keep an open mind, begin rethinking and take concrete actions around this topic, as you, the hiring managers, are the most direct and effective channel to create such change that we truly need in retaining the talents of both young and old.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As we move from growth to sustainability for the future, have we, as a country and Government, done sufficiently to enable this?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: For sustainable outcomes, I believe it is prejudiced to measure the outcomes purely on monetary terms.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: First, we are building a social ecosystem, not an infrastructure.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It is right to begin with the end game in mind.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This will necessitate the need to plan, design and build ahead of demand.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Take today’s healthcare in context, our healthcare capacity has yet to achieve an optimal point that supports all near-term needs, much less the future.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As we build more hospitals, nursing homes and care centres, it is equally important to look beyond the hardware infrastructure.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It is the holistic care ecosystem that we want our seniors to be able to age successfully in.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: What this means is that we must radically initiate at least one generation of healthy active seniors, where their needs are not dependent on healthcare infrastructure to manage multiple chronic illnesses or sickly conditions.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Instead, we want to build an ecosystem that provides quality social care that caters for their well-being, one which is less medically dependent as the seniors are socially active and mentally healthy.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Such an ecosystem will require investments of a different scale and in communal activities where the community or corporate organisations can be more actively involved.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Over time, we are seeing more value-for-money projects which are large in both physical and financial scale.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: We often raise questions when large expenditures are in view.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Naturally, people will look immediately to cost-cutting measures and easily follow the pursuit of low-cost solutions when, in fact, what we need is a balance between cost effectiveness and execution efficiency.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: On one hand, we understand the need to constantly scrutinise the projects under planning and development.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: We know the need to check whether projects are within budget, on time or whether any base parameters have changed with time and thus requiring adjustments to serve the primary purpose.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: On the other hand, as projects become more complex, what is not obvious and easily overlooked is how effective have we coordinated the execution efforts as a project team.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: How then, in the long run, can we ensure there is no wastage that collectively delivers more value than us purely squeezing the last dollar?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Lastly, the changing fabric of our social safety net.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: With shrinking family sizes, the nature of support required also evolves.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Over time, the social safety net may not be meant only for the low-income bracket.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: We should consider if strengthening this net signifies some intervention for the middle working class.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As we continue to ensure social mobility is a key pillar within our society, the changing demographics do justify the need of changing the fabric of our safety net to give it the composite strength, without which, it can be difficult for working family members, especially those who are the sole caregiver, to juggle between their work, children and caring for aged parents without external support.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Second, to enhance tax relief to children who are not living with their parents but are the primary caregivers.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Third, to consider modelling a time bank incentive scheme that provides rebates or care options for families who have contributed their time for other elderly within the community when they are still able.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, Sir, as a Singaporean, everyone has a part to play for the country’s development.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: We need to plan ahead and think not only for ourselves, but also for the future generation.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: However, the country's future development is full of challenges.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The short answer is: we must take charge of our lives and be responsible for our own future first.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As the saying goes, "The forefathers plant the trees and the descendants enjoy the shades".

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: At the same time, we should have foresights to plan ahead and build more with less resources.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is a prudent and inclusive Budget that aptly refocuses our attention on providing for the under-served and the elderly and looking at how taxes can help supplement Government revenues so that we are able to fund much needed and increasing social spending.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I support the Budget, but I also wish to speak on three areas that I feel we need to take a closer look at, whether in this Budget or future ones.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These areas are: one, older workers; two, women and flexi-work; and three, making taxes even more progressive.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In an earlier Sitting this month, some of our esteemed Members in the House filed a Members' Motion on the elderly, which is timely.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I had the privilege of speaking on the Motion, and I wish to reiterate some of the points I raised then here.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While I applaud the numerous schemes, programmes and initiatives to retrain older workers to help them reskill or cross-skill or deep-skill, what they also need are beyond skills and training.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: More importantly, our older workers need opportunities – opportunities to be given continued employment or job redesign or even opportunities to be mentors to younger workers.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The amount of knowledge, wisdom and experience they have garnered over years of working should be put to better use, specifically for our younger workers to learn from.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To elaborate, for older workers who may not be able to carry on with work that is rather physically demanding, they can undergo job redesign to become mentors or trainers to younger workers.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The organisation they work in can redeploy them as mentors or trainers who are able to train within the context and institutional knowledge of the organisation and be granted SkillsFuture grants for employee training, rather than engaging external training vendors who may deploy trainers who lack the experience, the contextual understanding or institutional knowledge of the organisation.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Another example is to retrain our older workers who are keen to explore working in a different industry, to be trained as early childhood teaching assistants or educarers, for example.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have brought this up before in this House.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Personally, I believe that older persons have much more patience to work with young children, compared to their younger counterparts.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Other than patience to nurture and help take care of the young children, it also provides the older persons an opportunity to laugh at the antics of the young ones and feel young again.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In 2016, Bangor University in the UK carried out an experiment in letting the elderly in a seniors day care centre and young children in Plant Parciau nursery in Caernarfon, Wales, a childcare centre, to interact and spend time together over several days.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It was found that, for the seniors, they felt happier and had a better sense of well-being.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For the young children, significant benefits were: one, there was an improvement in learning language, particularly dialects, and, in this case, it was Welsh; and two, a boost in their confidence levels.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This was because the children had almost undivided attention and encouragement by their elderly friends as they played.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am heartened that our Government is already piloting the co-location of childcare and elderly care centres over the next few years.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, I would also implore the Government to ensure the employment of more older workers in these dual-service care centres.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are many jobs that provide meaningful work for older Singaporeans to do, be it in mentoring, training or caregiving, beyond menial work, such as cardboard collecting or cleaning jobs, that some of our seniors feel they are destined to do once they reach their late 50s or early 60s.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It does not make sense that when our average life expectancy is at least 80 years old, our CPF contribution rates are cut at 56 years old.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Alternatively, if not cutting the CPF contribution rates may render our older workers less attractive to be employed, then at least make the reduction progressive over four or five years, rather than the drastic 11% cut in just over one year.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With more Singaporeans marrying later and having children later, it is quite inevitable that at age 55 or 56, we would still be supporting school-going children and elderly parents, as well as financing our housing loans.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The proportion of women who are actively working has been almost constant around 60% for the past few years.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In comparison, the proportion of men who are actively working is around 75%.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are various reasons that women may choose not to work or be employed.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These reasons range from childcare or elderly care responsibilities, to the decision to have a better work-life balance and work from home on a flexi-work basis.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Whatever the reasons, sufficient support must be given to our women in managing their numerous responsibilities.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, we need to continue our push to ensure better parity between men and women, be it in terms of salaries earned or in terms of familial responsibilities.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Men cannot be expected to always earn more than women in the household.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And women cannot be expected to take care of the family more than the men in the family.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Another concern that I have is that women are still not seen as a valuable source of manpower in the workplace.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Looking at the manpower statistics of 2017, there are still more women earning lower salaries compared to men.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I will speak about this in the COS debates.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While salaries are competitive and are based on merit and experience, there is still much that the Government can do to lead by example in closing the income gap between men and women, and in changing the perception of what women and men are capable of doing in the workplace.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For instance, there can be more women appointed to senior Civil Service or Administrative Service positions, the boards of companies and organisations, and even as ambassadors to other countries or to international organisations.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Other than appointments, the Government would also need to lead by example in allowing for more flexi-work for public sector and Civil Service employees, for both male and female employees.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Currently, flexi-work is more widely accepted in the teaching service.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One, that flexi-work is acceptable and can still render effective contribution at work; and two, that flexi-work is meant for both men and women, so that they are able to better manage work and familial responsibilities.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Taxes seem to weigh heavily on the minds of many Singaporeans, even in the lead up to the Budget announcement.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Comparing similar economies as Singapore, that is Taiwan and Hong Kong, there is room for personal income tax rates for high-income earners to increase.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In Taiwan, those whose assessable income is between S$105,000 to almost S$200,000, have to pay a personal income tax rate of 30%.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Those whose assessable income is more than S$200,000 would have to pay a maximum personal income tax rate of 40%.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Those whose assessable income is more than $500,000 and up to $1 million can be charged a personal income tax rate of 24%.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Those whose assessable income is more than $1 million can be charged a personal income tax rate of 26%.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In comparison, in Malaysia, the maximum personal income tax rate is 28% for those whose assessable income is more than RM1 million or S$335,000.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Another comparison, in Taiwan, the maximum personal income tax rate is 40% for those who assessable income is more than S$203,000.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Other than increasing personal income tax rates for higher-income earners, the Government can review the corporate tax rates, particularly for multinational corporations (MNCs) or large firms.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The current corporate tax rate for Singapore is 17%, flat.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Comparatively, the rate for Taiwan is 17% while that for Hong Kong is 16.5%.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While it may make it less competitive for Singapore to increase our corporate tax rate across the board, we can consider making it more progressive.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is a small increase, in order to keep Singapore globally competitive for businesses, but the revenue that can be generated to fund Government expenditure and social spending is significant even with this half to one percentage point increase.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Since personal income tax has already been made progressive, corporate income tax should also be made progressive, rather than the current flat rate that benefits high income earning MNCs or large firms significantly more than smaller firms.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For the imminent GST change, I can understand the need for the increase.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, the GST increment should be made gradual.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For instance, the GST can be increased 1% for one to two years, then another 1% for the next one to two years.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This staggered increment will give people more time to adjust to the increased GST and better manage their finances and expenses.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, I would implore the Government to look at how GST for e-commerce, especially in the buying and selling of luxury items, such as branded bags and accessories, can be enforced and collected.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While I do not have the data on this, I believe there is a substantial amount of revenue lost through e-commerce transactions, especially for large quantum amounts involving branded items.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There is still room for tax revenues to increase to front higher and increasing social spending, and I hope the Government will explore the suggestions I have made, even if not for this year's Budget, then for future ones.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I am very pleased that this year's Budget Statement by Finance Minister Heng Swee Keat aims at narrowing this divide.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: From supporting needy individuals, seniors and families, to encouraging the spirit of giving among Singaporeans, this Budget goes a long way towards enabling social mobility, which would narrow the class divide.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: However, Mr Speaker, Sir, the Government alone cannot bridge this gap.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Inequality is not a new phenomenon, nor is it unique to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: However, I would like to suggest that the country today is much better equipped to deal with this division than ever before.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: As Prime Minister Lee has pointed out just earlier this month, there is a concerted and coordinated effort by the Government to tackle the challenges of income inequality, social mobility and social integration together.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: The Government has intervened to help those who are less well-off in the areas of home ownership, healthcare and education, as well as means-tested assistance schemes for Singaporeans from lower-income households.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: But still, many Singaporeans look to the Government to resolve this class divide, a legacy perhaps of a time not so long ago when we looked to the Government's lead to transform mudflats into a metropolis.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: While there is trust between the Government and its people, there is also concern that, as The Straits Times opinion editor Chua Mui Hoong noted in a recent column, "today's citizens may be expecting too much of their leaders, thinking back to the pioneering generation.' In much of the discussion on inequality and the class division, many experts and Singaporeans have noted that the Government would need to do more to address inequality, which, left unchecked, would pose a serious threat to the country's social cohesion.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: There was markedly less chatter about what Singaporeans ourselves can do to address this divide.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: High social mobility in any country is influenced by structural as well as individual factors.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: The Government is already intervening more aggressively in structural and systematic policies.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: But what can Singaporeans, what can we do to address the individual factors?

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I am reminded of the words that we so readily recite every morning in the schools and once a year on 9 August.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: We each say, hand on heart, that "We, the citizens of Singapore, pledge ourselves as one united people, regardless of race, language or religion, to build a society based on justice and equality, so as to achieve happiness, prosperity and progress for our nation".

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: We, the citizens of Singapore, pledge to build a society.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: For as good as our Government may be, a community can achieve progress only if we acknowledge that change will come when we take ownership and make a collective effort to address inequality.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: And I would like to suggest that we begin where it always starts, at home.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: And as the country progressed, so did its people.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Social mobility matched economic growth as Singapore and Singaporeans worked hard to build their country and their lives.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: We have many inspiring stories of Singaporeans who have become shining examples of what it would take to succeed in spite of humble beginnings.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Our President, Mdm Halimah Yacob, the former Speaker of this House, is one clear example.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Her work ethics, resilience and consistent concern for the less privileged serve as a benchmark for many of us in this House, and an inspiration for every child who dreams of becoming President of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: What has moved many Singaporeans, in particular, is the credit that Mdm President gives to her mother for the person she is today.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: There has been much written about how parenting styles influence a child's development and social mobility.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Some may refer to this as parenting with heart and backbone, while others may say that it is about building resilience through positive psychology.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: It is really about learning how to get up when you fall, or to keep your chin up in times of adversity.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Many in this House might be familiar with this parenting style.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: But I wonder if "conscious parenting", as I would like to call it, is all that common in our very busy Singaporean households.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: As a business executive with no background in psychology or sociology, I can only share with Members my personal encounter with this particular style of upbringing.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: It might help explain why a person from a minority community, from an impoverished upbringing, with no "connections", and someone who is not a Government scholar, is in this Chamber today.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: The class divide in the early days were stark.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: But my parents kept us focused on the future.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: What we lacked materially did not seem too much because we always knew that things would get better if we worked hard enough at it.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Education and meritocracy, even in the early days of nationhood, served families like us – people who did not have much – very well.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I went to a mainstream primary school and never really felt out of place.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Most of the kids were from the same neighbourhood and we had similar backgrounds.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I was an average student from an early age.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I was far more interested in sports than I was in books.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: So, I did well enough to get into a good secondary school but not the school that my father wanted me to get into – the elite, top boys' school in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: You see, Mr Speaker, my father, who came from an even more impoverished background, had, through merit, made it into the top boys' school for his secondary education, and he wanted his son to do the same.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, it did not help that my eldest sister had made it to the elite top girls' school!

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: My father did not openly show his disappointment, though I could feel it.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: It was my first real lesson in "failure".

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: It inspired me to work hard and I ended up in the elite junior college (JC).

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: My first day at the JC was horrible.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: The majority of the kids came from the elite secondary schools and many of them were reluctant to mix.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Most knew one another because they moved in the same social circles and were family friends.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: They were driven to school, wore the latest sneakers and carried the trendiest school bags.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I went home after that first day of school and told my father that maybe I had made the wrong choice and should have gone to a more mainstream JC.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: My father said to me, "I did not bring you up to be a quitter.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: You got there on your own merit and you deserve a place in the school.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Just work hard, and the rest will take care of itself." So, I stuck with the school and, over time, I began to fit in.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I still did not get invited to the "cool" parties at the country clubs, but I made new friends – people from different races and different social backgrounds.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Many of these I made through school sports.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: And sports certainly played a key role in my integration in school when I faced a very stark class divide.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Through sports, being on the school team and playing in national tournaments meant that where I came from, where I lived in, what shoes I wore did not matter.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: We trained together, we won and lost together.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: We became brothers both on and off the field.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Some of my best friends today are friends I made playing sports.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: What I am today is very much the result of how my parents brought me up.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Their insistence that I face and overcome challenges, coupled with the positive reinforcement and support at home, taught me again and again that the positivity, perseverance and resilience would light the way to where I wanted to go.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: My parents never once allowed me to feel like I did not belong among the smartest or richest kids in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: They encouraged me to dream big and to take ownership of what I wanted to do and where I wanted to go.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: My teachers never held my background against me and the education system gave me the tools to succeed.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Many Singaporeans own their own homes, enjoy a high standard of education and healthcare, and go about their daily lives in a safe and secure environment.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Yes, there is income inequality and there always will be.
