speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: But the Government has taken the lead in addressing these issues with policies and assistance at every level and touchpoint.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: We have a meritocratic system that offers multiple pathways to social mobility.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, we must also create more opportunities for children of all income backgrounds to mingle and build lasting friendships.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: (In Tamil):   There is an ongoing debate in Singapore about the gap between the well-to-do and the less fortunate.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: There are many negative comments on this gap about the Government.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: The gist of it is that they say that the Government has not done much about it.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: What is true is that the Government alone cannot correct the situation.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I did not come from a well-to-do family and, in fact, the Government's policies have been the very reason that made me stand here and make this speech.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: To correct this situation, parents like us, communities, societies must encourage our youths to have faith in the programmes that the Government provides.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: We must make our youths as caring humanitarians.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: If they lead such a life, the gap between us will be reduced.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, Singapore was built on the values and hard work of our fathers and mothers.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: In striving to narrow inequality and class divisions, we need an all-in, whole-of-Singapore approach.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I am sure we are all now very intrigued about which school you went to.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I think we had an arrangement with the Government Whip that under the original schedule, I would be speaking today.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, I think The Straits Times was not aware of this.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But I hope that they would print a correction to correct any misimpression that has been generated by this report.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, Sir, I would focus my Budget speech on inequality.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This Budget has, as its third plan, a fostering of a caring and cohesive society.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The concept of care and cohesion, though not new, is timely, given the current public discussion of a class divide in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The recent study on social capital by IPS confirms what we already anecdotally knew.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It found, for instance, that, on average, Singaporeans who live in public housing have fewer than one friend who lives in private housing.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It found that people who study in elite schools also tend to be less close to those in non-elite schools and vice versa.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And earlier, the Member, Mr Ganesh Rajaram also shared his own experience, coming from a non-elite background going to such an elite JC.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We also see some measures in this Budget in the direction of mitigating the class divide.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, tax measures, such as raising the top marginal BSD rate by 1% for residential properties valued at above $1 million are geared towards requiring the better-off to pay more taxes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Another long-standing policy to mitigate inequality is that Government transfers are generally weighted in favour of those who live in lower-cost housing or have lower income, such as the GST Vouchers and service and conservancy charge (S&CC) rebates.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But, for all these moves made now and over the years, how well are we doing to reduce inequality and how much do we really know about the inequality that exists in Singapore?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What else do we need to look at or change?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Discussions on the status of inequality have tended to focus on numerical data, such as the Gini coefficient, which measures income inequality.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Nevertheless, Prime Minister Lee acknowledged in January that our Gini coefficient was still higher than that of many developed countries.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: All these point to high levels of income inequality.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Beyond numbers, it is also necessary to dig deep into the daily lives of poor Singaporeans and evaluate the reasons why they do not seem to be able to catch up with the rest of society.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In her recent book, "This is what inequality looks like", sociologist Prof Teo You Yenn shares powerful stories from her years of field work with families living in HDB rental housing.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: She writes, and I quote, "I saw how tough it is for them trying to balance wage work and care responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: By hearing their stories about jobs, I saw how hard they have to work and how little they get in return for their labour.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: By asking them about their children, I saw how much their kids struggled in school and how worried parents are that they would eventually have difficult lives.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: By listening to them talk about their crises, I heard about their feelings with humiliation, trying to access social assistance.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In paying attention to their everyday experiences, I saw how little dignity they are accorded in our society." What Prof Teo observed resonates with what we see, too.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While better-off Singaporeans plan for family holidays with their children, poorer families feel demoralised that they cannot afford to buy needed items that their children ask for.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While better-off parents are busy at weekends, sending children from one enrichment activity to another, poorer parents spend weekends working and worrying about whether their unsupervised children will fall into bad company.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Many of our lower-income residents work hard and even two jobs but may still be unable to pay their bills.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Richer children are served and even spoilt by domestic help.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Poorer children shoulder responsibilities, like caring for younger siblings and even being spokesmen for their parents who do not speak English.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In a Parliamentary answer in February this year, Prime Minister Lee emphasised, and I quote, "Every citizen, no matter what his social background is, must have the opportunity to do better and move up in society based on his efforts and talent.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Nobody should feel that his social position is fixed based on his parents' income level or position in life." Can we say today that the lot of our poorest fellow Singaporeans is due to their lack of ambition or talent?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Or does the system itself inadvertently make it difficult for them to succeed and thus perpetuate inequality?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For example, do Government policies support poor families with adequate and sustainable care for children?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Does our education system penalise those who did not have a leg-up in preschool?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Do housing policies unjustly discriminate against those whose marriages fail?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How have children been impacted by their parents' circumstances and were they supported or facilitated to break out of the poverty trap?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Earlier, the Member Mr Ganesh Rajaram shared his own experience of social mobility.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And I do not know how old he is.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But looking just at physical appearance, he could be born between the 1960s and 1970s.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And I think we can all agree that for persons born during that period, there was probably significant social mobility when compared to parents of the earlier generation.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But an important question is, moving forward today, for the new generations of Singaporeans, is social mobility still there or is it becoming more and more difficult for people to move out of certain social classes?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These are serious questions deserving our serious study.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To get answers to these critical questions, it is important to do longitudinal studies to track the fate of families over time.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Has the Government, for example, started commissioning independent studies on social mobility using longitudinal data?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Government has noted in the past that we must not allow an underclass to form, and so, the Government has to show commitment to this goal.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The competition in the education system is high.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Just look at the money spent on private tuition and other enrichment classes which, in turn, adds to the economic stress that families face.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Why is it so important to show a commitment to the goal of reducing inequality and increasing social mobility?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Because it is vital to our very existence as a nation.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We recite the words of the pledge daily.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How can we say these things about justice and equality, happiness, prosperity and progress for the nation, if we are perpetuating a society where citizens are not equal, where some are seemingly having little hope and doomed for failure, while others boom ahead?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Will there eventually be an erosion of trust where a class divide makes it harder for people at the bottom and the middle to identify with those at the top?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We fiercely guard our sovereignty and expect Singaporeans to defend Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But will the day come when Singaporeans, who find Singapore a cold and cruel place, have no motivation to defend it?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This will be a disaster at all levels.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If one compares the coverage of private insurance plans and the coverage under MediShield Life, one will observe that there is significant inequality in access to healthcare that affects the poorer and older Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As regards insurance coverage, there are some practices in the healthcare industry that need looking at.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: One such practice is that of some insurance policies providing full coverage for hospitalisation bills.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such insurance policies undertake to pay for surgeries as long as they are done as day surgeries or if the patients stay at the hospital.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: All charges will be paid by the insurance company "as charged".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such policies do not require the patient to pay any deductible or make any co-payment.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In contrast, MediShield Life understandably has deductibles and co-insurance to avoid over-consumption.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: One feature of MediShield Life, however, is that the annual deductible rises when one passes 80 years old.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Has the Government analysed how this increased deductible has affected the consumption and delivery of medical services to our most senior citizens?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To give one specific example, operating on a trigger finger release usually costs less than $2,000.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, those aged 80 and above cannot claim the expenses for the surgery, but those who are younger can claim part of the expense as the deductible is lower for younger people.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Why this reverse discrimination for our older citizens?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Coming back to the private "as charged" insurance policies, there is another aspect that needs review.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Has the Government studied the effect of such full coverage policy on the behaviour of patients and its implications?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: When a person has to undergo a minor surgery which could be done at the outpatient clinic, does he choose instead to do it as a day surgery or as an inpatient in a hospital, so as to be able to tap on the insurance for full coverage?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Does such insurance result in some unnecessary surgeries when more conservative treatments will suffice?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Are there inefficiency and a waste of expensive resources caused by such policies?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is important to review the kinds of insurance schemes in the market, so as to discourage over-consumption and inefficient use of resources.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There have to be deductibles and co-payments for all medical insurance schemes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Regulators have to direct their attention to this area.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We have to drill deeper into the sources of inequality and take concrete steps to remedy it.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: As a stakeholder in the private sector and a Member of this House, I am particularly interested in the Industry Transformation Maps (ITMs) that are supposed to pave the way for 23 industries to be future-ready.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Industry players and Singaporeans need to "A" adapt to the reality of technology disruptions and embrace the benefits of digital transformation.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Many industries are experiencing digital disruption, from print newspapers to television (TV) broadcasts, to brick-and-mortar shops, and traditional taxi services.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong said during the 2016 National Day Rally that digital disruption is the "defining challenge" facing Singapore's growth.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: There is no doubt that companies need to embrace digital technology, otherwise, their expiry date is near.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: We also need to help the workers to adapt.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: At the same time, the Government needs to be flexible and even-handed in their regulatory framework in managing the digital economy, which is the topic of my next section.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Regulators need to "B" blur the boundaries when it comes to regulating industry players, which no longer operate in industry-specific silos, but extend their tentacles into the provision of all sorts of conveniences for the consumers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The most successful companies are those providing services across different industries, building an ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Starting out as an e-commerce marketplace in 1999 in the form of Taobao, it now also operates Tmall, search engine eTao and, more famously, Alipay, which is China’s biggest online payment system.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: It has further ventured into finance and banking with its Ant Financial Group.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Closer to home, we have an Indonesian ride-hailing company Go-Jek.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: It started off as a modest motorcycle-hailing company in 2010.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Today, it offers private cars and cabs, as well as on-demand services, from beauty treatments and massages to home cleaning and food and cargo deliveries.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Like Alibaba, Go-Jek also launched an e-wallet called Go-Pay.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Go-Pay even facilitates mobile transfers between accounts and cash withdrawals from automated teller machines (ATMs) at partnering banks.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: We need to encourage such creative diversification from our own entrepreneurs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Hence, regulatory bodies need to rethink how to regulate such multimodal industries or "ecosystems" differently.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: It is important to strike a balance between over-regulation which would stifle creativity, and under-regulation which might create unfair competition to existing players.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Given the onslaught of cheap money under the guise of ride-hailing technology, all the taxi companies in Singapore have no choice, but to form an alliance with the two dominant ride-hailing companies.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: For commuters, it means more choices as they can now hail taxis from the taxi stands, on the roads, on the streets and from the taxi company's call centre or app, as well as through the ride-hailing companies, under different pricing mechanisms.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Out of 100 calls, 92 calls must be matched with taxis.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, with a good proportion of taxis responding to third-party ride-hailing app, it means that there are fewer taxis on the road to take on requests coming in through the taxi companies' app or call centre, which is what LTA looks at only.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This means that the taxi companies are more susceptible to failing QoS because of the effort to provide more choices to the commuters.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Ideally, LTA needs to consider taxi booking data from both the taxi companies and third-party ride hailing companies that dispatch taxis collectively.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This is an example of how the incumbent industry players are over-regulated while the new players, disguised as "technology companies" are under-regulated.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The reverse could be true in other industries.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: What it means is that regulators need to keep up with the times.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Indeed, an article in The Financial Times suggests that traditional rule-making is unable to keep up with digital businesses.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: One suggestion put forth for greater flexibility is that the Government can monitor the achievement of established targets, for example, accident rate, but it should not prescribe the means of achieving such targets.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Instead, the regulator could consider allowing the industry players to design their own approach. "C" for competitive.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: One of the ultimate outcomes of the ITMs ought to be making our local companies more competitive not just locally but also regionally and perhaps even globally.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, are there efforts being made to nurture local firms as we expand the rail network?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Can local firms eventually construct Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) tunnels?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Can homegrown technology companies eventually build trains or provide the signalling systems?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Most of the tunnelling works in Singapore are undertaken by foreign contractors like Japan-based Nishimatsu Construction, China-based Shanghai Tunnel Engineering Co, and German-based Zublin.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Local construction companies typically take on the role of a sub-contractor to these foreign companies.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Similarly, for rolling stock, such as the physical train itself, and the signalling system which is the brain of the train system, they are primarily provided by foreign firms, such as Thales from France, Alstom or Siemens from Germany, Bombardier from Canada and Kawasaki from Japan.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: From the inception of our MRT system until today, 30 years has passed, we have to rely on these foreign companies to replenish our rolling stock, upgrade our train or upgrade our signalling system.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In fact, the current signalling system in many MRT lines is like a black box to us.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In 12 years' time, when we double our train network length, will we face the same problem.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Many of these large international companies grew with government support.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Thales, for example, formerly known as Thomson CSF and Thomson SA, had the support of its government to privatise in 1998.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The move had helped the company to expand globally.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: For Alstom and Siemens, they are competitors, but they merged the train building business recently with the support of their governments in order to compete better with China.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Bombardier was founded in 1942 and, as recently as last year, the Canadian government provided interest-free loans worth over $370 million to the company to support its projects.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Of course, this would be advantageous, as working with these MNCs will allow us to learn their expertise, technologies and processes.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: For the first 180 km of MRT lines, our local firms played a supplementary role in building, supplying and upgrading the MRT system.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: For the next 180 km, I hope our local companies can play a significant role in building, supplying and upgrading our Singapore MRT system that we can be proud of.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The same goes for other industries where we think that it is important to acquire our own expertise, build on it and compete globally.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Finance Minister Mr Heng Swee Keat had said that ITMs have "to prepare our companies for a new phase of growth".

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: ITMs have to help companies and Singaporeans "A" adapt to the new reality of digital transformation, "B" regulators need to blur the boundaries when regulating companies in the digital economy, and "C", ultimately, ITMs have to nurture local companies to be competitive not just locally but also to win contracts and business in the region and the world.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Perhaps, the ABC for ITMs could be seen as part of the foundation to propel us into the future.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: She noted that the income gap of the rich and the poor is increasing and asked what the Government has done to narrow the gap.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I just want to explain to her that I also have 462 units of 1- to 2-room rental flats in my division, and we have been taking advantage of some of the Government's policies to help our rental flat residents.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I always tell them it will be a success if I can help them move out of the rental flats.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: There is another scheme on childcare subsidy that helps co-pay the childcare centres' fee.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: We have been helping a lot of the children to go into childcare centres.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In addition, all Members of Parliament who have rental flats also work very hard with different voluntary welfare organisations (VWOs) to help the residents to upgrade.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: There is a kidsREAD Programme, for example, which is spearheaded by the National Library Board (NLB), and we have capitalised on it and have volunteers to help the children from the low-income background to read better, so that when they go to Primary 1, they can do better.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In my division, we also have this project "Hand-in-Hand", where we get many volunteers and donors to give food to our residents every month or every other month.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: We also set up, for example, a provision care corner to help the rental flat residents in the primary school to learn piano, guitar and robotics, so that they can have more confidence and, subsequently, do better in school.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: We also have a youth centre for vulnerable teenagers in my division.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: All these probably are not confined to my own division.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Many other Members of Parliament who are hardworking on the ground will be able to take advantage of the Government's policies and grants to help rental flat residents to do better in life.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: These are things that we need to discuss further.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, I just wanted to clarify that point.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I will first touch on the area of care for our elderly.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe the trend will continue to grow.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Together with a projected increase in our elderly population relative to other age groups in the coming years, it is important that we get our policies on elderly care right.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government seems to be still finding its way in deciding how extensive the role of the State should be when it comes to caregiving.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If it prefers to continue to rely substantially on caregiving through an individual’s family care network, it should consider giving more support at every level to the supporting family as well as to caregivers, including supporting the caregiver who has to stop work, and deciding what is a decent level of support for the caregiver.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Further, with the growing number of elderly or elderly singles living alone, the Government needs to put in place adequate resources and the infrastructural support for assisted living.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Government policies often involve drawing a line between competing imperatives.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When it comes to policies affecting elderly care and their well-being, may I implore the Government to give priority to the consideration of enhancing elderly care efforts?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The enhancement of the Proximity Scheme Grant for both families and singles will ultimately benefit our seniors as children are encouraged or assisted by the enhancement of the grant.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Before the announcement, the one-time grant is currently given only to singles who buy a resale flat to live with their parents.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While it is good that the Government now recognises that singles are often a key source of caregiving support within their families, in my view, many singles end up taking a larger role in caregiving support than their married siblings who may be bogged down with caring for their children.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hence, such singles do not deserve a lesser grant than their married counterparts, whether they are living near or with their elderly parents.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In fact, arguably, many married siblings benefit more from living near their parents than their single siblings as they benefit from their parents helping out in caring for their children.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Whatever rationale the Government chooses to use to give married children a higher grant, I hope the Government will consider equalising the grant for the reasons I have given.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Ultimately, when we make things easier for the caregiver, single or otherwise, the ultimate beneficiaries are the elderly parents of the caregiver.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Without the caregiver, the state or the society may also end up having to provide additional resources.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should always take care that our policies, however well-intentioned they are, do not become too rigid that it becomes a burden or a source of stress for our elderly and seniors or their caregivers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Foreign Domestic Worker (FDW) levy will be increased in two ways.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am concerned this may affect households employing two helpers, one to handle all the housework and one to look after elderly parents who may be bedridden or even just require attentive care at all times while their children are working.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the second FDW is not allowed levy concession, this increase in levy will add to the financial burden of their children.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can the levy increase be exercised more equitably in favour of families needing two FDWs to look after elderly parents as well as doing housework?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can the Government not distinguish the example I mentioned from the situation of, say, a wealthy family living in a big house requiring more than one FDW?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Again, I hope the Government will regard enhancing elderly care efforts in priority to other considerations on this issue.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A Fengshan resident shared with me his frustration of having to pay the full Singles Premium for his 2-room flexi flat.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: He is approaching retirement in a few years.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To prepare for retirement, he is trying to save up as much as he can from his modest monthly income of $700.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: His existing savings are precious to him for the same reason.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: His excitement at getting a new 2-room flexi flat was somewhat dampened by the burden of the additional $15,000 Singles Premium he had to pay.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While I fully understand the rationale of having the Singles Premium, must it always be rigidly enforced against people of all ages from 35 upwards?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope the Government will relook how it applies its Singles Premium policy on elderly singles.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Elderly singles may require more support from the Government.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They will likely have fewer options than their married counterparts insofar as family financial support or family caregivers are concerned.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When they are not self-sufficient or cannot care for themselves, the state may ultimately have to step in anyway.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can we apply a little more flexibility for the benefit of these single seniors?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can we place a greater premium on elderly care and welfare in such a case?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, the Government can consider helping all singles aged 55 and above purchasing 2-room flexi flats for the first time on a shorter lease by reducing the Singles Premium.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   In his Budget Statement, Finance Minister Heng Swee Keat said that the ageing population is a challenge that we have to face.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: From 2006 to 2016, the number of senior citizens who live alone will more than double to nearly 50,000.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government estimates that the ageing population will continue to grow in the next few years, and we need to have more comprehensive measures to take care of our senior citizens.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At this point, it appears that the Government has yet to reach a conclusion on what kind of extensive role the Government should take on, in terms of caring for the elderly.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the policy objective of the Government is for elderly Singaporeans to be cared for by their own family members, more support should be given to each of these families in all aspects.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These include helping caregivers who have to quit their jobs to take care of their elderly family members.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In addition, with more senior citizens and single senior citizens living alone, the Government also needs to provide adequate resources and develop related infrastructure and facilities.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government needs to balance various needs in policymaking.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With regard to policies that affect the elderly, I urge the Government to prioritise the enhancement of policies related to caregiving.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Generally, prices of flats in mature estates tend to be higher.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Proximity Housing Grant encourages more families and singles to live close to their parents or live together with them in order to take care of them.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am delighted to see that singles can now enjoy Proximity Housing Grants of $15,000 when they purchase a resale flat near their parents.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For singles who purchase a resale flat to stay with their parents, the grant has also increased to $15,000.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is encouraging to know that the Government is aware that senior citizens are often cared for by their unmarried children.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singles tend to shoulder heavier responsibilities because their married siblings are probably caught up with taking care of their own children and are, therefore, unable to share the responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Therefore, I believe singles should enjoy the same amount of housing grants as those who are married.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Regardless of the basis for giving more housing grants to married couples, the same amount of grants should be given to singles who wish to live near or with their parents.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, I would like to ask the Government to consider increasing the subsidy for singles who choose to live near their parents.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When help is provided to the caregivers, regardless of whether they are single or married, their elderly parents will ultimately benefit.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If they are unable to care for their parents, the Government and welfare organisations may eventually need to render more assistance.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government needs to exercise flexibility in the implementation of policies.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am concerned that this will affect families that employ two FDWs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These families may require one helper to do the household chores, while another takes care of the elderly family member who is bedridden or needs to be cared for round the clock.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If they cannot enjoy the subsidised rate when employing a second helper, it could increase their financial burden.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Therefore, I would like to urge the Government to reconsider this decision.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is it possible to consider more reasonably the needs of families which require a helper to care for their elderly family member?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These families are different from the wealthier families that need two helpers because they have a bigger house.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A Fengshan resident shared with me that when he purchased a 2-room flexi HDB flat from the Government, he had to pay an extra premium of $15,000.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As he only earns a monthly income of $700, he needs to save as much as he can because he is retiring in a few years' time.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To him, this premium is a huge burden.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I understand the objective of this premium, but I also hope that the Government can review this policy.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Older singles are different from those who are married with a family, who can be supported financially by other family members.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Therefore, I feel that the Government should adopt a more flexible approach.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: By doing so, the Government can maintain the policy, while helping elderly singles who are less well-off to buy a home they can retire in.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I declare my interest as a shipping lawyer.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The MTP looks to using automation, digitalisation and artificial intelligence (AI) to develop new technologies, designs and operations concepts that can be deployed in Tuas and Jurong Port.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With the emphasis on strengthening maritime traffic management capabilities and enhancing operation efficiency and improving safety and security, it should benefit our port operators and related auxiliary industries in automation, AI and robotics.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have one of the world's leading ports.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thus far, despite our charges being relatively higher than our competitors, we managed to stay ahead through technology and efficiency, helped by our favourable location.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How long will we continue to enjoy this location advantage is anyone's guess.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will the proposed deep sea port in Malacca pose any problem for us in the future, especially if Chinese or other players can help to overturn the deficiencies which have long bugged the Malaysian ports?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When will the Northern Sea route start pulling away vessel traffic now passing the Strait of Singapore?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With polar caps melting further in future, will technology-enhanced port operational efficiency and traffic management alone always be sufficient to fight off challenges, such as savings of substantial travel time of 30% with the Northern Sea route?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our leading shipyards are the yards owned by the Keppel and Sembcorp Marine groups which are reputable leaders in offshore-related buildings, like oil rigs and semi-submersible and Floating Business Storage and Offloading (FBSO) conversions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With uncertain offshore markets, our leading shipyards should focus on developing new niche areas of ship and offshore building, like the way it developed its niche in offshore building over the years.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It remains to be seen whether this will become their new niche areas or be able to contribute to the level of growth that offshore building afforded them in the past one and a half decade.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The search to develop new niche areas should not be confined to our leading shipyards.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Business has been patchy for our other small players in recent years and the rampant demand for tug building a few years ago has subsided.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While the use of shipyard facilities in nearby Batam has helped some of our shipyards in managing their costs, competition by yards in other countries, especially China, meant that our yards are not in the market for the building of cargo or passenger vessels, with the exception of tugs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For most of these firms, in recent years, they have been occupied with repairs, conversions and the odd small building jobs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How many of our small and medium enterprises (SMEs) are in the position to compete in the LNG and offshore renewables identified in the ITM for marine and offshore engineering?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Besides this area, what are the future options that SMEs should prepare for?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our maritime business community consists of many more SMEs up and down the value chain, beyond ship and offshore building and port management.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I agree with the current push for innovation, building on autonomous systems, robotics and AI and data analytics, as well as for digitalisation under the current sea transport ITM.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But we must not forget those who may not benefit from this development.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many SMEs are players specialising in certain specific areas of business or capability.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Unlike Government-linked companies, the size of SMEs may limit their ability to scale up in order to compete for businesses with bigger or established players internationally.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Straits Times report of the launch of the ITM for marine and offshore engineering cited a pressing need for smaller firms to build up their capabilities so that they can benefit from this trend.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Perhaps, for some SMEs especially, it is not merely about building up alone but needing to work together with other players providing different expertise to take on bigger projects.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our local banks can help with the financial support and the Government can consider providing initial funding and support for setting up.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is different from efforts aiming to help SMEs directly as individual businesses.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: SMEs with different specialisations can be integrated to work together, develop products and pitch for bigger businesses and contracts internationally, as a consortium, tapping on one another's expertise and sharing economies of scale.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such a programme can include both existing SMEs from the maritime industry as well as those which are currently outside the sector.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A firm from outside the industry may well bring with them different ideas or different ways of handling comparable projects.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Technology Centre for Offshore Marine Singapore can definitely play a role in providing appropriate support for SMEs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There has been much talk about the Belt and Road initiative and potential benefits.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How can our shipping and logistics and offshore businesses make use of our relative strengths and resources to work hand in hand with our Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) neighbours in the Belt and Road initiative around Southeast Asia and beyond?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government can lead a study into the likely opportunities for our involvement in Belt and Road projects in the region and consider how our businesses can jointly market ourselves to complement and value-add to ASEAN companies to take on Belt and Road projects.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I wish to address two issues: one, the elderly, and two, leadership.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The Minister has identified ageing as one of the major shifts that will affect our future.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: He has rolled out a whole series of initiatives to address the issue, including more money for hospitals and senior care centres; strengthening the Agency for Integrated Care (AIC) and expanding the scope of the Pioneer Generation Office (PGO) and the Community Network for Seniors (CNS).

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: These initiatives will have a direct impact on the elderly over the coming months and years.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I have spoken about them several times in this House and I am glad that this is happening.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: However, I believe there is more we can do.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: For a start, can we look at the issue a little differently?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: But I wonder, is it time for us to reconsider the definition of elderly as those being 65?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: If we look around us, we can begin to observe many in their late 60s and 70s who are still healthy, active and gainfully employed.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I believe that the elderly of today is not a good proxy for the elderly of tomorrow.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In 20 years’ time, many Members in this House would be in their 60s and 70s.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Using ourselves as examples, the 40-year-olds of today are smart, tech-savvy and self-sufficient.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In 20 years' time, we will have a host of capable people who are mobile and independent.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The challenge for us is to build a society that encourages our seniors of the future to thrive and live active lives.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: There are five areas we should think about: (a) healthcare, (b) communities, (c) education, (d) volunteerism, and (e) connecting the four is technology.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In his Budget Statement, the Finance Minister has put the focus on infrastructure – more hospitals, eldercare centres and so on.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: While this is definitely necessary now, the future elderly in Singapore will need soft skills, especially an increased shift towards self-sufficiency.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I hope that more attention and resources will be spent to drive the improvement of soft skills in the healthcare sector.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We need to provide the elderly with the means to connect, engage and encourage one another.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The Minister has outlined three areas that contribute to this: the Silver Generation Office, the Community Silver Trust and the focus on Social Services Offices (SSOs).

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I hope we can encourage our elderly to continue their lifelong journey of learning.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: But the areas of study, objectives and methods of teaching for the elderly are different, especially as the number of highly educated and enabled elderly increases.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: There exists among our elderly a pool of talent and skills that is largely untapped.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: They are our retirees from the Civil Service as well as from industry.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: They are professionals, managers, skilled workers and so on.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: They should be encouraged to contribute not just to earn some extra pocket money, but also to pass on their skills, experience and wisdom.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This is an area that will grow fast and we will need to review the scope of this Fund.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I spoke about this last month during the Motion on the Elderly.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We should aim to be one of the global leaders in technology-assisted elderly living.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The road ahead is still long, but I believe this Budget has taken some important steps towards making Singapore a good place to grow old in.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Most Budgets looked at how to meet next year’s needs or, at most, the next few years.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This Budget looks at the future needs of Singapore beyond the term of this Government.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This is a very mature democracy which takes medium- to long-term decisions, in a way in which governments in the UK and America are not able to do because they are always worried about the next election….

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It’s a nice Budget because it has a good medium- to long-term view”.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: After the Budget was presented last week, I sat down with my volunteers and asked them what they thought.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I explained that we will be spending more, especially on healthcare, education and infrastructure.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I said we will need more money in future, hence the need for an increase in GST.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: They asked why the Government is raising GST when we have so much money.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This is a valid question which the Prime Minister and the Ministers have answered and must continue to explain.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: As their Member of Parliament (MP), I will try to convince them, too.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: But what we need to do is to ask ourselves where did the Reserves come from in the first place?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The answer, of course, is that it was the hard work of our Pioneer Generations working hand in hand with the Government to grow our economy and create wealth, and to spend within our means, and always putting something away for a rainy day.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: These three cardinal principles – growth, surplus, savings – have been followed faithfully by successive People's Action Party (PAP) Governments for over 50 years since Independence.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I remember during General Elections (GE), some Opposition members would come out with many ideas about how to spend the Reserves while the Government tries hard to convince the people to work hard and save.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Fortunately, the people have kept faith with the PAP.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This is why good leaders are critical for Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: But because of good leaders, we are a strong country.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: If we want to continue to grow, we need leaders who are prepared to tell people the not-so-nice things, leaders who take a long-term view, leaders who must convince people that they do care, but care in a responsible way.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We need leaders with vision, who can plan for a future Singapore which is more beautiful, sustainable and liveable than today.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Now, I personally feel that 70 is still too young to retire but that is not for me to decide.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The question of who will be our next Prime Minister has been the subject of much talk, from coffee shops to board rooms.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: There has been speculation as to why a decision has not been made yet.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The Prime Minister, the Emeritus Senior Minister and the 4th generation (4G) team have all said something.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: But instead of making the situation clearer, people read the tea leaves and speculate even further.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Because I think that the Prime Minister and his colleagues have been steadily building up a strong team to take us into the future.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: As the BBC commentator suggested, we are quite a unique democracy.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We have been planning for leadership succession of the team for many years.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It is not just about one man or woman.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: And we should ask ourselves, is the team ready to take over?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: They are the ones who will have to implement this difficult decision and follow through on all the other difficult steps on this road map to a better Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It is a team that is prepared to take difficult decisions and to take a long-term view.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It is a team that has a vision for Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I am confident that we are in good hands.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Before, I could even say hello, they went: Yi – Fan Feng Shun; Er – Long Teng Fei; San – Yang Kai Tai and so on.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Their father shared that the youngest one had learnt it in school and taught the greeting to the siblings.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The eldest child, a girl, is eight years old.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Her brother, the second child, is six years old and the youngest girl is five years old.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The father recently had heart surgery and is not working but is actively looking for a job.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Some time ago, they had sought higher subsidies from the eldest child’s school for student care fees but were not successful.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Now, after the surgery and with the husband not working, the family is feeling the financial pinch.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: They have some debts to clear as they had previously paid for various bills in the past with credit cards.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The father expressed his concerns as it was getting financially challenging for the family to afford the children’s expenses as their needs increase.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: My team is making the appropriate appeals and referrals to assist the family.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Their circumstances are specific to them, but some of the issues that they faced are not uncommon.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: An unexpected event, especially a health-related one, often derails a family’s financial plan.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: A bad financial decision in the past may continue to haunt the family for a long time.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Sometimes, financial assistance is not immediately available because of the eligibility criteria, though I have seen exceptions been made in appropriate circumstances.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: So, when we talk about the Budget or the various policies or programmes to help families, we must always bear in mind what happens on the ground, what is the impact on people, will this Budget and the various programmes help people in the long run?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There are many elements in this Budget that can help the family I spoke about.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Indirectly, the other initiatives targeted at supporting businesses for growing a vibrant and innovative economy like the extension of the Wage Credit Scheme, enhancement of corporate income tax rebate and the Enterprise Development Grant will all help to create a more conducive environment to look for a job and stay employed.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Hopefully, by the time the GST increases kick in, the family is financially stable.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Even if they are not, the GST offset package, amongst other things, would be in place to support them.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am glad that there are reviews and extensions of existing schemes within this Budget.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Policies and schemes need to be tweaked and retweaked.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We need to make sure that the policies and the various progammes match the needs of our people.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Eligibility criteria may need to be reviewed from time to time.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: New initiatives may need to be put in place.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is important to always be mindful to ensure that the Budget and any policy changes continue to improve the day-to-day lives of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I trust that this Government will do just that.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is an attractive notion to argue for more to be done to help everyone.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am acutely aware that the Government has to cater to all these needs whilst balancing the need to ensure fiscal feasibility and sustainability of the country.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The inevitable announcement has thus been made regarding the increase in GST.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There has been a lot of buzz regarding this, and many views have been put forth.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I think beyond just the banter of assent and dissent, and alternative suggestions, there is an opportunity to talk about our values and what defines us as Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Budget is not just about the economy and our fiscal needs but also about the principles that guide us.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I feel that this Budget and the recent Budget statements in the past few years have gotten all of us thinking about important questions relating to Singapore's future: what do Singaporeans expect of the Government, what do we do in difficult times, what do we do in good times?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There is an opportunity to ride on this and consciously involve the youths in these discussions and create for them a platform where they can be meaningfully involved in policy formulation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: After all, many of the things we are doing is for the future generation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am aware that there is already a lot of effort in engaging the youths, for example, through the efforts of the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth (MCCY) and the National Youth Council (NYC), of which I am a council member.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I believe though there is scope to enhance such engagements by having targeted approaches for the different archetypes of youths.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Not all are vocal and not all may be interested in giving their views.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: But they should be interested and their views matter.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We could look at sharing information and obtaining feedback in a medium that is more suitable and comfortable for the different groups.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This could mean repackaging information in bite size forms and engaging them through social media.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It means we go to them, have discussion sessions where they hang out after school, or where they seek recreation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We should also be open to implement meaningful ideas generated from the discussions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This could encourage more mature and constructive discussions in the youths here.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Such discussions will hopefully help to shape views and instill the youths with the same sense of responsibility and ownership of our Pioneer Generation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This sense of responsibility and ownership is necessary if Singapore is to survive.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The community needs to come together and do its part.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We have many schemes and programmes in place but there will always be gaps and those who fall through the cracks.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The community plays an important role to complete the support network and close the gaps.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Many came forward without hesitation to help their fellow residents in need.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: During one of my ang pow presentation sessions to the elderly in the past weeks, one senior citizen approached me.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: He told me he had brought walking sticks to be donated to the Residents Committee (RC) and asked that I tell the RC members to give them out to anyone who needs them.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: But this is, in fact, a significant show of caring and sharing.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This is the spirit of giving that the Minister for Finance spoke about in his Budget Statement.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In particular, I look forward to the enhancement of SG Cares and the one-stop platform Giving.sg.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: If I may suggest, we could look at the data available from this platform and understand behavioural inclinations.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This information could then be used to curate social nudges that may further create awareness of the different community efforts and encourage the spirit of giving.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In Malay):   A subject that became a hot topic recently was the issue of the GST rate increase which will be implemented within a four-year period.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Many have voiced their views on this matter.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Clearly, discussions about the Budget gave us an opportunity to think about matters that are important to our nation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Will our country continue to survive in the coming years?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: How can we continue to ensure that our country can still compete internationally in an ever-changing world?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: What should we do to provide a good life for our children who will inherit this nation from us?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There are three things that I would like to emphasise.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: First, it is important for us to think about the long-term impact of each decision made for our country.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We need to be prepared for a rainy day.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Some have asked, "Is there no other way?" Various suggestions may have been raised, but all of them will have an impact on the nation’s assets.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There are those who rejected the increase in the GST but, in the same breath, they asked the Government to enhance social assistance measures.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Government sometimes have to make decisions that are less popular but are important for the good of the nation in the long term.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Second, at the individual and family level, we also need to stay prepared for the future.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We must be open-minded, work hard to acquire new knowledge and upgrade our skills.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We need to pay attention to our children’s education, so that they will not be left behind in this current of rapid change.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In this regard, I welcome the Council for the Development of the Singapore Malay/Muslim Community's (MENDAKI's) efforts to enhance our community’s education.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I hope that MENDAKI and other Malay/Muslim organisations can continue to update the information and knowledge that can be conveyed to our community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: For my third and final point, I think that it is important for the people to continue playing a role in complementing efforts to assist the community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We can contribute in many ways, be it through donations or by helping out.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We must encourage the spirit of helping one another.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am confident that with the joint effort of the Government, families and community, a comprehensive support network can be established.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, let me conclude in English.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: My grassroots leaders translated the meaning of the greetings which the three children recited to me.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: They were wishes of good luck and blessings.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I certainly hope all the good wishes that the children wished for me also come true for the family and for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: May the five blessings arrive at our doors!

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: And may good fortune come from all directions!

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: These are the shifting of global economic weight to Asia and the emergence of new technologies.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: I interpret this interesting phrase "Global-Asia" as positioning Singapore to catch the growth in Asia with a global outlook.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The convergence of these two shifts, indeed, is the shifting of the global economic weight to Asia and the emergence of new technologies, in which the Fourth Industrial Revolution is taking place in the region stretching from South Asia to Northeast Asia through Southeast Asia.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: For the first time in modern history, the Asian economies combined are developing more robustly than Western economies.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The Asian engine is driving the global economy and transforming Asia from being a volatile region into a dynamic global centre.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The opening up of China to global capitalism by Deng Xiaoping also opened up the minds of the Chinese people to the world.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Many overseas Chinese talents returned from the developed countries of the West to China, bringing with them the knowledge and culture to advance China’s science and technology.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The political will to succeed and the hunger of the Chinese people to learn and live better lives fuelled rapid economic development.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: China is fast becoming an economic and military superpower.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Singapore has thrived in the past 50 years by making ourselves useful to global capitalism, especially by correctly identifying future trends before others do.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: We made ourselves useful to American-led capitalism in Southeast Asia and East Asia during the Cold War and, in the process, helped to transform ASEAN from a political grouping into an aspiring economic community.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: In the last three decades, Singapore correctly predicted the rise of China and was one of the first countries to share the know-how of economic development with China.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: We have reaped a lot of benefits from this first-mover advantage.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: But I am afraid this advantage is now irrelevant.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: China is leading the region to become the centre of global capitalism.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: As a small city-state nation, this also means transforming our culture and human capital, as well as our diplomatic relationships with the economic powers and interpersonal friendships between national leaders and citizens.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: In the past 50 years, Singaporeans’ ability to speak English well has contributed to fostering our relationships with Western countries at the centre of global capitalism in the region.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: There is a unique ethnic connection between Chinese Singaporeans and the Chinese in China due to ancestral and linguistic ties.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: I would even go further to argue that we should also learn our dialects as well.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: In China, speaking Mandarin ‒ Putong Hua ‒ is just the official language in official dealings.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: If one would like to connect better to the Chinese, not just rationally, but also affectionately, then the language to use is the local dialect.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: That said, we must also bear in mind that Singapore is, first and foremost, a multiracial and multilingual society.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: What does the rise of China as an economic and political superpower mean for a small state, such as Singapore?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: My view is that Singapore is, politically at heart, a Southeast Asian nation, defined by commercial trade winds, tropical hospitality, openness of the seas and the diversity of cultures.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: I believe that the ethnic politics and international frictions in our region will subside in time and ASEAN will soon become a more integrated community to protect our own interests against external dominance.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: As a Chinese-educated Singaporean, I am delighted to see Chinese being used in many countries today, especially in places where they see the value of Chinese tourists and investment dollars.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The Chinese language is, today, one of the most popular languages being learned by people all over the world.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Chinese culture is fast becoming less a scholarly curiosity but more a tool of soft power today.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: This has helped perhaps some Chinese-educated Singaporeans feel that they are finally freed of the feeling of inferiority.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Will China seek to turn the tables on its experience of European imperialism and become an imperialist power itself?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: This is not far-fetched if we consider that Japan did just that in the first half of the 20th Century.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Will China revive its old tributary empire and use sharp power to compel small states to submit to its will and pay it the equivalent of tribute today?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: There is a need to transform the Singapore industrial-era mindset and culture to make us relevant and useful to the future economy and contribute to the economic dynamism of the region.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: But besides focusing on economic opportunities, we should also have the new political scenario in mind while anchoring Singapore as a Global-Asia node.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: It is important that we see the political economy of the major shifts, instead of just the economic challenges and opportunities.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: I appreciate the Government's vision statements and the articulation of how Singapore should strategically position itself in the new era.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Do not let this opportunity to lead Singapore with this vision go to waste.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Some Members before me have spoken about how they wish more can be done for our seniors, about what more can be done to address inequality.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In my speech, I would like to touch on how we grow our economy so that we have more resources, jobs and tax revenues from a more buoyant economy to meet our needs so that we will have more to address the various issues that Members have raised before me.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Second, I would also like to touch on how we ensure Government spending is used effectively and efficiently.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is so that resources collected from the public can be used to best address needs.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Mr Low Thia Khiang, who has spoken before me, spoke on the importance of leveraging ideas and new technology.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We need to have contact points into globally innovative cities as so to have global access to ideas and technology.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Minister for Finance and his team have spelt out their plans through the Global Innovation Alliance (GIA) and the ASEAN Innovation Network.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I support the GIA and the ASEAN Innovation Network which are ways for us to be plugged into the ecosystem of ideas and new technologies.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We currently have many Singaporeans working and studying in the region, Singaporeans familiar with the venture capital and private equity circuits and Singaporean firms and their partners with investments in these cities.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Apart from strengthening our bilingual and bicultural skills, I suggest we more deliberately build our networks and leverage them to sense-make and get a better grasp of emerging trends in Asia – open platforms to bring in various partners to widen our reach and understanding of new developments and establish linkages back into Singapore to provide more opportunities for businesses and partnerships.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Second, we should invest in priority areas which are central to our economy and which can also develop new adjacent avenues of growth.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our investments in these sectors can provide us with a strong platform to develop new avenues of growth if we continuously reassess what the most valued part of the sector is.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Data and the use of data, for instance, have emerged as a change agent for many industries and spawned new businesses and business models.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For airports and ports, there is a lot of data from the travellers and trade that pass through our shores.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For instance, can we create our own global online travel company, given the amount of data we have about the preferences of travellers?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
