text: We can also leverage data to market to travellers even after they have left our shores.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Aviation and Maritime Transformation Programme described in this year's Budget thus builds on our capabilities in the airport and seaport.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We should challenge ourselves to mine these sectors for new development opportunities.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Third, we should equip our people and our companies to take advantage of new opportunities.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Skills upgrading allows workers at different stages of their work life to catch up on skills gaps which, if left unaddressed, could lead to long-term income gaps.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Skills upgrading and training have thus been a key initiative in successive Budget plans.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Further, to ensure that our young Singaporeans are ready for the workforce, I would like to suggest that internships be made available to all youths above 18 years old from the Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs).

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Internships can provide youths a reality check on the skills needed for the workforce and complement the education they receive from IHLs.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Lastly, I support the Capability Transfer Programmes that are being piloted in certain specialised fields.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is used, for instance, to bring in experts in data analytics, machine learning and AI to facilitate the transfer of specialised knowledge to our local professionals in fintech.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is timely help for our companies and industries which are facing skillset gaps in certain important fields.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I would next like to discuss how we can ensure that Government spending is used effectively and efficiently.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, I hope that Government agencies can constantly challenge themselves to manage costs while delivering good quality services.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: First, Government agencies should always strive to negotiate the best deal with suppliers when it comes to Government procurement for the benefit of taxpayers.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For instance, with the need to build more healthcare facilities for an ageing population, there is scope for economies of scale via centralised procurement of hospital supplies, equipment and information technology (IT) software.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And as the country steps up public renewal works, there is scope to demand discover what various agencies are procuring and if there are overlaps which allow more streamlined purchasing and better leverage.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A well-thought through centralised procurement process may go beyond simple demand aggregation to require standardisation of product needs across institutions.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I hope that the Ministry of Finance (MOF) can look into this actively to ensure that we are not being charged different prices across different institutions.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I hope more will be trained through such a programme.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Cash flow projections should take into account their maintenance costs and the lifespan of their replacement parts.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given the challenges in projecting cash flows, inhouse expertise may be required to make a fair assessment.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Government agencies, such as HDB, for instance, should consider having businesses, such as Essential Maintenance Service (EMS) develop lift expertise so that they are able to make a reasoned assessment on the costs of maintenance and replacement.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the meantime, greater care and scrutiny need to be put into purchase contracts to bind suppliers to their promises.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Third, I would like to see greater collaboration between the public, private and community sectors to configure resources to deliver optimal outcomes.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I have also seen how private operators, like Grab Shuttle Plus, complement our national transport infrastructure by introducing buses to Punggol during off-peak hours and serving residents who stay in less populous areas.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And in Gambas, the community came together to buy and share umbrellas rather than spend public monies building a high sheltered linkway which may not provide good cover for residents from the rain.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We should be open and enthusiastic in encouraging different configurations of public, private, community contributions to deliver optimal outcomes for citizens while minimising the burden on public monies.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: At the end of the day, everybody wins.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If increased spending is here to stay because we have to take care of our elderly and renew our infrastructure, let us seize the opportunities to grow our economy and revenues and, at the same time, make every tax dollar count.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Let us be united in our vision and apply our energies correctly.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Only then, can we overcome the challenges we face and create a stronger, better Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, some Members expressed hope that more can be done to help the elderly and the disadvantaged.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This Budget is precisely about how to allocate our resources optimally to create the biggest economic pie to support increasing expenditure, so that we can look after our senior citizens and the disadvantaged effectively.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Therefore, I would like to discuss two points.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: After decades of hard work, Singapore has made great strides in our ports and aviation industries.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These were achieved by our forefathers who were bold to explore in the face of great uncertainty.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As the new generation of Singaporeans, if we do not pursue success boldly, we will become mediocre.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These demonstrate Singapore’s determination to stay ahead and constantly strive to be stronger and better.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Of course, the value chain of today is very different from 50 years ago.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Even if you compare it to 10 years ago, there has been tremendous changes, with the Internet and big data creating disruptive impact on the transport industry.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As people say in Chinese ni shui xing zhou, bu jin ze tui (when you are sailing against the current, you must keep forging ahead, or you will be falling behind).

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We should keep up with the major long-term trends and actively pursue new business opportunities in the value chain, for example, investment opportunities in transportation big data, online travel services and more.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Only by doing so can we stay ahead in the face of global competition.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In addition, I also suggest setting up an international network for Singaporeans under GIA, so that overseas Singaporeans can also contribute to our development.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is also important to nurture our local talent.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We should ensure that both working adults who are currently employed and young people entering the labour market are better able to meet market demand, and that job training programmes are market-driven.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Therefore, to rein in costs, the Government not only needs a sound system, but it also needs to take a micro view to incentivise every public officer to save public funds.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For example, based on the premise of procuring quality products and services, Government agencies should always strive to negotiate for the best deal with suppliers, while achieving economies of scale and reducing procurement costs through centralised procurement and product standardisation.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: At the same time, the Government should adopt a lifecycle approach in procurement cost evaluation and control long-term costs effectively.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Government can also work with community and private sectors to optimise the use of resources.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I hope that we will not be trapped in a zero-sum game.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With Government expenditure growing steadily, we must make greater efforts to save public funds, be more meticulous in planning expenditure, and constantly challenge ourselves to improve the efficiency of money spent.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 2.50 pm.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: As the Prime Minister and his Cabinet colleagues have signalled for some time, our taxes must rise to pay for our future public spending needs.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Not only does this approach demonstrate our Government’s ability to plan for the long term, it also demonstrates, once again, its integrity.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Our Government does what it says it will do.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: And our Government keeps faith with Singaporeans whom it both represents and serves.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This is, Mr Speaker, Sir, only right and proper.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It should and must always be the Singapore norm.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But it is by no means the norm elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Singaporeans can be justly proud of their Government’s record of integrity, especially at a time when flip-flopping on policy decisions and policy positions is the order of the day in some countries.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Our Government is fulfilling its role of always acting in the best long-term interests of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It is right that we invest in our children because they will form the core of our future.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It is right that we take measures to help workers stay relevant.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It is right that we take measures to respect and help our senior citizens who have contributed so much to making Singapore what it is today.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It is right that we square up to and act to increase inclusivity by looking after those less fortunate to reduce income inequality and strengthen community cohesion.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It is also right, Mr Speaker, that public expenditure is governed by the principle of fiscal sustainability.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Every citizen understands that, whether they are managing a household's accounts or those of a business.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: To paraphrase Charles Dickens’ character Mr Micawber of David Copperfield: "Monthly income $5,000, monthly expenditure $4,500, result happiness.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This is eminently preferable to spending our Reserves and reducing the very source of net investment returns (NIR) which contribute so much to this country’s Budget revenue.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Utilising our Reserves as guarantees for loans to fund long-term, large-scale infrastructure projects is both innovative and wise.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: As the Minister stated in his announcement, this approach should enhance the Singapore Bond Market.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The approach is also fairer to all Singaporeans as it spreads the burden of costs across the generations in an equitable manner.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The Budget Statement demonstrated our Government’s commitment to sustaining a vibrant and innovative economy in two key ways.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Our SMEs and the FDI which the Economic Development Board (EDB) works tirelessly to attract and retain are two sides of the same coin.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The focus on sustaining a vibrant and innovative economy is the vital component to ensuring our country’s goals are achieved and, indeed, to ensuring its continued survival.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It is only with a vibrant and innovative economy that we can support and defend ourselves.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It is only with a vibrant and innovative economy that the little red dot can continue to punch above its weight internationally.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It is only with a vibrant and innovative economy that the Singapore passport allows visa-free entry to more countries than most other passports.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: If we are to do this, we would quickly discover that our rates of economic growth are less than other global cities.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I am well aware that other cities do not need to incur big ticket items, such as defence, in their budgets.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: However, Sir, for us to ultimately continuously punch above our weight, we need to compare ourselves with what other cities are doing.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: With this in mind, it becomes even more important that Singaporeans work together and find ever more visionary ways to grow our economy.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The need for continual innovation becomes even more imperative.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Many people here and abroad have complemented Singapore on its ITMs.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The amount of work which has gone into producing these ITMs is considerable and very impressive.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: My sense, from talking with businesses, is that there may well be a gap of understanding as to which ITM is relevant to them and what they should be doing.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This is an opportunity for the Government and businesses to deepen their existing collaboration and roll out targeted, quality communication on ITM execution.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The communication model could be that of the excellent quality of communication from MOF's team for this year’s Budget.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This is another vital component in sustaining all that Singaporeans and its Government have built since 1965.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: They certainly are of concern for our SMEs which provide most jobs for Singaporeans and for those businesses which invest in Singapore and which also provide jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: I support the key thrust of the Budget which is about sustainability.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Second, how should we support local firms to sustain and grow their businesses in order to provide better jobs and wages for Singaporeans?

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Third, how can we build a sustainable environment where Singaporeans can live, work and play?

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Doing so will provide a stable income for the Government to fund the increase in expenditure, particularly in the healthcare and security areas.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: However, more has to be done to help low-income Singaporeans cope with the potential increase in prices.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: As more Singaporeans are eating out these days, I propose that the permanent GST Voucher Scheme take into consideration the increase in cooked food and drink prices, especially in relation to serving sizes, when determining the quantum of assistance.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: All these shifts will pose immense challenges to our local businesses, especially the SMEs.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Many SMEs are still not coming forward to develop competitive edges and prepare for overseas business expansion.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Many of them also do not understand how they can seize business opportunities under the 23 ITMs.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: I would urge the Government to step up its efforts to engage and help our SMEs more effectively.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Many are reluctant to upgrade or expand their businesses.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: From the feedback gathered, while SMEs are keen on solutions, they are afraid of the process of adopting these changes.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: This will reduce greenhouse gas emissions, especially from power plants and industries.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: However, the carbon tax may not be as effective in reducing emissions generated from transportation and buildings.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: We must act fast and take bold steps to make our transportation and buildings eco-friendlier.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: As of 2017, we have about 160,000 goods vehicles and buses on Singapore roads.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Many of these vehicles are not green-certified and emit PM2.5 which is detrimental to the health and well-being of Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Many of these vehicles travel at night and in the early hours of the morning.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Pollution is less visible during these hours and our enforcement officers may not be present at these hours to enforce air pollution controls.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: As goods vehicles and buses are costly to replace or upgrade, the Government can consider providing low interest loans and subsidies to accelerate the replacement of our existing fleet of heavy vehicles.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Many of these buildings date back to the 1970s and are not equipped with eco-friendly features.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Only about 25% of our buildings, that is, about 2,400 buildings, are certified green under the Building and Construction Authority's (BCA's) Green Mark Scheme.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: To further expedite the greening of our buildings, I propose that BCA compile best practices on green building designs, mechanical and electrical installations, interior fittings and maintainable designs in order to guide developers, consultants, contractors and facilities managers.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: These best practices should also be included as part of the Green Mark Scheme.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Buildings, especially air-conditioned ones, consume large amounts of energy and contribute significantly to the overall greenhouse gas emissions.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: In Singapore, our hot and humid climate encourages more people to spend more time indoors in air-conditioned places, such as offices, shopping centres, restaurants.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: More HDB flat owners are also installing air-conditioners in their flats.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: The proliferation of air-conditioners will undoubtedly increase energy demand and add to emissions.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: To ensure the more efficient and prudent use of air-conditioning, we should encourage the installation of energy monitoring systems that will help building owners to track their electricity consumption and reduce wastages.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: An example of such a system is the Home Energy Management System (HEMS) in Japan, which allows for the control of electrical appliances, such as air-conditioners and lights, to reach optimal energy efficiency.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: To fight climate change, we need to expedite the adoption of renewable energy sources, such as solar energy.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: HDB has started the installation of solar panels on HDB rooftops.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: However, the progress is slow due to various financing constraints and pricing problems when solar energy is sold to PowerGrid.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: I hope the Ministry will address these problems and scale up the installation of solar panels in all high-rise buildings so as to build more solar energy banks.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: We can learn from many Japanese cities which have embarked on various successful eco-sustainability policies, incentives and education.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: In 2008, Japan selected 13 cities under the FutureCity Initiative to transform Japan into a low-carbon society.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: These are some examples of projects undertaken by the various cities.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: First, Toyota city has encouraged the use of eco-friendly cars through programmes which assist buyers in purchasing such vehicles.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: It has integrated eco-friendliness as part of its cultural identity under the "Do You Kyoto" project.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: In addition, Kyoto also subsidises households which utilise solar energy.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Many Japanese cities have also adopted the Comprehensive Assessment System for Built Environment Efficiency (CASBEE) to measure eco-friendliness.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: CASBEE may be used to assess eco-friendliness at various scales, ranging from individual buildings to entire cities.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: We have worked with our people, public and private (3P) partners to organise resource conservation projects, recycling and climate change education programmes to promote environmental ownership.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: I would urge the Government to provide more funding support to the community to champion green projects.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: I hope that more initiatives to make Singapore an eco-friendlier nation could be included within the Budget to make Singapore a sustainable green city.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Their answers were varied, fresh and often very surprising.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But I admit that it can be overwhelming to try to make sense of the conflicting forest of everyone’s different answers to the “How” and “What” questions about our economy.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: How should we encourage innovation or tackle inequality?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: What is the best way to manage our Reserves or the best tax system for us?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I find that the questions I keep circling back to – the ones that give me some compass of clear direction to help me navigate my own uncertainty and confusion – are always the questions of "Who" and "Why".

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Who do our Reserves or tax system serve?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And at the heart of it all, who are we?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Taking the time to slow down from our usual pace in Parliament to dwell on questions of purpose and identity may seem frivolous.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But I suggest to Members, they are the most crucial questions.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Because they bring us back into a space of choosing from what matters most to us.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I have found that whether we are debating about how we should spend our own personal dollars or the dollars of our nation, the core question we must keep returning back to is, "What is the meaning we care to make with all our money in the first place?" Our greatest fear should not be of failure but of success at things in life that we realise did not really matter to us at all.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, I fully support the Finance Minister's wonderful reflection in his speech that "a strong economy is not an end in itself; it is a means to build a better home and provide a better quality of life for all our people.” If our economy is a means to an end, then should we not discuss every year at Budget whether we as a people still share the same end-goals?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: In my first Budget speech in 2015, I shared my hope that, "Our country spent the first 50 years of our history getting rich.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I would love to see us spend our next 50 years charting our course towards becoming truly wealthy." My desire still stands.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, what is this vision of true wealth that we are longing for at the end of all our days of economic hustling?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: With each year, do we know and do we care to know whether we are moving closer to or further away from that end?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I find that one visionary end-state still resonates for most young Singaporeans across different beliefs and backgrounds and, that is, the one that was still that written down more than half a century ago which invited us to imagine that there will be a day when "We", the citizens of Singapore would find ourselves as one united people; able to regard one another less by race, language or religion; and more as fellow builders of a democracy, that was based on justice and equality.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Because we had somehow learnt that this life we got to live was never about creating prosperity and progress for its own sake, or for the sake of bettering only ourselves, but for the sake of bettering others alongside because we finally believed we were better together – rather than apart – as a nation.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It is our North Star, an ambitious promise we ask every young student to spend each morning putting their hand on the heart and swear that we will do whatever it takes and take on whatever cost to bring to life this vision.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And yet, as each young student ages into a young working professional, many of them feel their idealism for themselves and for the country being challenged at different levels of the Singapore system.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Along the line, we sense that the Singapore way is more like a tense high-wire act where we must learn to calibrate our ideals of communitarianism, democracy and egalitarianism on one end with the realities of individualism, authoritarianism and elitism on the other end.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So far, our country has managed to advance forward without falling off the line.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And even our critics concede that that is no small feat.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But whether our performance has been a gracefully balanced act or one ungracefully tilted too much towards pragmatism has been the fodder of much debate.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I have heard it said jokingly that pragmatism is our official religion.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And you know it is certainly part of our cultural DNA when you can hear it, not just in the voice of our parents and our policymakers, but in ourselves and our children.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And every tilt towards the side of pragmatism is simultaneously a tilt away from the side of our ideals.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And I want to stress I do not presume pragmatism to be bad and idealism to be good.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Every healthy individual learns to hold both options in tension within their mental construct and make their hard choices.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But I believe our idealistic young professionals and students who make up both our current and future tax base have the right to question us.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And, if not now, while we have substantial surpluses, then when?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: If not later, then are we saying never?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I came across an article online called "The Limits of Ideology: Lessons from Singapore" by an American CEO called Margaret Heffernan.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: She concluded her article like this – "What Singapore holds in reserve…is an asset western leaders would give their eye teeth for: a national surplus accrued over many years of fastidious economic management.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And while western leaders use insolvency as a perennial alibi for their failure to make coherent strategic choices, Singapore's Government has the money and the power to effect real change.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And should it fail to do so… no politicians in Singapore will be able to claim they did not see their chance.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: If, with the freedom to spend that most western leaders lack, Singapore cannot address its problems, then the principles it espouses will be discredited for good." And I get it.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: She is really cutting, but I can concede that she has a point.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Thanks to the prudence of our forefathers, we, of all nations, indeed, have a unique chance right here and right now, to set an example once more to the world of how a small nation can effect real change, impacting real people in real time.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And this substantial gift is given unto us for a reason and maybe it holds a meaning larger than our present imagination.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, we have quite a First World problem on our hands.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Should we spend more to help the people we have with us today or store more so we can help the people of tomorrow?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And it is a hard choice, because both are equally good choices.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But it is healthy to ask ourselves if we notice that we are in the habit of overestimating for the future.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Could we also be underestimating what we can do in the present?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The choice is really about whether we believe in growing our Reserves faster or slower.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I want to admit I am a terrible economics student, so I do need help in making sense of all of these.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I struggled to understand the International Monetary Fund's (IMF's) surveillance of member states' foreign exchange reserves adequacy because in IMF's assessment, it says we are excessively prudent.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, that is about three times over IMF's recommendation.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And I want to stress again that I am not assuming that IMF is right and the Government is wrong.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I am certainly not saying let us just take whatever a foreign institution says as gospel truth because I am sure as heck I do not know enough to make any kind of proper assessment.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I think it is helpful for the Government to provide a thoughtful and easy to understand response to the IMF's assessment because it does open up an important and deeply profound question for us to consider.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: What is this final number we need in our Reserves that will make us feel complete and secure?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And who would we be prepared to re-examine that number for?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: When we build up our own family's savings, how do we decide when is a good time to tap into it to spend on our children now, versus storing it up for them to use for their future children?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And we might say, well, that really depends on how urgent are the needs of my children now, is it not?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Is there a golden opportunity they need to seize?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We would probably take out a significant percentage of the investment returns of our own savings – while prudently protecting a baseline sum, of course – in a heartbeat if we believed doing so would make a significant and immediate difference to the well-being of our children in the present, particularly if it would help save their life, because no point saving for their future if they die in the present, right?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It is human to be much more liberal when it comes to spending on our own children and much more conservative when we choose how to spend on other people's children.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I deeply admire the Government’s devotion to long-term strategic over-planning and I get the deep anxieties we have around under-planning.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I appreciate that we cannot afford to get the mathematics wrong, but we cannot afford to get the meaning under the mathematics wrong either, because people do not listen to mathematics, they listen to meaning.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: If we hope to galvanise the support of the young idealists who make up our future tax base, we have to give them a braver and broader vision that warrants the bigness of our Reserves.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Otherwise, they can mistake it to be a story that is just about growth of Reserves for growth's sake.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, I hope that the Government can help us understand what is the real story better.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Inequality is a deeply emotional issue for many young Singaporeans and I dare say it is one of the biggest issues they care about.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, now is the time to really go talk to the next generation of Singapore taxpayers before 2021 hits, and to listen in to what really matters to them.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: A sociologist, Teo You Yenn's book, "This Is What Inequality Looks Like” is sold out and I have seen dog-eared copies already making their rounds among thoughtful young Singaporeans and some of them are buying one copy to keep and another to loan.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Because what she is saying in there about a need to deal with inequality through a systemic lens is resonating and connecting with them.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The Straits Times' journalist Chua Mui Hoong cited it in her own article, "Inequality is a threat – name it and face it", recommending it as a must-read for every politician and civil servant.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I am really glad that the Prime Minister himself is making inequality a "critical" issue to look at.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Our youths who have lived in public housing, gone to neighbourhood schools and depended on public transport all their lives will say that they did not need an official study to tell them what they have seen for a long time.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They can sense-make the class differences in everyday, ordinary interactions because it is the difference they feel at the doorway between the teenager who gets to order from Foodpanda and the teenager who rides through the rain to deliver it to him.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It is the difference felt by the young intern every lunchtime when she struggles over how to tell her colleagues that she has a very different idea from all of them about what is an affordable place to dine.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Even some of our more privileged youths are not comfortable with the growing divide either and they are driven to do something different about it through the system.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They are well-acquainted with how money can buy through tuition classes, college prep coaches, yearly overseas trips and diverse life experiences for someone else in their generation who is taking that same national examination, fighting for that same national trophy and going for the same interviews that they are.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They, too, want to jailbreak this pragmatic arms race of "every man for himself" meritocracy.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The lower-income youths welcome the $300 but they know how fast it disappears in a few bill payments.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, no once-off voucher can truly soothe the blow of a GST increase that hits them with every transaction on a day-to-day basis.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And meanwhile, they know, in the land of the rich, many treat the $100 as just chump change.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: For the short-term and disproportionate impact that they have, ad hoc packages are not cheap.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, are our well-intended ad hoc transfers drawing resources and attention away from dealing with challenges in a more sustained and structured manner?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Every year, after the GCE "A" level results, the media loves highlighting stories of kids who excelled in their examinations despite the most challenging of circumstances.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: This year, I came across a story of a 19-year-old Singaporean girl who grew up under an alcoholic Singaporean father who constantly abused her Indonesian mother.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And in primary school, she witnessed her desperate mother attempting suicide.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: This girl lived on a daily allowance of $2 and survived on loaves of bread and treats from friends.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: She studied in school all the time so she could help her mother save on electricity bills.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: She recounted that the temptation to join gangs was always present, but she had the presence of mind to ask herself, "Is that what I really want to be in the future, and is this how I want to define myself?" With the help of a resilient and loving mother, supportive friends and teachers, she ended up not just excelling at the GCE "A" levels, but she even joined Meet-the-People Sessions (MPS), interned at MSF, did volunteer work and reconciled with her father.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Why is it that we recognise this girl's story as an exceptional story, rather than the norm?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And do we want stories like hers to be more of a norm?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And if we do, what are we prepared to do at a systemic level?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I have met children growing up in rental flats with potential to live up very big dreams, a girl whose ambition is to become a criminal lawyer, an articulate boy who learnt public speaking because he binge-watched Technology, Entertainment and Design (TED) videos.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I met a neighbourhood school teenager who floored me with his serious conviction that someday he will enter Parliament to be, in his own words, "a voice for the voiceless".

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Singaporean children of low-income moms, single moms, and foreign moms.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Why should we not take any and every child born into Singapore with equal honour and belief and blessing?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Our young Singaporeans get it that we are a small and vulnerable nation and they get it that we need a monstrous amount of money just in case a perfect storm of horrors truly hit – and they are so many horrors out there: sea levels rising, global economy tumbling, silver tsunami, total fertility rate flatlines.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I mean, they get it; they have heard it.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We are a nation so well-versed with fears – a motivating force.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We have come very far in surviving as a country by not ignoring our fears.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But it is not the only emotion worth listening into.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Fear alone cannot bring us past that space of survival into a space of true thriving.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: When I live-poll young people in junior colleges (JCs), polytechnics and Institutes of Technical Education (ITEs) about what is that one word they associate with the future of Singapore, do you know what word consistently emerges as the biggest on their word cloud?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, yes, I think we have succeeded in engraining in them the message of our vulnerabilities.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And the emotion of fear, while useful, can become uninspiring and paralysing as a mood.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Our youths are hungry for a new kind of certainty.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: That certainty can only come from the promise of a new story, a story of a "Who" and a "Why" that is bigger than the sum of all of our fears about "What's" and "How's".

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Our youths need to hear the greater story of all the things that we want to do for love, not just fear.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And the story needs to come straight from the heart of every leader in the land about all of the meaning that money can buy, not just for ourselves, but for one another.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: At some point, we have to decide when to stop just operating in fear that the bottom will fall out of Our Singapore Story.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: There is a time for fear, and there also is a time for courage ‒ courage born from the fire of fighting for our ideals ‒ to simply say, in the face of fear, that "That is enough.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And it is time to let more of us have enough, too." And in that space of sufficiency, we shall find our satisfaction.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin
text: I want to say that I see the heart of the Minister for Finance for the people.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin
text: I believe in his openness to find new ways forward and I trust his courage to make hard choices.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin
text: So, my hope is that he and this Government can work together with a new generation of idealists and pragmatists to help them dream of a better future that they will all be so very proud to call their own.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: It is, therefore, apt that Budget 2018 is also an inclusive Budget and, perhaps more than any other, I will remember this Budget as one in which the Minister for Finance named VWOs as one of the stakeholders, alongside workers, businesses, the Government and citizens, to build a better Singapore for everyone.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: Here, I declare my interest as the President of the Society for the Physically Disabled (SPD) and a Board Member of SgEnable.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: So, how do I see the role of VWOs in nation-building?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: I liken this to a family, where one parent looks after the welfare of the family and keeps the house in order, while the other parent brings home the dough.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: VWOs, by virtue of their being on the ground, are best placed to increase and strengthen intra-community networks and bonding.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: We must, therefore, strategically develop this role, collaborate with grassroots organisations.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: We can, and we should, build the kampung spirit, the neighbourhood care network.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: How tragic it would be if a person were to perish in a natural disaster because the neighbours did not know he had existed.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: I do not need to say any more.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: Is this the kind of neighbourhood that we live in?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: It has been a few years since we popularised the term "kampung spirit".

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: Let us step up to the plate and just do it.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: In the days of nation-building and consolidation, social development spending was way below that of other Ministries.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: The Government has recognised the importance of building up the vulnerable and weak segments within our society.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: It remains my dream that, one day, charities will not depend on charity.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: The same set of challenges facing us, as the Minister for Finance says, can be turned into opportunities for us.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: But it seems to me that the four strategies laid out in the Budget will not work if we are only implementing the schemes, if we are only encouraging take-up by individuals and organisations.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: We need to radically change our mindsets and world views.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: We need to change the way we do things.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: In the face of disruption, we must be prepared to disrupt the way we do things, disrupt our own comfort zones.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: These are terminologies not alien to us, having been frequently spoken of and discoursed.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: Unfortunately, familiarity sometimes has a way of immunising us against the true import of the terms.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: When we talk about innovation, we frequently think in terms of acquisition and effective, efficient use of technology.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: I use my mobile phone without a clue as to what happens inside in cyberspace and, where applicable, even in the virtual world.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: My purchase of a mobile phone, and any proficiency – which I do not claim I have – in using the phone and the downloaded apps, do not make me innovative.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: Embracing change, such as upgrading to the latest version, does not make me innovative.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: Now, if I can tweak my mobile phone and change it into a loudhailer, that might be innovation, but it might also explode in my face.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: It is when I embark on a quest for the better, for the best, when I say nothing is impossible, when I dare to dream, when I dare to fail, then I might – I might – innovate.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: And yet, I might not, for I might fail.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: It is imperative that we develop this psyche.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: If we cannot, whether as businesses or individuals, we will have neither the courage nor the drive to innovate.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: We will be nothing more than buyers and users of technology, machines and skills.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: We will be nothing more than persons attending training courses.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: The Government schemes will be tapped upon for expenditure, but we will not achieve our aim of fostering pervasive innovation throughout our economy.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: But we can also catalyse such change upstream, through education.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: It has continued to review its curriculum and pedagogy to prepare future-ready leaders.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: Hence, I have a few suggestions which I hope MOE will consider.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: While basic subjects remain important, I submit we should review our curriculum and make structural changes to our education landscape.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: Before I go further, Mr Deputy Speaker, allow me to talk about Deepmind's AlphaGo.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: AlphaGo is not just a computer game of Go.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: It is a programme that defeated the reigning three-time European champion, Mr Fan Hui, in October 2015 in a 5-0 win and, just last year, it defeated the legendary grandmaster Mr Lee Sedol, winner of 18 world titles and widely considered to be the greatest player of the past decade.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: AlphaGo earns a ninth-Dan professional ranking that is the highest certification ever for a Go player, a computer programme getting a ranking over a human being.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: Unlike AlphaGo, AlphaGo Zero did not learn to play Go using human amateur and professional games.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: It learnt to play Go simply by playing games against itself, starting from completely random play.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: It is now arguably the strongest player of all time.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: It gives us a glimpse into what world we are living in, what world our children will live in.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: Think of our children facing AI in their lives, careers and challenges.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: We communicate with human beings in human languages; our children will need to communicate with machines in their languages.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: We need doctors when our bodily functions are compromised; we need machine physicians to intervene and fix machines when functions have been compromised.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: We apply human psychology in interactions with one another; our children will need to understand the psychology of machines.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: Language, physiology, psychology – I use words hitherto applied to human beings.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: Could it be that, in the world to come, there may be little differentiation?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: How can we, our young people, live, thrive and harness AI in such a world which is no longer science fiction?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: This could potentially broaden the skillsets and perspectives of our students.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: With industrial 4.0, we need more than academic competencies.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: We need to nurture from young the appetite for risk, the comfort level for problems, the courage to fall and to stand again.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: In line with curriculum change, therefore, we must effect environmental change.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: The environment in which children cram or are hothoused for better grades should be changed to a "push-frontier" environment, in which children challenge one another by creating problems and by devising solutions to those problems, an environment in which children are challenged with different risk permutations and are allowed to grapple with defective or inadequate responses, simulations of real-life scenarios in which they analyse, brainstorm, role play and make judgement calls.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: Instead of clearly defined experiments within each subject, students could be challenged to use a combination of their knowledge and skills across subjects to achieve certain outcomes.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: A push frontier environment will encourage creative thinking, the ability to conceptualise problems, create problems, solve problems, and live with problems.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: It will build confidence and the courage to be different.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: The courage to create will shape a different world view, a different view of success and failure.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: To be sustainable, this environment must be housed in the school.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: I note the already heavy commitment of students.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: The Government has done much to try to level the playing field.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: But the fact remains that, all things being equal, children from more advantaged backgrounds will have access to more enrichment and tuition classes, and, when assessed on the current academic models, outperform their peers.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: As long as this situation persists, we run the risk of not harnessing the potential of all our young people.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: The current system has been abused such that inequity continues to be perpetuated and deepened.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: We have children study together, grow together, spend time together ‒ greater opportunity to level up, greater opportunity to bond.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: When they go home, parents should be encouraged to reduce reliance on external contractors in providing additional teaching and hothousing and use the time for family bonding.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: We require a change in the way we define success and failure.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: The Chinese have a saying,行行出状元, meaning there are top scholars from every trade.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: I had previously used this to encourage those who did not perform academically.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: To my mind, it connotes that one is only valued if one is at the top of one’s trade.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: Everyone is important, not just those at the top.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: I am not encouraging sloppy or irresponsible performance.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: But I am saying that everyone is to be valued, regardless of whether you are at the top or at the bottom.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: Each time we get into the car, we put our lives in the hands of the last mechanic who serviced it.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: Most of us do not need a mechanic who is top of his trade.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: We just need one who is competent and responsible.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: We should also value "failure" as an alternative outcome.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: Penicillin may not have been discovered but for a messed-up experience on something else.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: Of course, Dr Fleming was not the only one to be credited.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: The rest of the team were hardly to be known as 状 元..

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: We should also re-examine scholarship criteria used in Government, commercial and IHL scholarships.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: What criteria qualities do we want in our future leaders?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: Responsibility, courage, risk-taking, the ability to fall and stand again?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: Are we prepared to grant a scholarship to a student with a B-score, in place of one with straight As?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: If the first student had scored his Bs because he had to overcome an illness, or because he had to work to supplement his family income, or because he had to care for a sickly parent or a sibling, are we prepared to have scholarships for students on the basis of courage and risk-taking?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: Unless we review our scholarship criteria, I submit we may not have, and we would be hard put to find leaders that we will need in the age to come.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: I welcome the measures in Budget 2018 and, in particular, await more information regarding the Capability Transfer Programme.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: In relation to the forging of strong partnerships, can I request that we take a long hard look at how we now attract foreign companies to Singapore?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: We could consider a progressive model of ensuring that the right to the grant of privileges or to continue to enjoy such privileges is reciprocated by an increase in the transfer of knowledge and skills to employees and local enterprises.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: We could require vigilance in systematic and structured training and transfer of such skills to local employees and enterprises.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: Next, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, a few short words about migrant workers.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: Migrant workers could range from Work Permit holders to senior executives.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: We have never been xenophobic, and despite vociferous noises from certain quarters, we must never be.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: Some of our friends returned to their homelands, but our forefathers stayed on.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: Today, our children and loved ones work and live overseas as migrant workers.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: We hope for them, our children and loved ones, to be cared for and respected in those communities, and we hope for them to do well.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: Let us then be hospitable to migrant workers in our midst and hope that they, too, will do well.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: And to our migrant worker friends, you are our guests.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: Please respect our culture, our rules and even our accent.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: Whether you eat or drink, cross the road or cycle, please respect our culture, please respect our rules.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: There are many among us who have carried themselves honourably and they are our shining examples.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: And we are confident that with mutual respect, together, we can achieve a win-win for all.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: An aim around us, hearts big enough to accept someone who has failed, minds broad enough to see alternatives, rather than failure.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: The Government may pave the way for us, but how we take that road and where we find our destination are up to us.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: Let us take this journey together as Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: We will fall, but we will lift one another up.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: We will succeed in honour of their memory, we would succeed for ourselves, and we would succeed for our children.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: Because with the Singapore spirit, we will triumph.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Dr Tan, do you have a clarification for Ms Chia?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: As far as I understand it, not being an economist myself, nowhere in the report does it mention protection against currency speculation and other forms of stress which may subject a country's reserves to.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: My clarification, Mr Deputy Speaker, is that I am not sure, at least speaking as a lay person, how Ms Kuik's speech in mentioning the IMF and Singapore's Reserves lead to the recommended conclusion that we might not be maintaining the Reserves as much as we should?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin
text: I have no idea what the Member is asking.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin
text: I could not hear what he wanted to ask.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: Or alternatively, it might be just me because I fully acknowledge that, like Ms Kuik, I am also not trained as an economist.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: As an interested lay person, I am trying to understand the argument better.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: But would Ms Kuik agree that maybe we shall leave it more to the expert folk to educate both of us on this issue?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin
text: I think in the speech, I said quite clearly I was a terrible economics student and I do not really know much.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin
text: I really would appreciate the Government's clear and easy-to-understand response to that because I did not know how to make sense of it.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: You would not want to know my economics grade!

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: I do not know whether, on a Point of Order, it is proper for me to ask.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: I do not direct it to any particular Member, but to various Members who spoke largely about equality or inequality within our community.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Ms Chia, you can seek a clarification if you are asking someone to clarify.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: But if you are asking the general House, no one would want to answer you.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: If I may ask the hon Member, Ms Kuik, and if I recall correctly, also Ms Sylvia Lim, I think there had been much discourse on inequality in our community.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: I am wondering whether the hon Members were thinking of inequality or inequity.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: Are they thinking about the Government or the society not having taken enough measures to make sure that everyone is equal or are they talking about not taking enough measures to equip and level up each child to their potential?

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Ms Kuik, I am afraid Ms Sylvia Lim is not in the House, so you would have to answer.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Ms Chia asked either of you, and only you are here.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin
text: I guess we may differ in our thinking about how much is enough help for people.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin
text: I speak especially for children with single mothers and foreign mothers.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin
text: We have talked a long time in this House about the differences of views about why they cannot get adequate housing and all that.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Ms Chia, are you happy with the answer?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: The point I wanted to make was that there is a difference between an inequity and equality.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: Nobody is equal and I do not think it is ever possible to make everyone equal.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: So, perhaps, the Member could be referring to inequity rather than inequality.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Ms Kuik, are you referring to inequality or inequity?

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Are you clear on the clarification raised by Ms Chia?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin
text: Could the Member redefine "inequity" and "inequality" in your point of view?

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: So, she is asking Ms Chia to clarify.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong
text: So, perhaps you could be thinking of requesting for more equitable treatment rather than equal treatment.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin
text: I do not want to hold up the debate.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin
text: I am quite happy to discuss with the Member in the Members' Room later about inequity and inequality.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I will try my best to keep things simple.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think, listening to the debate, I suspect the question from Dr Tan to Ms Kuik was actually whether she thinks MAS is putting too much away in Reserves.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I understand that was the point in the speech.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But I guess she can clarify and the Finance Minister can answer that question.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: That is the only clarification, does Ms Kuik think that MAS is putting aside too much?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: From what I understand from Ms Chia's point is that equity is about fairness.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, if someone does more, he deserves more, whereas equality is everyone gets the same.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think what Ms Chia is asking Ms Kuik is whether or not she is looking for fairness to everyone as opposed to equality.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: That is my contribution to clarify for everyone.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Vikram, you are seeking a clarification from Ms Kuik or you are trying to clarify Ms Chia's clarification?

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I think Ms Kuik is happily seated and we will not let the debate carry on upon the clarifications.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In no other democracy will a Finance Minister announce a tax increase four or more years in advance, with a general election in between.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: No government will willingly announce a decision to raise taxes and especially not one which wants to continue to be in government.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: To do so takes integrity and courage to be willing to lay upfront the challenges facing our nation and explain what we need to do to surmount these challenges.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Faced with high costs of living, such a move is painful and worries many.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Enhancing financial assistance and support packages would, therefore, be imperative in helping our low-income and perhaps even our middle-income families and Singaporeans to cope.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But emotions and concerns aside, we know that money needs to be raised to fund new projects and programmes.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The Finance Minister had, in his speech, explained in detail why he has taken such an unprecedented move.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Indeed, we are faced with many challenges – technological disruptions, rapid ageing in our population, mature infrastructure that needs to be maintained, new infrastructure that needs to be built, and more.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We need to respond decisively, as one people.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: How we respond now will determine if Singapore can continue to be a thriving nation amidst a highly competitive world, one in which our young will continue to have a bright future and our seniors are properly taken care of in their old age.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Budget 2018 takes a long-term and strategic view.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It sets out a programme to transform and revitalise our economy; to boost infrastructure and build a Smart Nation; to strengthen our hardware and social infrastructure and prepare for an ageing population.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These are important priorities, to keep Singapore strong and viable, and the best home for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: To fund these priorities, we need to raise revenue.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The Finance Minister has set out three ways to do this.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: First, impose spending controls and cutting Ministries' budget growth; second, finance some of the infrastructure developments through bonds; and third, raise GST.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: My view is that we should do these three ways in that order.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In other words, first, ensure that our Ministries and Statutory Boards are run in the most efficient manner.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I do not advocate starving the public services of much needed resources to do their jobs properly.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But if we are to raise taxes, we owe it to Singaporeans to make sure that what the Government has already collected is not squandered.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In the same vein, could we make better use of this year’s surplus?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I understand from the Finance Minister that this is an exceptional surplus, and we cannot always count on having exceptional surpluses.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Second, the Minister announced that bonds will be issued to fund infrastructure projects.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So far, market reports appear to be positive, with some believing that this will "turbo-charge" the debt market.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: What safeguards are in place to ensure that we are able to meet the payments and also fulfil our projects going ahead?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I believe Singaporeans will understand the rationale and tradeoffs for raising GST, however painful it is for our citizens, provided that the Government works very hard to deliver on promises and prove that every revenue dollar raised is efficiently and effectively used for the public good.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singaporeans have trusted this Government for decades and made many painful sacrifices for our nation’s long-term good.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We must never squander this trust and must do our best to protect Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Deputy Speaker, allow me to continue in Mandarin.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In Mandarin):   Deputy Speaker, Sir, how society respects the elderly and care for the disadvantaged not only shows how civilised we are but also reflects on our moral upbringing and common beliefs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, respecting the elderly and caring for the disadvantaged cannot just be empty talk, but must be put into practice.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We must "walk the talk" through the institutions, policies and actions to ensure that our seniors and the disadvantaged are well looked after.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With our population ageing rapidly, the Government must introduce policies and adjust the allocation of resources decisively, and perhaps even carry out a major "facelift" to prepare for an ageing population.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With regard to caring for our elderly, the Government has done a lot and has accumulated a lot of valuable experiences.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It has also made many improvements in healthcare subsidies and pro-elderly services.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For example, with the launch of the enhanced healthcare subsidies, many elderly residents no longer require help from the Macpherson ComCare Fund, which we initiated voluntarily to help low-income senior citizens defray medical costs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In addition, the CNS pilot programme launched by the Government also produced good results, and Macpherson is honoured to be part of the trial.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In the past, we used to have to approach the Ministries separately to seek help for our elderly residents.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If a certain Ministry does not have enough resources, we had to knock on the door of other Ministries.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: CNS has been able to provide regular health checks for seniors, and they have become healthier and more active.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With the help of neighbourhood volunteers recruited through the network, the elderly who live alone no longer feel lonely and helpless.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: From what we can see, the Government can help turn our common ideals into reality and, thankfully, the Government has worked on this relentlessly.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, it is also equally apparent that the people's response and support are of vital importance.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If nobody is willing to donate money, then the Macpherson ComCare Fund will not be able to help the elderly who cannot afford to see a doctor.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If no one volunteered, then we cannot take care of senior citizens who live alone, on a large-scale and organised way.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: On a higher level, if people do not support the Government, national programmes cannot be implemented, no matter how great they are.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is the duty of elected leaders to set the future direction and strategies of a country, and the responsibility of the entire Government to implement policies effectively.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, the success of a country’s strategy is not just dependent on the Government.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Otherwise, the Government would be speaking without a voice and punching without weight.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: How then can they implement necessary policies for the long-term good of the country?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: How then can they ensure the disadvantaged or minorities whose interests are at odds with the majority, are taken care of?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: How then can they implement programmes that ensure the competitive advantage of the country and its people, or even the ability to compete effectively in the international arena?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We all know what the Government has done to take care of our senior citizens.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But I also hope that the Government can do more to create a more pro-elderly environment.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As we grow old, we inevitably face limits in terms of physical strength, but that does not mean we no longer have a part to play, nor does that mean it is the end of life.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If we can make the necessary adjustments, our twilight years can also be interesting.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Some elderly Singaporeans may choose to continue working, some choose to be volunteers, while others choose to learn new things, and some may even pursue dreams that were out of reach when they were young.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Regardless of what they choose to do, we should ensure that our environment supports and not limit them, so that they can do what they are good at and continue to make a difference.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In this way, our senior citizens will not develop a negative attitude.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Instead, they will maintain active lifestyles, live more meaningful lives and become truly happy senior citizens.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In English): As we justify the need for hard measures in order to sustain fiscal sustainability, I hope we will not inadvertently attribute the cause to our elderly, which is the primary narrative on the ground now.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: An ageing population is one of the key contributing factors, but we know that it is not the only one.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And we must recognise that being old is not being useless.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We need a paradigm shift across all levels and sectors of our society that seniors are assets and not liabilities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We just need to create the right and enabling environment for them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Much of what we have today, including hardware and social infrastructure, was designed decades ago when our population was still young.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is time to refresh these to welcome a different population landscape with a different set of requirements.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We need to ensure adequate support for our elderly today and tomorrow, so that we are all empowered to age gracefully and actively in the comfort of our own homes and community.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Given our expectations on social spending, it is imperative that we maximise the impact of every dollar spent.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We must enable our elderly today and tomorrow to continue leading an independent and graceful life.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This will ensure effective use of resources and better planning.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In any case, it is the same target stakeholder group.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: From policies to qualifying criteria and service standards, AIC is better positioned to design and deliver a seamless suite of programmes to care for our seniors holistically.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: MacPherson is fortunate to have been one of the pilot sites for CNS.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
