text: Within just over six months of implementation, we have observed tangible benefits on the ground and received positive feedback.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: At the agency level, AIC plays a coordinating role, though it is very much a "deal maker" as well.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In the past, if seniors have needs or encounter issues requiring our assistance, we have to approach the agencies one by one and be subjected to their available resources, which is time consuming.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Most of the time, it would be extremely challenging to get a common date that the agencies can agree on.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: At the local level, our seniors with different needs are matched to the local VWOs for further engagement or services according to their organisational strengths.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This is more targeted and demonstrates the many-helping-hands approach.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In terms of benefits to seniors, services are more structured and holistic, with proper follow-ups.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Seniors do not just go through health screenings, they are given practical advice on suitable diet and exercise, and there are dedicated people who would follow up or check in on them to ensure follow through.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Seniors, so far, have been very appreciative of this.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Beyond health services, our single elderly are now more socially connected and better cared for.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Take Mr Toh, a 66-year-old senior in MacPherson, for instance.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: He lives alone and expressed that he felt lonely with nobody to talk to.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This was brought up to CNS and a befriender was arranged to visit him on a monthly basis.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: He was also invited to join active ageing activities at the MacPherson Community Club or in the community.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Mr Toh is now a much happier person.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With the integration at the national level, I believe the benefits will be much more.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But I hope the Government will go further in creating an enabling environment for seniors to continue to thrive in.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: First, let us design to include and empower mainstream elder-friendly designs and make them pervasive, so that seniors can lead a normal and productive life regardless of where they are.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Apply elderly-friendly designs to the development of common spaces, facilities, machine interfaces, workflows, public processes and more.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: There are some inevitable physical constraints as one ages, but that does not necessarily mean that one can no longer do meaningful work or lead an active life after becoming old.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With the right environment, these constraints can be compensated and seniors can continue to thrive.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: No institution or country so far has been an authority in terms of setting elderly-friendly design standards.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singapore can take the lead in setting elderly-friendly standards and be the authority in this area.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Second, create a favourable environment and employment opportunities for seniors.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: There are seniors who want to work, either out of passion, or sadly, out of financial need.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Regardless, given that we have seniors who do want to work, let us help them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Third, and this is more for seniors who are less independent, proliferate digital eldercare to supplement shortage of eldercare manpower and help more seniors live independently.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: There may soon be a point in time when there are more who need care than those who can care.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I have spoken at length during the Motion on Support for Senior Citizens earlier this month, and I will speak about it again during the Committee of Supply (COS).

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But the point is that if you can leverage technology more, if you can leverage digital eldercare more, we can help more elderly Singaporeans, those who may have difficulties moving around, and even paraplegics or those who may be semi-paralysed, to be more independent and continue to enjoy the comfort of their own homes.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Of course, it is not enough for the Government alone to work on it.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Our seniors need to believe in themselves and step up, too.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I firmly believe that our seniors are much more capable than being mere recipients of care.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As we enhance our healthcare, we can expect longer and more healthy years.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As our economy evolves, there will be less reliance on physical strength at the workplace but more use of intellect and wisdom.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As each population becomes better educated and more savvy in the digital space, there will be less fear and deeper entrenchment of technology in our everyday lives.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I am also against self-defeating thoughts, such as lao le bu zhong yong 老了不中用, which means that we are useless after we aged, which can be self-fulfilling.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Whether it is to remain active economically or socially, it is a choice our seniors have to make.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But the point is that we need to keep active and we need to keep trying.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Being active brings meaning to life, it helps us look forward to every new day.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singapore weathered through many disruptions and we have transformed time and again.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, I hope we will continue to possess the quality of resilience and discipline, so that we can deliver a progressive yet compassionate Singapore.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I also note that the Minister and his Ministry are putting in a lot of effort in communicating his ideas and the rationale in his decisions through various channels to engage our people.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As we grow our economy and meet the challenges ahead, there will be demand for more skilled manpower.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I see a growing pool of retirees, whom we should look to, to rely on, as a good source to meet our skilled manpower needs.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many of our retirees are healthy, well-educated, well-informed and with good work ethos.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, an accountant may have a passion to teach preschoolers, or an engineer, a passion in the nursing profession.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With more childcare and healthcare facilities being built, we definitely need extra manpower.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For some of our retirees, it is not always about the money.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Rather, it is about doing the things that they have always wanted to do and are prepared to be retrained to take on this new career.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: After her retirement, she became a full-time caregiver to her two grandchildren.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Her neighbours knew she doted on children and would occasionally ask her to babysit for them when they had errands to run.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Morin has always obliged as she loves children very much.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Last year, Morin approached the Henderson-Dawson PAP Community Foundation (PCF) Childcare Centre at her block to volunteer her services.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As the teachers saw a gem in her who had so much love for the children, the centre offered her a job and she readily took up the offer.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: She now interacts with the children, plays with them, keeps them comfortable, and gives them all the love and tender care, like how she cared for her grandchildren when they were young.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: She also assists in the overall maintenance and hygiene of the centre, including sanitising the play equipment and kitchen utensils.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Morin has been working in the Henderson-Dawson PCF Childcare Centre since February 2017, and is enjoying every day of it.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: At 69 today, she is healthy, experienced and committed.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: She sees her work with PCF as a second career.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If they are prepared to take the flight to a new beginning, then let us offer them the conversion training and be the wind beneath their wings.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I now turn to the subject of "Building a liveable city and a smart nation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have done much to make our home a truly liveable city, from having a strong economy, building good infrastructure ranging from affordable housing, healthcare and education institutions to a host of other amenities.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our elderly, the generation of Baby Boomers born in the 1940s to 1950s and, among them, a good number belong to the group who missed formal education, were working in manual work and are somewhat struggling to understand and keep up with the new digital age.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is a vicious cycle where because they were doing harsh manual work, it took a toll on their health.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Because they were not earning much, they do not have the luxury to afford many things and they lead a spartan life.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some do not have good family support and have to fend for themselves.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In my Henderson-Dawson ward, many of them I meet enjoy walking around the neighbourhood parks, chatting with neighbours at the void decks or markets and the coffee shops or visiting the community centres (CCs) and senior activity centres (SACs) to socialise and enjoy the liveable city.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But more can be done for them in our Smart Nation journey.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: All the talk about the Digital Age, the Information Age frightens some of them.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These residents are just spectators in the high-speed world of information, connectivity through smartphones, smart TV, iPads, chat apps, quick response (QR) codes, e-banking.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our CCs and SACs have been running computer classes and given many of them hands-on opportunity to touch and navigate through the “www”.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: At the CC or library, there are silver Internet hotspots, but the operating hours may not suit their time schedule.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Plus, mobility may be an issue for some.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Seniors need their own time and space to tinker and learn at their own pace and in the comfort of their own homes.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In helping them to get into the Digital Age, it would also help to bring them closer to the younger generation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They can talk to them about some basics of the Internet of Things.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The key is that the seniors would not be alienated.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In fact, getting them on board would help them better engage and participate in the various Government initiatives.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, they can gain access to health information and be empowered to care for themselves or their spouse.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In this show, they will pose a set of three questions for viewers to think what would be the correct answer.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, real-life freak accidents are shown with morbid three-dimentional (3D) graphics.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There are episodes which even captured real phone calls, so you can hear what fear and anxiety sound like.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Then, the viewer is given a choice of three possible options, two of which result in death or serious injury.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: One initiative I have in mind for “Do or Die” show is for our SG Secure.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We can play out the scenario of a major fire catastrophe, sudden cardiac arrest or choking incident.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: After watching the show, I believe what is learnt in a fun and audio-visual way is likely to stay in the mind.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The lessons learnt will enhance and contribute to our Total Defence strategy.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: One is never too old to dream another dream and make that come true.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, I stand in support of the Budget proposed by Minister Heng Swee Keat and his team.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The IMF blog in April 2017 attempted to define several key principles underlying good fiscal policies and smart fiscal policies.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The blog read that in a world of dramatic economic disruptions and globalisation, smart and good fiscal policies facilitate change, harness a country's growth potential and protect people who are hurt by the disruptions.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There is a call by IMF for more room to install more growth-friendly, inclusive, strong and prudent fiscal policies around the world.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: National budgets are the key means by which fiscal measures, such as spendings and taxation, are implemented.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Budget 2018 continues with the aim of building a vibrant and innovative economy through a slew of more than 20 initiatives to anchor Singapore as a Global-Asia enterprise node.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It continues with its aggressive plan to train more Singaporeans in a world of technological and business disruptions.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Budget 2018 also passes the test of promoting inclusion.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But Budget 2018 is, at the same time, prudent.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: By putting a cap on Ministry budgets, it encourages public servants to do more with less, respecting that money is hard-earned, whether at the national or personal levels.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In addition, by having the AIC to coordinate activities for seniors and strengthening the Social Service Offices (SSOs) to link up the Many Helping Hands on the ground, Budget 2018 reduces overlaps and directs resources to where support is most needed on the ground.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In a sense, Budget 2018, Mr Deputy Speaker, is somewhat "better than good".

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I believe that better national budgets are those which confront issues head on; and takes the courage to put in measures important, sometimes unpopular, to secure our future; going beyond the here and now.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But at the same time, it promises Singaporeans that those in the lower- and average-income brackets will not have to bear the cost of this GST hike because it has the permanent GST rebate feature that comes with it.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For Budget 2018 to be the best ever, I have several inputs for the Minister to consider for incorporation, especially during implementation.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Not all of these inputs fall under the direct purview of MOF, but I am hoping the Minister will help to facilitate some of these inputs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Most of them concern mindsets because, as they say, the real battlefield is often in our minds.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: As a member of the Council for the Future Economy (CFE), I have personally witnessed the painstaking efforts by Council members and their subcommittees in developing ITMs to anchor Singapore as an innovation, technology and enterprise node.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But maps are maps, and they need tangible support and resources to become realities.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Budget 2018, with its slew of 17 measures in this space, is certainly moving in the right direction to support the making of a vibrant and innovative economy.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: However, Sir, a vibrant and innovative economy is not developed from Budget allocations and programmes.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is not developed from only speaking up, and Member Mr Louis Ng spoke about that earlier.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Although that is a good starting point, it requires a conducive setting of a culture of pervasive innovation, and we know that cultures are not built overnight.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In fact, research says that a purposeful attempt at culture-building takes at least three to five years.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: As in raising a child, fostering a culture of pervasive innovation takes a village.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Fostering pervasive innovation requires more than plug-and-play solutions.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It needs a whole society to create an environment that encourages and celebrates a sense of playing, tinkering and experimenting, something that preschools, like My First Skool and MOE Kindergartens, are starting to do.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, I think Budget 2018 should actually allocate more resources to do a deep independent dive on what is stopping us from seeing more pervasive innovation in, one, the private sector, especially amongst our SMEs; two, in education institutions from young to older ones, and families, and especially, in the Public Service which is watching over this space.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Another hindrance to fostering a culture of pervasive innovation is likely the lack of vision and limitations caused by existing processes and tools.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There is a story of a man who went fishing.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Each time he caught a big fish, he will throw it back into the water.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And if it is a smaller fish, he kept it.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, an observer nearby found this incredulous and asked him why he did that, why throw back the big fish and keep the small fish?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And this man replied, "Sir, you do not understand.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The dish in my kitchen for the fish is only seven inches long, and if the fish is any bigger, then it would not fit in my dish!" That is why he threw it back.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The question then remains: how can we achieve a better balance between being fearless and visionary and having to be accountable and answer for one's actions, especially failure?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And that may lead us to having more results and outcomes in trying to build a culture of innovation and ensuring innovative outcomes in all of our different aspects of the Budget.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Second, on asset expenditure, a 2017 report by the Centre of Creative Leadership says that newer business models are presenting threats to traditional models, and the traditional models are the ones that are centred around assets, for example, a hotel property; services, for example, a recruitment company or online retail mall or technology products, such as an Electronic Road Pricing (ERP) system.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This report states that in a rapidly sharing economy, a "network orchestra" model that provides platforms to bring partners together for transactions and collaborations is almost now a new normal.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Hence, the rise of highly valued assets which do not themselves own physical assets, companies, such as Uber, AirBnB, Expedia and the like, are on the rise.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I, therefore, cannot help but notice that, in Budget 2018, several of the big-ticket infrastructure expenditure revolve around physical infrastructure – the high-speed rail, the airport and the mega Tuas port.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Needless to say, to operate these physical assets would require the corresponding software infrastructure.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But there still ought to be a sharper focus on creating non-physical assets and investments.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Tharman Shanmugaratnam, at an IMF conference just a couple of days ago in Jakarta, spoke about the huge opportunity offered by the vision of a single digital economy for ASEAN and the potential of financial technology (Fintech) and other financial innovations.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: What are we doing to position ourselves as a leader in the provision and export of non-physical assets to serve not only ASEAN but the rest of the world?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Are there any ways by which good solutions that we use internally in Government or in the Public Service can be developed with export as a goal and monetised to add to the national coffer?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Thirdly, on building a future for the vulnerable.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In executing our five CDCs' charter to enhance awareness and adoption of SkillsFuture, I find that not enough Singaporeans actually believe or fully appreciate the speed of change and the risk we are all in in a disruptive new economy – jobs that have disappeared or will be disappearing, like word processors and typists, data entry operators, some travel agents, insurance agents; jobs that we see today that never existed before, such as digital market specialists, drone operators, content creators, data scientists, app developers, Uber drivers, driverless car engineers.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: At the macro level, even if the economy looks good and the unemployment rate looks good – lo, Minister Lim Swee Say had famously said many times that the labour market is not short of jobs, it is short of citizens who possess the appropriate skills, the right skills, to fill the jobs of the new economy.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: If ordinary Singaporeans are affected by all these massive changes, what more those who are not as mobile, not as adaptable, not as culturally-sensitive to work in the global market or cognitively able – the vulnerable and the lowly-skilled, not out of choice but out of circumstances, what will happen to them?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: How do we ensure that, indeed, when the tide rises, all boats will rise?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Fourthly, Sir, on bringing out the best in Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I am not certain how many Singaporeans, especially those in the middle- and higher-income brackets, are appreciative of Budget 2018's gift of the SG ang pow as a sharing of surplus from the last financial year.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But I am almost certain that there will be no end of critics who say the ang pow is too little or too much.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: A $100 SG Bonus "hongbao", for some, could mean just an additional dinner out for the family or for himself.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But to another citizen, the bonus adds to the cash flow to purchase that milk powder or diapers for the family baby or disabled elderly parent.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This is not a job for the Government alone.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is a job for all of us – Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is for all of us, as a country, to imagine that we can become even better versions of ourselves.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There is the story of a farmer who often wins awards for growing the best corn in his locale.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, when a journalist asked him for his secret of success for growing this best corn, the farmer replied, to the journalist's surprise, that he shared the corns with his neighbour farmers.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The journalist was surprised and asked, "How can you, Mr Farmer, afford to share your best seeds with your neighbours when they are your competitors?" To this, the farmer explained, "Sir, you need to know this.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The wind picks up pollen from ripening corns and blows them from field to field.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: If my neighbours grow inferior corn, the cross-pollination will affect the quality of my own corn." And herein lies the story of successful people and nations – why they should never just stick to Success, worldly Success, but move to Significance.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Like the farmer, if we wish to grow good corn, we must help our neighbours grow good corn.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: If we want a peaceful life, we must help our neighbours be peaceful as well.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: If we want to do well, we must seek to help others do well, too.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In the world of business, I saw many top busy local business leaders, some of them in the Council for the Future Economy, some in the CDC I work with.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: They are busy business leaders but they gave unselfishly to causes beyond themselves – leaders like Mr Robert Yap from YCH Group who helped start the Logistics Academy for the logistics sector, many of whom are his competitors.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Leaders like Mr Vincent Tan of Select Group who is unselfish in encouraging the food and beverage (F&B) sector to try out new technology and SkillsFuture initiatives; leaders like Mr Kang Puay Seng and his partner who, during their days starting Mr Bean, trained and supported adults with disabilities to prepare and sell soya bean products; and leaders like Mr Wee Ee Cheong and Ms Wee Wei Ling who used their business platforms in the banks and hotels to create jobs for the disabled.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There are many more giants like them with whom I engage in my CDC and charity work.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In North Carolina in the United States (US), students in a school’s technology centre create prosthetic arms using 3D printing for others in need and, at the same time, hone their advanced manufacturing skills.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Two young staff of mine in the CDC, Caleb and Sherlyn Yap, a couple, help villagers in Thailand and Cambodia start chicken farms as a livelihood.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Each year, they use their annual leave to do that.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I see in this young Singaporean couple not only kindness and contentment but also a sense of purpose and a sense of meaning.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Budget 2018 had put in six measures, no less, to foster a spirit of giving.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It will come in useful for the emerging and existing needs that we identify in each of our Districts.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Our Camp Explore programme curates good enrichment classes, holiday programmes.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I remember Ms Sylvia Lim and Ms Kuik Shiao Yin have been talking about these to close the inequality gap.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: They say it is possible to give away and become wealthier, richer.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: It is also possible to hold on too tight to what we own and lose them all.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I record my thanks as well to the to the Tamil translators, in particular, led by Mr Palaniappan, for preparing, with the Tamil Language Council, a very useful glossary of English-to-Tamil translated words.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Anything that I say from this point onwards in Tamil that may sound intelligent is thanks to them.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Anything which I may say which does not sound sensible is my fault alone!

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Having said this, it is only fitting, Mr Deputy Speaker, that I begin my speech with a few words in the longest surviving classical language in the world, an official vernacular in Singapore, and my mother tongue language, Tamil.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: (In Tamil):    Mr Deputy Speaker, last week, Finance Minister Heng Swee Keat gave a praiseworthy, forward-thinking Budget Statement.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The Statement reminded me of a couplet written by a great sage called "Thiruvalluvar" which says that the best way to guard oneself is not to slight the powerful or the elders.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Applied to the Budget Statement, this means we should not abandon our respected elders who sacrificed for our nation's progress, do not ignore their advice, understand their dilemmas and, importantly, do not forget their dreams.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, the Budget policy serves as a supportive "walking stick" for elders.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I believe it will encourage a spirit of giving in every Singaporean.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Through this Budget policy, this fundamental tenet is not only reserved for this year, but, like a banyan tree, can grow roots deep into the community and support a fiscally sustainable and secure future for all of us as well.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It will also support our gurus or our elders.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I was one such caregiver to a grand aunt and a grand uncle.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: One such example in my case is with my grand aunt and grand uncle.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: They are fortunate because there are quite a few members around but they do not have children of their own.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: So, they turned to family members who do not live with them.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: They have an extremely good Town Council in a mature HDB estate where they live.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: As an example, they had not planned for their financial retirement.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: So, every time they needed money, the one asset they would use would be the one that is over their head.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: So, you sell your house and use the income that you have for the next few years.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: How many Singaporeans may be in the same boat but may not have the same kind of MP who would sit down with them and explain to them what they could do, or may not have family members who are either legally trained or professionally trained to guide them over the next steps?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: This is the question that troubles me, Mr Deputy Speaker.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I think this is something that we should be thinking about.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: As we look at the next steps beyond our elderly – and I firmly believe and support the welfare-centric Budget that Minister Heng has put before us but I do think and I will speak about this in a moment – we have to spend more time communicating the importance of such a Budget to Singaporeans.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: And I must record my thanks at this point to, beyond everyone else, the Jurong Town Corporation and the Monetary Authority of Singapore.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But the question still comes: when we are not combating a deficit, why are we tightening the purse strings?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Is it because we fear that our small and open economy is vulnerable to fluctuations in the global economy and financial markets?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: We are accustomed to Singapore and its limitations as a low-lying, small island state.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: What stands out to me in this Budget that Minister Heng has put before us is that it does not seem to be driven only by fears.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: On the contrary, there is a savvy inherent in his proposed measures.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Minister Heng suggests, for example, that Government Ministries, much like private enterprises, will need to look for more productive and innovative ways to run their own agencies.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Simply put, they should adopt a corporate work ethic.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond adopting a corporate culture, Mr Deputy Speaker, the Government has a solemn responsibility to explain, in plain and practical terms, how these taxes tomorrow will benefit us, our elderly and our children in further time to come.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The Government may wish to explain why Singaporeans should go from maintaining their own parents alone, which is their current social and legal compact, to assisting with the maintenance of the nation’s elderly as a whole.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The Government should explain whether Singapore will continue to be a "liveable" city if we are consistently ranked amongst the most expensive cities in the world.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: If there are new gaps, will the Government then think about revising upwards the current GST, as an example?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: If the answer is, which I imagine it should be, "well, yes, it will be reviewed from time to time", the recurrent question that Singaporeans will ask, and they will ask it now is: why not rely a little more heavily, not completely, but a little more heavily, on NIRC?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Why can they not be increased to finance our needs?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: This will come back again and again every time there is an increase in GST and in any other tax.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Alternatively, they will ask "should we not have more progressive wealth taxes"?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: So, the best way to deal with this now, when we are planning for 2021, is to speak to Singaporeans at this point.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: In all honesty, Mr Deputy Speaker, the questions and clarifications that I am raising, while directed at Minister Heng and MOF, really are at the Government as a whole, because they warrant a broader conversation.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Singaporeans’ concerns over public expenditure are real, and they need to be heard, if possible, so that they can be addressed.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: They need to be heard in a context where this message can be unpacked.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: And I say "unpacked" because I enjoyed the healthy debate that we had today.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The clarification over inequality and inequity ‒ that is interesting to me.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But that is because I am an academic, Mr Deputy Speaker.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: That is because I am legally trained, and that is because of the people who spoke.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I know from my own experience that two of them are expert JC debaters and one is a really good lawyer.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Minister Heng mentioned in his speech that "Our Singapore Conversation" (OSC) in 2011 or 2012, if I remember, gave him a window into what Singaporeans were thinking at that time.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It gave him a unique opportunity, in his words, "to converse with Singaporeans about their aspirations for themselves and for Singapore”.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: As a member of that Committee, together with many other people in this House, I would affirm the value of the OSC as a participatory process, and I would ask the Government to take measures to ensure that new dialogues could signal some semblance of "participatory budgeting".

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: These conversations would perhaps be by the Ministries individually with groups that have relevant concerns: where persons, Singaporeans, are given a sense that their views matter and could one day help determine how public finances are spent and how Budgets are implemented; where it is made plain that welfare-centric expenditure tracks demographic trends.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: We have heard this, and I believe it to be true, as I am experiencing it as a caregiver.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But this has to be explained to people who may not have the same burdens or the same considerations on their mind all the time, beginning with the needy aged.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: So, that is the first demographic trend that we have all agreed on.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But in time to come, I am sure there will be other demographic trends which require our welfare-centric concern.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Singaporeans are not fully accustomed to responding to these welfare-centric trends, and we should take the time to explain the importance of doing so.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Traditionally, Mr Deputy Speaker, socioeconomic issues have fallen solely within the remit of the Government and, sometimes, through civil society.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But going beyond this, surely our corporate citizens also have a role to play, and they should be giving back in some way or the other.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: We also want to thank the Tamil interpreter for helping to translate what you said earlier.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is clinical in its approach to dealing with what Singapore needs in the future.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is not bogged down with theoretical purity.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It provides assistance to those who need it most.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It does not discourage prosperity nor does it discourage diligence.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In short, this years’ Budget is ambidextrous – a mix of left- and right-leaning policies.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It shows that we are not concerned as much about theoretical purity as we are about doing what is correct in each circumstance.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are problems with either extremes in economic theories.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: From the now-dissolved Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR), we can see that there is a problem with socialism in the form of Marxist Communism.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Even in China, we see the need for exceptions to socialism in the form of free economic zones in Shenzhen and other designated cities and the Special Administrative Region in Hong Kong.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Today, Shenzhen is known as the Silicon Delta.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On the other extreme, we see the breakdowns of pure capitalism ‒ unbridled capitalism.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: According to David Korten, extreme capitalism has the same problems as that of extreme Marxist socialism.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, economic power concentrates in unaccountable centralised institutions – the state, in the case of Marxism; and the transnational corporation, in the case of capitalism.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The rich get richer, and the poor get poorer.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is because those who control wealth accumulate it at a faster rate than the economy can produce it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This trend continues, unless something disrupts the status quo.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Muller, the author of "The Mind and the Market: Capitalism in Western Thought", says it this way: "Inequality is an inevitable product of capitalist activity...Indeed, one of the most robust findings of contemporary social scientific inquiry is that as the gap between high-income and low-income families has increased, the educational and employment achievement gaps between the children of these families have increased even more." Hence, pure, unbridled capitalism has its problems ‒ that of extreme, entrenched income divides.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, what we need in Singapore is to have a flexible fiscal policy.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We cannot be rigid or be slaves to fiscal ideology just for ideology’s sake.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And this is, in my view, what this Budget seeks to achieve.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Financial analyst Ram Ramesh wrote in the Trinidad Express and he expresses it this way: "Labels, such as socialism and capitalism, are making men in power forget that their role is to administer the right medicine regardless of what label it carries… In these times, it is not the philosophical underpinnings that will guarantee   survival but their own ability to adapt to the rapidly changing economic landscapes.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Not adapting can cause them their very survival." In other words, when we are too inflexible, we are unable to respond to changing situations.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: When we are too concerned about avoiding a certain label or fitting into a particular mould, we tie ourselves to a deadweight and we lose.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, what we need is a flexible approach – an economic policy for our time, for our future, and for the best for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: An array of fiscal options should be on the table with one caveat – that our foundations do not change.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Three, stewardship, that is, making difficult national decisions today for the sake of a better future tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are more foundations, but, to me, these are among the most crucial.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, what we need is a flexible fiscal policy anchored onto unshakeable foundations but without a single-minded fixation on theoretical purity.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Dr Goh Keng Swee was known for being a practical economist, doing what works and not necessarily aiming for theoretical purity in economics.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: An example is in how he "envisioned an important role for the state-government promotion of public goods and externalities… through institutions   as the Economic Development Board (EDB) and the Jurong Town Corporation (JTC)" while being “for the most part… a believer in the efficacy of the markets and the private enterprise system.” This illustrates how we should not be afraid to try less popular policies and be free to think out of the box.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Just as that economic policy was suited for its time, we, too, need an economic policy that speaks to our time ‒ not just our current needs but for our future together as well.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is clinical in its approach to dealing with what Singapore needs in the future.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In short, this years' Budget is ambidextrous, as I have said, a mix of left- and right-leaning policies.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On the one hand, we have policies leaning towards the left.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And, on the other hand, we have policies leaning towards the right.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We are doing all these while also retaining and preserving some right-leaning policies, for example, personal income tax was not increased.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is why I view the budget as a strategic fiscal plan to meet the needs of Singapore and Singaporeans present and future.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is also the reason why I do not agree with Mr Pritam Singh's criticism of the Budget.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If I heard correctly, Mr Singh mentioned that he is unable to support the GST hike at this point in time.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I take that to mean that he is not closed to a GST hike but just not "at this point in time".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I also take it that Mr Singh knows that we are not raising the GST now.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, the real query for us to answer is this: why are we announcing now a hike that is to take place three years or more from today?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The answer is stewardship, honesty and being upfront with the people we serve.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This includes expanding healthcare infrastructure, such as public hospital, community hospital and nursing home capacity; enhanced subsidies for specialised outpatient clinics, as well as intermediate and long-term care and subsidies on premiums on MediShield Life.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These also accommodate longer life expectancy and an ageing population.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There is even more need to "take action" and strengthen our security and defence in the face of "turbulent geopolitics" and the threat of a terror attack at its highest.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Video Trawling and Analytics System to detect, track and recognise faces is being developed; and officers are being trained with simulations and are being equipped with pistols that can hold more bullets.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Further, all MHA departments are expected to be housed at a single complex by 2023 for better coordinated responses in a crisis.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To help everyone reach his or her potential, expenditure per child has increased.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is a colossal task to give every child a good foundation from a younger age, especially preschool.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We are also rolling out programmes to increase financial literacy, digital skills in helping mid-career Singaporeans reskill and upskill in the changing economic landscape.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And we are being upfront with the people we serve.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That is why I disagree with Mr Low Thia Khiang's position that we should not have disclosed the future GST increase now so as to get "buy-in" for the broader vision of this Budget.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We cannot conceal from the people we serve that this revenue will be needed in three or more years.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Much of the increased expenditure is important for meeting the needs of Singaporeans in the long term, for the future.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That principle of stewardship is not to be scoffed at or dismissed lightly.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Pritam Singh also mentioned that we keep on piling accolades on people at the top.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That took me by surprise and I would like to respond to that point because the statement goes against a lot of what I and many in this House stand for.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In fact, many of us in this House stand for the uplifting of the vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We do speak for the voiceless and we celebrate each step taken towards a better life.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A resident whom I serve currently stays in a rental flat with his wife and three daughters – all five of them.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Their daughters are all studying at the moment, one in JC, the other in polytechnic and the eldest at university.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Recently, he shared with me that the family has secured a HDB loan and they will be moving to a flat they can call their own.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It reminds me of another family, a single mother who works as a security guard to raise her family, living in a rental flat.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We worked hard to piece together and appealed to HDB for her to purchase her own HDB flat.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I should say thank you to HDB for that, and she is now a home owner.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We both celebrated when we heard the news.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Caring for the lower-income and, at the same time, being business-friendly so that the economy thrives, and being honest with the people we serve about Singaporeans' future needs and how to meet them.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Pritam Singh has suggested using the revenue raised from land sales to fund expenditure.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In particular, Mr Singh suggested a cap on the amount of earnings that can be used, such as not more than 20% of the value of average land sales over 20 years or 20% of land sales for that year, whichever is lower.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The point here is that we do not want to build in a formula which promotes indiscriminate or rash sales of land to increase revenue for immediate spending.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, instead of building in a formula which promotes possible indiscriminate quick sales of land to increase revenue for immediate spending, it is more fiscally prudent to allow land sales to form part of the Reserves and then investing those Reserves to achieve healthy NIRC.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Ms Sylvia Lim is of the view that because the reversionary title of 10- or 99-year leases return to the Government, land sales is not one-off, that we can use the revenue from land sales and not put all of that in our Reserves.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As stewards, we cannot have a single-minded fixation on theoretical purity.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And when we are able to see that where we are born is not where we will end, we win as a nation.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) and Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I hear across the different speeches that they essentially agree with the many programmes proposed in the Budget.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) and Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In fact, they want the Government to do more – in education, take care of the elderly, doing more for the women, more for the disadvantaged.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) and Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: And in one Member's speech, she focused her speech on inequality and emphasised that inequality is a threat to our nation, that we have to "take concrete steps to remedy it".

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) and Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The Workers' Party agrees with many of the Budget proposals.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) and Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Mr Low Thia Khiang said that this is a forward-looking Budget to anchor Singapore firmly in the future.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) and Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: But, yet, the Workers' Party says that the GST is a distraction.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) and Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In this Budget, we have outlined to Singaporeans how we can take care of our seniors, to better prepare our children for the future, to prime our businesses, to help our workers in the dramatic economic changes taking place and the technological disruptions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) and Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We want to help the disadvantaged in society more.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) and Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: And yet, after all the speeches that I have listened carefully to in this Chamber, the Workers' Party thinks that finding the ways to fund all these programmes is a distraction.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) and Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They agree with the programmes but that talking about how to fund these programmes is a distraction.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) and Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I think it is critical, honest and right that we outline to Singaporeans how we intend to chart Singapore's future forward in a sustainable manner.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Yes, because the Minister is referring to my speech where I said it is a distraction.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: So, I thought it would be better that you announce the intended GST increase of two percentage points at another time.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: We can then have a full debate here.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Thus, I wonder whether it is better to announce it separately and have a debate here, or to debate it at the Budget.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: We have never said that the Government will have to fund everything without any revenue.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: We are looking at whether there are possibilities of other revenues.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: We can have a full debate on this.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: My point was that this is an important Budget, a Budget that is looking forward to the future.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: But the GST increase can be a distraction because then we end up debating whether there is a need to increase GST.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: I quote, "I hope he", meaning the Minister for Finance, "can be upfront with Singaporeans now so that they are not blindsided by the Government as they were with the sudden 30% increase in water price".

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: You cannot have the cake and eat it.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: I am not asking you to hide the increase or intended increase in GST.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: I am not asking the Government to do that.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: What I am saying is that, by all means, announce it well before you want to increase it.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Then, we can debate it at the election rally.
